William Howard Fischer
Grand Master, 1927·1928

Will H. Fischer, our sixty-first Grand Master, is small of stature,
but in intellect is the peer of any. of his illustrious and distinguished
predecessors. The family Bible records that he was born in. Yolo County,
California, September 1, 1875, and from other sources we learn that he
attended the public schools and Hesperian college at Woodland until he
reached the age of 20, when he engaged in newspaper work, and as
cub reporter, special writer, editor and manager he established an enviable
reputation with the public press. As a reporter he soon developed in large
degree what newspaper men aptly call a "nose for news," which has been
an asset in all his varied employments. After twenty years of service as
a newspaper man, in 1915 he became Director of the Taxpayers' Association of California, in which capacity he did constructive work, the
most conspicuous perhaps being his inauguration of a movement which
resulted in the reorganization of our machinery of State government in
1921. Shortly thereafter he entered the employ of the Southern California
Edison Company, and has been steadily advanced until now he is assistant
to the President of that vast corporation.
Brother Fischer received his craft degrees in Humboldt Lodge No. 79,
at Eureka, the first degree February 9, second February 16, and the third
February 25, 1909. He became a Royal Arch Mason and a Knight
Templar at Eureka in 1914, and very soon thereafter he removed to Los
Angeles and affiliated witli the Masonic bodies in that city. At the organization of Wilshire Lodge No. 445, he was chosen as Master, and the
following year was appointed Inspector, in which position he served with
zeal until his appointment in 1922 as Grand Orator. He is also a member
of Los Angeles Consistory, 32d degree.
In all the years since 1914 Brother Fischer has served the fraternity
faithfully and well, and has always been in demand on important committees of Grand Lodge. To his constructive work we are indebted for
the certificate system of. vouching for and admitting members to Grand
Lodge.
At the annual communication of Grand Lodge in 1924 he was chosen
Junior Grand Warden, and regularly was advanced until in 1927 he was
elected and installed as Grand Master, in which exalted station he has
endeared himself to the brethren of the jurisdiction as a wise counsellor,
an energetic 'head of the Institution, and a most lovable man.
Our retiring Grand Master is blessed with a wife who is known
widely for her intellectual attainments and as an amiable and comforting
helpmeet.

Grand Master, with song and
Prayer by the Grand Chaplain
Almighty God, Lord of heaven and earth ! whose we are and w.hom
we serve, we ~ffer to Thee the sincere homage . qf our heart~ and pray
that. Thy Blessing may rest upon us gathered together in Thy Name and
Presence. Guide us in our deliberations. May the spirit of wisdom be
~oured out upon us, that in the affairs of this Grand Lodge, the highest
interests of our beloved institution may be furthered and Thy Name glorified. Appreciating the glorious heritage which is ours, may we loyally
maintain thos~ truths and principles handed down to us from the generations that are past. May we realize our responsibility, and so live that
we may transmit unimpaired the pure light of Masonic teaching to generations yet to come.
.
We offer Thee grateful thanks for the blessings of the past year,
.for the peace and harmony that has prevailed throughout this grand
domain. Look with Thy Favor upon the Grand Master and his officers
who direct its affairs. Grant that all things may be established upon
the best and surest foundation.
·

7

We would remember before Thee those who are dependent upon our
care. Our aged brethren and the little ones, in our Homes. May we
esteem it a privilege to minister to them and to supply their needs, and
to bring comfort to lonely hearts. Supply the needs of those in distress
through cyclone and flood.
Look graciously upon our Nation and at this time guide and direct
our citizens in the choice of him to whom shall be given the chief magistracy of our country. Defend and guard our liberties. Save us from the
spirit of lawlessness and dishonesty, and grant that under Thy protection
we may dwell in righteousness and peace.
Bless thy servants the President of United States, the Governor of
this State, and all in authority. Bless our Courts of Justice, and those
who administer the laws. May they discern the truth and impartially
administer the same in Thy fear alone. And may all the people through
obedience to Thy law show forth Thy praise among the Nations of the
'e arth. In the time of prosperity fill our hearts with gratitude, and in
the day of trouble suffer not our trust in Thee to fail. Amen:

MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Obedient to the requirements of our Constitution I submit herewith
a report of my activities as Grand Master, together with certain observations and recommendations for your consideration.
Constitution of Lodges
I was installed as Grand Master on October 14th last and in the
evening of that day constituted Menlo Park Lodge No. 651. On the following day I became conscious of the development of an illness which threatened pneumonia, but journeyed from San Francisco to Turlock in company
with Past Grand Master Arthur S. Crites, and constituted Livingston
Lodge No. 658. From there I proceeded to Fresno in company with
Brother Crites and Inspector Thomas A. Dille of the 83rd District. In
Fresno I was forced to take to my bed, and was unable to continue with
further constitution ceremonies. The remaining Lodges which had been
granted charters were at my request constituted as follows :
By Past Grand Master Samuel E. Burke:
At Los Angeles, Monday, October 17, 1927:

official contact with our constitutent Lodges to acquaint the latter as
well as ourselves with matters of mutual interest and concern.
I may add that I have been the guest of Masters and Wardens
Associations, clubs and inspectoral and other groups on many occasions,
and have held a large number of private conferences with Lodge officers.
I acknowledge with gratitude and appreciation the numberless courtesies
which have been extended to me and my fellow-officers in connection
with these delightful associations with our brethren.
Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens
During my administration I have had the most earnest and helpful
cooperation of the Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, the Right
Worshipful Senior Grand Warden and the Right Worshipful Junior
Grand Warden. To each of them I am obliged for the most loyal and
active support, and to each of them I am indissolubly linked by the
sincerest ties of affection. Wherever I have been, whatever the conditions obtaining, I have known that Brother Hutaff in the far North,
Brother -Wollenberg in the Bay region and Brother Ross in the far
South, were watchful of the interests of the Craft, and alert to carry on.
On numerous occasions each of them has conducted important investigations and handled weighty affairs, thus rendering high service to Grand
Lodge and easing the Grand Master's burden. Twice it has been necessary for me to absent myself from the jurisdiction in order to make
eastern trips, and during both such absences our strong and capable
brother, the Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, in accordance
with our Constitution, has exercised my official functions.
Owing to the large number of Lodges in our jurisdiction and the
vast extent of territory over which the authority of our Grand Lodge
<'.xtends, I believe the time has come when those who hold the offices I
have mentioned should be called upon more and more, by succeeding
Grand Masters, to share in the active duties of the supreme .office. Such
service cannot fail to add materially to the training and experience of
the junior elective officers as they advance from year to year'; and I have
no hesitancy in saying that no man can bring to the discharge of the
duties and responsibilities of the Grand Master's station a measure of
ability or experience which will outrun its requirements.
I desire also to acknowledge my obligation to the Past Grand Masters of this jurisdiction. From time to time I have called upon one or
an~ther of them for assistance, and their response in every case has been
prompt and generous. Some have conducted ceremonies, others have
advised as requested and some have given .me the benefit of their great
knowledge of our laws. Others have ~erved on special committees to
which I have delegated specific matters.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

In this connection I cannot refrain from an expression of appreciation of the wisdom Grand Lodge has displayed, particularly in recent
years, in recognizing, in the election of Grand Masters, outstanding
Masons residing in various sections of California. While personal qualifications, manifested and measured through long service in Grand Lodge,
are and should ever remain the standard controlling selection, it is a fact
that the efficiency of Grand Masters, as well as the interests of Grand
Lodge and the craft at large, are promoted if reasonable consideration
of regional representation is given in choosing the four principal officers
of this august body.
Permanent Grand Lodge Meeting Place
It will be recalled by those who attended the 78th annual communication of Grand Lodge that our sessions were held in the ballroom
of the Scottish Rite temple, this city. This was due to the existence of
a condition which for several years past has given rise to increasing
dissatisfaction, relative to the inadequacy of this room properly to accommodate our membership. The room which we occupied last year provided
some advantages in the way of seating capacity, but in virtually all other
respects was unsatisfactory. It is generally conceded that, as a physical
picture, in 1927 the aspect of Grand Lodge was calculated to remind an
observer of a political convention rather than a communication of our
august- body.
I have, therefore, expressed the desire, with which there has been
general accord, that our sessions this year be held here as in years past.
Brother Frank C. Ruppel of our Committee on Finance and also of the
Temple Association, has undertaken to assure us of better ventilation,
while our Grand Secretary, with the splendid cooperation of Brother
Ralph Wiley, has arranged for the installation of an amplifying system.
Requirement has been made that visitors shall not be admitted to the
gallery until fifteen minutes after the beginning of each of our sessions,
thus providing an opportunity for members of Grand Lodge to be
seated. I am aware of the fact that despite these provisions, which
appear to have exhausted the possibilities, your comfort and convenience
remain but poorly served.
It is obvious that we must have a new and permanent meeting place
properly adapted to our requirements. Owing to the large number of new
Lodges constituted within recent years, our normal attendance has increased far beyond the expectation of the designers of the temple in
which we are now assembled. Throughout the jurisdiction there is a
growing tendency upon the part of Wardens as well as Masters to avail
themselves of the information and inspiration of our communications,
while the same tendency manifests itself more and more, as the years
flow on, among Past Masters of Lodges.

Masonic Temple Association of California
In accordance with conditions clearly indicating the wisdom of the
procedure, a reorganization of the Masonic Temple Association of California has been undertaken and carried forward successfully.' The reorganized association will be known as the Masonic Temple Association
of California, Inc. The articles were filed on August 20 and a certificate
issued. The corporate books have been procured and proper procedure
instituted and approved in the office of the Commissioner of Corporations.
The plan of reorganization involves the conveyance of the property
of the old association to the new corporation, for evidence of indebtedness equal in amount to the outstanding stock. This transaction, with
which I am in full accord, probably does not require confirmatory or
other action by Grand Lodge at this time but is reported for your
information.
Conference of Grand Masters
On February 20 of this year I attended the. annual conference of
Grand Masters, the same being held at the Willard Hotel in Washington, D. C. The conference was called to order by Brother John A.
Dutton, then Deputy Grand Master, now Grand Master of New York,
in the absence of Grand Master Harold J. Richardson of that jurisdiction. Organization of the conference began with Grand Master James
T. Gibbs of the District of Columbia presiding temporarily. Grand
Master Howard R. Cruse of New Jersey was elected permanent chairman and Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary J. Claude Keiper of
the District of Columbia was chosen as permanent secretary. The Grand
Jurisdictions of Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana,
Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota,
Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey,
New York, North Carolina, Nor th Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon,
Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee,
Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia and Washington were represented, in
most cases, by Grand Masters, and in others by Deputy Grand Mas.t ers
or Past Grand Masters.
By virtue of its representative character and the eminence and attainments of its members, the conference was extremely impressive. It would
be interesting to review the proceedings at length, but considerations of
the space allotted for this address serve to preclude a comprehensive
report. I think you will be interested, however, in the following paragraph with which Grand Master Cruse, of New Jersey, opened his inspiring address :
'

GRAND LODGE OF ~ALIFORNIA

15

"This great fraternity that we represent, in my humble judgment,
is distinguished by its universality. The language of. Freemasonry
is a universal language, spoken at the Equator and answered by the
Northmen. The wisdom of Freemasonry is the universal wisdom,
drawn from the thought and the travail of a thousand generations.
The signs of Freemasonry are universal signs, derived from the
childhood of the race. The symbols of Freemasonry are universal
symbols, great with a nameless age. The religion of Freemasonry is
a universal religion, ripe with the worship of ages; and the tenets of
Freemasonry are expressed in universal charity and brotherhood that
manifest themselves in sympathy, service and sacrifice."
The agenda of the conference covered the following subjects:
1. Laws relating to expelled or suspended Masons, and jurisdiction
over rejected candidates.
2. Uniform receipts for dues.
3. Application and affiliation frQm a Grand Lodge not recognized
by all American Grand Lodges.
4. Inter-jurisdictional relief.
5. Uniform regulations covering visitation.
6. Use of cipher codes.
7. Consideration of policy with reference to the manner of election
or appointment of officers of Grand Lodges.
·The reports covering these topics consisted mainly of a review of
the laws and practice in the several jurisdictions. No action was taken.
It appearing to me that it would be valuable to Grand Masters to know
the sense of such a conference concerning the matters discussed, I consulted with a number of those in attendance and reached the conclusion
that the reticence of the conference was due to a prevailing fear upon
the part of its individual members that any such action might be misconstrued as a preliminary step looking toward the ultimate formation
of a National Grand Lodge. My inquiries developed to my satisfaction
that there was no disposition in any quarter to promote or foster such a
movement.
Accordingly, when called upon to speak at the dinner given in the
evening; following the conference, I made bold to mention this matter,
and advanced the suggestion that the conference to be held February 20,
1929, should go on record as opposing any niovement calculated to be the
forerunner of a National Grand Lodge. The definite assumption of this
policy, I pointed out, would probably warrant the annual conference in
expressing the sense of those attending. The action would be in no
measure official or binding, nor would any jurisdiction represented be in
any degree obligated to concur or conform.· The net result; however, in
actual experience, would undoubtedly be manifested, in 'the course pf a

16

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

few years, in a more decided tendency to harmonize the laws of the
several jurisdictions in matters of inter-jurisdictional practice. Such a
result, in my opinion, would be desirable. The Most Worshipful Melvin
M. Johnson, Past Grand Master of Massachusetts, strongly seconded the
foregoing suggestion, and at the conclusion of the di.n ner, when informal
discussion became general, I gathered the impression that there was
probability of procedure in the 1929 conference along the line I have
indicated.
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association
On February 21 and 22, following the conference of Grand Masters,
participated in the eighteenth annual convention of the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association at Alexandria, Virginia.
The morning sessions of February 21 and 22 were held in the Lodge room
of Alexandria-Washington Lodge No. 22, while the afternoon session of
February 21 was held in the uncompleted amphitheatre of the Memorial;
which is in course of construction on Shooter's Hill. overlooking the city
of Alexandria. During the afternoon of February 22 we united with the
people of Alexandria in an observance of Washington's birthday. In this
observance, President and Mrs. Coolidge also took part.
If it were permissible under my restrictions, I should like to set
forth at length the impressions which were mine as I sat with the Grand
Masters and Past Grand Masters of forty-Jour of our American jurisdictions in the old Lodge room made sacred to Masonry by virtue of its
association with the active Masonic life of Brother George Washington.
This Lodge room has been ably and often described, but no description
could carry with it the thrill of inspiration which it imparts to a reverent
Masonic pilgrim.
Presiding over our sessions was that wise, indefatigable and personally impressive Masonic veteran, the Most Worshipful Louis A.
Waters, Pa·st Grand Master of Pennsylvania, President of the Association. The place, the occasion and the purpose of the meeting combined
to impart to those assembled a surge of the deepest feeling. The visit to
the monument, likewise, served to emphasize the sentiment and fortify
the determination of each and all of us. This great work must' go forward to a ·glorious completion. I can have but scant sympathy or patience
with the views of those who oppose this enterprise.
The monument is ideally located on a site which many of the forefathers favored for the Capitol of the United States, overlooking the
historic city of Alexandria, the broad sweep of the equally historic Potomac and the majesty and beauty of the city of Washington. In ifs
lines. proportions and dimensions it represents a beautiful expression of
architectural artistry and skill. In its plans it provides for every purpos'!

17

which may properly be associated with a fraternal monument erected to
perpetua.t~ the memory and to impress upon the oncoming generations
the nobility of .character of that greatest of patriots, statesmen and
Masons-that mighty leader "whom God made childless that he might
becom~ the father of a nation"-George Washington. Moreover, this
memorial stands and shall stand, a visible symbol o f the unity, the strength,
the loyalty and mutual faith and reciprocation of all Masons who live and
labor and achieve and dream and aspire beneath the folds of the flag
that Washington made the emblem of a free people.
. ~oking forward adown the endless vista of the years I seem to see
pilgrimages of Masons from every State of the Union, and from every
land where men love liberty, making their way in solemn procession to
this glorious shrine of Masonry, there to refresh their ideals there to
refortify the dignity of manly character and there to drink deep from
the fount~ins of inspiration that flow from the memory of him who was
"first in peace, first in war and first in the hearts of his countrymen."

Anniversary of Initiation of George Washington
I confess that owing first to illness and then to the many activities
which required my attention in the days immediately following my
assumption of office in October last, I was somewhat tardy in .sending to
our constituent Lodges notice of the request of Grand Lodge that they
severally observe, on or about November 5, 1927, the 175th anniversary
of the initiation of George Washington as an Entered Apprentice Mason.
Despite the fact that my notification did not allow Masters time for extensive planning and preparation, I am glad to state that at one date or
another in the month of November, practically all of our Lodges held
services commemorative of the event to which I have referred. From
the reports received I entertain the opinion that such services proved inspiring to a very large number of our brethren throughout the jurisdiction.
Perpetuating the Memory of Washington
In accordance with a resolution adopted at our annual communication
in 1927, I appointed a committee consisting of Brother Harry L. Todd
of San Francisco, the Most Worshipful Albert E. Boynton, Past Grand
Master, and the Right Worshipful Gustav A. Hutaff, Deputy Grand
Master, "to consider the best method of perpetuating the memory" of
George Washington, said committee to report during our present communication.
Public Schools Week
. With profound gratification I am able to report that the ninth annual
observance of Public Schools Week, in the measure of its general success,
appreciably exceeded the observances which had preceded it. The observance was held duri~g the week beginning Monday, April 23rd, and
the reports from Lodges now in the hands of our committee indicate that
with relatively few exceptions the meetings throughout the State were
largely attended and extremely enthusiastic.

Our Educational Program
For many years our Grand Lodge has been definitely committed to
the policy of carrying on educational work in constituent Lodges. In
the year 1915 the first Committee on Education was appointed, and from
that time until the present a continuing interest has been manifested
in this particular endeavor. For a number of years the Committee on
Education functioned at a great disadvantage, because no appropriation
was made to support its plans and efforts. In the year 1917 the first
appropriation was made. The record of appropriations to date is as
follows:

Since the beginning of · appropriations more results have followed
our work in the educational field, but. I believe it is accurate to say
that. many members of Grand Lodge have questioned whether the results
achieved were sufficient to justify the expenditures made. At the outset

21

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of my term as Grand Master I determined to devote a great deal of my
personal attention to direction of the activities of the Educational Committee. Only a few changes in personnel were made. The Committee
was also slightly enlarged in order that broader contact might be had
over the jurisdiction with our constituent Lodges.
Considerable time was given to investigation of the requirements of
Lodges and the methods to be adopted. In due course my own ideas
became settled and I thereupon called a meeting of the ~ntire Educational Committee at San Francisco, at which meeting a general discussion was held and plans adopted for the year. Subsequently, on
January 14 of this year I forwarded to the Masters of all Lodges a
letter outlining the revised plan for educational work. This called for
the preparation by our Committee on Education of at least one program
per month, the presentation of which was made mandatory. Masters
were instructed that the monthly program might be presented either at
a stated meeting, a degree meeting or a special meeting called for the
purpose. The suggestion was made that musical or other features might
also be introduced. Masters were asked to have the papers as forwarded
by the Committee used as bases for the preparation of addresses either
by members of their own Lodges or by other qualified brethren. They
were also requested to encourage, after the presentation of each such
address, a general discussion by the brethren. The suggestion was likewise made that Lodges in small or remote communities, or where speakers
could not be obtained, would be deemed to have complied with the plan
if they caused a brother to read the paper. The requirement was further
made that each Master should from month to month fill out a report
form supplied by the Committee and forward the same to the Inspector
of his District. Inspectors at the same time were given specific instructions as to the plan and were required to transmit each month to the
Grarid Master the reports submitted by the Masters of their respective
Lodges.
Through general letters to Masters and Inspectors, as well as
through many hundreds of individual letters and a great number of
addresses and interviews, I have continued to impress upon those having
charge of our Lodges the importance of earnest cooperation to the end
that we might ·be enabled, for the first time, to observe and measure
results in an orderly manner.
I am happy to say that the degree of cooperation accorded and the
general results obtained have been highly satisfying and encouraging.
At the general meeting of the Educational Committee at which the
program was adopted I stated that I would be content with a very modest
measure of success in the first year of the experiment, because if we
obtained any really appreciable and measurable success we could depend
upon the future to magnify it from year to year. That a remarkable

result has actually been obtained, observed and measured is a fact in
proof of which I shall presently submit for the information of Grand
Lodge a few figures compiled from the formal reports of the Masters of
Lodges.
Our beginnings under the new system were necessarily crude and
entirely experimental. We were pioneers. Our machinery for the preparation and dissemination of programs had to be constructed. Our information was limited. The system, it may be stated, is still in a developmen~al
stage and no one will claim for it a patent of perfection. We feel, however, that the observations thus far made possible have permitted us to
expand and improve the work; that early dissatisfaction among certain
Lodges has given place or is giving place to genuine satisfaction; that
resistance originally prevailing in a few Lodges has to a great extent
been converted into hearty acceptance ; that experience has given to our
Committee a wider knowledge of the requirements and desires of Lodges,
and to Inspectors, Masters and Wardens a broader understanding and
more enthusiastic appreciation of the spirit, purpose and possibilities of
the plan.
At first the Committee forwarded to the Lodges one program each
month. It was realized from the beginning that no one program would
meet the requirements. and desires of all Lodges. As soon as the system
was fairly in operation we enlarged the number of programs to three
per month, one program relating to a strictly Masonic subject, one to a
scientific subject and one to a subject of general interest, bearing usually
on citizenship.
The programs prepared and sent out thus far are as follows :·
February- Automobiles in American Life.
March-The Romance of Aviation.
April-Masonic History in California.
May-Crime in California.
June-Radium and Rays. The Lambskin Al!ron.
July-Patriotic Program.
August-Literary Program. Masonic Questions and Answers.
September-Masonic Courtesy and Etiquette. What the Universe is
made of. California Courts.
October-The Legend of Hiram. The Wonders of Chemistry. Credits and Their Uses.
November-George Washington, Master Mason. The Marvels of the
Heavens. Newspapers and News.
As previously indicated, all reports in connection with our educational
meetings have come directly to me. The reviewing of these reports and the
compilation of consolidated figures have represented a task the magnitude

of which can scarcely be appreciated by anyone who has not actually
acquitted himself of such a task. I am glad, however, to have had the opportunity to contribute to this effort, because I am persuadc:d that as ·a
result thereof, I am in a position to report to Grand Lodge that we .are on
our way to achievement. In my opinion our accomplishments of the y~r, in
this connection, have completely justified our expenditures in moqey and

I should like to pursue this subject at length. I should deem it a
great privilege to read to you the thousands of reports ~nd letters which
I have personally scanned and studied. I am, however, conscious of the
time limitations under which we labor and I shall therefore proceed to
lay before you a few salient and outstanding indications of the results of
our labors.
I have considered the interest of Lodge members,·. as reflected in
attendance, the primary index of success. It was necessary therefore to
compare attendance .at our educational meetings with attendanc~ prior
to the institution of the educational plan. In most instances the educational programs have been presented at stated meetings, although some
Lodges have presented th.em at special meetings. Seeking to secure ·the
fairest comparison possible, covering the entire jurisdiction, I have compared attendance at Lodges at the stated meetings of October and November, 1927, and January, 1928, with the attendance at educational meetings
held in the months of February, March, April and May, 1928. I "would
have reported upon the educational meetings for a greater number of
months were it not that there is always an appreciable lag in reports.
I have the comparable figures from the Lodges within all of our Inspection
Districts with the exception of five. In three of these five Districts the
comparable data are incomplete and from two Districts I have received
no reports. In one of these two Districts the Masters of the Lodges
involved have given me .unsolicited assurances that they are most heartily
in favor of the educational plan and that their Lodges have experienced
excellent results. The five missing Districts involve a total of 22 Lodges,
which are accordingly eliminated from the figures which I shall here
quote.
.
With the foregoing explanation I desire to advise that the average
total attendance at Lodges at the stated meetings of October and November, 1927, and January, 1928, was 19,307 and the average total attendance
for the months of February, March, April and May, 1928, was 23,567.
This shows an average increase, per month, of 4,260 or otherwise ex'pressed, an increase of 22 per cent.
I have set up my compilations by Inspectoral Districts and find that
89 Districts show increased attendance while 15 Districts show decreased

attendance and ·one District shows no change. Among our Special Districts four show increased attendance and one a slight decrease.

22

~

Let us now consider the 89 Inspectoral Districts showing net increase
in attendance. These Districts embrace 457 Lodges of which 341 individually show increase, 90 show decrease, 15 indicate no change in attend~nce and 11 are not considered because of incomplete reports.
. . Among the foregoing 89 lnspectoral Districts 34 Districts show an
increase for every individual Lodge.
We shall now consider the 15 Inspectoral Districts showing net
decrease in attendance. These 15 Districts embrace 78 Lodges of which 42
show increased attendance, 35 show a decrease and one reports no change
in attendance. It will be noted that in these 15 Districts the number of
Lodges showing gains in attendance exceeds number showing losses. The
total losses, however, slightly exceed the total gains. It is exceedingly
interesting to note that among these 15 Districts not a single one reflected
decreases for each individual Lodge.
I dare say that the instances in which educational programs can be
properly charged with decreases in attendance are extremely rare.
Aside from the figures on attendance, which clearly reflect a 22 per
cent increase in the jurisdiction as a whole, there are other interesting
developments to consider. In the months of February, March, April and
May, 1928, a total of 3,118 speakers, other than the officers of Lodges,
led the discussions on the subjects assigned by our Educational Committee. This means that a considerable number of our brethren, who otherwise would not have been called upon, were given opportunity to contribute
their talents to and renew their interest in our constituent Lodges-also,
a great deal of new talent was discovered.
A still more important and significant fact, as disclosed by the reports,
is that a total of 12,292 members participated in general discussions of our
program subjects.
The number actually participating doubtless exceeds this figure, as
it was the frequent custom of Masters, in preparing their reports, to say,
"Discussion was general" or "Numerous brethren joined in discussion,"
etc. Such generalizations, of <;ourse, we could not convert into figures.
I · hold that the development of men is, in the last analysis, the supreme
opportunity and responsibility of Masonry and l think it will not be
denied that great developmental values are involved when in a period of four
months, more than 12,000 members of Lodges can be induced to overcome
their reticence and shyness and join with their fellows in interesting, noncontroversial discussions of timely and enlightening subjects.
Reports in hand show that approximately 75 per cent of the Lodges
pres"e nted their .edµcational programs at stated meetings and 25 per cent
at degree meetings or other special meetings.

The suggestions which Masters have forwarded with their reports
have been of great value, and it is desirable that such suggestions should
continue to be forwarded from month to month, as they indicate to those
in charge of the work the type and character of programs most likely to
meet with the favor of the brethren. We have some Lodges at the present
time that clearly favor programs on strictly Masonic subjects, some that
enjoy scientific subjects and some that prefer to discuss topics of more
general interest. The aim of the Committee has been to meet these varying
requirements. With the continued advice of Masters and Inspectors this
phase of the work can be still more intelligently developed.
When all is said and done, the underlying purpose has been and will
continue to be the stimulation of the intellectual life of Lodges. It has
been necessary to adopt a set program in order to get this movement
under way. In my opinion, however, our basic purpose w ill have been well
served in instances wherein individual Masters, exercising their judgment,
shall adopt monthly programs of their own, induce the discussions heretofore referred to and report to the Grand Master from month to month
the information called for on the forms supplied by the Committee. There
is not, nor should there be, the slightest desire or intention to restrict
Masters in the exercise of their originality and ingenuity. On the other
hand, the intent and desire is to encourage the exercise of these faculties.
The mechanical part of the system is devised mainly to establish and make
permanent a habit of procedure among the constituent Lodges.
During the hot summer months, as might be expected, my observations
indicate that our Lodges desire to make their meetings as brief as possible and I, therefore, offer to those who shall hereafter have this work
in charge a recommendation that the presentation of programs during two
months each summer, at the option of each Master, be made non-mandatory. December witnesses the annual election and installation of officers
in our Lodges, and I would likewise recommend that we dispense with
the educational program in that month.
I recommend that th~ usual appropriation be made in further support
of the work of our Committee on Education.

B:other Leon 0. Whitsell, our Senior Grand Deacon, and Brother Percy
Kmg of Napa. To the work of the Committee I have given the full support of my office. Our Very Worshipful Grand Secretary has likewise
extended the utmost cooperation, while the Deputy Grand Master and
Grand ~ardens, together with officers and members of many Lodges,
have assisted most effectively in the effort to emphasize the value of
Masonic History in this jurisdiction and to perpetuate the ·memory of our

At Coloma
In the course of the year several important historical observances have
taken place. The most notable of these was the general observance at
Coloma on Saturday and Sunday, June 2nd and 3rd, 1928. This observance
was planned and held in recognition of the 75th anniversary of the Lodges
chartered in the year 1853, as follows: Madison Lodge No. 23 at Grass
Valley; Mariposa Lodge No. 24 at Mariposa; Georgetown Lodge No. 25
at Georgetown; Palmyra Lodge No. 26 at Placerville ; Trinity Lodge No.
27 at Weaverville; Golden Gate No. 30 at San Francisco; Gold Hill Lodge
No. 32 at Lincoln; Ophir Lodge No; 33 at Murphys; San Diego Lodge
No. 35 at San Diego. Owing to the distance of their location from the
scene of the observance, Trinity Lodge and San Diego Lodge were unable
to participate. The other Lodges were represented, although the duties
of host fell most directly upon Palmyra Lodge, Georgetown Lodge and
Hiram Lodge.
After arranging the preliminaries for this observance and outlining
its general character and program I was required to absent myself from
the jurisdiction for several weeks, and it became necessary to turn over to
our able and energetic Senior Grand Warden, Brother Wollenberg, the
heavy burden of immediate direction and development. Brother Wollenberg in turn called to his assistance the Masters, officers and members of
the pioneer Lodges I have particularly indicated, together with other
Grand officers and brethren of the Craft. A monumental achievement
stands to the credit of Brother Wollenberg, Brothers Ellis and Whitsell of
our History Committee and the scores of officials and brethren who
cooperated with them.
Interest was widespread. A 'complete special train ran from the city
of Los Angeles to the scene of the celebration. By train and auto many
brethren from San Francisco joined in the pilgrimage, while hundreds of
brethren from Sacramento, the valley counties and the mountain counties
moved to the historic site where, on January 19 in the year 1848, gold was
discovered at the old Sutter Mill by James W. Marshall.
By my request the brethren had been advised to array themselves in
the costumes of the old mining days. Garbed as were the men who
trekked across prairies and over mountains to reach the new El Dorado in
the Days of '49, and equipped after the fashion of the pioneers, our
brethren when assembled were individually lost in a motley composite,
kaleidoscopic in character and worthy of becoming the inspiration for the
masterpiece of a supreme artist.

The program on June 2nd included such events as the re-discovery of
gold, placer mining operations after the fashion of early days, the arrival
of pack outfits, the comedy of Chinese miners, whipsaw and broadaxe
contest.s, horseshoe pitching contest, wheelbarrow contests and a tug of
war by teams consisting of Los Angeles and San Francisco brethren,
resulted in the ducking of some of our southern brethren in the waters of
the American river. Brother Howell 'B. Murphy of Placerville, impersonating a pony express rider, arrived and swam his horse across the river
to deliver what purported to be the first Masonic charter. Nearby was
located a camp of Washoe Indians, living in pristine simplicity.
In the afternoon the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior and
Junior-Grand Wardens, Grand Lecturer, Grand Secretary, Grand Marshal
and other brethren were ushered upon the scene in a stagecoach once used
regularly between Placerville and Carson City in the days of the gold
·
excitement.
The day was warm, and in ·the latter part of the afternoon many of
the brethren, including notables whose names I forbear to record, journeyed a mile down the stream and reproduced, for their own edification,
and greatly to their comfort, the scenes which were so familiar in boyhood
·
days around the old swimming hole.
At 8 :30 o'clock in the evening a number of our brethren affiliated with
the Square and Compass Players of San Francisco, presented an historical
drama in three acts entitled "Men of Destiny." . This drama had been specially written and was directed by Brother Jesse M. Whited, Past Master
of California Lodge No. 1 and Chairman of our Committee on Correspondence. Act 1, which was in two scenes, portrayed historic events, deeply
influenced by Masonry, at Lassen's Ranch and Sutter's Fort in the year
1846, events intimately associated with the great movement which brought
this western land under the permanent protection of the Stars and Stripes.
Act 2 was a reproduction of the historic scene which accompanied the
organization of our Grand Lodge at Sacramento April 17, 1850, and Act
3 represented a reunion at the Masonic Temple at Placerville on June 27,
1853. In each of these scenes and acts gifted brethren represented with
fidelity and distinguished artistry the eminent men of the days that have
gone.
Music was furnished by the bands of Ben Ali Temple,
A. A. 0. N. M. S. and Sacramento Pyramid No. 3 A. E. 0 . S., while
members of El Dorado Chapter, Order of De Mo lay and the Boy Scouts,
both during the day and evening rendered valuable service.
The natural setting for the drama was one which adapted itself
ideally. On the smooth face of a gently sloping hillside a stage had been
constructed. Gazing upon the scene while seated upon the ground, more than
2500 brethren from every section of California gave rapt attention as the
glorious story of the participation of Masons in the controlling events of
the early days was developed. High in the heavens hung a golden mobn, its

light reflected in the swift and musical waters of the American River.
The wooded hillsides sent forth their charm into the night. A serious
reverent spirit dominated all who beheld this magnificent spectacle. The
occasion, the environment, the inspiration of it all, combined to leave upon
the minds and in the hearts of those in attendance an impression which the
rushing years will not erase.
On Sunday morning June 3, after an old-fashioned breakfast served in
the open, the brethren, many of whom had been joined by their wives and

delivered by the Reverend Irving B. Bristol, cif Sacramento. Led by the

of American men and women these many years. Following this devotional service the brethren began journeying toward home, and within two
or three hours the historical observance at Coloma had become a beautiful
memory.

Pelton Monu:nent at Camptonville
One of mankind's most pleasing customs is that of erecting monuments to perpetuate the memory of those who through their achievements
have won illustrious places in history. Monuments to the great have been
raised by governments, societies, groups and individuals. It S:eems particularly fitting that as a patron of the arts and sciences the Institution of
Masonry should from time to time pursue this custom as a means of
attesting its appreciation of Masons who have contributed largely to the
advancement of civilization and the welfare of mankind. In the year
1878 Lester A. Pelton, a member of our Gravel Range Lodge No. 59,
brought forth an invention (patented in 1880) which may be said to have
revolutionized industrial processes throughout the world. This invention is
known as the Pelton Water Wheel. Brother Pelton ·conducted his experiments and perfected his invention in his little workshop at Camptonville.
Today in the great field of human industry no name stands higher than his.
Some months ago Brother Acton M. Cleveland, Past Master, advised
me that Gravel Range Lodge desired to erect, on the spot where the Pelton
Wheel originated, a suitable monument to perpetuate the memory of
Brother Pelton. Gravel Range Lodge No. 59, he stated, was not in a
financial condition which would justify the expenditure of a sum sufficient
for this purpose. He therefore desired to know whether, in my opinion,
our Grand Lodge would finance this project. · The proposal appealed
strongly to me, and after reflection I informed him that I would make a
recommendation at this time.
A letter from Brother Cleveland under date of September 10 states
that the Meek Mercantile Company, which owns the land where the Pelton
workshop stood, will donate the same as the site for the monument The
Pelton Water Wheel Company haii agreed to provide a 700-pound bucket
of the latest type to be made a part of the monument, and the Miners'
Foundry and Engineering Company has donated one of the oldest Pelton
wheels extant, also to be made a part of the monument. The structure
will be about 12xl2 feet at the base and 10 feet high. At the top it is
planned to place the old wheel, while the large bucket will form the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

33

central feature. On native California granite will appear a proper inscription setting forth the significance of the monument, the date of its erection
and the fact of its erection by our Grand Lodge. The cost of this work,
greatly reduced by the donations which have been offered, will not exceed
$600 and I recommend that Grand Lodge appropriate that amount.
The suggestion has been made that the financing of monuments
establisliies a· precedent which if followed may later involve considerable
sums for various projects. I doubt whether any large amount of money
would ever be required for monuments to be erected by Grand Lodge.
In any event each proposal of this kind should stand upon its own merits
and be judged in connection with the conditions attaching to it. I feel
that our brethren of Gravel Range Lodge have made a happy suggestion;
that the monument is one which should be raised, and that the assistance
of Grand Lodge should be forthcoming.
Decisions
Most of the questions which have been submitted to me I have found
to be covered by our law and it has only been necessary to refer questioners to the Constitution and regulations. The following matters are
reported for the consideration of Grand Lodge :
1. Several Masters have desired to know whether final conviction
and imprisonment for certain crimes not enumerated in Section 192 would
cause the automatic expulsion provision of said section to operate, I have
held that the rule of inclusio unfos est exclusio altcrfos applies.

2. In connection with the operation of the same section I held that
a brother convicted of an offen~e enumerated in Section 192, but granted
probation, was not subject to automatic expulsion.
3. I have held that Section 192 cannot be given ex post facto application.
4. I have held that the 60-day period mentioned in Section 108 of the
Constitution runs from and after the day upon which the objection is
made. (But see Section 108 as amended October, 1928.)
6. I have held it to be not an impropriety for a Lod&"e to make a
modest donation, from its refreshment fund, for the purpose of assisting
to pay the expenses of an Inspector at an annual communication of Grand
Lodge. (Not approved.)
7. I have held it to be in bad taste, although not directly prohibited,
for a Lodge to advertise a public dance under its auspices "to raise funds
for building a hall."

Objection Before Initiation
In my opinion section 108 of our Constitution should be amended. The
section now provides that an objection made after the election of a candidate but before his initiation, unless withdrawn within sixty days, has the
effect of a rejection by ballot. I have heard of a number of instances
wherein this section has been abused. Quite recently my attention was
drawn to a case wherein, apparently, the objection entered against a
candidate who had been elected was interposed for the purpose of coercing
him to purchase the interest of a business partner. I believe that every
member of a Lodge is presumed to be on notice with referemie to the
election of caadidates. Ii a member does not attend his Lodge the fault
is, his own. The right subsequently to enter objection remains a valid
right, but in my view the candidate who has passed the test at the ballot
box is also entitled to certain rights of protection against whimsical or
vicious objections. :t therefore recommend that the Committee on Jurisprudence be requested, to prepare and submit at this Communication an
amendment to section 108 in such form as to eliminate the present provision
that "suah objection shall unless ,withdrawn. within sixty days have the
effect of a rejection by ballot" and substitute in place thereof the form of
procedure set forth in sections 110 and 111, or an apJ?ropriate procedure
similar thereto.

99, one whose petition has been 11:eceived by a Lodge may not withdraw

conceive this to be fair to a petitioner, and I believe that this pw\tision
of our law invades legitimate personal rights. I can see no good reason
why we should compel a man to go to election or i:eiection against his
will. I therefore recommend that the Jurisprudence Committee prepare
and submit to Grand Lodge at this Communication such amendment of

Revision of Funeral Ritual
Coinciding with the opinion of many who believe that our funeral
ritual strikes an unnecessarily mournful and harrowing note, I have
deemed it proper to cause an effort at revision to be made. Brother
Frank B. Belcher, Worshipful Master of Wilshire Lodge No. 445, volunteered his services in this connection and has prepared a revised ritual
which will be submitted at this communication and referred to our Committee on Ritual for consideration and report. In the performance of this
task Brother Belcher has examined the rituals of a number of our sister
jurisdictions. The duty so generously assumed by him has required much
time and effort, and I wish to make acknowledgment of my appreciation
of his valuable co-operation.
It is understood by all, I am persuaded, that ·any revision of our
funeral ritual presents points of delicacy. The sentiment of many of our
brethren with respect to the existing ritual is very tender. On the other
hand there are many, of whom I am one, who feel that the attitude of
society toward the Great Adventure has been modified. In the. older days
the natural tendency to grieve over the departure of a dear one was more
or less a rtificially emphasized and encouraged upon funeral occasions.
Death was referred to as the end of life. The popular imagination was
taught to conceive of it as a tragedy, deep and dark, hopeless and bitter.
The rituals of societies such as ours were profoundly influenced by this
concept.
Present day society, while responsive to the normal human impulses
of grief, and fully conscious of the awe and mystery which cannot be
dissociated from death, takes what many of us hold to be a more intelligent and in fact a nobler view. We have come to believe more firmly in
the assurances of religion and in the abundant testimony of the earth,
the sea and the stars, and the comforting voices that whisper within our
hearts. We are stronger in the faith that death is not the end, but a
mere transition from the physical to the spiritual plane of activity and
function.
In conformity with that belief, should we not, in paying our respects
to the memory of our departed brethren, subdue the note of woe, and
sound, if we can, the harmonic of a greater and finer faith? Should we
not soothe rather than aggravate the distress of those who are left behind
and bring to them at the graveside a realization that "in the night of
death hope sees a star and listening love may hear the rustle of a wing."

Physical Qualifications
On several occasions Grand Lodge has given consideration to the
physical qualifications to be required of candidates for our degrees. The
traditional practice of Masonry required that candidates should be
physically whole. Our law is 'based upon this original practice and yet
we leave much to the discretion of Masters, demanding only that candidates ~hall be physicaily able substantially to conform to the requirements
of the degrees.
The discretion thus granted has on many occasions been abused, not
with wrong intent, 'but because .of the failure of occasional Masters to
apply sound judgment. I take it that every Grand Master has been called
upon many times to pass upon the question of the qualification or disqualification of candidates who have lost one or another of their limbs. I believe our law can and should be clarified.
In this connection I have been frequently moved by the appeals of
World War veterans who suffered physical disqualifications while in
service overseas defending our Government, our people and our institutions. Most if not all of these men are receiving Government allowances,
many of them to the extent that · there is small probability of their
becoming charges upon any Lodge. I have felt that if we could consistently do so we should make some special provision in their favor. We
make special provision with reference to residence of candidates actually
in the service of the Army and Navy. It has therefore appeared that we
might, in some measure at least, recognize the claims of those who have
shed their blood and lost one or another of their physical members in our
defense.

39

· Aside from this consideration, there are many men of outstanding
mo:al and intellectual qualifications, and financially competent, who through
accident have suffered the loss of a hand or foot. , I know many such men
who are anxious to become Masons and whose membership would be
hailed with satisfaction by our Lodges. Some of these men are so
equipped with artificial limbs that they can and do perform the functions
of natural members. I discovered a case in which one of our Lodges had
voted. to receive such a candidate. This gentleman unfortunately had
lost both feet. He had been voted upon and the first degree had been
conferred upon him before the matter came to . my attention. I required
the Lodge to sus1,Jend all further proceedings until such time if ever as
our law had been modified.

Clandestine Grand Lodges
A few months ago, in the city of Fresno, a clandestine body known
as "Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge, A. F. & A. M. of California," held a
Communication. It appears that we now have two or three clandestine
Grand Lodges in California and I submit that this matter should be made
the subject of an orderly investigation accompanied by a report at our
next Annual Communication setting forth recommendations as to procedure. I am advised that the agents of such clandestine Lodges can be
prosecuted for fraud under certain circumstances, but it is admitted that
it is somewhat difficult to find evidence to support effective action. I
recommend that the incoming Grand Master be requested to appoint a
special committee to go thoroughly into this subject so that at our Annual
Communication in 1929 we may be fully advised.

I quote these cases merely as examples. Such analysis ' as I have been
able to make would indicate that in no instance is the fina.ncial difficulty
of a Lodge or temple association due to dishonesty or . illegal practice
upon the part of those having charge. In most instances the trouble seems
to lie in the fact that, in their desire for temples .comporting with ·the
dignity of Masonry, the brethren have been betrayed by their enthusiasm.
Several cases might be noted in which the members of Lodges have been
required to pay dues ranging from $24 to $36 per year as a con;equence
of misdirected enthusiasm. But high dues are not so bad as the dissension
which sometimes ensues.
·
No Masonic building project should be undertaken, .and no financial
commitments should be made until after provision for meeting all charges,
not only for the acquisition of land, the erection of edifices and the purchase ·o f furnishings, but also for interest during construction, insurance,
etc. With liberal deductions from conservative estimates of income, a
Lodge or Lodges singly or jointly undertaking the construction of a
temple should see in advance sufficient earnings from the building and
revenues from members to ensure ability, after construction, to meet
carrying charges, maintenance, taxes and insurance without crippling
Lodge treasuries and preventing the exercise of normal M'asonic functions.

ln any average case the reviewing and directing functions of a Grand
Lodge committee such as has been suggested, would result in confirming
the judgment of the members of a Lodge whose project was feasible and
free of doubt, but it would give a timely and. emphatic warning in those
cases in which the project; as to plans and financing, could not stand the
scrutiny and criticism of an impartial and disinterested committee; indeed,
in case a building project was faulty and foredoomed to failure, such a
committee could forestall the effort and thereby save the Lodge, its
members, .and Grand Lodge from embarrassment, if not from disaster.
It is better to wait than to dissipate the harmony of a Lodge and
destroy the enthusiasm of its members. The "Lodge Over Simpkin's
Store" is better off Masonically with its modest but sufficient treasury
than a financially distressed and discordant Lodge housed within a temple.
I am happy to report that, in the absence of the legislation which will
be considered here, ~ut appreciating its desirability, Culver City Lodge No.
467 recently presented to Brother Jeffries of our Finance Committee a
statement of the financial situation of the Masonic Temple Association
of Culver City, which proposes to build a temple there. Brother Jeffries
has reviewed said statement and approved the soundness of the project.
I have no doubt, therefore, that this undertaking will be carried forward
successfully.
Each of the reports from temple associations mentioned herein has
been submitted jointly to Brother Jeffries of our Committee on Finance,
and Past Grand Master Hervey, Chairman of our Committee on Policy

persuaded that the craft in this jurisdiction is prepared to accept the
legislation which will be submitted at this communication.
Insurers and Insured
During the year I have repeatedly emphasized, in the course of addresses to our brethren, the necessity of resisting any and all efforti upon
the part of individuals, organizations or associations improperly to exploit
Masonry for business purposes. It appears that the point and purpose of
my statements on this subject were occasionally misinterpreted and the
conclusion reached that I was hostile to so-called Masonic insurance companies. At the instance of one of these companies, Past Grand Master
Bradford S. Webster visited me and asked for a statement of my position.
Subsequently I had occasion to meet three or four officials and representatives of such companies, and through the courtesy of Brother Webster
I was supplied with a file of the literature used by several such companies
for advertising purposes. To Brother Webster and to the representatives
of companies, I believe I succeeded in making my position clear; and I
feel it to be not improper to state it here. I am a firm believer in life insurance and I would like to see every Mason carry a reasonable amount

I believe the selection of an insur ance canier is in all respects

a. personal business matter. In justice to his dependents it is the duty o.f
a Mason te make proper investigation to the end that he may know the
financial responsibility of the insurer. The rule of caveat emptor applies.
I have no prejudice against or unfriendliness toward any insurance company whlch may, for the promotion of its own interests, restrict the
selection or its risks. to Masons, but the adoption of such a policy by an
insurance organization does not and cannot give it even the slightest
claim to. Masonic recognition or a preferred position among Masons.
In my conference on this subject I voiced objection to the advertising
0£ any organization as a "Masonic" insurance company and laid down the
~la.rati0t1, on behalf of Grand Lodge, that any improper solicitation
among Masons. would be Fesented. I particularly stl'essed the reprehensi~

An examination of the literature of these companies subsequently
<£isclosed the fact that practically all, if not all really objectionable matter
has been eliminated from their advertising. I had their assurance that
their practice would be strictly in keeping with the position stated by me,
and to their credit and as a matter of justice, I should add that no complaints. of improprieties have come to my attention.
In this connection I re-emphasize my belief that it is the du~y of every
Mason,. particularly those having dependents, to make proper provision
for insurance. Time and again we witness the tragic spectacle of a departed Mason's widow and orphans cast upon the world without financial
resources or experience,. and repeatedly we are touched by pathetic cases
of suffering by Masons and their families, due to accidents or illness encountered by the bread-winner. These conditions can be prevented or at
least atJJel.iorated through insurance. Our Lodges, as a rule, respond as
generously as possible to the calls of the distressed, but their resources
are limited and in most instances they cannot provide that measure of
succor which the vicisiiitudes. of ou-r brethren in fact rtquire.
A great deaL of misinformation exists among the profane, and indeed
arnong tM j.nitia.te, with refetence to the financial responsibility of
MallO!ilic Lodges oo distressed members and their families. We do a
noble work, it is ~r,ue, and all the funds of our Lodges a.re constitutionally
defined as tmst. fu11ds for relief ; but there is an impression, too widespread, that our Lodges undertake to guarantee ample relief. This is not
tniie. We can help our brethren only to the extent of our ability, and
such Jae* must be. extended, in ev.ery case, with due reference to our
obligations as a whole. Masonry is not an insurance fraternity and may
not be. so considered. It has no machinery and no plan based upon insur.ance principles.

Lodge Clubs and Internal Organizations
Americans have a genius for organization. It has been said that
whenever three or more of them meet, they organize, elect a chairman,
adopt by-laws and assess dues. As a people we indulge a peculiar passion
for joining. American men also seem to possess another outstanding
idiosyncrasy. At one time or another each of us passes through a silly
season, the duration of which is controlled by the shape of the individual
head. Some men never recover from it, while others emerge in time and
are restored to normalcy. It is during this silly season that we develop a
fondness for horse-play. We follow the rule of "monkey see, monkey do,"
and become imbued· with the idea that the submission of our persons to
slap"stick indignities so inflicted as to tickle the risibilities of beholding
multitudes will promote our standing as good fellows and thus contribute
to a, blissful success in life. Many men, eminent even in Masonry, have
at one time or another found a drooliing delight in subjecting themselves
to the manhandling of horse-play organizations, and subsequently in perpetrating hilarious outrages upon their "less informed" brethren. There is
s~11aly a male intellect, no matter how brilliant or how Stygian, that
esc:apes eiOier a temporary or a prolonged attack by this mysterious
malady.

Mason, of course, was usually a shining mark, although all comers were

My first opinion upon learning of the existence of what I will call the
"horse-play" clubs was that I should issue an edict abolishing them as
inconsistent with the dignity and welfare of our constituent Lodges. 1
believed them then, as I now believe them, to be calculated to produce
cliques, endanger harmony, and lower the tone of Masonic Lodge life.
Further investigation indicated that some of these clubs had been
in existence for a considerable time and were to some extent excusing or
justifying themselves by certain activities not undesirable. Moreover, I
was not in possession of the fact as to whether this form of internal
organization had spread throughout the jurisdiction. Subsequent investigation convinces me that it is practically localized in Los Angeles county.
After giving the matter much t)lought I concluded not to issue an
edict, but on the contrary to ask the Lodges having such clubs to assist
me in working out a solution of the problem presented. I felt moreover
that before any definite action should be taken, Grand Lodge should be
given an opportunity to consider the situation and define and enforce a
policy. I requested the Lodges conducting such clubs, or permitting such
clubs to meet in their Lodge rooms, to arrange for a suspension of the
activities of the same pending the judgment of Grand Lodge. I take
pleasure in saying that so far as I am advised, the Lodges concerned have
complied with my request.

their purpose the social activities and entertainment of the members of
their respective Lodges ; eight clubs exist for charitable purpose of the
Lodge members ; eighteen clubs have for their purpose social entertainment
and charity; eleven clubs are organized for the purpose of insurance, and
of those eleven, eight pay a benefit insurance based upon total membership
and three pay a fixed 'sum for each death, as follows: Beacon of the West
Lodge, $100.00 for each death ; Guardian and Hollenbeck Lodges, $250.00
. for each death. One club, affiliated with South Gate Lodge No. 320, in its
by-laws provides that it shall concern itself with the character and qualifications of candidates for public office, and to inform its members thereof.
The name of the club is an Instructor Club, which is a misnomer. We
find that ·five clubs charge only an initiation fee, ranging from $1.00 to
$5.00; nine clubs charge dues only, ranging from $1.00 to $4.00 yearly;
nineteen clubs charge both initiation fees and dues, the initiation fees
ranging from $1.00 to $7.50 and the dues from $1.00 to $6.00 yearly. The
insurance clubs have a fixed fee of $1.00 to $2.00 for each death benefit.
We find that twenty-two clubs are under the control of the Master of the
Lodge and the balance are entirely governed by officers of the club. We
find that sixteen of the clubs meet monthly; five quarterly ; two semiannually and three yearly and ten upon call.
The committee in its report asserts that the rituals used by certain of
the clubs contain parU; or passages subject to criticism, while the rituals
of others are passed without comment except that they are calculated to
produce m:irth.
The report, which is signed by Brothers Elson, York, Benjamin and
Mullen, but not signed by Brothers Rueber and Johnson, offers three
findings, or recommendations, which may be briefly stated as follows:
1st: That clubs operating for the purpose of furnishing relief to the
survivors of a deceased member should be encouraged, but should be placed
under a uniform code of by-laws and subject to the control of Grand
Lodge, with due regard to the laws of the State.
. 2nd: That clubs providing for a form ~f initiation or cereqionial
present a serious problem, because the young Mason, hastening to join them,
is apt to suffer a shock to the ideals which Masonry has inspired· in him.
I quote the committee: "It is said that the older member may look upon
these ceremonies with a great deal of tolerance and in his wisdom may not
display the same characteristic in_terest in this form of entertainment, and
t~.at such an experience should not compel him to lose sight of the real
purpose of Masonry ; but forgetting for the moment that these clubs,
together with their rituals, are operated and conducted exclusively among
Masons, within the Lodge building, and supported by the officers of Masonic Lodges, we cannot, in our opinion, differentiate between the adolescent and the mature when it reflects upon the reputation, character and
standing of our fraternity."

The Inspectoral Service
Much might and should be said in praise of the work of our Masonic
Inspectors. The year has been an extremely active one. Conditions arising

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

52

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

from our new system of educational work, the effort to finance the Masonic
Club at the University of California, Los Angeles, and many other matters,
as well as the increasing duties associated with their customary work,
have required me to make numerous and heavy demands upon them; and
~ith only a few exceptions they have responded promptly in the heartiest
spirit, with the most capable cooperation. To them I offer my sincere
thanks. We cannot over-estimate the services performed by an efficient
and . attentive Inspector.
Not through legislation, but rather through the evolution of circumstances and requirements, the importance of the office of Inspector
has been greatly enhanced in recent years. Today an Inspector is required
not only to perform the service required by the Grand Lecturer, but also
to execute important commissions as a direct representative of the Grand
Master, to whom he is responsible for his appointment. He must possess
alert intelligence, industry, and diplomatic and executive qualifications
of a high order,. in addition to his proficiency in the ritual. The office
must continue to grow in importance if Grand Lodge is to give to its
constituent Lodges an expanding program worthy of the opportunities
and responsibilities of Ma~onry. Appointments to this office should not
be made by favor, or merely in recognition of ritualistic proficiency. The
service demands strong, capable men of first quality. It represents a call
to high duty. If at any time there be found among the ranks of the Inspectors any who have outlived their enthusiasm or their willingness or
capacity to cooperate with the appointing power, the Grand Master should
feel no hesitancy in permitting them to retire so that more active and
interested brethren may take their places.
·considering conditions as they now exist, I believe that our Inspectoral
system, regardless of an occasional unsatisfactory personal equation,
should be continued in force. The problem, if any there be, relates to the
upbuilding of standards of efficiency and personnel. This problem can be
completely solved if each s·ucceeding Grand Master will give it his careful
consideration. I do not believe that the plan of appointing District Deputy
Grand Masters, as heretofore advanced, would produce the results expected of it. I am of the opinion that the annual term of Inspectors
should begin December 1st of each year, rather than February 1st, as at
present, thus coinciding more nearly with the term for which a Grand
Master is elected. I recommend that Section SS of the Constitution be
so amended as to determine the term of an Inspector in accordance with
this observation.
Masonry in Business
Throughout the year I have emphasized and re-emphasized the impropriety of the use of Masonic titles and designations for business or
political purposes .. I believe the campaign I have conducted has accom-

53

plished results. This does not mean that improper methods will not
again be used. There must be constant watchfulness and frequent admonition. From time to time discipline must be applied. The number of
those willing to make improper use of Masonry is really small. A continuous appeal to our Lodges will keep the abuses to the minimum.
Complaints have been made to me concerning the financing and management of certain promotions among "Masons only." In particular two
of the outstanding promotions referred to in these complaints are a
country club in Los Angeles County and a resort in the Santa Cruz
mountains. In both instances, however, the causes of complaint arose
prior to my assumption of office. I have failed to find authority or jurisdiction to deal with these matters and have, therefore, had no alternative
but to suggest to those making such complaints that their recourse, if any,
was in the courts of the land and not in the courts of Masonry.
Emergency Relief
Again the Storm King has brought distress to many of our brethren.
The public press of Sunday, September 16th, published the news that a
devastating wind storm had destroyed lives and property in Porto Rico
and Florida, and on Monday, the 17th, I directeil ·the Grand Secretary
to at once contribute from our Emergency Relief fund the sum of $SOO.OO
to the San Francisco Chapter of the American Red Cross, for the use and
benefit of its fund for the relief of the distresses in Porto Rico. A telegram was also dispatched to the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of
Porto Rico expressing the sympathy of the brethren of California, asking
if any organized Masonic relief had been established on the island, and
requesting a statement as to the needs of the craft in the storm area. The
following cable was received in answer to our proffer of assistance:
"San Juan, P. R., September 22, 1928.
Grand Master and brethren of Porto Rico greatly appreciate expression
of sympathy and offer of assistance. Making careful survey of destruction of buildings and Masons in distress, and will advise as soon as details
available.
Jose G. Torres, Grand Secretary."
No further direct advices have been received, and inasmuch as the
total Masonic membership in Porto Rico is about 4,000, we may fairly
assume that the Red Cross is adequately handling the situation there.
On the 17th I also caused the following telegram to be sent to the
Grand Secretary of Florida.
"Your brethren in California send sympathy to the people of the
tornado district. Please wire your needs and meanwhile draw on us up
to two thousand dollars."

Subsequently the Grand Master of Florida wired that· the committee
directing Masonic relief work in the storm-stricken area of that State
reported conditions much worse than two years ago; that there were
more than two thousand dead and ninety per cent of the homes in the
storm district destroyed or damaged, with large numbers of our brethren
homeless or destitute. The money we offered by ·wire has been paid and
receipted for by the Grand Secretary of Florida, to whom all contributions were requested to be sent. The Grand Secretary, in a letter received
by me October 4, said that "California was the first State to offer assistance to our brethren in their time of need, and it will long be remembered
by the Grand Lodge of Florida."
We are ready at a moment's notice to augment our contributions if
intimations come from the stricken districts that further funds are desired.

Temple of Sunset Lodge No. 352, my hosts presented to me a beautiful
Studebaker automobile of the commander type. I have utilized this magnificent gift on many occasions, with the utmost satisfaction and enjoyment
and, I trust, in the interests of the Craft.
A short time later I was surprised to receive .a beautiful desk stand
and set of pens from Santa Monica Lodge No. 307 and Palisades Lodie
No. 637.
Another pleasing surprise came during our historical observance at
Coloma when, on being asked to emulate the custom of the Days of '49
by panning some gravel from the American River, I found in the bottom
of the pan a beautiful set of cuff links made from nuggets, the gift of
Palmyra Lodge No. 26, Hiram Lodge No. 43, and Georgetown Lodge
No. 25.
I have previously acknowledged the splendid co-operation given me
by the Deputy Grand Master and Senior and Junior Grand Wardens. I
wish to add a word of appreciation of the constant co-operation which has
been acicorded me by each and every one of our grand officers. I am likewise indebted to our Past Grand Masters.

Conclusion
In the foregoing paragraphs I have reported upon many matters which

minor importance which I have not noted, but each of which engaged my
energies or my judgment. Except for the work which continues from day
to day and from month to month I leave to my successor in office a clear
desk. I bespeak for him the same abundant measure of loyalty and cooperation which you have accorded to me, and for which I am deeply
grateful.

LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

Los Angeles, November 2, 1927.
To All Masters of Lodges in the Jurisdiction:
At the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, October, 1927, it
was recommended by my predecessor that the 175th Anniversary of the
advent into Masonry of George Washington should be observed by the
Craft throughout our jurisdiction on November 4, 1927. In his Message,
G~and Master Jones stated that "when we consider the part played by
th~s great man in the history of our nation and in the life of Masonry in
this country, and when we view the imperishable glory that his membership has reflected upon our Fraternity," the propriety of a formal observance of the anniversary is apparent.
George Washington, shortly before reaching the age of 21 years
was initiated in Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4, Fredericksburg, Virginia:
November 4, 1752, nine days after his twenty-first birthday, March 3,
1753, he was passed to the degree of Fellow Craft and on the 4th day of
August following he was raised a Master Mason. He was during his
entire adult life a Freemason, and no opportunity was ever permitted by
him to pass without manifesting his interest and confidence in the Fraternity. He was installed April 5, 1788, as the first Master of AlexandriaWashington Lodge No. 22, and served two terms-eight months while
President of the United States. He died full of years and honors on the
14th of December, 1799, and the body of our illustrious brother was consigned to the tomb December 18, with the rites of Masonry.
I am aware that it is too late for Lodges to formulate extensive
programs, but I request that this letter be read in each Lodge, to be followed by a talk by some brother with reference to the Father of Our
Country, whose history is an inspiration to achievement.
Masters holding this observance, however simple, are desired to
report the fact, with program, to the Grand Secretary, in order that we
may have a record.
Fraternally yours,
WILL H. FISCHER, Grand Master.
Attest:
]OHN WHICHl>R, Grand Secretary.
