LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

Los Angeles, January 14, 1928.
To All Inspectors, Jurisdiction of California:
Dear Brethren: Attached hereto you will find a letter of instructions
I am sending to the Masters of all Lodges in the Jurisdiction relative to
monthly educational program. Please read the same carefully at once.
I will expect the complete co-operation of Inspectors in connection with
the execution of this general program. I am firmly of the opinion that
the work contemplated by this program will considerably increase attendance at and interest in our Lodges. We must build up, in addition to
our ritualistic teachings, a keener intellectual life in our Lodges. I know
this plan will get results if carried out in good faith.
Each Inspector is therefore required to secure the monthly reports
from all Masters in his District and forward the same to me at 1107
Edison Building, Los Angeles, not later than the end of each month. I
intend to analyze all of these reports and make them the basis of statistics
which will definitely indicate results.
The burden of execution will fall definitely on the Masters. You are
expected to give them every encouragement and to render such assistance
as you can. We do not expect perfect results the first month or the first
year, but we expect to be able to note ( 1) universal compliance with the
program, (2) steady growth in attendance and interest.
I am instructing the Committee on Education to send to each Inspector in the Jurisdiction, each month, a copy of the program exactly
as forwarded to the Masters of the Lodges. Inspectors are expected to
consider themselves specially obligated in this matter. The Grand Master
must rely on his Inspectors, whom he regards as his direct representatives.
Assuring you that I will appreciate your monthly reports, your advices
and co-operation, I am,
Earnestly and fraternally,
WILL H . FISCHER, Grand Master.

LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

Los Angeles, January 14, 1928.
To all Masters of Lodges in the Jurisdiction of California:
Dear Brethren: Our educational program for Lodges within this
jurisdiction has been worked out and duly approved. The program is
built upon a new basis and ih my opinion promises to arouse widespread
interest among Lodge members as time goes on. In the immediate future
you will receive from our Grand Lodge Committee on Education the program to be carried out in each Lodge in the jurisdiction for the month of
February. Thereafter you will receive the program for each month about
30 days in advance. This will allow you ample time to secure speakers
and make other necessary arrangements.
The execution of this program in each Lodge is hereby made mandatory. Each Lodge is hereby required to present the program once a
month.
The monthly program can be presented on the occasion of the stated
meeting, or following a degree meeting, or at a special meeting for that
specific purpose. This will be at the option of the Master. . Regularity
as to the time or nature of the meeting is hereby recommended. If the
program is presented at a stated meeting or a degree meeting, the work
in hand should be cleaned up by 9 o'clock at the latest so that the members
can have the advantage of the program and get 'home on time.
Masters may, of course, provide musical or other features to accompany the educational program, if they so desire.
The program each month will be forwarded to the Master direct,
and he will be accountable for its presentation. Each program will be
accompanied by ample instructions from the Committee, which instructions. will be approved by the Grand Master.
Masters are hereby required to supply to their respective Inspectors,
on or before the end of each month, fully filled in, the report slip which
will accompany each monthly program. Inspectors will forward these
slips to the Grand Master and they will be carefully analyzed so that the
Grand Master will be able to report results definitely to the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge in October next.
These programs will be so arranged that Lodges in all larger communities will be able to secure qualified speakers on the subjects assigned.
The Master is expected to use diligence and enthusiasm in selecting
speakers who can handle the various subjects intelligently and interest-

ingly. The Committee on Education will supply a paper each month,
comprehensively c<Wering the subject. These papers are ' to be given to
the speakers, in order that they may prepare themselves well in advance.
Discussions following the presentation of the subject are to be encouraged,
but Masters, of course, must be careful not to permit these discussions
ever to follow the line of disputation.
Lodges in small or remote communities, where speakers cannot be

GRAND LODGE, F. & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
SAN FRANCISCO, CAJ.IFORNJA

PROCLAMATION
NINTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

To all Masons in tht Jurisdiction:
The American public school is one of our most cherished institutions.
It reaches every boy and every girl in the land. It is for the sons and
daughters of the rich and of the poor alike. It is the most democratic
of our institutions, offering equal educational opportunities to all. It
should be the concern of all the people .as it is of the Masonic Fraternity.
It was because of their interest in and regard for, our public schools
that the Masons of our jurisdiction instituted, and are fostering, P~blic
Schools Week. It has established a close contact between the public and
its schools. It furnishes an opportunity to present to all the people the
aims, purposes and achievements of the present day school ; and its annual
observance has become a community affair of the greatest civic, social
and educational value.
Now, therefore, we, Will H. Fischer, Grand Master of Masons in
California, do now proclaim the week commencing MONDAY, APRIL
23, 1928, as PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK in the Masonic Lodges in this
i.urisdiction; and we do request and direct that during that week there be
held in every community in California and Hawaii · in which there exists
a Lodge of Masons at least one public meeting for the Ninth Annual
Observance of Public Schools Week.
We do likewise request and direct that wherever practicable the
meeting be held in the auditorium of a public school; and that it be particularly remembered that the observance of Public Schools Week is a
community affair in which we seek the active co-operation of all local
civic organizations and the participation of all the people in the community.
We do furthermore request and. direct that no "work" be done by
any Lodge ·on a night on which any meeting for the observance of Public
Schools Week is held in the town or city in which the Lodge is located.
Dated at Los Angeles this 30th day of January, 1928.
W1u, H. F1sCHER, Grand "Master.
Attest:
JOHN WHICHER, Grand Secretary.

SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA

February 14, 1928.
To the Worshipful Master and Brethren:
At the 78th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge held in San
Francisco in ·October, 1927, the Masonic Club House, University of California at Los Angeles, an incorporated organization, caused to be introduced a resolution requesting the consent and approval of Grand Lodge
to a proposed campaign to raise the necessary money for the purchase
of land and the construction of a Masonic Club House adjoining the new
university campus at Westwood, which is located between Los Angeles
and Santa Monica. The request was duly referred to our Committee on
General Policy and Purposes, which reported thereon, and in consequence
of said report the desired authorization was given by unanimous vote.
Conforming to the action of Grand Lodge I have held numerous
conferences with the Board of Directors of the "Masonic Club House,
U. C. L. A.," and at my suggestion the Board has been reorganized in a
manner entir~ly satisfactory. The by-laws of the corporation have been
amended ,to provide that the Directors shall serve in rotation, five to be
named by the Grand Master each year. This .places the control of the
organization entirely within the power of Grand Lodge.
The necessity for the proposed Club House, which will duplicate the
splendid work of our Club H ouse at the University of California at
Berkeley, is obvious. Masonry should be expressed through exactly the
same service at the Northern and Southern universities.
The U. C. L. A. is now in course of construction, contracts having
been awarded on three of the main units. It is planned that the new
buildings shall be occupied in the near future. A very large attendance
is inevitable.
In financing the Club House at Berkeley a quota was fixed for all
Lodges and the response was generous in all parts of the Jurisdiction.
The same plan has been adopted for financing the Club House at U. C.
L. A. I have therefore authorized the Directors of the "Masonic Club
House, University of California L. A." to proceed with a campaign and
fix a quota representing an average contribution of $1.00 per capita for
the total membership of your Lodge. This quota is light, and I have no
doubt that it can be easily and quickly raised. I earnestly request that
each Lodge in the Jurisdiction accept its quota and give to the movement
the benefit of complete, prompt and effective co-operation.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

63

Past Grand Master Dana R. W eller has been selected as General
Chairman of the campaign, and through his organization will communicate with you from time to time. The period set for the drive covers
the months of March, April and May. We earnestly desire the privilege
of laying the cornerstone of the building before the next communication
of Grand Lodge. For the information of all concerned it can be stated
that no commissions, fees or salaries are to be deducted from the contributions except possibly a small sum for stenographic assistance, postage,
etc. .The entire work is voluntary and without private profit of any
character whatsoever.
I have requested the Inspect~rs of the several districts to co-operate
actively with the Directors and the campaign organization of. the "Masonic Club House, U. C. L. A." and will greatly appreciate a harmonious,
active and full response on the part of the brethren of all Lodges in this
Jurisdiction. No other activity involving the raising of money is contemplated this year.
With my kindest regards to my brethren and with appreciation of
the assistance I know they stand ready to give in this important matter,
I am,
Fraternally,
W ILL H. FISCHER, Grand Master.

LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

San Francisco, March 26, 1928.,
H' orshipf11l Masters, Wardens and Brethren:
I deeply appreciate the active co-operation of the officers and brethreii
of the Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction. Our program this year is '
perhaps somewhat heavy, but if we all continue our efforts we ·should be
able to dispose of it in advance of the vacation period and then enjo'y a·
well-earned rest. In return for our labors we. shall witness· the success
of several important projects for the welfare of the Craft. The following is for your information :
1. Education Program: Taking the Lodges as a whole;· the ptogram
has aroused deep and favorable interest. · Hundreds of highly successful
meetings have been held. The number of failures has been very small.'
It is obvious that no general program can meet the exact requirements.
of every individual Lodge, or the ideas of every individual Master. We
are therefore planning to develop several optional programs, which will
be sent out in due course. As a matter of fact, we are trying an important
experiment. We are receivir;ig general co-operation in the finest spirit,
and it is most helpful. The time is not far distant when we shal,1 \cnqw
quite accurately the requirements and desires of each Lodge, and we can
then be governed accordingly. Meanwhile, the constructive comments of
all Masters are sought.
2. Historical Observance: Is scheduled for June 9 and 10. Full
details will be supplied for May stated meetings, at which time we shall
ask each Lodge to advise how many members are going and make reservations accordingly. Plans are going forward rapidly. This represents
a heavy task for your Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden and many
brethren who have volunteered to help, as well as the members of our
Lodges on the Mother Lode. We visited Placerville yesterday during the
storm and had to dodge floods on the return trip. E verybody wet and
muddy; but it is all in the day's work.
3. Public Schools Week: Plans appear to be well developed, and
we are all expecting excellent results. It is our hope that every Lodge
will work heartily in making the observance a truly significant community contribution to the welfare of the schools.
4. Cl1tb House, University of California, L . A.: It is interesting to
note that one of our Lodges located at Berkeley collected its quota in ten
minutes and expects finally to send in 300 to 400 per cent of its quota.

65

This is because the work of the original Masonic Club House at U. C.
is fully understood and correctly valued by our Berkeley brethren, who
are anxious to see this fine service duplicated at U. C. L. ,.A. The appeal
for this cause is awakening a pleasing response all over the Jurisdiction.
The lot-a magnificent one facing the Campus at U. C. · L. A.-has now
been purchased. It is my hope that all quotas will be filled by the end
of May, so that plans for the building can be prepared and the cornerstone laid before Grand Lodge convenes in October. Meanwhile, Lodges
are requested to send in their collections to the Campaign Committee as
rapidly as pos'sible. 'This will help.
With every wish that happiness will abide with you all, that the true
spirit of fraternity will ever prevail, and that together we may continue
fo go 'forward to · achievements worthy of Masons and Masonry, I am,
,G ratefully and Fraternally,
WILL

H. FISCHER, Grand Master.

Masters, W.ardens and Brethren: .
.
In my general circular letter of April 16th, reference was made to
the Historical Observance to be held in June at Placerville., Definite
arrangements have now been completed to hold a Special Communicatiqi;i
of Grand Lodge near the historic town of Coloma ( six miles from Placerville) on Saturday, June 2nd (that being the full of the moon). Ar>,
interesting program will be presented, commencing Saturday. noon, con~
tinuing until the afternoon of June 3rd-all in commemoratlo~ ~f th~
seventy-fifth anniversary of the Mother Lode Lodges chartered in 1853.
Jesse M. Whited has written the story of events Masonic of those days,
which will be presented as a pageant full of color and life, to be played
under the blue dome of heaven, where the assembled brethren may all
hear and see. Special talent will present vocal and instrumental music,
and the old-time fiddler will add to the attractions.
A tent city will be erected with accommodations for two thousand
brethren. Owing to the necessity of living in tents for the two days, the
ladies cannot be included in the a rrangements. Ample provision will be
made for meals on the camp grounds, but those who attend by auto must
bring their own blankets, towels and flashlights.
Brethren who have motor camp outfits may bring them. Space will
be set aside for auto camps. The American River water will be warm
and inviting for those who will want to indulge in swimming; so bring
your swimming suits.
. Golf togs were unknown in 1853. Blue jeans and red shirts were
more in fashion. Come dressed appropriate to the spirit of the occasion.
The cost of .erecting a tent city and establishing necessary kitchens
and dining tables will be no in·considerable sum, but a group of enthusiastic Masons of Sacramento will care for this problem at cost. We
must, of course, guarantee the number to be fed. F our meals will be
served-lunch and dinner Saturday, and breakfast and lunch Sunday-t
a price of five dollars per person for the four meals. A cot in tent will
be provided at a cost of one dollar per person.
It is imperative that the committees know how many will attend.
Send to John Whicher, Grand Secretary, Masonic Temple, San Francisco,

Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Brethren All : The members of our ancient craft join with the people
of El Dorado County in felicitations to the Masonic Lodges whose
seventy-fifth birthday will be observed at the historic town of Coloma,
on the second day of June. It is fitting that the celebration of this diamond anniversary should be holden at the place made world-famous by
the discovery of gold-an event which resulted in a speedy influx of
sturdy young men to this then far-off Eldorado and the establishment of
Freemasonry on the Pacific Coast.
To
who join in his historic observance we commend that great
Masonic virtue, Brotherly Love.
Sincerely and fraternally,

all

WILL H. FISCHER, Grand Master

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

·• To present some of the outstanding work the Masons of the early
days did in the acquisition of California, the formation of the State government, the organization of the Grand Lodge and the presentation of
the charters, it has been necessary to condense into three acts many
events that were separated as to time and place. With this exception the
incidents and characters are historically and correctly portrayed.
The dramatis personae are members of "The Square ·and Compass
Players," who in the past have entertained the Brethren with the Masonic
plays, "An Eighteenth Century Lodge,". "The Legend of the Temple,"
"The Traitor," and "When Thrones Trembled."
The historical groundwork was furnished by Brothers John Whicher,
yrand $ecretary,; Arthur M. Ellis of Los Angeles, and Leon 0. Whitsell
of San Fra11cisco, members of the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic
History.
. The members of Sacramento Pyramid No. 3, Ancient Egyptian Order
of Sciots, their Band and Guard compose the members of the Third Exploration Expedition, the Lodge members in Acts II and III, and furnish
the musical numbers incident to the evening's production.
The gavel used in Acts II and III is the one used in the initial meeting
of .California Lodge No. 1, held October 17, 1849. The Holy Bible is the
o~e used at the initial meeting of Tehama Lodge No. 3, F. & A. M.,
December 4, 1849. The jewels are the original ones used by Georgetown
Lodge No. 25, at their meeting in May, 1852.

SYNOPSIS
AcT I
Scene I-Lassen's Ranch, May 24, 1846.
Scene II-Suttcr's Fort, July 11, 1846.
The Third Exploration Expedition commanded by Captain John C.
Fremont, U. S. A., accompanied by Kit Carson, left the Bay of San Francisco, early in 1846, on its way to Oregon. Nearing the northern part of
Upper California they were overtaken by Lieutenant Archibald H. Gillespie of the U. S. Marine Corps, who left Washington in November,
1845, carrying important instructions from the Government to Commander John . D. Sloat, Consul Thomas 0. Larkin and Captain John C.

71

Fremont, outlining the policy of the United States regarding the ·requisition of California. Fremont was attacked by Indians, but defeated them
with slight loss. The coadition of affairs in and around the Bay of" San
Francisco and Monterey caused Captain Fremont to alter his plans and
return to Sutter's Fort. While there the Americans captured Sonoma,
rais8d the Bear Flag and established the California Republic. Captain
Fremont shortly thereafter was ordered to take possession of Sutter's
Fort and Upper California in the name of the .United States.
ACT II
Masonic Hall, Sacramento, April 17, 1850.
In March, 1850, Connecticut Lodge No. 75 and New Jersey Lodge,
U. D., located at Sacramento, and Benicia Lodge, U. D., l'ocated at
Benicia, issued a call to the Masonic Lodges then in existence in California
for a meeting to o·rganize a Grand Lodge for the State of California. ·
Under Masonic laws this call was illegal. When this was called to
the attention of the original signers of the call it was withdrawn and a
new one issued for a meeting to be held April 17, 1850. This was participated in by all the regular Lodges and resulted in the formation of
the Grand Lodge, F . & A. M. of the State of California. The ·First Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was held in Sacramento on May
7, 1850, the original Constitution providing that there be semi-annual
sessions in May and .November.
ACT III
Masonic Hall, Placerville, June 27, 1853..
The Grand Lodge on May 5, 1853, issued charters to the following
Lodges located on the Mother Lode: Madison No. ' 23, Grass Vail~y ;
Mariposa Lodge No. 24, Mariposa ; Georgetown Lodge N o. 25, Eldorado;
Palmyra Lodge No. 26, Placerville; Trinity Lodge No. 27, Weave~ville:
Gold Hill Lodge No. 32, Lincoln; Ophir Lodge No. 33, Murphys.
The Grand Master in due time delivered the charters.

LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

May 28, 1928.
To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of all Lodges:
Brethren: Throughout the Jurisdiction the activities of Lodges and
indivlduai brethren in connection with the raising of the funds necessary
for · the erection of the Masonic Club House at the University of California, L. A., have been proceeding e_nergetically. Numerous Lodges
report that· they have filled their respective quotas. Others report good
progress, while a number of Lodges have not as yet indieated the result.
· Masters and committees representing many Lodges have sent requests either to· me· or to the campaign committee of the Masonic Club
House, U. C. L. A., for an extension of the period during which the
active work of · securing this money is to be carried on. In view of all
the conditiOns I believe such an extension is advisable and I am therefore
notifying all Lodges that the period is extended for one month at which
time definite reports of progress will be expected.
There is general approval and enthusiasm for the Club House project.
I am· persuaded that the brethren throughout the Jurisdiction understand
the necessity for the success of the project and I am confident that we
will. be able to report such success to the Grand Lodge at its next Annual
C~mmunication. May I ask, therefore, that in all cases where the full
quota has not yet been secured there be a continuance or renewal of
active work during this period. Let us get this work out of the way by
the end of June.
Make reiµittances to Masonic Club House, U. C. L. A., 632 Roosevelt
Building, Lo~ Angeles.
Deeply appreciating the co-operation which is being manifested by
our Lodges an.d their officers and trusting that the coming vacation season
will bring deserved rest and much happiness to all our brethren, I am,
Fraternally,

GRAND LODGE, F. & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
WILL H. FISCHER, Grand Master
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

July 5, 1928.
To all Masters:
Brethren: On June 30th I was present at a meeting at San Luis
Obispo, which meeting was attended by a considerable number of Masters
and Wardens who had gathered for a reunion. Among other subjects,
our Grand Lodge educational system was discussed and given, as a result
of such discussion, the heartiest approval. During the evening, however,
some points arose which suggest what here follows:
I wish to make it clear to Masters of lodges that the programs . as
prepared by the Committee on Education are not intended to be given a
rigid presentation. The purpose of these papers is to suggest ideas to the
speakers, but the speaker is to have all the latitude he desires. The only
requirement is that he refrain from entering upon controversial ground.
In other words, this program is intended to give to the Masters and to
the speakers ample range for their ingenuity and originality, and it is
intended that the Master shall be free to adjust these programs to what
he conceives to be the best manner of presentation to his particular lodge.
I have found some Masters who believed that the programs had to be
given word for word as prepared by the Committee. This was neve·r
intended. The Committee's effort is directed wholly to giving to Masters
and speakers some good ideas on which to start in the preparation of
programs.
As an example of what I mean, consider the July patriotic program.
This program was made very short on account of the heat in many
sections of the State. Any Master should feel free to substitute other
poems or statements for those sent out by the Committee, or, if it appears
desirable, to discard the material sent out by the Committee and have a
speaker address the lodge on a patriotic subject. Our .main thought for
July is to get organized thinking in the Craft along patriotic lines; and
the same thought applies to all programs from month to month.
From this time forward the Committee will send out three programs
each month, and the Master has the option as to which one he will select.
One program will be on some subject of general interest, one will be on
a scientific subject and one will be on a purely Masonic subject.
From the foregoing you can see the trend of development in the educational work. I have no doubt that the future will see an · even wider
range of optional programs and that ultimately, when the system has been

79

GRAND .LO:DGE OF CALIFORNIA

·firmly established, the only requirement will be that a lodge present some
one definitely educational program each ·month." Thi·s phase ~f 'our develop~
me!jt will be fully discussed in my report to Grand Lodge in October, and
I think will be pleasing to all lodges.
Masters should also understand that music am! any other features
they desire may be introduced along with the educational programs. Some
lodges give these programs around the dinner table before their meetings
begin. Others put through their stated meetings promptly and give the
programs early in the evening. Various plans are being used, with great
success by many Qf our lodges, whose Masters advise me tha't this work
is very popular among their members.
I am sending these thoughts along in the hope that they will be helpful
to you in still further stimulating interest in this highly important activity.
With kindest regards and thanking you all for the splendid co-operation you are gtvmg my efforts to advance the welfare o'f our ancient
Institution, I am,
Fraternally,
WILL H. FISCHER,

Gra11d Master.

P. S.-This is a political year. Let us remember that .political discussions, as such, are not permitted .in Masonic lodges. It is my hope
that all the brethren will do their duty as individuals and vote their convictions at the polls, but no Master should allow the injection of political
discussions into the proceedings of his lodge during its sessions.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY

Handbook For Secretaries

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
This being my twenty-first annual report, it may not be inapropos
to say I am now of mature age, and that the . passing years h.ave
endeared me most strongly to the legion of loyal brethren who so
generously have accorded me their friendship and encourag.ement d~rin~
the more than two decades of my service-years filled with the lights
and shadows that go to make a full life, and notwithstanding I am now
living on borrowed time, I take joy in each new morning, and keen
delight in the friends and affairs of today.
As ·required by the Constitution, there is herewith presented a
statement of all moneys received for account of Grand Lodge, for the
Masonic Homes and for the Emergency Relief Fund, and a summary
of disbursemen;s, together with a notation of all unfinished business.
The detailed and itemized statement of all disbursements has been filed
with the Committee on Finance, as required by the Constitution.
I also have appended an account of receipts since the close of the
fiscal year, July 31, 1928, to and including October 3rd.

Pursuant to the authorization of Grand Lodge at the last. annual
communication, the Handbook for Secretaries (formerly known as
Record Book of Example Lodge) was revised and printed, and one copy
mailed to the Secretary of each Lodge.

Membership
The membership of chartered Lodges as of July 31, 1927, was
128,665, and of Lodges under dispensation to September· 30, 1927, 644,
making our total membership last year 129,309.
For the year ended July 31, 1928, chartered Lodges have a membership of 133,908, and the ten Lodges under dispensation, reporting
September 30, have a membership of 394, our total membership now being
134,302, a net gain for the year of 4993. The net gain of last year
was 6897.
Our registry now contains 562 Lodges under charter, and ten
Lodges working under dispensation. I append herewith. some figures
showing our work in five-year periods.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON SYSTEM
OF KEEPING FINANCIAL RECORDS OF LODGES
To the M: .W: .Grand L odge of California:
At our last Annual Communication a resolution was adopted, providing for the appointment of a committee of three "to prepare and submit
to Grand Lodge, at its Annual Communication in 1928, a tentative system
of books and forms necessary and appropriate for keeping the financfal
records of the Lodges of this jurisdiction, together with the recommendations of said committee as to the advisability of the adoption of such
system."
This was a commission which was calculated to appall the members
of the committee, and we entered upon the work with full knowledge
that many capable Secretaries were of different minds concerning the
details of keeping the financial records of Lodges. We consulted with
numerous expert bookkeepers and found that many good forms are now
in successful use, and each expert Secretary insisting that while the other
fellow's system was good, the one in use by the particular Secretary with
whom we talked, was the best that could be devised-for that particular
officer. In other words, each such Secretary was satisfied that his system
was satisfactory and sufficient, yet admitting that other systems would
doubtless prove better for the other Lodges. Generally, however, we
found it was the consensus of opinion that uniformity in keeping the
financial records of our Lodges was desirable. We have therefore prepared forms that reflect practically a composite of ·all the better systems
now in vogue in this jurisdiction. They are simple and easily understood,
and in our judgment as complete as any set of financial records for·
Lodges should be, and all included in one cover or binder.
The forms include cash receipts from all usual sources, cash disbursements, general ledger, and membership ledger. This last-named
form constitutes on one sheet not only the financial record of the individual
member, provided by section 152, Constitution, but also takes the place
of the Roll Book required by section 151. We have also added a form

PROCEEpINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE 01" CALIFORNIA

for the use of Secretaries in making up their annual returns to Grand
Lodge, it being a onecsheet recapitulation of all work for the fiscal year.
By the use of this sheet Secretaries will be enabled to report at the end
of the year the exact number of members on the roll, with all losses and
gains and the. amounts due to Grand Lodge and the Masonic Homes,
without reference to any other records.
Objection may be made that some Secretaries may not be familiar
with bookkeeping. We have kept this in mind, and believe the system
presented is so plain that those who possess but .an eleme~y ~nowledge
of the art of keeping financial accounts can use 1t, and that 1t will accomplish all that is desired for Lodges whose Secreta·ries are skilled in
bookkeeping.
Complete copies have been prepared, and are now on exhibition in
the office of the Grand Secretary, for the scrutiny of all members of
Grand Lodge and others who may be interested.
Briefly described, the system may. be said to consist of looseleaf
sheets, placed in a serviceable binder in overlapping arrangeme~t, he~d
in perfect alignment, with .index alphabetically. arrang~d always. m plam
sight on its exposed margin. The books are made UP·.m three sizes: one
for a maximum membership of 175, one for 375, and a larger one for
575 members. A book to contain accounts for Lodges having a membership of more than 575 would be too heavy for convenient handling, and
for such Lodges we recommend that two or more books be used.
We commend these records to your careful consideration, knowing
full well that any set system will not satisfy every Lodge o~ every
Secretary, but we recommend that it be adopted and the use ~f it made
mandatory as to each Lodge. formed after this date, and opuonal as to

MASONIC RELICS, WESTERN STAR LODGE

96

existing Lodges.

JOHN WHICHER,
HOWARD
SENTER,
ONEY McC. NICELY,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON LIBRARY
To the M: .;W : .Grand L odge of California:
Your Committee on Library desires to call your attention to the
urgent need of a means whereby the numerous inquiries coming from
Secretaries and Masters of Lodges may be satisfactorily replied to, calling
for authentic authorities in shape of Masonic works that may be gotten
from Grand Lodge library from time to time. The circulating system
would fill this long felt want and supplement any other plan for Masonic
Education that may be brought forward during the coming year. Owing
to our vast increase in membership and the present paucity of books upon
diversified Masonic subjects,· that would be so helpful to those seeking
light, it would be entirely impossible to take care of the needs from
our ·present assortment of books.
Your Committee on Library cannot undertake the great and exhaustive work of gathering the proper books, purchasing shipping cases
and otherwise launching this most comprehensive plan of education without an initial expenditure far greater than would be required to continue

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

98

the work after it has once been established. We are equipped to carry
out the circulating plan. This Committee would therefore request an
appropriation of $1,500 for the coming year.
DENMAN S. WAGSTAFF, Chairman Library Committee.

Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and Finance.

It seems proper that, as Vice-President of the Masonic Temple As~o­
ciation of California I should report the formation of a new corporation
through which to hold and operate the property and affairs of the
Masonic Temple and the transfer to it of all of the property of the old

company.

99

The directors have, for a long time, considered this action necessary.
The name adopted is "Masonic Temple Association of California, Inc."
The directors of its predece$sor are now its directors.
The work of reorganization consumed several months and, except
for the necessary filing fees, printing and supplies, was done without c<ist
to the association. Brother Frank C. Ruppel, who has acted as secretary
since the death of Brother Edward Peabody, has performed that service,
as well as in the arduous clerical labor involved in the reorganization,
without compensation, while the legal work was handled by Brother
Olin L. Berry, likewise without remuneration. Sever~! other members
of the craft assisted by acting as directors of the new corporation until
such time as the transfers of property had taken place and the directors
of the old corporation were installed.
The objects which prompted the reorganization have been accomplished and the new corporation is functioning satisfactorily.
WILLIAM P. FILMER, Vice-President.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON MEETING
PLACE OF GRAND LODGE
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee to which was referred the subject of a perµianent
meeting place for Grand Lodge reports as follows : The committee was
appointed December 22nd, 1927, and the M.".W.".Grand .Master requested
it to proceed with its labors at the earliest possible date. With this
object in view the committee met on January 7th, 1928, and considered
the question of constructing a Grand Lodge Auditorium in the Temple
in San Francisco.
An architect attended this meeting and he and the committee, for the
next three months, gave careful consideration to three plans:

101

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

1. To use the large room on the ground floor on Oak street for
an.·auditorium with the store on the corner of Van Ness and Hickory
avenues as reception and anterooms. The architect reported that such a
room would seat but 1300, and to fit and furnish it would cost about
seventy-five or eighty thousand dollars. The space for seating under
this plan would be inadequate.
2. The architect considered the question of enlarging the present
Gr.uid Lodge room, which would entail the exclusion of four heavy
columns now . supporting the .dome and so change the room as to place
the .Gl'and Master's station in the West with galleries on the ends of the
room instead of on the sides as they are now. This would entail a cost
of i$150,000 and render the room objectionable for Commandery meetings,
for which it is now being used. Such an arrangement would seat but
1500, .and-while it might suit the requirements of the present, would not
take care of the future.
3. · Consideration was given -to the building of an auditorium on the
top floor of the building, .eliminating the offices of the Grand Secretary
and Grand Recorder of the Grand Chapter and Grand Commandery and
all other offices on that -floor, going through the .roof for the ceiling. It
was found that this room with galleries could be constructed to seat 1700
at a cost of '$150,000. The plan, however, precluded the possibility of
reception ·and committee rooms, and additional further objection was
found in the necessary use of columns. The offices of the Grand Secretary, Grand Recorder and other offices would have to be placed on the
groµnd floor.
Your committee therefore reports against the advisability of any
futther attempt to use any part of the Masonic Temple for this purpose.
We believe the time has now come when consideration should be
given to' the·- .purchase of a site and the erection of a permanent Grand
Lodge building in which would be placed a suitab~e auditorium for ~ur
Grand Lodge meetings, capable of seating 2500, with adequate reception
and committee rooms, space for a library and museum and offices for the
Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge and the Grand Recorder of the
Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons, Grand Recorder of the Grand
Council, Royal and Select Masters and the Recorder of the Grand Commandery, if desired, in the same building. It should be known that the
offices of these functionaries are very inadequate.
The offices of the Grand Secretary and Grand Recorder are much
too small for the rapidly growing business of the Grand Lodge and
t}ier bodies and the offices of the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer do
~ot at all s~rve the purpose. Copies of the Proceedings of the many
grand jurisdictions are annually sent to the Grand Secretary and filed by
him. It is therefore necessary that adequate facilities be established and

kept ready for these at all times. At present there is no library or even
sufficient shelving for books. There is no museum for the valuable· reli<:s
we now have, and there being no opporturuty for .display precludes the
possibility of obtainiag many specimens that might otherwise be sent to us.
We secured the services of a highly responsible real estate operator
who submitted several sites. From these we selected the one we considered best adapted for the purpose and secured an option without cost
to purchase the property. The option is good for two weeks from October
2d, 1928, to include October ' 17th, 1928. This site is situated· on the
corner of Golden Gate Avenue and Hyde Street. Its size is 137% feet
square and its cost is $145,000. Its present income is $550 per month.
It is central, is available to the Grand Lodge membership and the price
we consider reasonable.
It may be proper to state at this time that the Directors of the
Temple Association have discussed the proposition of selling the Van
Ness Avenue and Market Street Temple, when the time is propitious,
and if such sale is effected Grand Lodge will be adequately reimbursed
for its outlay on the proposed Temple.
Architects have submitted elevations and tentative plans for a
building, which we herewith submit.
The financial plan for purchasing the site and erecting the building,
assuming the cost to be about $750,000 for the site, building, and furnishings
is attached.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND MASTER'S
MESSAGE AND REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the M." .W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to which was referred the address of the Most
· Worshipful Grand Master, having had the same under consideration,
desires to report herewith as follows:
In the very complete and comprehensive account of his stewardship
as delivered this morning by the Most Worshipful Grand Master, there
was revealed in the most impressive and inspiring manner not only a
digest of all his activities in the administration of the affairs of his high
offiee1.-but in addition thereto a true picture of the wonderfully fine man
and Mason in whom has been vested the duty and responsibility of guiding
and directing our great fraternity during the past twelve months. An
indefatigable worker, a clear and constructive thinker, a concise and
able speaker-all combined in a personality at once congenial, affable and
sympathetic-serves but · inadequately to express some of those personal
attributes which have endeared Grand Master Will H. Fischer to all
members of the Craft whose i>rivilege it has been to see and hear and
come in contact with him. Your Committee feels that enough could not
be said in his praise.
·The continual growth and affluence of the fraternity in California
makes increasing demands upon those whom we elevate to places of
distinction in our institution. When the true situation is realized we
cannot remain unconscious of the fact that when we honor one of our
number by selecting him to preside over this grand jurisdiction, we at the
same' time put upon him a tremendous task ; one to test to the utmost
his physical and mental capacity. In so far as this task and its test are
concerned, the past year has proved no exception, and we feel that the
Grand Master has measured· up to the responsibility in a way that proves
him a most wdrthy descendant of a long line of illustrious ancestors in
the Oriental chair he is soon to relinquish.
'The earnestness and sincerity with which the Grand Master has
dealt with the problems of the Craft justly entitle him to the cordial
appreciation of your Committee and this Grand Lodge.
In view of the fact that the adoption of this report will carry with
it reference to the proper Committees the various recommendations of
the Grand ·Master, for later consideration by Grand Lodge, your Committee feels that discussion of these at this time is unnecessary. We
therefore recommend that the various sections of the address requiring
committee attention, be referred as follow:

REPORT OF EDUCATIONAL COMMITTEE
To the M .'.W.".Grand Lodge of California:
Your Educational Committee for the year 1928 respectfully submits
herewith a report of its activities during the year:
. The statistics of the Committee's activities include the receipt of
twelve hundred letters ; the writing of fifteen hundred letters; the presentation of ninety-five addresses by the Executive Director and members
of the .Commi~ee; the presentation and mailing of twenty-five pamphlets
on various subJects sent to 750 names on the mailing list; the awarding

107

of the prizes in the essay contest, which was instituted last year, the
awards having been made by Past Grand Masters Adams, Burke and
Reese from a total of seventy essays submitted; the holding of general
conferences in San Francisco, Fresno and San Luis Obispo.
But we hope we may be pardoned if we may present a short statement, historically, of the progress of the educational movement in the
Grand Lodge of California.
The present Conunittee and system devised by it were instituted in
1925, and reference is respectfully made to the reports of the Educational
Committee of that and subsequent years. The primary point dwelt upon
in the reports of the three preceding years is that an educational program
is one, not for a single year or few years, but rather one which must
extend over an unlimited number of years and proceed to a gradual
development. Necessarily the early years of such a program must be in
some measure experimental.
.
We hope you will bear with us, however, if we refer to the "Synopsis
of Subjects and Methods of Presentation" set forth in our report for
the year 1925. W ithout burdening you with details therefrom, we believe
we may successfully assert that the program as laid down in that synopsis
four years ago has not been materially departed from but, indeed, that it
has been generally followed and is being gradually developed. A review
of the subjects of the publications issued by this Committee, together
with the statement as to the methods of using such publications, develops
the fact that the original program has been adhered to· and has met with
the degree of success originally anticipated.
For the year 1926 and 1927, the method of procedure was followed
as organized by the Committee in 1925, and the progress made under
that method of procedure pointed out the strength and weakness of the
system. The strength of the system is obvious. We believe it cannot
be denied that a program which seeks to diffuse light among the members
immediately stands upon its own footing and attracts the attention of all
thinking men. The variety of subjects offered forms a veritable little
library, and if you were to take a complete set of these . publications ~f
thi°s Committee you probably would be much impressed with the material
afforded you. Hear, if you will, the list of these subjects:

l'v!aiter announced that he desired to have all Lodges, without, exceptiQn,

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
In accordance with the legislation enacted by Grand Lodge at the
Annual Communication of 1926, a Board of Control was appointed by
the Grand Master to supervise and direct the various Boards of Relief
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge.
At the 1927 Communication of Grand Lodge, the Board of Control
so appointed presented certain recommendations in connection with its
report, and these recommendations were adopted and approved by Grand
Lodge.
The report of your Board of Control here presented is in accord with
the legislation of both of the aforesaid Communications as well as the
recommendations of this Board adopted and approved at the 1927 Grand
Lodge Communication.
The recommendations so approved included the following:
1. (a) That all Boards of Relief be required to report for the
same period and that this period coincide with the period in which Lodges
report to Grand Lodge, namely, for the year ending July 31st ; that reports
of Boards of Relief must be filed with the Board of Control on or before
August 25th of each year.
(b) That Boards of Relief be required to submit at the close of each
year ending July 31st and before August 25th, uniform financial and
statistical reports, and also requests for reimbursement on uniform
blanks, which must be secured from the Grand Secretary.
2. That uniform records for cash transactions be adopted.
3. That each Board of Relief keep a ledger record of each case' of
relief, with a card record for indexing and cross reference; this record
to contain a complete financial account with the case and with the Lodge.
4. That at the close of each year the Board of Control be authorized
to cause an audit and survey to be made of each Board of Relief ; that
the officer, who has charge of the books of said Board, be required to
have his books in readiness for such audit between July 31st and August
25th of each year, and that the expense of such audit be charged to the
respective Boards of Relief.
5. That a uniform code of By-Laws for Boards of Relief be drafted
and that the Board of Control be authorized to draft such uniform code
for .such Boards, subject to the approval of the Grand Master and Grand
Lodge.
·
·
6. That all Boards of Relief be required to carry fidelity insurance
and that said insurance be arranged for and carried through Grand Lodge..

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

111

7. That all Boards of Relief be required to carry employers' compensation insurance in accordance with law.
9. That all Boards of Relief be placed upon a business basis, and
that the salaries of the officers of such Boards be regulated according to
the services performed.
10. That the Board of Control be empowered to formulate a plan
similar to that now in operation by the Masonic Relief Association of the
United States which will provide a central clearing house of all relief
cases and which will furnish to all Boards of Relief of the jurisdiction
a .record of all applications for relief .and relief applications granted,
particularly of all applicants who have imi)osed upon or attempted to
impose upon the Boards of Relief.
Immediately following the close of .the Grand Lodge your Board of
Control communicated with the officers o.f each of the respective Boards
of Relief giving notice of the recommendations approved by Grand Lodge
and requesting the support and co-operation of each of said Boards in
carrying out the legislation so approved.
Forms for uniform financial statistical reports were prepared and
submitted, as well as forms for uniform records for cash transactions.
With but one or two exceptions the Boards of Relief have adopted
the recommendations approved by Grand Lodge and the directions of the
Board of Control, and with these exceptions the desires of Grand Lodge
for uniform standardized record and account keeping have been
accomplished.
Coriferences have been held during the year with representatives of
the various Boards of Relief in an effort to secure a better understanding
of the Grand Lodge legislation and of the efforts of the Board of Control
to administer the duties placed upon it by Grand Lodge. T hese conferences have been held as much for the purpose of enabling the Board
of Control to become acquainted with the Boards of Relief procedure
and activities, as to inform Boards of Relief officers as to the legislation
of . Grand Lodge and the desires of the Board of Control.
. -The conferences have been beneficial, and, while they have "not
accomplished altogether -the purposes sought; while there has not .been '
entire unanimity in their results, yet we believe that the Bo;lrds of Relief
officers in the main have appreciated what your Board of Control has
set out to do, and that they are now acting in entire acco~d with these
effort~ and purposes,

The relief fund tra~sactions and expense fund transactions of this
Board are recorded in separate books and checks are drawn on separate
bank accounts. For the purpose of the comparative statement of all
Boards of Relief we have combined the operations of the Relief Fund
and the Expense Fund.
Medical and legal cases are referred to various brethren, who serve
gratuit9usly in many cases.
Checks are signed by the Secretary or Assistant Secretary or the
Treasurer, one signature being sufficient.
The books of the Los Angeles Board of Relief were audited by M. L.
Higgins, certified public accountant, to May 31, 1928. The bank statements and canceled checks were in the hands of the Treasurer and we did
not reconcile the book balances with the bank statements as of July
31; 1928.
Board of Relief-San Francisco
The Board of Relief is located in the Masonic Temple at Market
and Van Ness, occupying two of three rooms, the third room, which is
the common entrance room, being occupied by the Employment Bureau.
Transactions are recorded in a cash book having two columns, one
for relief receipts and expenditures and the other for an other items.
The .relief items are posted to a subsidiary record with each $tate and
foreign ju~isdiction, from which the total amount by jurisdictions is
obtained f~r report purpos~s annuaUy. The other items are analyzed
semi-monthly and posted to a summary, The Secretary indicated his
willingness to install. a columnar cash book with columns for recording
relief items by jurisdictions and an other items in a single column. This
is a step in the right direction, and will materiaUy assist in the preparation
of the required figures as well as in auditing the books. Relief cases are
recorded in a bound ledger with an index in front.
Legal and medical assistance is rendered without remuneration by
members of the fraternity.
· Checks are signed by the Chairman and .Secretary.
We inspected the following bonds, which are in the custody of the

Board of Relief-Oakland
The Board of Relief is located in the Masonic Temple at Twelfth
and Washington streets, in separate quarters from the E mployment
Bureau, which is housed across the street.
Beginning December 1, 1927, a columnar cash book in the form

recorded in a loose-leaf binder, with an index before each letter of the
alphabet.

Resume of Report
We will say, in conclusion, that the recommendations of the .Board
of Control are beginning to show results in the various Boards visited,
and the Secretaries all show a disposition to follow the instructions .of
the Board of Control. They welcome an audit. of their accounts and
have furnished us with all assistance possible in facilitating our work.
Now that a uniform accounting period has been adopted and the columnar .

cash book installed at most of the Boards, we believe that there should
be little difficulty in obtaining accurate reports from the various Secretaries.

Non-Membership o.f Lodges
In its report to the Grand Lodge Communication of 1927 your Board
of ·Control recommended, "that when Boards of Relief shall be organized,
or where Boards of Relief are already organized, all Lodges within the
jurisdiction of said Boards of Relief shall be required to hold membership in
such Boards of Relief and contribute their per capita share of expense of
said Boards of Relief; provided that Lodges adjacent to said concurrent
jurisdictions may upon application unite with said Boards of Relief."
This recommendation the Board of Control voluntarily withdrew, deeming
the time insufficient in which to prepare and submit the necessary amendment to the Constitution. The Board of Control, however, is still of the
same opinion, and believes that every Lodge within the jurisdiction of the
Baaed of Relief shall be a member of that Board of Relief and shall
contribute its pro rata share of the maintenance of said Board. Your
Board of Control now submits to the Grand Lodge its recommendations
that the Jurisprudence Committee be requested and instructed to prepare
and submit at this communication an amendment to section 83 of the
Constitution, which will provide for and cover the recommendations
aforesaid.

Recommendations
Based upon the experiences of two years and following upon the
recommendations submitted and approved in 1927, your Board of Control
now makes the following recommendations:
1. It is recommended that the Board of Control be given power and
authority to compel, with the consent of the Grand Master, any and all
Lodges to become members of a Board of Relief where one exists ·and
also where in its judgment, a Lodge is located sufficiently near to such a
Board. It is furtfier recommended that the Jurisprudence Committee be
requested and directed to prepare such legislation amending section 83
of the <Constitution as will authorize the Board of Control to act in
accord with this recommendation.
2. It is recommended that there be created in the office of the Grand
Secretary an Information Bureau, to be under the direction and authority

123

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the Grand Secretary, the duty and powers of which Bureau shall be
the dissemination to the Lodges and Boards of Relief of this jurisdiction,
information regarding applications for relief and relief granted to applicants who have imposed upon or attempted to impose upon said Lodges
or Boards of Relief; and it is further recommended that all Lodges and
all Boards of Relief be directed and required to furnish to the Grand
Secretary any and all information regarding relief granted to applicants
who have imposed upon or attempted to impose upon the said Lodges or
Boards of Relief.
3. It is recommended that Boards of Relief and Lodges which have
been reimbursed by Grand Lodge by and with the approval of the Board
of Control and the Finance Committee, at the Annual Communication of
Grand Lodge, be required and directed to forthwith report to the Board
of Control and the Grand Secretary any and all reimbursements for
relief extended which have been made subsequent to said Annual Communication, ·and for which reimbursement has already been made by
Grand Lodge, and to remit to the Grand Secretary any moneys received
for such reimbursement.
4. It is recommended that Boards of Relief or Lodges immediately
report to the Board of Control the neglect or failure of Lodges, whether
in the jurisdiction of California or elsewhere, to respond to request for
reimbursement or which refuse to reimburse the said Boards of Relief
or Lodges for relief extended, in order that the Board of Control may
endeavor to prosecute efforts to secure reimbursement, and to make such
efforts at once without waiting until the close of the year for such· reports.

Comments
Your Board of Control apprecfates the co-operation and support
which have been extended during the year by the respective Boards oI
Relief and their officers. The work of this Board of Control is even yet
only preliminary. Many changes were recommended a year ago after
less than a year's experience. These recommendations were submitted to
and approved by Grand Lodge and thereafter transmitted to the Boards
of Relief. The response has been most encouraging and gratifying. The
Boards of Relief have accepted and have put into ac:tual practice the
changes recommended.

A -,State~wide Masonic Employment Servi.c::e ·
Your Board of Control· has made considerable study and has conducted some investigai.ion of the Masonic employment situation in
California. The records of our own employment service show thllt the
nuwb.er of , placements made by the re.spective service organizations do
not compare fa.vora.bly with the nuinber of men and women who appcy
fQ( iemplpyment.
Notwithstanding the fact that the jurisdiction is prosperous, as evidenced by bank deposits, the absorption by the communities of stock and
bond issues, the multitude of automobiles, the vast amounts .of money
that are spent for amusements and luxuries, it is understood that there
is · an increasing amount of unemployment.
The problem of helping our brothers who are out of work is a very
definite one, and the · justicll an<J wiidoJll· of it are beyond dispute. Your
Boari! .Qf Con.trot is satisfied that our present plan. of solving the J>roblem
falls short of meeting the sit1,'at.ion, that it is eJ>pensive and th;it it is not
sufficient. In no way is there a better opportunity to put into practice
the ideals of service and. Masonic brotherhood than in this particular
manner. The Masonic ., fraternity prides itself on its charity. But this
work is not chas:ity.. We are pledged to aid and assist a worthy distressed brother. And ·there .is never a time when a brother needs aid
and assistance so. much· as when he is out of work and seeking a job. He
is not asking--chuity ;. he .wa~ work to provide a living for himself and
his f~y.
While the Employment Service is doing its best in this jurisdiction
the work that should be done is not being accomplished. By reason of

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

127

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
''

our numbers and by reason of our influence we should be able to do more
for our members. There are places in this jurisdiction where during
certain portions of the year labor waits for laborers while other places
have a surplus of laborers and no labor. Mendocino might need men in
its lumber mills or in the forests while San Francis~o might have many
men out of work who would be willing to take the jobs. Only by having
active committees constantly on the job can this great fraternity make
this work really efficient.
Your Board of Control believes that the real solution of this pr<;>blem,
the only way in which the work may be co-ordinated and standardized is
in the appointment and employment of a State Employment Service Secretary, whose duty will be to assist in the organization of Committees in
the respective districts of the State; to advise and direct such Committees;
to gather information regarding employment and to furnish such information to all other sections of the State for the benefit of the members of
the Fraternity. Your Board of Control does not deem it advisable nor
is it willing to make this recommendation at this time, but it believes
the time is not far distant when the problem will be so much more
serious than it is today that the appointment of an Employment Service
Secretary will become imperative and that it will be recommended and
approved by Grand Lodge.
Your Board of Control does favor, however, and hereby recommends that in each Inspector District of this jurisdiction the District
Inspector be authorized and empowered, when and where conditions may
necessitate and seem advisable to appoint an Employment Service .Committee which will act for the district; which will acquaint itself with
employment conditions ; which will prepare lists of industries and get in
touch with employing officials ; which will keep a list of men out of work;
furnish information to other districts and Boards of Relief of positions
open ; and seek to serve both employers and applicants.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Our first conclusion is that it has now been demonstrated that work

alon~ the line of the Masonic history of the State is of value and should
be aided by Grand Lodge. This is based on the reception which has been

accord~d various historical celebrations and observances had among

137

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

presentations that may be desirable with reference to the history of some
particular Lodges which are unable to handle them successfully themselves without aid.
ARTHUR M. ELLIS,

Masonic Lodges of the State during the past year.

PERCY KING,

It is our view that the most pressing problem before us is the collec~10~ ~nd pres~rvation. of the materials for such history. A few aged
md~viduals still survive whose recollections should not be allowed to
perish. Contemporaneous newspaper accounts, letters, diaries, photographs, old Lodge minutes and various sources of information should be
g~thered toge.ther and studied. The course of events moved very rapidly
wit~ the earliest Lodges, and some of them (particularly in the mining
reg10ns) passed out of existence long ago, but not until they had performed notable service. It is our belief that we shall be unable to
handle the situation satisfactorily unless a field agent is put to work
directly on such matters.

LEON 0. WHITSELL,

.

The. next pro~lem we feel is that of encouraging and assisting local
Lodges m gathering and preserving their own histories. Los Angeles
Lodge . No.. 42 will celebrate its 75th anniversary next spring. your
Committee 1s now at work assisting this Lodge in the preparation of a
book which it plans to issue on its history during the period of 1854-1868
when it was the only Masonic Lodge in Los Angeles. Similar under~
takings on the part of other Lodges should be encouraged.
Our first request is that the membership of the Historical Committee

b~ increased from three to five, the members of which shall represent
different parts of the State and be so distributed as to place one member
of the committee at least in close touch with every Lodge whose work
should be aided.
Secondly, we request that the sum of fifteen hundred dollars be
· appropriated for the purpose of employing a trained student of history
to serve as a field agent, all of the materials collected by him to be
deposited with and to belong to Grand Lodge. In addition there doubtless
wtU be the necessity of an .expense account, covering t'raveling, stenographic work and photography.
' : Thirdly, we recommend that the Grand Master be empowered to
appoint special Grand Lodge Committees as occasion may arise to assist
pariicular Lodges· that are unable to properly care for matters of an
hi1>torical character pertaining to them. We have in mind particularly
some of the smaller mining town Lodges. It seems to us also to be
desirable that special committees be appointed to aid in dramatic or other

Committee.

Adopted, excepting the requests for appropriations,
which were referred to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the M:.W:.Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit for the year just closed my twenty-first annual
report as Grand Lecturer. I have visited every district in the jurisdiction,
have held Lodges of instruction, both day and night sessions, and found
the officers and brethren were all anxious and ready to perfect themselves
in the ritual. A marked improvement is noticeable in this respect, particularly in the candidates' lectures, which is very gratifying. I have given
much instruction to the officers and brethren in my office, and have at all
times assisted the brethren when called on so to do.
I have received reports from all the Inspectors. They report the
Lodges under their supervision in good condition, although many of them
have not been doing as much degree work as usual. Most -of them are
actively taking up the Educational program and getting a great deal out
of it. I am deeply appreciative of the help and co-operation of the
Inspectors, who have all responded · promptly whenever . it was possible
for them to do so, to whatever calls that were made upon them. They
have all been most anxious to serve.
There are two things that are absolutely required in a good Masonic
Worker : First, he must know his lines; and second, he must know what
they mean in order that he can impart them understandingly and feeling)y;
He will then get out of that meaning just in proportion to the industry
with which he studies, thinks, imagines and reasons. All tpese are hidden
away in our Masonic ritual, waiting for each Mason to discover and
possess them for his own.
Masters should be particularly careful in the reception o.£. petitions~
and receive only those who are good men and true. The character and
efficiency of Freemasonry is determined by the character and efficiency of
the individual Master Mason. Therefore a petition for the degrees should
not be accepted from any one unless he is a moral, upright man, ·a loyal,

PROPOSAL FOR MONUMENT TO LESTER
ALLEN PELTON
Past Grand Master Jones, by request of Grand Range
Lodge, No. 59, presented the following :
WHEREAS, Brother Lester Allen Pelton, in the year 1877-78 invented
the famous Pelton Water Wheel, an invention which revolutionized
world industry, an invention used extensively throughout the world today.;
his . figures on hydraulics having been tested and adopted by the umverslties of the country ; and
WHEREAS Brother Pelton was an early Californian pioneer, residing
at Camptonviile, where he established his work shop, experimented, and
made the invention, he being an honored member of Gravel Range Lodge
No. 59, F. & A. M.; and
.
WHEREAS in honor of this esteemed .brother, Gravel Range Lodge
No. 59 plans {he erection of a suitable monument to the memory of this
inventor on the site of his old workshop where he experimented and
made th~ invention, thus linking this impo.r tant invention and person with
other early. day Masonic pioneers; therefore, be it

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PHYSICAL
QUALIFICATION
To the M:. W: .Grand Lodge of California:
Your special committee appainted by the Most Worshipful Grant!
Master to consider the subject of physical qualifications for Masonry
begs leave to repor"t.
The committee has given careful consideration to the entire subject.
Brother Whicher has secured information "from most of the other jurisdictions in this country as to the manner in which these jurisdictions
handle the subject. There is no uniformity. Your committee has further
carefully considered the history of the matter in this jurisdiction. It has
been one of great difficulty and confusion. Many Grand Masters have
called attention to this and to the necessity of simplifying and clarifying
the subject. In 1914 (Proc: 1914, pp. 9, 173) this Grand Lodge recognized
the necessity of taking action, and amended the Constitution to do away
with the old rule that a candidate must be able to comply literally with
the physical requirements, and adopted the rule that one who could comply
"substantially" with such requirements might be admitted. Instead of
clarifying the matter, this has · in practice simply resulted in confusion
worse confounded. No test is laid down, or in the nature of things can
be laid down, for what is "substantial" compliance. The result is that
every Grand Master has ·been burdened with a multitude of individual
applications from Lodges to determine whether particular candidates
were or were not physically qualified. In the very nature of things, the
Grand Master could not, in most instances, have any personal acquaintanceship or make any personal examination of the candidate. The view
of one Grand Master as to whether a particular injury disqualified a candidate might be entirely different from that of the preceding or succeeding
Grand Master. The present condition imposes an undue burden upon the
Grand Master, is unfair to the fraternity and to deserving candidates.
Your Committee has worked out a plan which, if it meets with your
approval, it is hoped may solve the difficulty. The Committee respectfully
recommends that section 94 of the .Constitution be amended by adding
thereto the foltowing :
"And the question as to the physical sufficiency of the candidate shall
be left to the sound discretion of the Lodge. Where the candidate is
unable to comply literally · with the physical requirements, the Master '
shall state the. nature and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before
·
ballot is ·takeri."

If this amendment shall meet with your approval, it will leave to
each Lodge to determine for itself whether a candidate can substantially
comply with the physical requirements. The Lodge is in the best position

141

to determine this question. The investigating committee and the officers
of the Lodge can see the candidate, can see and determine the nature of
his disabilities and the extent to which _they disqualify him. '.'.he~ can
also make full investigation as to his financial condition and the hkelihood
of his ever becoming a charge upon the fraternity. Moreover, each
ember of the Lodge, before voting, will have from the Master a state:ent of the nature and extent of the candidate's disabilities.
One objection might be urged to this plan, namely; that. some persons
might be taken into the fraternity who would at some time b.ecome a
charge upon it. This, of course, is always possible. However, th1~ Grand
Lodge has already determined that it is not necessary £.or a. candidate to
be able to comply literally. Some one must deter~me m each case
whether the candidate can substantially comply. Is 1t not ~uch more
likely that the Lodge itself can determine this accurately and Justly, both
as to the fraternity and as to the candidate, than can any other officer
or body, who does not know the facts of t~e particular. case? There are
many men with some physical disqualifications who will make excellent
Masons. This Grand Lodge has already deter.mine~ . tha.t it wants to
admit· such candidates, unless their physical d1~quahfications. are such
that they cannot substantially comply. We agam call attention to t~e
fact that some one must determine this, and the Lodge seems to be m
the best position to do so. There is no reason to - suppo~e t~at ~ Lod~e,
with full knowledge of the nature and extent of a cand1dat~ s d1squ~l~fi­
cations, will unanimously vote to admit him, if ther~ is any fair probab1hty
that such physical disqualifications will render him a charge upon the
fraternity.
.
The Committee originally considered making some special excep~1ons
in favor of men who had incurred their physical. disabilitie~ in ~e m.1htary
or naval service of their country. After considerable discussion it .was
felt unwise to base any distinction upon this ground. The Comrmttee
recognizes in full the consideration that is due. to any. ma~ who has bee~
di$Clbled in the service of his country. But 1t has hkew1se ~elt that . it
would be unfair to permit a man, who had incurred a particular disability from this cause, to be admitted and to exclude some other man
who had received a similiar disability in some other worth~ man~er. ~or
example, if a man has lost his left hand in saving the life of a child,
he is entitled to consideration perhaps as much as a man :-Vho .has lost
his left hand in battle. If both men possess all other qualifications and
are in such financial condition that they are unlikely ever to become a
burden to the fraternity, both would seem .to .be e?tit~ed . to . favorable
consideration when applying for membership m this mst1tut1on. The
Committee, therefore, recommends the amendment in the form above

stat~d so that all worthy men may receive equal consideration. If adopted,
this amendment will simplify 'and clarify the condition for which i 'remedy
is urgently" needed ..

Lodges having made contributions, 511; Lodges not having contributed, 56. This includes Lodges exempted by the Grand Master.
It has always been the desire of the Board, as well as the ambition
of the members of the organization who are students and faculty members, that the Club House should be ready for occupancy and the organization completely ready to start its work of ministering to the needs of
the Masonically affiliated students at the time the University moves to its
permanent location at Westwood.
It was the original announcement of the Regents of the University
that the transfer would take place in September, 1928, subsequently
deferred to February, 1929. However, in August of this year it was
decided by the Regents that the move should be delayed until September, 1929.
Inasmuch as it then became apparent that the building would not need
to be completed until August, 1929, your Board deemed it advisable to
invest the cash on hand, in accordance with its previous policy, as disclosed
by the foregoing financial statement, in securities legal for savings banks
and thus earn sufficient to materially reduce the expense necessarily incident to a campaign for funds. It is apparent, however, that steps
should now be taken to formulate final plans for the erection of a building
and that to that end competent architects should now be employed.
While it appears that upon a final checkup and completion of efforts
already initiated, sufficient funds will result to pay for the site and erect
the building, it yet remains to provide for the furnishings. With this
in mind, your Board has already set up a committee to seek subscriptions
from those individuals and organizations desiring to furnish a room or to
make a considerable donation to that end. Several organizations have
expressed a desire and willingness to take a direct interest in this part
of making ready for service to our young men and women. It has seemed
to us proper to thus separate the activities. There is no doubt on the
part of your Board but that sufficient funds will be provided by popular
subscription to completely furnish and equip the Club.
With this report we ask leave to submit the following resolution:
Resolved, that the Masonic Club of the University of California at
Los Angeles be authorized to employ architects for ·the preparation of
plans for the erection of its building at Westwood, and with the approval
of such plans by the appropriate Committee of this Grand Lodge to erect
such building and make it ready for occupancy on or before September
1 1929 · and also that said Club continue its campaign for funds until
s~fficien~ has been realized to completely furnish and equip the Club
House so to be erected.
THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS,
IRA F. THOMPSON, Chairman.

The report, including the resolution, was adopted.

REPORT OF MASONIC CLUBHOUSE, U. C., AT
BERKELEY
To the M:.W:.Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California, Inc., deems it unnecessary to make an extended report of
the activities of the Club House during the past Masonic year. The
institution has functioned faithfully and satisfactorily. Thousands of
contacts are made each semester with the members of the student body
who hail from Masonic homes or who have Masonic affiliations. The
institution continues to hold a most commanding place among the activities
of the Berkeley Campus. Words of commendation from administrative
officers and members of the faculty of the University are freely given.
Under the able administration and supervision of Mrs. J. H. Quinn,
resident hostess of the Club House, its work has attained even greater
results than in past years. The influence of this good woman among our
students at the University is most remarkable. She has the confidence
and esteem of the student body to a very great degree.
There has been practically nothing to disturb the peace and harmony
with which the affairs of the Club House have been carried on. It
continues to be the one center where the young people of our constituency
find opportunity for social intercourse and recreation, and to engage in
certain activities which they would not otherwise have.
The building and property of the Club have been well cared for and
preserved. Repairs and betterments have been kept to a minimum, and
the item of depreciation is remarkably small.
The assessment of 10 cents per member, levied at the last Convocation
of Grand Lodge for the support and maintenance of the Club House,
will enable the Trustees to make a very appreciable reduction of the
unsecured indebtedness to the First National Bank in Berkeley.
There is submitted herewith the budget for the Masonic year beginning October 1st. There is also presented an audit of the accounts of
the Trustees and the management of the Club House for the past year.
