REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON NINTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
To the M:. W.'. Grand Lod~e F . .& A. M. of (;alifornia:
Each year fp,r several years past your Committee on Public Schools
Week has been able to report ~hat the latest Observance was the . most
successful ever held. This year not only is this again true, but .such was.
the success of the Ninth Annual Observance that it is very inadequately
· '
expressed merely by comparison with results in previous years.
Just as the result of an election can often be confidently predicted.
fro~ . a "snap tally" of a few scattering J?recints over a widely diffused
territory, so do the first twenty-five or thirty reports received from the
Lodges fairly indicate the extent of the su~cess o( the annual observanc.e.
of Public. Schools Week. Your Committee is not however disposed to
be over sanguine with respect to the general'resulfbecause of early reports
of particularly 'successful observances; because there is always kept in·
mind the fact that the promptness and detail with which a Master makes
his report is indicative of the heed he has given to the suggestions 'of the
Committee, and of the Industry and intelligence that· is probably ·respon-'
sible for the success he has achieved. For instance, the very first report
received this year was from a Master who it appeared had inaugurated
his arrangements immediately upon receipt of the notice from the Grand
Master fixing the date for the observance; and whose committee included
a representative from each of the civic organizations in his community.
No detail had been overlooked; and they had even provided for transpor-.
tation to and from the meeting by arranging to have the school busses
run over their regular routes for the convenience of the people who did
'
not have cars of their own.
While all _the early reports indicate.d t~is year, as ,they h;t~e for.
several years past, that the latest observance' had been the ni6st sue-

147

cessful ever held the measure of that literally astounding success was not
fu!ly realized until all the reports were in; and in passing it may be
said that there were only ten Lodges in the entire jurisdiction that did
not report.
In this connection your Committee desires to express its appreciation
of the form in which a large number of Masters presented their reports.
Last year we called attention to the reports of two particular observances
that were not only extremely comprehensive but seemed to us to be models
as to form; and we also made mention of the fact that reports in similar
form had been received from several Lodges. This year there was a
noticeable increase in the number of Masters who had not confined their
reports to merely answering the questions on the blanks sent out but who
had a?1plified th.em. with de.tailed information of the work done by their
committees. This information was furnished as had been suggested on
.sheets of uniform size with the blank; and constituting a part thereof
were copies of all notices, announcements, invitations, programs and newspaper clippings all carefully indexed. Reference is again made to this
matter be_ca~se as we said last year it is in our opinion extremely significant. It indicates the probability that the attention and care with which
the report was pr~pared had been given to every detail of the arrangements ; and that this was responsible for the resulting success.
· Perhaps the most noteworthy fact in connection with our latest observance was the decided departure from its original form. The first
observance, it will be remembered, was confined to the public meetings
held th~oughout the state. The main feature of these meetings was the
speaker s address, and there were but few contributions to the program ·
b_y school children. For some years thereafter the public meetings continued to be the main, and in many instances the only feature of the
obse~vance with the pupils of the schools participating in the program.
~uring t?e !~st two or three years however there has been a decided trend
in the direction of an observance extending over the entire week with
the meetings as only incidental features. In many places visits to the
schools with practical demonstrations of the actual work being done·
constitute the dominant feature of the observance. These visits are of.
two. general classes. In one the visitor sees the school in operation either
during the regular school hours or at special evening sessions held for that .
purpose and has an opportunity to meet and talk with the principals and
te~c~ers. In the other,. a special program is provided. In some instances
t~1s is a school entert~inment in the auditorium with contributions by the
different classes, and in others there are demonstrations in special classes.
. The re~orts indic~te that these visits not only resulted in awakening
an. interest in the public meetings that were held, but served another, and
perhaps more valuable, purpose. In themselves they served to bring about
that close contact between the public and its schools which is one of the ·

149

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAXI:J LOD GE OF CALIFORXIA

primary purposes of Public Schools Week. Apparently they not only
proved extremely interesting to the visitors, but were greatly appreciated
by the teachers. The following quotation from a report from one of the
Lodges is illustrative of similar comments found in many, "The Principal
of one of the smaller schools said to one of our Committee that during
the entire time that he had been principal of that school he had never
before had a visit from a parent who had come only with the thought
of showing his interest in the work being done; but that that week he
had met and talked with twenty."
In evaluating the benefit of these visits we too frequently have in
mind only two groups ; one representing the school composed of the principals and classroom teachers, and the other representing the public composed in great part of the parents. There is however a third group. It
is composed of the school children. To them these visits mean as much as,
and perhaps more than, they do to either of the other groups. It gives
them pleasure of course, as it does everyone, to display their accomplishments ; and they take the same pride in it. This however is the least
of the good that is accomplished. It is made evident, perhaps for the first
time to some of them, that as school children they are objects of keen
interest and public attention. Because of this, and of the recognition and
appreciation of their accomplishments, they are encouraged to a renewed
effort that might not have been induced through mere school routine.
In passing it may be said that the parents of the children in attendance
were not the only visitors to the school. In more than one report mention
is made of a visit by one or more of the service clubs in the community;
and one report details a visit by a Rotary Club that instead of holding its
meeting during that week at the usual place had its luncheon served in
the High School by the Domestic Science class. It appears that so interesting did the members of the club find their visit that they invited
speakers from the school to address them the following week and explain
more fully the things they had seen on that occasion.
The wealth of the pupil programs as shown by the reports is simply
amazing. · While they were exceedingly varied in character, the central
thought of each was to illustrate some of the objectives of modern education, in meeting the homemaking, mercantile, agricultural and industrial
.needs of the community. It was something far different from the ordinary
"school exhibition." There were not · only demonstrations of the modern
methods by which the so-called fundamentals are taught, but the visitors
were given an opportunity to learn at first hand something of what is
being done in social studies, and through what are in some schools curricular, and in others extra-curricular, activities. Included in the latter
are, in addition of course to music and band and orchestra work, folk
dancing, dramatics, pageantry and supervised play. There were also of

course exhibits of every sort including the handiwork of students in the
shops and special classes; and an opportunity was given to see the boys
at work in the foundry, blacksmith, electric welding and machine shops
and girls busy in the sewing, millinery, and home economic classes. Incidentally the visitors saw in the shops not only boys but girls. A photograph appearing in one of the papers published in one of the larger cities
shows a girl engaged in work on a trash can with an oxy-acetelyne welding
torch; and there were on display a set of such cans and other campus
equipment that had been made by the students.
The exhibits to which we have just referred constitute one of the
most attractive and interesting features that can be provided for an observance. One Master reports that although the program provided for
the meeting was concluded at 9 :45 P. M., the majority of the extremely
large gathering were still in attendance, as midnight approached, viewing
the exhibits displayed in the lobby; a~d that he did not know how long
they would have remained if the Principal had not conveyed a hint that
it was time to go by dimming the lights.
The offer of a p_rize by one of the Lodges was mentioned some years
ago in our report as an original feature. This is now apparently becoming very general. Prizes are offered in contests. and competitions of
various sorts such as for the school or class having the greatest number
of visitors in proportion to its enrollment and for the best essays and
in other scholastic projects, including the old-fashioned spelling bee.
The award is made at the public meeting, or at the last of these if there
be more than one. It is particularly interesting to note that the donors of
these prizes are not only Lodges and Masters and Wardens' Associations, but ?Isa Posts of the American Legion, Woman's Clubs, Local Improvement and Parent-Teacher Associations, Service Clubs and other
civic organizations.
In this connection reference may be perhaps here made ta a competition which attracted considerable interest while in progress and the
result of which was given considerable newspaper publicity. As one of
the attractions of a meeting which was "crowded to the doors of the
auditorium of the High School" in which it was held there were two gold
watches offered as prizes to the pupils of the graduating class for the
best exhibition of good citizenship. One was provided by a Post of the
American Legion to be given to the boy, and the other by the Woman's
Community Club to the girl, who had best shown the qualities of good
citizenship during their high school careers. It developed that there was
an outstanding girl in the graduating class to whom was awarded the
prize offered by the Woman's Community Club; but no senior boy qualified for the citizenship award offered by the American Legion. This
fact was "played up" in the papers and was the occasion of considerable
comment not altogether favorable.

Public Schools Week there appeared every morning, commencing the
week before the date' set for the observance, and continuing until its
close' ' a two column "box" article with a standing head setting forth
th(! object of Public Schools Week. These columns carried not only ?ews
of the observance with the program of the week, but also educ~t1onal
items of general interest and re-prints of articles on education in the
modern school. There were also full reports of visits made by the writer
to e~ch of the local schools telling just what he had observed and giving
detailed information of the methods of instruction. Every morning after
th~ observance began there was published the nm:nber of visitors to each
school d~ring the preceding day. In addition to the m'.'-tter appearing in '.
the. ~pecial columns there were published communications that had been
invited with respect to the school system in general and the local schools
in ·partkul~r. This would certainly indicate that the ~pathy that once
existed in that community had been very effectually dispelled; and we
do riot think it is too much to claim that it is due in part at least to the
annual observance of Public Schools Week.

While we have· made reference to the newspaper publicity only as
an evidence of public interest, in passing it should be said that all the
radio stations were likewise very generous in alloting time to not only
the general committee, but as well to local committees in various com·
munities.
We have always had the earnest support of the leading school administrators, and the most prominent educators in the state have always
been ready and willing, frequently at a sacrifice of their own comfort and
convenience, to accept invitations to speak at our meetings; but never
before did the school people generally throughout the state, particularly in
the smaller communities, take such an active part.
As evidence of this there may be mentioned the action of the superintendent of one of our smaller counties. He sent out a circular letter to
all the teachers and school trustees in the county ~ailing their attention
to Public Schools Week and requesting that every school in the county
contribute to the exhibit of school work that was to be displayed in the
auditorium of the High School in which the public meeting was held·
and in this connection it is interesting to note that he suggested that fo;
the exhibit in penmanship instead of the teachers sending in the best
specimens of handwriting it would be far more effective and instructive
to have a series of papers of the same pupil or pupils extending over a
period of time thus indicating a steady improvement in their work. He
also fixed the day on which the Public meeting was to be held as the
date for the Trustee's Institute in order that every trustee might attend
the meeting and incidentally have an opportunity to compare the work
of his school with that of other schools in the county.
This will convey some idea of the support that was received from
the superintendents of schools everywhere, both of cities and of counties.
In on~ of the largest cities in the southern part of the state the City
Superintendent of Schools was in direct charge of all the school programs.
Amon~ othe~ extremely attractive events he arranged for an essay contest with prizes to be awarded to the winners at the last of the four
public meetings to be held during that week.
These are but two of innumerable instances that might be cited as
evidence of the splendid support received this year from the school people.
It was not confined to superintendents and school administrators but
the classroom teacher was likewise an important factor in the succe~s of
the observance. The increased interest of the school people was probably
due in great .part to th~ bulletin issued by State Superintendent Cooper and
to the circular letters issued by Superintendent L. E. Chenoweth, Presi·
dent of the Association of California Public School Superintendents, and
the late Mark Keppel, President of the California Teachers Association.
As has been repeatedly stated, it is not our policy to mention any
Lodge by name in these reports either with praise or otherwise; and this

153

year more than ever before would it be impracticable to do so. There
were scores of instances, probably more than a hundred, where the extraordinary success achieved really merits commendatory and detailed
specific reference; and to name all the Lodges entitled to credit would
seem to be calling the roll of the Lodges in this jurisdiction. It was .
particularly gratifying to your committee to note the care, good judgment
and zeal with which the arrangements were made and the many instances
of extraordinary ingenuity displayed in devising plans to attract the
attention of the people, and to awaken their interest. As a part of the
publicity for one of the meetings the committee secured the services of
an aviator who dropped tickets from his aeroplane as he circled the
city. Mention may also be made of a Master who evidently entertains
the belief that everybody wants to go where it is believed everybody is
not welcome. He caused it to be made known that no one would be admitted to the public meeting which had been extensively advertised unless
he had a ticket. He however had printed and distributed a sufficient number of tickets. to provide one for every man, woman and child in the
community-with a reserve supply at the door. There should be no
necessity of course for this sort of thing; but we must remember that
it is a condition and not a theory that confronts us. If the attendance
at any particular meeting is not as large as the Master believes it should
have been the reason he usually gives is that the public are not interested.
If it be indeed true that no very great interest in our annual observance
is evinced by the people of any community, it is not at all improbable that
it is because the right scheme has not yet been found to awaken that
interest. We do not mean by this to intimate that a sincere and earnest
effort has not been made; but only that either the right sort of program
was not provided or the proper method was not adopted to secure the
active cooperation of the civic organizations in the community; and it is
more than likely that the people do not yet understand that the observance
of Public Schools Week is a community affair, and not merely a Masonic
event to which the community is asked to give its support. In previous
reports we have called attention to specific instances of extraordinarily
successful observances following failures that were attributed to lack
of public interest. Again this year the reports furnish evidence of the
fact that it is largely a question of men and methods; and a striking
example is furnished by the experience of a Lodge in a small city in the
southern part of the state to which we purpose making a somewhat extended reference.
In 1925 the Master of this Lodge reported that the meeting was a
failure-there being only forty-one persons present including nineteen
children, and twelve adults who had a part in the program; and he attributed the result to his belief that the people were entirely satisfied
with their public schools and would not give up an evening to the sort

Exhibits in the business sections of the various communities in the
county with especially decorated windows drawing attention to Public
Schools Week. Exhibits to be from the Domestic Science, Manual Training or other departments and where desired by the merchant tied in with
his particular business.
Publication in the newspapus of articles from teachers and pupils
on work being done in the schools.
The publicity actually made use of included posters prepared by the
children carrying the slogan "Visit Your School" and displayed in store
windows; letters written by the pupils as part of their school work and
taken home to their parents ; articles contributed to the newspapers by
teachers and principals on educational topics in general and the local
schools in particular, and also radio announcements of the programs of
the week.
The schools were divided into four classes: (a) high schools with
not more than ten teachers, (b) high schools with eleven or more teachers,
(c) elementary schools with not more than ten teachers, and (d) elementary schools with eleven or more teachers; and a banner was awarded
to that school in each of these classes which had the greatest number of
visitors in proportion to the school enrollment. In the largest city of the
county every school participated with a total of 12,209 adult visitors during
the week; and in the county outside the city, sixty of the one hundred and
sixty schools participated. Of these, 27 reported an adult attendance
of 2838.
The observance to which we have just referred is but one of the
large number of those in which the Lodge this year occupied no different
position from that of the other organizations represented on the Committee of arrangements. The Lodge was, of course, the nucleus of the
movement and the Master was charged with the responsibility of arranging for a joint committee composed of representatives from the
various civic organizations in the community. This was usually accomplished with the assistance of the chief educational administrator; and
the Master's first conference was always with the school people. After
the Joint Committee was organized the Lodge acted through its representative or representatives ·on that Committee just as did each of the
other organizations. Incidentally it may be said that the best work was
done by the Master who made no attempt to obtain any particular prominence for himself or for his Lodge or the Fraternity. One Master
reporting with respect to the cooperation received from the Civic Organizations wrote, "Everyone of them thought that it was the most important
cog in the machinery." Of course this was just as it should be. It was
not our affair to which they were giving their support any more than it
was theirs receiving support from 11s. It was a real community undertaking
to the success of which each was loyally and jealously contributing.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

157

Naturally enthusiastic as we are with respect to the amazing success
of our latest observance we would not want to be understood as attempting
to convey the impression that it was in every instance as successful as
it was generally. There were some meetings where the attendance was
not what it should have been; and it is interesting to note the difference
in the nature of the reports made thereon. One Master frankly admitted
that he feared he had delayed too long in commencing his arrangements ;
another had unwittingly selected a date that too late was found to conflict
with that fixed for a more attractive affair; and a third believed that
he had "tied in" with the wrong organization, and stated that the same
mistake would not be made next year. It is exceedingly gratifying to
note that none of these Masters was apparently at all discouraged and
that all were looking forward to a real success next year.
Reports of a different nature came from three localities in each of
which there is more than one Lodge and where they have never held a
particularly successful observance. There they are still harboring the
belief that there is something peculiar to their particular communities
that can not be overcome ; and they are still complaining of "lack of
public interest." We are compelled to confess that it is difficult to understand why they have not been more successful because it would appear
from their reports that an earnest and conscientious effort has been made.
We do know however that "what man has done, man can do" ; and there
have been so many extraordinarily successful observances following repeated failures in the past (to one of which we have in this report called
particular attention) that we are firm and steadfast in the belief that
there is no city, town nor hamlet in California having a public school
and where there is located a Masonic Lodge in which a successful observance of Public Schools Week can not be held. The form of the
observance will vary of course. That which may be attended with great
success in one place may prove a dismal failure in another. In this connection it is to be noted that the meetings at which the lack of attendance
was deplored constituted the entire observance in those communities. There
was no attempt made to include any of those other features of a successful observance to which we have herein, and in previous reports,
referred; and the arrangements had not been made by a committee composed of representatives from the community. None of these meetings,
by the way, was a "frost" ; but the attendance was not as large as it
should have been.
Wherever the meeting constituted the entire observance, its success
was naturally measured by the attendance. We therefore feel justified
in again here repeating what we have heretofore said and what cannot
be too frequently reiterated with respect to this failure of attendance at
the public meetings :
It is of course desired that all our meetings shall be well attended; but
if that desire were everywhere accomplished it would be extraordinary.

159

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF .;ALIFORNIA

The · fact of the matter is that we are prone to expect too much. Those·
arranging the meetings work hard and earnestly and, -not unnaturally,' are. disappointed, and pethaps disheartened and ·dis'coura~ . if their
efforts do not result in attracting the attendance for which they hoped.,
They. lose sight of the fact that they are contending with a condition that
in itself· militates against• the· probability of a large attendance. Indeed
paradoxical as it tnay seem, there 'would be no need for holding meeting.s:
if they were as well attended as they should be. The lack of attendance
of which we complain is.. evidence of that apathy that brought about the·
condition that gave birth to the idea of Public Schools Week; and it is to
o'llercome and -dispel· that apathy that these meetings a-r e being held.
In one of our early reports ·we stated that it seemed impassible to~ '
determine whether it was in the urban or in the· rural communities that
the most successful observances were held. This continues· to be the case-. ·
In the strictly rural communities, particularly the smaller ones, the meet-·
ings .are still the main, and usually the only, features- of the observance ;i
and there they are crowded to the doors. This is however likewise the<
condition, or at least was this .year, in -the larger centers where the meetings ;
were .only incidents of the observance. In the largest cities the most sue- :
cessful meetings were apparently the ones held in schools irt those districts
which had an identity of their own. This was no doubt due to the fact
that there there exists a condition analogous to that of a small ·homo~
geneous community with a "community spirit" not apparent ·in other parts
of the same city. On the other hand, there was no small community.· in ·
the State where there appeared· to be a wider and more nearly general
interest than was exhibited in some large. cities and towns.
..
· From this we draw two deductions confirming a belief heretofore expressed. The first is that the success or. failure of any observance of '
Public Schools Week is not determined by the size of the community, its '
geographic location or the character of its population. The second is
that there is always everywhere a real genuine interest among the people'
in their schools; and thaf whether or not it ·is evidenced in the form we.desire -rests with us: In · other · words, colloqui~lly speaking, "it is the··
man behind the ..gun." ·
We !iave ·referred to our 'fat~st observance as ail asiouiiding success.
This ·was· not from a desire' to deal only in superlatives, but because it '
was literally true. Having in mind the nature of the movement in whieh
we are engaged, and the conditions under which it ' was undertaken and
is being carried on; our success has been simply amazing: Where a definite·
tangible result Is to be accomplished there is an appeal that is wanting
in ' the annual observance of Public Schools Week. The "i:nan in the
street" will hark to a cry for assistance in adopting or rejecting a con- 1
stitutional or :charter amendment, or in the election or defeat •of a candidate foT flublic office. That is not only something ~n which he has,.or ·

can be induced to take, a direct personal interest, but the result will be
very soon apparent. Soon after the issue is joined comes the decision,
and then it is all behind him. Furthermore, these are movements he can
evaluate. The value and importance of ours cannot be demonstrated or
even defined; they must rather be sensed. To appreciate its worth one
must have vision. With knowledge of its ultimate purpose he must pro·
ceed with faith in the accomplishment of intangible results. Our concern
is not alone with things and persons, but with ideas and ideals. The result
of what is being done today may never be known by those who are doing
it. To recruit an army engaged in such a crusade is not an easy task~
Each year, too, our leaders are changed. The Master who because of
the knowledge he has gained, and the experience he has had, could do
even better work than he did, turns the command over to his successor.
It is in the face of such difficulties that our success has been achieved.
That we have done, and are doing, good work in the cause so dear
to every Mason's heart is the testimony of those best qualified to know-the
school men of this State; and it is because of their belief that they so
gladly work with us. Furthermore, and we say this with some hesitation,
because of course it was not undertaken with any such idea, it has undoubtedly redounded to the credit of the Fraternity. In the reports of
meetings mention is frequently made of allusions by speakers who are not
Masons to the splendid work being done by the masonic Fraternity in
fostering Public Schools Week.
We have said that the ultimate responsibility is on the Masters of
our Lodges. To them, therefore, is primarily due the credit for the unprecedented success of the Ninth Annual Observance. Of course it goes
without saying that that success would not have been achieved without
the wonderful cooperation that was received from the school people and
from the individuals and civic and other organizations in their communities. For so much as came from those who are not of our own
number it is fitting that acknowledgment be made lest it might appear that
we are claiming for ourselves credit to which we are no_t entitled. To
voice our appreciation of their work is eminently proper; but any expression of gratitude therefor coming from us as Masons would seem
to imply a belief that the public schools are less their concern than they
are ours. Our hopes, desires, aspirations and obligations with respect to
the public school system are presumably likewise theirs. The Grand
Lodge of Masons in California is only the agency through which each
year there is provided this opportunity for a practical demonstration of
good citizenship. All good Americans should avail themselves of it,
becau.se as was said in an editorial published, during the recent observance,
in one of the most influential newspapers in the country, "Every good

American tries ceaselessly to improve and upbuild our public school
system-for that is the main highroad to an even higher and high.er
standard for every thing that is American."
All of which is fraternally submitted.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES MASONIC HOMES
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:

CHAS. ALBERT ADAMS,

ROBERT A. ODELL,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Herewith we present our annual report as Trustees of the Masonic
H:ornes of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1928, with a roster
of residents to and including August 31, and of funds received since the
end of fiscal year, to September 30.
As required by the Constitution, the Board met immediately after the
close of Grand Lodge in October, 1927, and organized as follows :
President, Charles M. Wollenberg, Senior Grand Warden;
Vic:e-President, James B. Gist, term expire!' 1931;
Samuel E. Burke, term expires 1928;
Chas. Albert Adams, term expires 1929;
Albert E . Boynton, term expires 1930;
Gustav A. Hutaff, Deputy Grand Master;
John Stewart Ross, Junior Grand Warden;
William P. Filmer, Treasurer ex-officio;
John Whicher, Secretary ex-officio.
The first report of the Trustees of what was known as the Widows
and Orphans Home was presented to Grand Lodge in 1892-thirty-six
years ago. Subsequent to that time the scheme of the Home was enlarged
to include Master Masons and mothers of Masons. The first building
erected for the care of those dependent upon the fraternity and who could
not be supported by the Lodges, was completed and dedicated by Grand
Master Thomas Flint Wednesday, October 12, 1898, and the first Lodge to
take advantage of the privilege of the Home was Pacific Lodge No. 136,
a member of which Lodge was admitted March 13, 1899, and died in 1907
at the ripe age of 81. The first widow admitted was from Silver Gate
Lodge No. 296, who arrived March 25, 1899, and lived in comfort until
she reached the age of 82, and passed to her eternal home. The first child
to become a resident of the Home was from King Solomon's Lodge No.
260, the date of admission being June 18, 1899. Since then 521 men, 295
women, 300 boys and 237 girls, (a total of 1353) have been cared for by
the Lodges at the Home, and at the present time (August 31) there are
259 aged residents at the Decoto Home and 183 children at Covina. Your
Trustees are also caring for 19 dependent men and women and 25 children
outside the Homes, at a monthly expense of $1,030.00.

Masonic Rights of Daughters
A number of the women residents at the Decoto Home are there by
virtue of the recently adopted policy of Grand Lodge to recognize adult
daughters ·of Masons as being entitled, as of right, to Masonic relief.
Within the past twelve months fou~ women were admitted whose moral
claims to recognition were of questionable value. All of them had been
married to men of their own choosing and not members of our Fraternity.
Soine of them, indeed, had never been dependent upon a Masonic father.
One was born in .1860, and her father died in 1861. In the course of time
she grew up and married a non-Mason; her husband died, and she ·again
married a man who was not a Mason.
"The poor shall never cease out of the land," and as citizens we ·all
have a duty to perform in caring for the distress of those of our fellowmortals who, because of sickness and poverty are unable to maintain
themselves. As Masons, we have an additional and particular obligation
to aid worthy distressed Master Masons, their widows and orphans. 'That
is as far as our Masonic duty extends. There ·is a growing tendency fo
add to our basic law, obligations not contemplated by the Masonic Institution, and while admitting our civic obligations to all poor and distress~d
persons, without regard to creed, color or fraternal affi!iation; we respectfully submit to Grand ·Lodge whether we as Masons should not reser\ie
our family charities to those contemplated' by ancient Masonic law and
custom.
The three principal tenets of Freemasonry are Brotherly Love, Relief,
and Truth, and these virtues have been defined by likening Brotherly LOve

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

164

165

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

as the column of Strength, which binds our members as one family in the
bonds of fraternal affection. Truth is called the column of Wisdom, and
Relief the column of Beauty, "whose ornaments, more precious than the
lilies and pomegranates that adorned the pillars of the porch of King
Solomon's temple, are the widow's tear of joy and the orphan's prayer of
gratitude."
For many years i~ was the settled policy of the Grand Lodge of
California that our Masonic obligations adhere to the ritual. Grand Master Tinnin (Proc. 1886, p. 486) was asked this question:
\
"Can a Master Mason's daughter, after her marriage, reinstate her
claims (on our Fraternity) by virtue of being the daughter of a Master
Mason?"
"Answer: No. When she married she severed her rights in the Order
by and through her father, and thence can only retain her rights therein
by and through her husband."
Past Grand Master Belcher one of our outstanding authorities on
Masoni.c jurisprudence, laid dow~ the Masonic law (Proc. 1893, p. 220) to
be that "the daughter of a Master Mason, whether of tender years, or
if unmarried, of mature years, is a member of his family, and is, if in
need, entitled to ask for and receive assistance from Masons wherever she
may be."
Our settled law with regard to widows is that if the widow of a
Master Mason remarries to one who is not a member of our Fraternity,
she is not thereafter entitled to Masonic consideration. And that is the
law in every jurisdiction in the world.
We ask your thoughtful consideration of this question of the rights
. of adult daughters, and recommend that you give expression, at this annual
communication, to the following statement of policy :
That the daughter of a Master Mason, after marriage to one not a
member of our Fraternity, is not entitled, as of right, to Masonic relief.
Building at Decoto
In our annual report last year, it was stated that the funds of the
Homes had been so conserved that the Trustees felt they were justified in
commencing much needed new dormitories at the Decoto Home, plans
for which were exhibited to the brethren present at Grand Lodge. We are
- now pleased to report that a new steel and brick dormitory, immediately
adjoining the southerly side of the old administration building, is nearly
completed and will be ready for occupancy this winter. It is four stories
high, . with basement for the use of Lodges and brethren who_~i.sit the
Home in large numbers, equipped with kitchen and other fac1hbes for
. picnic banquets. The cost of this dormitory, including neces~ary road
work and excluding furnishings, will be $250,000. When fimshed, the

married couples now domiciled in the administration .building · will be
housed there, and serious consideration will then be given to the problem
of repairing or razing the old building. That structure is now more
than thirty years old, and because of_ its bad physical condition, due in
part to the seismic disturbance in 1906, it must be given a general overhauling, or be torn down and replaced by a steel frame structure.
Cemetery at Decoto
Your Trustees have sold to the Citizens Water Company of Niles
a strip of land twenty feet wide with additional space for a reservoir, in
all containing .65 of an acre, with the assurance that water mains will be
extended to the Home cemetrry. When this work is completed, we expect
to have water in ample supply to keep the cemetery grounds in presentable
condition.
Roads at Decot o
We were fortunate in securing the services-which were donated-of
Col. John H. Skeggs, district engineer of the State Highway Commission,
to advise the Trustees with respect to the construction of permanent roads
through the grounds, and to make a survey and recommendations. The
survey has been completed, and the roadways will soon be repaired and
constructed accordingly.
Improvements at Covina
For the better protection of the Home against the hazard of fire, we
have installed 2y,( gallon soda and acid fire extinguishers of approved
design, and two 40-gallon fire extinguishers mounted on wheels.
The heating p\ant at the Covina Home, is now inadequate to supply
the buildings which have been erected since the original installation, and
we are now remodeling the plant, substituting new and larger boilers for
those previously in use, extending the chimney up 25 feet, moving the
hot water tank and heater to a new position and installing a steam heating
element in the tank; insulating the boilers and piping, and installing an
automatically-controlled unit oil burner. T his needed work will be completed this month.
Student Loan Fund
This Fund is being added to by friends of the ch ildren, and one boy
and five girls are now participating in its benefits. One girl is commencing
her third year at Pomona College, her school record continuing to be
good. During the vacation period she was gainfully employed and is
happier for the experience. One girl is in her third year at the University
of California and gives every evidence that she is making the best of her
opportunities. One girl is attending the State T eachers College at San
Jose. One girl is attending the training school for nurses at the Children's
Hospital, San Francisco, and one at Santa Barbara hospital training school

has displayed marked ability as a cartoonist has been awarded, by the
Trustees, a scholarship in a school of drawing.

Christmas Dinner at Covina-and Donor
Mr. John F. Taylor of Pasadena, a wealthy retired capitalist, who
had previously donated a valuable quartz lamp to the hospital, visited the

168

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Home a few days before Christmas and indicated that he would like to
furnish the Christmas dinner. He left a check for one hundred dollars
£6r this purpose, and requested that a large letter G should be a part of
the dining room decoration on that occasion, and that the Lord's prayer
be recited by the children as "grace before meat." All this was done.
Summer Employment for Children
Fourteen of the older girls were gainfully employed during the school
vacation, working as helpers for mothers, care of children, and general
house work. Each home into which a · girl was placed was personally
inspected and approved by the Superintendent before placement was permitted. The total wages earned by these girls was more than five hundred
dollars a month. The older boys did not make as good a showing at summer employment, only five of them securing employment. However, credit
should be given to five other boys who remained at the Home for necessary care there while the children were enjoying camp life at Balboa. In
addition to these employments, many of the older children at the summer
camp were employed at odd jobs at Balboa and Newport. Thirty-five
children spent their vacations with relatives.
We respectfully request that the per capita tax for maintenance for
the year ending July 31, 1929, be fixed at twenty-five cents.

C. M. WOLLENBERG, President,

J. B. GrsT, Vice-President,

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
To the B oard of Trnstees :·
I hereby present for your consideration the following report for the
year ending August 31, 1928.
The past year has been an important one, as new and necessary improvements are being made to enlarge the usefulness of the benevolent
work carried on here by the Fraternity.
The new building, now under construction, when completed and furnished, will meet the requirements of the Lodges in this jurisdiction for
some time to come, besides adding materially to the comfort of the members of the Home.
There are now at the Home 259 residents, 141 men and 118 women.
During the year there have been 70 persons admitted, 44 men and 26
women. There have been 33 deaths and 2 departures.
The general health of the Home has been good, with the exception
of those who are infirm and feeble, owing to advancing years.
The facilities afforded by our hospital department enables our physician and nurses to give every care and attention to those who are ill. Day
and night nurses are in constant attendance. There are at the present time
36 members of the family being cared for in the hospital.
All the members of the Home are encouraged to render some service
in keeping with their strength and in their leisure hours to interest themselves in healthful and wholesome diversions for their general well-being.
A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of the
Home by their services in the carpenter and paint shops, the care of the
garage, mail, passenger and expresij service, kitchen, pantry, vegetable
room, laundry, store-room, clerical work, attending phone .calls, care of
flower beds, lawns and light work in a general way.
The ladies of the Home attend to the making, marking and mending
of .linen, sheets, pillow slips, table cloths, etc. They also assist in preparing
fruit and vegetables, work in the kitchen and dining rooms and take care
of their rooms, halls, and general household duties.
There has been no change in the management of the farm. The
greater part of the hill ranch has, as in the past, been leased either on
shares or cash rental. Our share of the hay crop has been more than
sufficient for the needs of the farm department, the surplus being sold in
the local market. The orchards have supplied plenty of fruit for table
use, the surplus being sent to the drier and stored for future use. The
garden has furnished a variety of vegetables and greens. The chicken
ranch has supplied all eggs for table use ; all over and above our needs
have been sold in the San Francisco market. There seems to be no

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

182

183

PROCEEDINGS 01'' THE

decrease in the supply of water from our deep well pump. Our reservoirs
are full at all times and equal to all demands made upon ·them for household, lawns and irrigating purposes.
Library: Our library continues to grow, there are now about 5,600
volumes on the shelves of the main library and branches located in the
club rooms and hospital department. The Masonic Hill branch .of the
Alameda County Free Library is well patronized and enables our family
to obtain many of the latest books and an opportunity for special ones.
In addition we are the recipients, through members of the Fraternity, of
daily papers, magazines and periodicals, which are placed on the tables
of the library, men's club rooms and ladies reading rooms.
Social Life: Many .splendid programs md stage plays have been
provided during the year by visiting Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters and
friends for the entertainment of the members of the Home. The evening
gatherings often close with dancing. Every Monday. evening the members
of the Home enjoy a moving picture entertainment. During the winter
months a social is given every Tuesday evening at which time a program
of vocal and instrumental music, readings, recitations, community singing,
cards, dancing, stage sketches, etc., is given. These programs are made
up entirely by the members of the Home. Choir practice every Friday
evening. The usual services are held every Sunday afternoon, after which
a few musical numbers · are given by the Home orchestra. All these
meetings are well attended.
A reading class for the blind meets daily in the men's library. At that
time the daily papers are read to them by one of the ladies of the Home.
A number of the members of the family have radio sets in their
rooms. The privilege is specially appreciated by those who are blind, and
those who are confined in their rooms in the hospital department.
Arrangements have been made whereby the me.mbers of the. family, a
few at a time, can make trips to Oakland and San Francisco and nearby
towns. Regular trips are made, by auto, each week on Tuesday, Wednesday
and Thursday. Also occasional visits to nearby Lodges and Eastern Star
Chapters.
Grand Master Will H. Fischer and officers of the Grand Lodge have
made a number of visits to the Home during the year and a large number
.of brethren from various Lodges have spent many pleasant hours with us.
I wish to express my appreciation of the services rendered by the
employees throughout the year, and also my gratitude to the Board of
T_rustees f~r the counsel and support they have at all times given me.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

Report of Superintendent, Covina

To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
The number of children at present enrolled in the H ome is 183; a
year ago the enrollment was 159; the increased membership in the Home
fills it approximately to the capacity of its present accommodation. Of
those now in the Home 75 per cent are half-orphans, 8 per cent full
orphans, while 17 per cent have both parents living. In most of these latter
cases one or both of the parents is completely disabled, so as to be incapable
of supporting the child. In 14 per cent of the cases some payment is made
by parent or relatives toward the maintenance of the child in the Home;
the total amount of such payments during the past year has been $4,485.00.
Of the 183 children now enrolled in the Home, 8 are under school
age, 106 are attending grammar school, while 69 attend high school or are
receiving vocational training.
Health
Health condit ions in the Home during the past year have been excellent. No epidemic has occurred, with the exception of a small number
of mild cases of measles. About thirty children have been operated upon
for the remo'val of tonsils.
Dental care has been placed upon a regular and systematic basis, insuring that every child will have needed dental work performed regularly.
Careful attention is given to providing our children with an abundance
of good food, properly selected for their needs, and well ~ooked. An in_iportant factor in our dietary is a plentiful supply of milk, produced m
our own dairy, fresh eggs from our own poultry plant, and vegetables
from our own garden. The children have, also, plenty of oranges from
our own trees.
It is gratifying to note that children coming to us almost invariably,
after a few months, show a marked improvement in physical vigor and
general health.
An important factor in the promotion of the physical well-being of
our ·children is the summer camp at Balboa. Two months are spent there
with plenty of sunshine and good exercise. It is a striking fact that the
amount of illness among our children during the camp at Balboa is almost
negligible.
Housemothers
The immediate task of dealing with our children and regulating the
many concerns of their young lives falls upon the shoulders of six housemothers and one male supervisor. We are fortunate in having had during
the past 'year only two changes in the personnel of this part of our staff.
These people are working in a spir.it of fine devotion, and are giving their

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

best efforts to their important and responsible work. Their hours are
long and their work makes heavy demands upon their physical arid
nervous energy.
Morale and Behavior
The morale and general behavior of our large family is most excellent. Our efforts to secure responsible and thoughtful conduct on the
part of our older boys and girls have in general been met with the most
gratifying response. "Boys will be boys,'' is an old saying which we must
keep in mind in making allowance for youthful shortcomings; but it is
al~o true, as one wise trainer of youth has recently remarked, that "boys
will be men" at no distant time, and with each succeeding year of the
child's development he must be brought further ·on the road toward
adulthood.
A student of child life recently said: "There are 8,760 hours in a
year; the average boy spends 3,650 in bed, 1,000 hours in school 600 hours
in eating, 300 hours in dressing, and 100 hours at church; the' remaining
3,110 hours will determine his life and character." Less than twelve per
cent of the child's time is spent in school. Our work in the Home at
Covina is to care properly for the child during the eighty-eight per cent
of his time when he is not in school.
.
Use of Money
During the past year we have been developing a system of placing
money-earning opportunities before our older children and in turn requiring them to buy certain of their necessities, as well' as their luxuries.
We believe that this practical experience in the earning and handling of
money is of great value in preparing them to manage their own affairs
in the world in which they must shortly take their places. If the boy or
girl who is not industrious, thrifty, or careful gets along in the Home
as comfortably as the one who possesses those qualities, he is likely to
develop an attitude of wastefulness and inappreciation for what is being
done for him.
In our Domestic Science cottage, where our high school girls live
four at a time, we have recently adopted a plan which is producing good
results. These girls are given a stated weekly allowance in cash, with which
they must do their own marketing and provide themselves with food stuffs.
They go into the Covina market like any housewife and shop around and
get the most they can for their money. Their menus must be submitted as
evidence that they are securing a well-balanced diet.
Are the Children Happy?
. The question is often asked: "Are the children in the Home happy?"
This is indeed a natural question, in view of the fact that their very
presence in the Home implies a background of misfortune, if not of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

205

tragedy. Yet despite the fact that they are deprived of some things which
Nature intended to be every child's inheritance, there can be no doubt
that most of them are leading happy lives in the Home. Their characteristic attitudes are free, spontaneous, and unsuppressed. As they grow
older they come to look upon the Home with feelings of pride and affection. If a visitor inadvertently refers to the Home as an "orphanage,"
they feel that he is ill-informed, that he has failed to catch the spirit of
the place.
Care is taken to build up their self-respect, to make them feel that
they are not objects of charity but rather wards of Masonry. They are
imbued with the idea that if they but make good use of their opportunities and do their best, they are under no more obligation than that of
any child to his parents.
Their recreational life is well provided for. Weekly picture shows
are furnished, through the good offices of the Los Angeles Masters' and
Wardens' Association. A vigorous and active Boy Scout organization is
maintained, to which Brother William Hoogendyk of Covina devotes
much time and effort. Substantial additions have recently been made to
the playground equipment. The Home is well represented on the athletic
teams of the Covina high school.
Frequent visitations by Masonic organizations, particularly those in
and around Los Angeles, constantly impress the children with the loving
care and solicitude of Masonry toward them. These organizations and
individual Masons, too numerous to mention, have performed acts of
helpfulness, indicating their warm and friendly interest in our boys and
girls.
Auditorium and Swimming Pool Needed
Our chief needs in the way of plant equipment are an auditorium and
a swimming pool. The only place which we have at present for assembling
the children for picture shows and other entertainments is a room in the
basement of the main building, in which the view is much obstructed by
large piers and in which the ventilation is poor. The present swimming
pool is much too small, and is not provided with any means of filtering or
disinfecting the water.
Vocational Training
Owing to the special circumstances which place them as wards in the
Home, most of our children will be called upon to be self-sustaining at an
early age. For this reason we are making a special effort to accelerate
their decis\on in the matter of vocational choice. We regard it as desirable
that the boys, especially, shall have chosen a vocation by the time they
finish the second year of high sch_o~I, and that they spend the last two
years of the high school period in some specific training by which they
may later earn their living. Inasmuch as vocational training opportunities

PROCEEDINGS OF '.CHE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNlA

are not available at Covina, this plan involves their removal to Los Angeles
or elsewhere during the latter part of the time they are under our charge.
For such boys and girls we find suitable boarding homes from which they
may conveniently reach the shop or school where their training is received.
Our responsibility toward our wards should continue until they have
become firmly established in employment in which they can succeed. To
do less than this is to risk losing the result of all our years of work with
any given child.

Private Placement
There are some children who do not get on well and cannot make
the best·development as members of a large group such as we have in the
Home. This will always be the case, no matter how well ordered the Home
may be or how well it may be adapted to the needs of the average child.
The best modern practice in the care of dependent children indicates that
such cases should be placed in private boarding homes, with a quieter
atmosphere and a more highly individualized treatment than is possible
in the large institutional group. By this method we have obtained excellent results in some cases.
Where the boarding home is used it should be thoroughly investigated
before use, and care should be taken to see that it is suited to the special
needs of the child. Once the child is placed therein, we should maintain
careful supervision so as to make certain that he is being well treated and
that he is making satisfactory progress.
.
Respectfully submitted,
J.M. DOWNEN, Superintendent.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

To theM:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns has pleasure in reporting that all the
Lodges of the jurisdiction have filed their a~nual returns and the requisite
dues have been paid.
The reports show that fewer candidates have been raised than in the
preceding year. This · should not give any cause for worry. It is a
reflection of business conditions. Even then there has been a net gain in
membership for the year of five thousand lacking seven.
We ought always t~ remember that it is the quality of the membership
that makes the strength, or the weakness, of our fraternity, and not the
mere matter of nu~bers. It is for the Lodges to see to it that a high
standard of membership is maintained and there will be no cause for
anxiety.
The amounts for dues for which the Lodges of the jurisdiction were
indebted for the year ending July 31, 1928, together with the Lodges
under dispensation for the term ending September 30, 1928, all of which
have been paid.

To the M.· .w.· .Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Accounts, whose duty it is to approve all Grand
Lodge expenses for the year, pursuant to Constitutional requirements,
beg leave to report that we have called at the office of the Grand Secretary on the last Saturday of each month and audited all bills, claims and
demands against the Grand Lodge as were received by the Grand
Secretary.
In checking over bills of the various Committees which receive appropriations from this Grand Lodge, we notice that the same do not require
the approval of this Committee, and in line with business efficiency we
believe that it would be to the best interest of the Grand Lodge that all
purchases should be made through the Grand Secretary's office, and paid
in the same manner as prescribed in the Constitution.
PAUL NATHAN,

DEFINITION OF "ORPHAN"
Brother C. 0. Hamilton presented the following, which
was referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolved, that the word "orphan" wherever used in the Constitution
or in any Regulation, shall hereafter be deemed to mean the son or
daughter under the age of twenty-one years of a deceased Master Mason;
and no man or woman over the age of twenty-one years shall be entitled
to relief as a matter of right as the son or daughter of a Master Mason.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE TO PERPETUATE THE
MEMORY OF GEORGE WASHINGTON
To the M: .W." .Grand Lodge of California:
At the last session of the Grand Lodge, held in October, 1927, a
resolution was introduced and unanimously adopted, providing for the
appointment of a committee to devise ways and means for the purpose of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

best commemorating the memory of our illustrious and Worshipful
Brother, General George Washington, in suitable memorial or monument.
Your committee begs leave to report that subsequent developments
during the recess of the Grand Lodge indicate a strong probability that a
most appropriate and inspirational memorial can be provided for in the
new federal building to be erected by the United States Government in the
. .Civic Center at San Francisco, construction of which will begin immediately upon transfer of the proposed site to the Government.
Your committee desires at this time to report progress and requests
that further action be held in abeyance pending further developments.
HARRY L. TODD,
ALBERT E. BOYNTON,
G. A. HUTAFF,

their views. A building project seems to excite a commendable enthusiasm
which is not always translated into wise action. The brethren who sponsor
a building operation do not always support the project until the costs are
finally liquidated. A Lodge investing its funds in an over-ambitious
temple project, or in a building operation that is not prudently financed,
usually finds its funds crystallized in a long-time, debt-ridden investment,
and the usefulness and financial ability of the Lodge is impaired, if not
destroyed. Grand Lodge encourages the ownership, by the Lodges, of
the property they occupy, and looks with pride and approbation upon all
well-considered, businesslike undertakings of this character. But Grand
Lodge deprecates improvident and unwise action in these matters on the
part of _its subordinate Lbdges. If a Lodge is plunged into debt, or falls
into distress, or meets with disaster by reason of its building operations,
it causes a reflection, not only upon the Lodge and its membership, but
upon Grand Lodge and Masonry in general. The financial distress may be
more poignant to the Lodge than to Grand Lodge, but its influence and
effect is felt far beyond the limits of the subordinate Lodge. Grand
Lodge cannot escape a greater or less responsibility for these unwise
expenditures, because ultimately all the assets and property of a Lodge
belong to Grand Lodge, and a distressed Lodge is prone to turn to Grand
Lodge for advice and help, even if it does not ask for financial assistance.
Under such circumstances it seems to your Committee that it would be
expedient and proper for Grand Lodge to have some part in the preliminary plans and financial arrangements· of a subordinate Lodge which
contemplates investing its funds in a temple project, rather than to wait
for a consideration of the matter until the Lodge is in difficulty. We
believe that the subordinate Lodges would welcome the impartial and
independent advice and assistance of this Grand Lodge before it becomes
involved in a building enterprise and its funds are invested in a permanent
and frozen form. Moreover, we believe that Grand Lodge should not '
permit funds of a subordinate to be invested in the securities of a building
corporation until after a proper analysis and check of the proposed plan
has been made by or on behalf of Grand Lodge. Legislation is being
proposed requiring subordinate Lodges to submit the plans and proposed
final arrangements of future building projects to a Committee of this
Grand Lodge and prohibiting investments of Lodge funds to be made in
such enterprises until such Committee has approved the plans and proposed
financing. Your Committee recommends the adoption of such legislation.

246

Committee.

The report was adopted and the committee continued.

INVESTMENTS BY LODGES IN MASONIC BUILDING PROJECTS
Past Grand Master Hervey, for the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, presented the following report,
which was adopted and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee has carefully considered the recommendations made
by the Grand Master and the suggestions of the Finance Committee with
respect to the investment, by Lodges, in stock, bonds, debentures and
other securities of Masonic building corporations, and is in entire accord
with the opinion of the Grand Master on this subject.
The Lodges should enjoy a large degree of liberty with respect to
the conduct and management of Lodge affairs, and Grand Lodge is careful
to avoid making undue restrictions on the activities of its subordinate
Lodges. In pursuance of this policy, no legislation has ever been enacted
to control the investments of subordinate Lodges, and. they have had the
power to invest their funds in Masonic building enterprises, and otherwise,
as to each Lodge seemed best. The result has not been satisfactory.
Many Lodges have become seriously involved by reason of ·unwise and
imprudent investments of their funds in corporations organized to build

PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE TEN-MILE LAW
The master of Orange Grove Lodge, No. 293, presented
the following, which was referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence :
At the 1926 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, Section 82A
was adopted providing for a concurring jurisdiction of all Lodges within
ten miles. This section and its practical application has been a source of
great irritation and embarrassment to many of the smaller Lodges in the
rural districts of the State. While this section may be working satisfactorily in cities, it is not working out in the less populous sections ;
therefore, be it

Resolved, that Section 82A be repealed.

the by-laws of Lodges, and with the exception of a few minor corrections,

To the M. ·. W. ·.Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Secretary's report discloses two Lodges under dispensation
that were held over from our previous Masonic year. Eight others have
petitioned for dispensations during the year, ~king ten in all for consideration by your Committee on Charters. With these ten, Grand Lodge
will have issued charters to 156 Lodges during the past seven years, or a
yearly average of 22 new Lodges. This yearly average has not been
maintained during the year 1927, nor our present year, although in those
two years our membership rolls have increased by 11,890 Master Masons
(net gain 1927, 6,897; net gain this year, 4,993). The Lodges already
constituted seem to be handling the load very ably.
It is our duty, as a Committee on Charters, the better to protect this
Grand Lodge, to be convinced in our minds that the Lodge under the
probation (which we call a Dispensation) is doing good Masonic work in
a fair amount and with inward harmony, with the assurance that the
organizing members are respected and of high standing in the communit)'.
where the new Masonic family is to have its home; the Constitution
requires (Section 75) an examination of the work and proceedings. To
some degree the Committee may be said to have the resp<2nsibility of the
careful Mason who knows that it is his personal Masonic duty, when
asked to sign a petition for membership in our Institution, to scr.utinize
the conduct and learn the reputation of the man who asks for his signature
in order to obtain the right to enter our doors. Our positions are similar,
but the careful Mason must be even more careful than we are.
The Chairman has had the high privilege of serving on this Committee for three consecutive years. During that time the personnel of the
body of the Committee on Charters has changed; appointments have been
given by the Grand Masters and then substitutions have had to be made
at the following Communications, due to absences that were unavoidable.
One instance of an absence that will be permanent, fills our hearts
with grief. The Committee as appointed by Most Worshipful Will H.

Fischer, at the time of his installation on the last day of the Communication of Grand Lodge one year ago, included the name of a beloved brother
who is no longer here, Thomas Ingram of Grass Valley. A member of
many standing committees of this Grand Lodge in years gone by, Inspector
of his Masonic District for nine years, Senior Grand Steward two years
ago, this excellent brother is deeply missed today.
Conceding that the earnest Mason will not lightly lend his name to
anyone not deserving of our privileges; will not willingly ever contribute to
the placing of an ugly or defective stone in the great edifice we call Free
Masonry-with that feeling must the brother, unknown to us, who many
years ago signed the petition of Tom Ingram, now be able to review with
great pride, the Masonic record he built so well. Genial, kindly, a good
neighbor, following openly and without false shame or restraint the daily
practice of manly affection for Masons of his Lodge and his district and
his Grand Lodge ; a willing worker who sought no reward for his work;
Brother Ingram was one of those men who make very foundation stones
of an Institution of morality like ours. Good deeds and kindly acts were
his. He was friendly and he knew nothing of envy. He was a true
Mason.
In the name chosen by the second of the two Lodges under dispensation, held over for this year's Communication, we find a laudable attempt
to honor a revolutionary leader who was one of George Washington's
Masonic generals. Henry Knox was born in 1750 and died in 1806. He
was an American patriot, prominent in the Colonial militia ; fought at
Bunker Hill and at Monmouth and at Yorktown; at the age of 34 he
became major-general and senior officer of the United States Army ; and
the following year became our first Secretary of War.
The dispensation petitioners inadvertently asked for the name
Henry T-V. Knox Lodge. The "W" is an error; the General had no middle
name or initial. In asking for a charter, the petition requests that this
be issued as "Henry Knox Lodge." This correction is proper and should
be made; the Constitution (Section 75) · permits it and we shall so
recommend.
A Lodge cannot be named for any living person (Constitution, Section 73). Another laudable attempt, intended to honoi: the name of a
highly regarded California Mason, is found in the formation of John P.
Jarman Lodge at San Jose. Brother Jarman died in May of 1921. That
was a year in which this Grand Lodge lost by death three of its Inspecto;s: Brother Jarman, Brother Granville D. Warren and Brothe.r
Edmund E. Knepper.
Brother John P. Jarman was well known to members who have been
attending Grand Lodge for a number of years ; in many places he is
referred to in the Proceedings of 1921. The Grand Lecturer's report
(page 470) mentions our recent loss; the address of M.".W.".Grand

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND LECTUREWS
REPORT
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to which was referred for consideration the annual
report of the Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer, makes the following
report:
The report of the Grand Lecturer is characterized by the modesty
which is typical of the present holder of that important office. I t presents
in simple form his observations resulting from the performance of his
duty in visiting every single district in this extensive and diversified
jurisdiction. Only one who is a lover of the fraternity, who constantly
cherishes the utmost faith in its principles and purposes, and who has
made the very atmosphere of Masonry the dominant thing in his life,
can perform so ably and efficiently the duties that devolve upon him.
We are pleased to note from the report that the conferring of degrees
is not occupying an unreasonable part of the time of the Lodges, and that
while the ritualistic work of the officers is of a standard befitting the
dignity and beauty of our Masonic endeavors, sufficient time is now
found earnestly and sincerely to engage in important educational work.
Through it Lodges are being stimulated to greater effort and, we believe,
with much value and profit to the individual members. Through the cooperation of the Educational Committee with the various Lodges and by
reason of the program material which is being furnished, there has
resulted practically in all of the constituent Lodges of our jurisdiction a
happy combination of ritual and general educational effort. It is perhaps
too early, as yet, to evaluate what is being done, but surely much good is
resulting.
The Grand Lecturer vividly points out the care that should be exercised by the Lodges in the reception of petitions, and well may we repeat
his epigram "that the character and efficiency of Free Masonry is determined by the character and efficiency of the individual Master Mason."
We do welcome the admission to the fraternity of good men and true,
but we must recognize the fact that merely having the reputation of being
a good fellow is not the open sesame to our institution. The time-honored,
exacting standards of admission which have kept Masonry in its respected
position during the years demand the same and even greater attention to
those who now would enter our portals. The suggestion by the Grand
Lecturer of a special committee appointed by the Master, whose duty it is
to confer with the petitioner, contains much of value and should be carefully considered by the Masters, especially in those Lodges where some
difficulty is incurred in procuring the proper investigating committees.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

253

Such a special committee allows a close personal observation of the
petitioner and often discovers and corrects erroneous impressions held by
him. This practice, which has been in operation in many of the L odges, has
resulted in fewer rejections at the ballot, thus preserving a degree of
harmony which ballot rejection too often disrupts.
With regret we note the passing of two of our beloved Inspectors of
Grand Lodge-Brother Dr. Clarence A. Tillotson and Brother Ernest
Henry Verble-both brethren well known to Grand Lodge, beloved by
all with whom they came in contact, upstanding men in their several
communities, and ardent, sincere and enthusiastic in their Masonry. Grand
Lodge will pay proper tribute to their memories.
There is a tinge of sadness in the Grand Lecturer's report concerning
the condition of several Lodges. These are situated in localities which
were populous in the rough and ready pioneer days of the discovery of
gold, teeming with life and industry, but now being numbered among the
ghost cities of the West. For sentimental reasons some of the brethren
hold to their Mother Lodge and kindly brethren hesitate to break that
sentimental tie. We feel satisfied that some form of relief will be found
by our leaders for these brethren and these Lodges, which will take care
of their present plight.
We congratulate the Grand Lecturer on his twenty-one years of
untiring service in behalf of the Craft, and we wish for him in the succeeding years that measure of success which he would wish fo r himself,
the opportunity fo r still greater service to the fraternity.

C. S. BALDWIN,
WM.

s. THOMPSON,

ARTHUR J OEL,

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred Trial Record
No. 572, from Progressive Lodge No. 578, F. & A. M., beg leave to report
as follows :
·

•

The record (page D) discloses that the charge of unmasonic conduct,
with three specifications, was preferred by the Junior Warden of Progressive Lodge, at the direction of the Master of said Lodge, and that
the same Master who had directed the Junior Warden. to prefer the
charge, presided at the trial. This procedure is in plain and express
violation of Sections 197 and 202 of our Constitution, and of Decision
No. 5 of Grand Master Jones, as approved by Grand Lodge in 1927 (Proceedings, Vol. 40, pp. 394-586); it is an invasion of the Constitutional
right of the accused to a fair and impartial trial before an unprejudiced
and unbiased tribunal, and for this reason, amongst others, the finding of
guilty will have to be set aside and the case remanded for a new trial.
The record shows that the impartiality and even-handed justice which
this Grand Lodge demands of all tribunals working under its authorization, were conspicuous by their absence. The Senior Warden was present
as "adviser to the . \Vorshipful Master," a position not warranted by our
law, although the Senior Warden in this case acted as chief prosecutor,
in addition to being the Master's advisor as aforesaid. Thus we have
the prosecutor advising the Judge how to rule. The Junior Warden who
had preferred the charges, also acted as a prosecutor; so did the Secretary, who was not busy because a shorthand reporter was taking down
the evidence ; and the Master asked many questions that had better been
left unasked. Such conduct is thoroughly reprehensihle and must not
occur on the retrial of this case.
The record also shows that the Lodge voted to have seven Trial
Commissioners and then elected nine, eight of whom acted.
The sessions. of the Trial Commission were held on Sundays, in
defiance of Section 78 of our Constitution, which says that no meeting
shall be held on Sunday, except for funeral purposes. (Decision 3S8,
Proceedings 1923, pp. 461-707.)
The record also shows that, although the accused lived in Los Angeles,
in which city the trial Lodge was located, the Secretary forwarded the
summons to the accused by registered mail, instead of serving it on him
personally, or leaving it at his ordinary residence or place of business, as
provided in Section 199 of our Constitution.
The fact that this error was cured by the appearance of the accused,
does not excuse the negligence of the Lodge Secretary, who is not shown
to have made the slightest effort to obey the plain letter of the law.

For the foregoing reasons, amongst others, we offer the following
resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved, that the judgment of the Trial Commission herein be and
· the same is hereby reversed, and the cause remanded for a new trial.
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred Trial Record
No. 578, from Oak Grove Lodge No. 215, F. & A. M., beg leave . to
report as follows:
The accused, upon conviction and imprisonment for the felony of
grand theft, was declared expelled by the Master of Oak Grove Lodge
No. 215, at its stated meeting held on May 3, 1928, under the procedure
laid down in Section 192 of our Constitution, as amended in 1927, which
provides that "fifteen days' notice of the action to be taken by the Lodge
(i. e. the declaration of expulsion by the Master at the next stated
mectting) shall be given by registered mail." The record shows that the
notice of the proposed expulsion was forwarded to the accused by the
Secretary of Oak Grove Lodge, by registered mail, on April 20, 1928,
and that the stated meeting was held on May 3, 1928, ~hirteen days thereafter. When action to be taken is such as will deprive a Mason of his
membership in the Craft, every act required by the Constitution must be
fully complied with. As the fifteen .days' notice was not given, the Master
of Oak Grove Lodge, at the stated meeting held on May 3, 1928, had not
acquired the jurisdiction to declare the accused expelled, and the whole
proceeding is therefore void. A new notice will have to be given at
least fifteen days i>rior to the stated meeting at which action on such
notice is to be had.
yYe, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved that the action of the Master of Oak Grove Lodge No.
215 at the st~ted mcteting of that Lodge held on May 3, 1928, declaring
the accused herein to be expelled from all the rights and privileges of
¥asonry, be and the same is hereby annulled and declared null and void,
and that the record herein be returned to said Lodge for prompt and
appropriate action by said Lodge in the premises.
