Trial Record No. 565, from Bethlehem Lodge No. 453, is a case
wherein the accused was acquitted and an appeal filed by the accuser. It
appears that the judgment of the Trial Commission was announced in
Lodge at a stated meeting held January 3, 1928, and that notice of appeal
was not filed until February 7th. Section 207 of the Constitution requires
that where an appeal is taken, notice thereof shall be given to the Master
of the Lodge in writing within thirty days after his announcement of
the result of the trial. This provision is mandatory. There is a request
by counsel for the accuser for a special dispensation permitting the matter
of appeal to be postponed until the 1929 communication of Grand Lodge,
in order that additional evidence may be presented.
Inasmuch as no lawful appeal is pending, the request of the accuser
for a special dispensation is denied.
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred trial record
Number 571, from Exeter Lodge Number 424, begs leave to report as
follows:
The accused, a member of Exeter Lodge, was charged with unmasonic
conduct as set out in nine specifications alleging that on different dates
during the years 1923, 1925, 1926 and 1927 he had been convicted of
certain misdemeanors. At the trial a certified copy of an abstract of
judgment of the Justice's Court of Exeter township was introduced in
evidence. This document related to only two of the nine specifications.
No further evidence of any character was submitted. Nevertheless, the
accused was convicted on eight of the nine specifications. No proof of
the identity of the accused with the individual named as the defendant in
the abstract of judgment was offered. This proof of identity seems to
be a common stumbling block to Masonic trial commissions. Undoubtelily
trial commissioners usually know that the accused is the same individual

260

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

previously convicted in the courts. But this knowledge on the part of
the commissioners is not sufficient. The record must disclose proof of
identity. Non-disclosure of such proof in the instant case is fatal and
would of itself warrant a reversal of the judgment. But there are in
this record other defects equally fatal. There is no showing that a vote
was taken upon the charge of unmasonic conduct. Section 205 of the
Constitution specifies in clear and unequivocal language that a vote shall
be taken upon the charge of unmasonic conduct. Indeed, the section
referred to goes further and states the reason why a vote upon the
charge must be taken in the following language : "And a similar vote
shall thus be taken upon the charge of unmasonic conduct and be thus
recorded, as it might be that the facts proven and found did not constitute
a Masonic offense." A third fatal defect appears ln this record in that
it entirely fails to disclose that any vote was taken upon the sentence as
is required by the provisions of Section 205 of the Constitution. For the
reasons herein specified your Committee is of the opinion that the judgment, if it can be said there is a judgment, must be reversed, and therefore
offers the following resolution and moves its adoption:

Resoli•ed, that the judgment of the Trial Commission finding the
accused guilty be, and the same is hereby reversed and the case remanded
for a new trial.

Definition of "Orphan"

5. Your Committee has considered the resolution introduced by
Brother Charles 0. Hamilton, Inspector of the Fifteenth District, reading
as follows:
" Resofoed, that the word 'orphan' wherever used in the Constitution
or in any Regulation, shall hereafter be deemed to mean the son or
daughter under the age of twenty-one years of a deceased Master Mason ;
and no man or woman over the age of twenty-one years shall be entitled
to relief as a matter of right as the son or daughter of a Master Mason."
Your Committee is in accord with the spirit and policy set forth
in said proposed resolution. Under the provisions of the Crvil Law, a
minor attains his or her majority when he or she becomes twenty-one years
of age. After attaining majority a person has no further legal claim
upon his father or mother for support. The principle upon which charity
is extended to the relatives of a deceased Mason is that the deceased
wo~ld have been legally and morally obligated for the care and support
of such person were he alive. We do not think that the Masonrc liability
should be extended beyond the limit proscribed by the rules of the law
of the land.
It is true that this Grand Lodge has once, or oftener, held that the
woman continues to be an orphan during her natural life, regardless of
hei; status as a spinster, wife, or widow. Grand Lodge has not gone so
far as to hold that a woman who is bereft of her father. after she attains
age of tw~nty-one years, is an orphan; but if it were held that a woman
orphaned while a minor child, continues to be an orphan for the remainder
of her life, it would be entirely consistent and rational to hold that a
woman losing her father at an~· age, would thereby become an orphan.
Furthermore, your Committee fails to find any reasonable ground
for a distinction between the distressed son and distressed daughter of a
Mason. If the Mason's female child is a potential charge on his Lodge
dnring her lifetime, why should not the son of a Mason also be a
potential charge during his lifetime on his deceased father 's Lodge?
Your Committee feels that Masonry should be fair, even to the
degree of indulgence, in providing for the needy who are entitled to its
ministrations, but we are firmly of the opinion that Grand Lodge should
not extend its liability, and that of its subordinate Lodges, to unreasonable
or improvident limits.
Your Committee, therefore, recommends that the resolution be ·
adopted.

The report and resolution were adopted.

Lodge Clubs
8. Your Committee recommends that the subject of Lodge clubs and

'and study. The problem is one of difficulty and your Committee is

under the guidance of the 'Master, should have and maintain full control

activities within, or in connection with, the Lodge. Perhaps Masters of

in its ritualistic ·work, but in all its activities and efforts.

Sw~n

It appears that about 1735 the Lodge of St. John had been established

Grand Lodges of Germany
21. Recently a letter was received, addressed to the Grand Lodge of
California by high officials of the National Mother Grand Lodge of the
Three Giobes, at Berlin, complaining of the action of one of the subordinate Lodges of our obedience which refused to accord Masonic recognition
to a member of a subordinate Lodge holding obedience to the National
Mother Grand Lodge of Germany. In response to this letter the chairman of your Committee wrote to the Grand Master and grand officers
of the Nation~! Mother Lodge of Germany, .assuring the!ll of our
fraternal regard for their Grand Lodge and our recognition of its

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

sovereignty and rights, and explaining the· seeming Masonic discourtesy
which arose from a misunderstanding of the facts and not from any lack
of fraternal courtesy and good will.
It has been generally understood that at the commencement of the
late war all the German Grand Lodges withdrew recognition from the
grand bodies of Masonry of the allied countries that were the enemies of
Germany in that war. Reports to that effect were printed in Masonic
periodicals and in the Pl.!blic press. If such statements were true, then
the attitude of these Grand Lodges was narrow and intolerant and
·calculated to strain whatever cordial relations might theretofore have
existed. Your Committee has had no direct communication from any of
the German Grand Lodges on this subject, but, from the letter above
referred to, assumes that the National Mother Grand Lodge has not
severed its fraternal relations with this Grand Lodge.
For the information of Grand Lodge, the following is a brief summary of the conditions of Masonry in Germany:
Before the war there were eight Grand Lodges in Germany and five
independent Lodges which were not under the jurisdiction of any Grand
Lodge. Two of these Independent Lodges were located at Leipsic. The
Masonic Handbook for 1927-28, containing a list of German Grand
Lodges, includes a Grand Lodge at Leipsic having 2,200 members. We
have no information respecting this Grand Lodge, but assume that it was
formed by some of the Independent Lodges. The eight Grand Lodges
which were in existence at the time of the war are as follows:
(1) The Grand National Mother Lodge of the Three Globes, seated
at Berlin, with a present membership of 22,700.
(2) The Grand Lodge of Hamburg, . seated at Hamburg, with a
present membership of 5,000.
(3) The Mother Grand Lodge of the Eclectic Union, seated at
Frankfort-on-the-Maine, with a present membership of 3,500.
( 4) The Grand Royal York Lodge of Friendship, seated at Berlin,
with a present membership of 11,400.
•
(5) The National Grand Lodge of All German Free Masons, seated
at Berlin, with a present membership of 22,300.
(6) The Grand Lodge of The "Sun," seated at Bayreuth, with a
present membership of 4,000.
(7) The National Grand Lodge of Saxony, seated at Dresden, with
a present membership of 7,200.
(8) The Grand Lodge "Concord," seated at Darmstadt.
The only one of these Grand Lodges recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California is the Grand National Mother Lodge of the Prussian

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

273

states called "of The Three Globes" (Grosse National-Mutterloge "zu
den drei Welt Kuglen") with which we established frate~nal relations in
1881 (Proceedings 1881, page 26).
Speculative Craft Masonry seems to have been introduced into Germany from England in the first half of the eighteenth century, soon after
the Duke of Hanover ascended the throne of England. In 1733, it is
stated, the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of England issued a dispensation for the formation of a Lodge in Hamburg. Soon thereafter
"Absolom" Lodge was instituted and is still in existence. This Lodge
initiated Prince Frederick, who afterwards became King Frederick II
of Prussia (Frederick the Great), at Brunswick, in 1738. The Grand
Lodge of Hamburg was subsequently organized by Lodges, some of
which were of English origin, and Grand Lodge had decades of checkered
history due to the "Strict Observance" movement and development and
also to dalliance with Rosicrucianism. In the latter part of the eighteenth
century the Gra~d Lodge returned to the English type of Free Masonry,
but in 1811, by reason of Napoleon's interdict, all connection with England
was discontinued and in that year the present Grand Lodge of Hamburg
was organized by twelve Lodges. This Grand Lodge has had a long
and successful history and, after checking the information now in our
possession and ascertaining the attitude of that Grand Lodge toward the
Masons of England and America, your Committee will be disposed to
make a recommendation for the recognition of the Grand Lodge of
Hamburg.
The introduction of Masonry into Prussia is usually credited to
Frederick the Great, who reversed the antagonistic policy of his father
who had interdicted the institution. Upon succeeding to the Crown,
Frederick openly acknowledged himself a Free Mason and presided over
his Lodge and for many years was Grand Master. He authorized the
erection of a Lodge at Berlin in 1740, which took the name of "The Three
Globes," and which, in 1744, became the Grand Lodge of the same name.
This Grand Lodge chartered Lodges without as well as within Prussia
and assumed the title of "Grand Royal Mother-Lodge of the Three
Globes." From 1764 to 1782 this Grand Lodge was an exponent of the
new "Strict Observance" practices and ritualism and other Masonic
vagaries of the time, to which all its Lodges except the Royal York gave
their adherence. In 1797 the Grand Lodge of the Three Globes adopted
new constitutions and disavowed and renounced the last remnants of the
"Strict Observance" system and based itself upon the three symbolic
degrees. From time to time since 1797 new constitutions have been
adopted in a progressive effort to establish a representative system and
to modify the essentially aristocratic character of the early years of the
Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodge has steadily grown in influence and

275

GRAND LODGE .OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF THE

274

usefulness and has greatly prospered notwithstanding the distresses and
disturbances of the Napoleonic wars and the century-long agitation and
difficulty over the Jewish question. This Grand Lodge was recognized by
the , United Grand Lodge of England in 1869 and is in fraternal accord
with numerous Grand Lodges, including California.
The Mother Grand Lodge of the Eclectic Union has always been
entitled to high regard because of the filial persistence with which it has
adhered, under most difficult circumstances, to its connection with England
and its resistance, . in the face of every allurement, to the blighting inftuence of the "Strict .Observance" and other "Masonic Aberrations." It
has always confined itself to the three Craft degrees and has worked in
accordance with the English ritualism. The records of the Lodge are
complete for the entire period of its existence and no confusion exists as
to its policies or its performances.
After receiving assurances that this Grand Lodge has not severed
relations with the Masonry of the English-speaking co~ntr1es your Committee will be heartily dispo:SCd to recommend the recognition of tlie
Mother Grand Lodge of the F.clectic Union.

To the M: .W: .Grand Lodge of California:
Since the report of this Committee at the last .session of the Grand
Lodge, another year has slipped silently into the Past, carrying with it
much of light and shadow, ;oy and sorrow, leaving in its train many
aching hearts and empty pla<:es once fi1led with those whose hands met
ours with fraternal greetings, and wh<>!le eyes looked into ours with 'the
lig'ht of fratemal love.
In looking ove~ the list of those who have· been by the Supreme
Grand Master translated from this imperfect to that a:ll pe.rfect, glorious
and celestial Lodge above; we cannot wonder that they have been made
a part of the celestial household, for they are of natures noblest, and
while we shall sorely miss them as we foregather in our various places
of meeting, we shall only grieve for ourselves, that we can no longer
enjoy their fellowship.

This complex and perplexing puzzle called life no longer contains any
mystery to them ; the broad fields o.f human relationships as well as the
eternal verities stand fully revealed to them, and ~e are fully persuaded
that in no small degree, , the practice of the great moral principles of
Masonry, contributed in the preparation for the enjoyment of that blissful
haven of rest to which they have been called and of which they are now
a part.
Limited space prevents our giving these departed brethren little more
than a passing notice, but we have a more enduring record of' their many
virtues graven upon our hearts than could be related on many printed
pages. Let us who remain strive earnestly to merit an equally wellearned place in the hearts of those we shall in due time leave behind.

Henry Taylor, of Los Palmas No. 366, Grand Organist in 1924, is among

in 1893 and 1894 and presided as Superior Judge of Sierra county continuously from 1890 to 1920, a period of 30 years. His reputation was
that of an h~:mest man and an updght judge.
Broth~·r John Francis Ellison was born at Falls Church, Virginia,
and died '!t Red Bluff, Qctober 30, 1927. He served his Lodge as Master .
in 1893, and from 1891 to 1927, a period of 36 years, he presided as Judge ·

judges in the State. He was frequently called to preside in cases outside
of his county, and his decisions . in many instances mark epochs in California jurisprudence. His was a noble soul and his life a beacon light to
his fellow· men.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Decisions of Grand Master

To the M. ·. W. ·.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which was referred the decisions of the Grand Master, has considered the same and reports thereon
as follows :
In Decision 1, the Grand Master held that the provision of section
192 of our Constitution adopted in 1927 and to the effect, in substance,
that any Mason who "shall suffer a final judgment of conviction and be
imprisoned in pursuance thereof," for certain specified offenses only, on
production of a certified copy of the final judgment of conviction and
notice to him of fifteen days, shall stand expelled from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry, has no application with regard to offenses not
specified or referred to in the provision.
In Decision 2, he held that where a Mason was convicted of one of
the offenses specified in the same provision, but was admitted to probation
and was never imprisoned, the provision has no application, for the
simple reason that the provision is made applicable only to one "who shall
suffer a final judgment of conviction and be imprisoned."
In Decision 3, he held substantially that this provision could not be
held to operate retroactively so as to appiy to a conviction had prior to
the enactment of the provision in 1927, the language of the provision so
enacted being "who shall suffer," etc.
Each of these three decisions was clearly correct, the first because the
provision does not purport to apply to any but the offenses specified
therein, and the second and third because no other conclusion can fairly
be reached in view of the language of the provision.
We recommend that these rulings of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.
Decision 4, section 108 of our Constitution, is to the effect that
where a candidate has been elected to receive the degrees, objection
may nevertheless be made at any time before his initiation by any member
of the Lodge, and that in the event of such objection being made he shall
not receive any degree until the objection is withdrawn, and that such
objection shall, unless withdrawn within sixty days, have the effect of a
rejection by ballot. Under our ~ell-settled law such objection may be
and is made privately by the member to the Master of the Lodge. The
Grand Master held that the sixty-day period fixed by the section begins
to run on the day the objection is so made to the Master.

281

This decision was clearly in accord with the plain language of the
section, which makes the objection effective on the date when made, and
renders its continuance for sixty days without withdrawal a rejection. It
should be noted that the language of this section, applying only to
objections made after election and before initiation, differs from the
language of section 101 with regard to an objection made to the Master
before report of the investigating committee, as to which it is provided
that such objection shall preclude a ballot unless withdrawn and unless it
be withdrawn within sixty days shall have the effect of a rejection by
ballot, and that as to any such objection the Master shall report the fact
to the Lodge, and the sixty-day period shall commence to run from the
date of the meeting at which the fact of objection is so reported to the
Lodge. But such is not the rule declared by section 108 as to objections
made after election and before initiation. We are of opinion that for the
purpose of establishing a Lodge record of the fact of objection and the
time when the sixty-day period commences to run, section 108 should be
amended to conform substantially with the provision of section 101 in the
regard specified, and will submit such an amendment.
We recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.
In Decision 6, the Grand Master held it not to be an impropriety for
a Lodge to make a modest donation from its refreshment fund for the
purpose of assisting to pay the expenses of an Inspector at an annual
communication of Grand Lodge. We are forced to the conclusion that
the making of such a donation is a violation of our law as now written.
Sections 88 and 89 of our Constitution are very clear and explicit as to
the uses that can be made of Lodge funds. Sections 88 and 89 make all
such funds (except when donated to and accepted by the Lodge for any
proper specific purpose) trust funds set apart for the payment of the
necessary expenses of the Lodge, and for the special calls for charity for
which it was instituted, and provides that the Lodge cannot us~ or permit
the use of such funds or any part thereof "for any other thing whatsoever,
except that it may make an appropriation therefrom for the purpose of
a Past Master's jewel for its retiring Master or for floral pieces for a
deceased brother," and except also that it may expend twenty per cent
of its total revenue "for purposes of refreshment and the promotion of
fraternal intercourse." The donation here referred to by the Grand
Master, laudable as may have been its purpose, was for none of the purposes specified in these sections. If it be desired to enlarge the uses to
which the refreshment fund of . a Lodge can be put, this can be accomplished only by amendment of our Constitution.
We recommend that Decision 6 of the Grand Master be not approved.

Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Decision 7. The Grand Master held it "to be in bad taste, although
not directly prohibited," for a Lodge to advertise a puMic dance under
its auspices ...to raise funds for building a hall." This expression of
opinion on the part of the Grand Master, in which we personally concur,
does not involve any question of law, and we believe does not call for
any action on the part of this Grand Lodge.

before initiation by objection privately made to the Masfer and not withdrawn within sixty days (Section 108 of the Constitution). He thinks
that in this regard no distinction should be made between an applicant
who has not been initiated, and one who, having been elected, has received
the first, or the first and second degrees, where the objection is to advancement, and a · hearing is had thereon at which the identity of the objector
is disclosed, and decision is made by the Lodge as to the validity of the
objection. Of course there is an essential difference between one who
has been made an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft Mason, and one
who has not been initiated. The former is already a Mason, with certain
Masonic rights, while the latter is precisely as he was before the ballot.
The rule stated in section 108 of the Constitution has been in force ever
since the institution of this Grand Lodge. Its purpose is the same as
our law requiring a unanimous secret favorable ballot on an application
for the degrees, with disclosure of the vote of any member strictly prohibited, viz., to effectively protect Masonry against the admission of
improper material. The theory of the secret ballot is that such secrecy
is essential to the full and free discharge by the members of a Lodge of
their all important duty in the matte.r of acceptance of applicants for the
degrees. There is no good reason why, the protection of the Craft against
improper material being the only thing in·volved, the absolute duty of a
member to privately make effective objection to the initiation of one who
he conscientiously believes to be dangerous to Masonry should not continue
in full force up to the time of initiation, just as it existed at the time
of the ballot. Of course the power to thus effect a rejection may be
improperly used for unworthy purposes, but the same thing is true of
our secret ballot in the Lodge.
We believe the suggested change is inadvisable and recommend that
no action be taken.

282

Adopted.
Decision 8. The Grand Master was, of course, compelled to hold
that, under our law (Section 129 of the Constitution) a life membership
cannot be acquired by a member except by the payment of money into
the treasury of the Lodge by or on behalf of the member, and that the
Lodge <:alDlot, ~:y any device or form of bookkeeping whatever, accomplish what would be in effec_t a donation by it of a life membership.
We recommend that the decision be approved.

Adopted.
Decision 9. The Grand Master held it not to be an "impropriety"
for the brethren of a Lodge to participate with their families in a simple,
private picnic on the Sabbath day, provided such picnic be a private
affair for members and their families, with no advertising, sale of tickets,
or commercial feature. This body has ~aid that it is not in keeping with
·the dignity of Masonry, or in conformity with our law, that Masons
should. assemble as a Lodge or as Masons on any Sunday, except for some
purely Masonic purpose, and that the advertising or sale of tickets for
Sunday pleasure outings are dearly opposed to the principles and teachings
of Masonry (Decisfon 388). We have no disposition to question the
correctness of that ruling. The facts here, howeveT, are so stated by
the Grand Master as not to show any assembly prohibited by Masonic
law, and his decision to that effect on such facts should be approved.
We so recommend.

Adopted.
Decision. 10. The ruling that the wife, child or other dependent of
an e~p1tlled Mason is not entit111d to Masonic relief is obviously correct
and should be app!!<Wed. We so recommend.

Adopted.

Amendment to Section 108, Constitution
In view of what we have said in commenting on Decision 4 of the
Grand Master, we recommend that Section 108 of the Constitution be
amended by adding thereto the following:
"Whenever any such objection be made, the Master shall report the
fact at the next stated meeting of the Lodge, and the sixty-day period
specified herein shall commence to run at the date of such meeting."

The report was adopted and Section 108 of the Constitution was amended as above set out by unanimous vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence then presented, with
its approval, the following proposed amendments to the
Oonstitution:
Special Committees
Sec. 28. Special committees may also be appointed by the Grand
Master, whenever it may be deemed necessary by the Grand Lodge and,
whenever, during the intervals between the communications of the Grand
Lodge he shall deem it necessary so to do.
The Grand Master shall annually appoint a member of the special
committee of three on investments of Lodge funds in Masonic building
corporations, provided for in Sec. 87.

Adopted by unanimous vote.
Funds of Lodge-Financing of Building Projects
Sec. 87. A Lodge must retain the control of its own funds and
property. It cannot incorporate or intrust any of its funds or property
to a corporation formed within itself. It may, through Trustees provided
for in a standing resolution, who shall always be under its control, hold,
mortgage, sell and otherwise dispose of its property and funds, which may
be invested and reinvested as the Lodge shall direct. No money, except
that dispensed by the Charity Committee and that due the Grand Lodge,
shall be drawn without its express consent appearing in the record, and
no warrant shall be drawn therefor, unless there are sufficient funds to
meet it, except in extreme cases of Masonic necessity or charity.
No Lodge shall hereafter invest any of its funds in any manner or
obligate itself in any way for the purpose of acquiring or erecting a
Masonic Temple, Masonic Hall or other structure for the occupancy, in
whole or in part, of a Masonic Lodge, until after the plan for financing
such building, and the plans and specifications of such structure, together
with estimates of costs, shall have been submitted to and approved by a
majority of a special committee, consisting of the Grand Treasurer, the
Chairman of the Finance Committee of .Grand Lodge, and a member
appointed by the Grand Master.

Adopted by unanimous vote.

Automatic Expulsion

The Committee on Jurisprudence presented with its
approval the proposed amendments to Sections 192 and
192A of the Constitution as follows:
Sec. 192. When the charge is for an offense which is the subject of
proceedings in Courts of the land, the Masonic trial may, in the discretion
of the Master, be deferred until such proceedings are concluded. In the .
event any · Mason who is a member of a Lodge under the' jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of California shall suffer a final judgment of conviction
of a crime classified as a felony under the law, and be imprisoned ·in
pursuance thereof; or shall be adjudged an habitual criminal; it shall be
the duty of the Secretary of the Lodge of which such Mason is a member,
upon learning of such conviction, to procure, at the expense of his

286

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge, two certified copies of such final judgment of conviction, one of
which certified copies shall be filed in the records of the Lodge. Thereupon sixty days' notice in writing shall be given to such Mason by registered mail, forwarded to his last known place of address, notifying
such Mason of the filing of such record of conviction in such Lodge and
requiring such Mason within such period of sixty days to elect in writing,
if he so desires, to have a trial in such Lodge on the charge of unmasonic
conduct based on the offense or offenses of which he has been convicted
in a court of the land ; which written election shall be filed with the
Secretary of such Lodge within said period of sixty days. If such
Mason shall elect to have such trial in said Lodge, it shall be the duty
of the Junior Warden of such Lodge to prefer charges against such
Mason based on the offense or offenses of which said Mason was so
convicted in such court ; and proceedings shall thereafter be taken in the
same manner as provided for other trials by the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge. If no such election shall be filed by such
Mason, as above .provided, within such period of sixty days, then, at the
next stated meeting, after such sixty days from the mailing of such notice
shall have elapsed, the Master shall announce to the Lodge the fact that
such certified copy of a judgment of conviction has been filed and that
the required notice thereof has been given. Thereupon the Mason so
convicted shall stand expelled .from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, and it shall be so noted in the minutes. The Secretary shall
transmit to the Grand Secretary a copy of the record of such minutes, a
certified copy of the final judgment of conviction, and a statement of the
giving of the sixty days' notice and failure of such Mason to elect to
have a trial in said Lodge; which shall constitute the record required by
section 207.
Acquittal in said courts or the refusal of a grand jury to indict for
an offense, is no bar to a Masonic trial.
Whenever it shall appear by the record of conviction from another
Masonic jurisdiction, recognized by us, that a member of one of our
Lodges, resident in such jurisdiction, has been suspended or expelled for
unmasonic conduct in such jurisdiction while a resident thereof, it shall
be the duty of the Junior Warden of the Lodge in this jurisdiction of
which he is a member to prefer charges against him for the acts and
conduct alleged in the charges preferred in the foreign jurisdiction and
of which he was there convicted, and the same proceedings shall thereupon
be had as in ordinary cases ; provided, that the record of conviction of
the foreign jurisdiction shall be received on the trial as prima facie
evidence of t·he guilt of the brother of such acts and conduct.

Sec. 192A. In the event any Mason who is a member o f a Lodge
under a foreign jurisdiction shall suffer a final judgment of conviction·
in the State of California, and be imprisoned in pursuance thereof, of a
c;rime classified as a felony by the laws of California or the United
$tates, or shall be adjudged, an habitual criminal, it shall be the duty of
the Grand Secretary, upon learning of such conviction, to procure two
cer~ified copies of such final judgment of conviction. Thereupon sixty.
days' notice of the fact of the procuring of such certified copies . of conviction, and the action to be taken thereon, shalt be given to such Mason
by registered mail, forwarded to his last known place of address, and
requiring such Mason to elect within such sixty days, if he so desires, to
ha;ve a trial in such Masonic Lodge within the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California, as the Grand Master may designate for the purpose;
such election to be in writing and transmitted to the Grand Secretary at
his office within such sixty days, by the accused or upon his behalf ; in
which event it shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of the. Lodge
designated ,by the . Grand Master for the trial of said matter, to prefer
charges in such Lodge against such Mason upon specifications to conform
to the offense or offenses of which such Mason has been tried in the
courts of the land; the trial thereafter to be had under the same procedure and in the same manner as provided for other trials under the
Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge. Should such Mason
not ·elect to have such trial within such sixty days as above provided,
thereupon, · on the expiration of such period of sixty days, the Grand
Secretary shall transmit one certified copy of such final judgment of.
conviction to the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of the jurisdiction
of which the Lodge to which such convicted Mason belongs is constituent,
and shall file the other certified copy of such conviction, together with a
statement of the notice given, and the failure of such Mason to have
such Masonic trial, in the records of the Grand Lodge ; whereupon such
c'onvicted Mason shall automatically stand expelled from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry.

Adopted, and the section amended by unanimous vote.

Pelton Water Wheel
Your Committee on Finance, to which was referred that portion of
the Grand Master's address, wherein he calls the attention of Grand Lodge
.to the fact that Brother Lester Allen Pelton, the inventor of the Pelton
Wa1er Wheel, was a ·member during his lifetime, of Gravel Range Lodge
No. 59, and also to the efforts of the members of that Lodge, at this
:time, rto appropriately perpetuate the memory of Brother Pelton, by the
erection of a suitable monument upon the site of the old workshop of
this inventor, in Camptonville, has given the same consideration.
It is pleasing to know that the man who conceived this epoch-making
invention, was a member of the fraternity, and we commend the Grand
Master for having included this account in his Annual Report. It is very
fitting that the records of Masonry should show that this inventor was a
member of the Craft. We also commend the brethren of Gravel Range

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge for their zeal in planning to perpetuate his memory. The Committee, however, is doubtful of the propriety of Masonry attempting to
perpetuate the memory of its illustrious members who have achieved
distinction outside of the Masonic field, or of those endeavors to which
Masonry is dedicated-such as humanitarianism and education-by other
than appropriate mention in its records. Your Committee, therefore, is
of the opinion that Grand Lodge should not make the appropriation requested by ·the Brethren of Gravel Range Lodge, and so recommenqs ..

Adopted.

Temple Stock of Redondo Lodge No. 328
Your Committee has considered 'the request of Redondo Lodge No
328 that the Grand Lodge purchase 20,000.00 of the stock of the Masonk
Hall Association of Redondo.
Your Committee has had before it the requests informally of many
Masonic Hall Associations throughout the State, for financial assistancf
and, while your Committee fully recognizes the need for financial assist·
ance, they know of no way by which this Grand Lodge could enter into
the purchases of stock in Masonic Temple Associations with any degrel"
of safety. Your Committee, therefore, recommends that the request of
Redondo Lodge No. 328 for the purchase of this stock be declined.

Adopted.

. Permanent Grand Lodge Meeting Place
: · · Your Committee. on Finance has considered the report of the Special
Committee and also the Grand Master's recommendation on this subject.
Past Grand Masters Filmer and Henderson, members of this Special
Committee, met with your Committee on Finance for an extended discussion. We believe that all will qree th~t there is a need for this new
builaing, 'but 'set over against this need are many I>erplexing question~
to decide.
· '. . Of the pre.sent outstanding capital stock of one million dollars of
the Masonic 'remple, in which we now meet, the Grand Lodge owns
$590,000.00, or practically 60 per cent. If this building could be sold so
as to realize on this investment, your Committee would look with favor
on a new undertaking. It is conceded that a new meeting place will cost

PROCEEDINGS OF THE • ' ·

338 .

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

at least $750,000.00, which is approximately $6.00 per n:iember for · the
entire membership in this grand jurisdiction, and this amount would fall
upon Lodges, many of which are now straining under their own financial
burdens.
. ': ~, •.,
Your Committee feels that the needs of the Grand ·Lodge· may be
divided under two headings :
First, more commOdious quarters" for the ~ffices and committee rooms
·
of the Grand Lcxige;
Secondly, a larger meeting place for the Annual CommunicatiOn. · •
As this larger meeting place would only be required four qays . e~ch.
year, it does seem to your Committee that if our present room it too
small, we can find a church or hall somewhere which will suffice, wrthout
the expenditure of so large a sum as will be required to build a new meeting place at this tirrte, and where the Grand Lodge atmosphere could be
maintained.
As for more space for the Grand Lodge officers, we have discussed
with directors of the Temvle Association a plan to rearrange the space
on the fourth floor of this Temple with a view of carinJr for the needs
of the Grand Lodge for several years to come.
Your Finance Committee recommends that the report of the Special
Committee be not concurred in, but as the subject is of such importance,
we reeommend that the Special Committee be continued.
Your Finance Committee further recommends that the incoming
Grand Master, the Grand Secretary, and the Grand Treasurer be a
committee with authority to arrange with the directors of the Masonic
Temple Association for additional space on the fourth floor of this
building, and that they be further authorized to expend from the funds
of this Grand Lodge, a sufficient amount to remodel the quarters and
refurnish the same.
The Special Committee has devoted a great ·deal of time and thought
in the matter of the new building, and great commendation is due them
for their earnest efforts.
·

Adopted.

Grand Lodge Week Activities Committee
During the last few years the expenditures of the Committee having
in charge the entertainment of the Grand Lodge, have increased from a
few hundred dollars to several thousand dollars, there having been expended in 1927 approximately $5,000.00, and your Committee on Finance
is informed that the total expenditures for the 1928 Communication will
exceed $5,000.00, which includes a bill of the Masters and Wardens' Club
of Alameda county of $2,230.00.
In the past there does not seem to have been any check on these
expenditures. Your Committee feels that some definite limit should be
placed upon the amount of money which can be expended upon the entertainment of the Grand Lodge.
After consultation with the chairman of the Activities Committee
your Finance Committee recommends that the total expenditures for
entertainment of the Grand Lodge in any communication shall not exceed
$3,000.00, and no expenditures shall be made without same having been
authorized by the Activities Committee.

Adopted.

CEREMONY OF DEDICATION OF VAULT OF
WESTERN STAR LODGE, No. 2·, F. & A. M.
SATURDAY, _SEPTEMBER 15, 1928
Compiled by JOHN WmcHER, Grand Secretary,
and published by order of the Grand Master
WILL H . FISCHER, Grand Master, Officiating
(Grand Lodge will be opened in Lodge Room )

Grand Master (States object of meeting, and that Grand Lodge had
caused to be built, as a part of this building, a vault in which to house and
preserve the relics, documents, antiques and articles of Masonic historic
value possessed by Western Star Lodge.)
Grand Master: The ceremony of dedicating this vault is, like all
Masonic ceremon~es, symbolic. Freemasonry is well defined as "a: science
which is engaged in the search after Divine Truth, and which employs
symbolism as its method of instruction." It is this peculiar character as
a symbolic Institution, this entire adoption of the method of instruction
by symbolism, which gives its whole identity to Freemasonry and has
caused it to differ from every other association that the ingenuity of
man has devised. It is this that has bestowed upon it that attractive form
~hi~h has secured its own perpetuity.
A symbol is defined to be a visible sign with which a spiritual feeling or idea is connected. It is the expression of an idea which is derived
from the comparison or contrast of some object with a moral conception
or attribute. Thus, the plumb is a symbol of rectitude, its physical qualities being compared or contrasted with the moral conception of virtue
or · rectitude of conduct. The plumb becomes, after we have been taught
its symbolic meaning, the visible expression of the idea of rectitude or
uprightness of conduct.
And so, in the dedication of this vault, erected fo r the purpose of
p'reserving the priceless relics of Western Star Lodge against the fury
of the elements and the devastations of time which destroy our temporal
buildings, we make use of the symbolism of Masonry to inculcate in the
minds of our brethren the lessons of Faith, of Loyalty, and to perpetuate
the memory of the pioneers of our Craft who bore the burden and heat
of the day when Freemasonry on this western coast was more of a
vision than a fact. As was said by the Prophet Isaiah, "Mine elect shall
long enjoy the work of their hands."
In the earliest ages, the cave or vault was deemed sacred. The first
worship was in cave temples, which were either natural or formed by

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

350 .

351

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

art to resemble the excavations of nature. Of such great extent was this
practie:e of subterranean worship by the nations of antiqtrity, that many
of the forms of heathen temples, as well as the naves, aisles and chancels
of churches subsequently built for Christian worship, are said to owe
their origin to the religious use of caves.
From this, too, arose the fact that the initiation into the ancient
mysteries was almost always performed in subterranean edifices, and
when the place of initiation-as in some of the Egyptian temples-was
above ground, it was so constructed as to give to the neophyte the appearance, in its internal structure, of a vault.
As the great doctrine taught in the mysteries was the resurrection
from the dead (as to die and to be initiated were synonymous terms) it
was deemed proper that there should be some formal resemblance between
a descent into the grave and a descent into the place of initiation.
'The vault was, therefore, in the ancient mysteries, symbolic of the
grave; for initiation was symbolic of death, where alone Divine Truth
is to be found. Freemasons have adopted the same idea. We teach that
death is but the beginning of life; that if the first or evanescent temple
of our transitory life be on the surface, we must descend into the vault
of death before we can find the deposit of Truth which is to adorn our
second temple of eternal life. It is in this sense of an entrance thtoagh
the grave into eternal life that we are to view the symbolism of the
vault. Like all myths and allegories of Masonry, the historical rela:tion
may be true or false, but even if invented by imagination, the lesson is
still there, taught in symbolism.
The legend of the vault is intimately connected with the symoolism
of the Lost Word, the search after Truth, which is. the unity of God and
the immortality of the human soul. A distinguished Masonic student has
aptly said that "the symbolic Word-the knowledge of Divine Truthis never thoroughly attained in this life, or in its symbol the Master
Mason's Lodge. The corruptions of mortality which encumber and cloud
the human intellect hide it as with a thick veil from mortal eyes. It. is
only beyond the tomb, and when released from the earthly burden of life,
that man will become capable of fully receiving and apprecia.ting the
revelation. For it is only after the decay and fall of this temple of life
which we as Masons have been building, that from its ruins, deep beneath
its foundations, and in the profound abyss of the grave, we find that
Divine Truth, in the search for which life was spent, if not in vain, at
least without success, and the mystic key to which Death only could
supply."
I deem it not improper at this time to say that the brethren vriro
acted in behalf of Western Star Lodge and the Grand Lodge of California
in the preparation of the plans by which the vault. has been constructed,

are to be particularly commended for having so carefully kept in mind
the purposes for which it is to be used; for having erected a chamber for
1
the safe keeping of valuable Masonic relics, which in every way meets
the requirements for which it was designed. The skill and ability dis- '
played in the execution of the trust reposed in the members of the Grand ;
Lodge Committee at the inception of this undertaking have received, as ·
they so well deserve, our entire approbation, and it is our hope that the·
enterprise may continue as a lasting monument to the ·genius of our
Institution.
Deputy Grand Master: Most Worshipful Grand Master, the plan
upon which the vault is constructed having met with your approbation,
it is the desire of the brethren that it should now be dedicated according
to ancient usage.
Grand Master: Agreeable to the request of the brethren, the vault•
will now be dedicated according to ancient form and usage. After Grand
Lodge is called to refreshment, the Grand Marshal wilt form the officers
of Grand Lodge in, procession.

(Grand Lodge is then called off "For the purpose of dedicating the
vault of Western Star Lodge No. 2.")

clear.)
(In the doorway of the vault there should be a pedestal or smalt

which is alcohol or other substance that will readily burn.)

(Officers of Grand Lodge wilt form in front of vault door, near
back wall, Grand Master in center and about two paces in front of

Grand Master: Brethren, in accordance with the teachings of our
Institution, it is our duty, before entering upon any important undertaking,
to invoke the blessing of God. We will, therefore, unite with our Grand
Chaplain in an address to the Throne of Grace.
Grand Chaplain: Thou, 0 God I Creator of the Universe I the Great
Jehovah who laid the foundation of the earth I We invoke Thy presence
and Thy blessing upon our labors this day. Enable us to properly com-·
prehend and practice the precepts of our fathers who established and
here carried on the work of charity and brotherly love. Teach us, our.
Heavenly Father, to appreciate the blessings which Thou hast vouchsafed
us, and inculcate in our minds and hearts the glory of friendship and the

s~irit of. fidelity which should animate the members of our Mystic Craft.
Endow us with reverence for the memory of our brethren of other
clays.. May the vault to be dedicated this day be an inspiration and a
sh;ine to· all who love Truth, and an enduring monument to the integrity
311d good conscience of these Thy Servants. We beseech Thee, our God
a;nd our Father, to let Thy blessing continue upon. our Nation and our

first dedication in 1774 was in all its essentials identical with that which
is performed at the dedication of our Masonic temples today. To those
unmindful of its symbolism it will be nothing but an unmeaning form;
but it is in truth and in fact, as are all 011r ceremonies, fraught with
significance.
In ancient times the priests were commanded to cast salt upon tAl'
altars to be dedicated, and upon the houses, so that "peaoe, humony and
brotherly love shall perpetually reign." To cat salt with any one, was to
partake of his fare, to share his hospitality, and to enjoy his favor, .or
to be in his confidence. Hence, salt became an emblem of fidelity and of
intimate friendship. The domestic sanctity which thus attached itself to
salt was much enhanced in influence by its religious applications, so that
it became symbolical of the most sacred and binding of obtig:rtions.
Accordingly, a covenant of salt was accounted a very solemn bond.
The building in which we are now assembled has been heretofore
solemnly dedicated to Freerna90llry, Virtue and Universal Benevolence,
in the ceremonies of ·which the Masonic elements of consecration-com,
wine and oil-wore employed. We will, therefore, on this occasion,
depart from the form used at the dedication of a Masonic Temple, and
will employ the element used by the fathers of Israel, by sprinkling salt,
the emblem of hospitality and friendship, upon this vault, and dedicate it
as an important and integral part of this Masonic Temple.
This brief explanation will, we hope, bring a clearer understanding of
the significance of the ceremony.

Grand Master : We read in the Holy Writings that when all the work
that Solomon had made for the house of the Lord was finished, he
assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the chiefs
of the fathers of the children. of Israel, and then the house which was
etectl!d to God was dedical'ed to His Holy Name.
We have gathered here in imitation of the children of Israel to
dedicate a vault-a repository-for the preservation of the relics of our
bi:ethren of the days of old, thus perpetuating a custom which has come
.
down to us from time immemorial.
Among the ancients, every temple, altar and statue was dedicated ~o
some divinity or to some special cause. The Hebrews extended this
ceremony to cities, walls, gates, and even to their private h~uses; and
it was a custom in Israel to dedicate a new house to Gi>d with prayer,
praise and thanksgiving. This was done in order t~ secure th~ Divine
RFes.ence and blessing; for it was believed that no pious or sen.s1ble ~an
could expect tp dwell safely in a house which was not under the 1~med1ate
protection of God. They made a distinction between consecration a?d
dedication, for sacred things were both dedicated and consecrated,. while
profane things, such as private dwelling houses, were only dedicated.
'Fhis distinction has always been observed among peoples generally, many
of whom (and in the early ages, all) consecrated their churches to ~e
worship of God, but dedicated them to, or placed them under the especial
patronage of, some particular saint.
You will r.emember that a similar practice prevails in our Institution,
and that while we consecrate our Lodges to the honor and glory of. G~,
we dedicate them to the memory of the Holy Saints John, and the bu1ldmg
it~eH is dedicated to the purposes for which it is set apart.
Our temples are dedicated to Freemasonry, Virtue, and Universal
:$enevolence ; and you may be interested· in knowing that this. was the
form ·o f dedication of the first. edifice ever erected as a Masomc hall of
which we have authentic information ; and that the ceremony of that

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
October, 1928
By JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
I herewith submit my Eighth Report as Chairman of the Committee on Corre,s pondence. The views expressed under the various
subjects, as heretofore, are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
The subjects engaging the attention of the Fraternity are practically the same as those that have been prominent in Masonic
activities for the past few years. There can, of course, naturally be no
unanimity of opinion as to the best method of solving the various
questions, each Jurisdiction being a law unto itself, depending upon
the viewpoint of the individual Jurisdiction. Some view "with
alarm," while others "point with pride."
In this Report are set forth at length the opinions or actions that
are general to all Jurisdictions. Conservation of printer's ink and
paper will allow for the consideration of only the most interesting and
important ones. For this reason we are sununarizing in the following
paragraphs general statement as to others that cannot be considered
at length.
COURTESY DEGREES: Some Jurisdictions have criticised the
action of those who will not confer the Entered Apprentice Degree on
request. There undoubtedly are emergency cases, where such action
would be proper, but generally speaking in the long run a Lodge that
is responsible for the entry of an applicant into the Fraternity should
assume the burden of initiation. In some instances the basic idea of
"Courtesy" has been entirely overlooked and the request based along
mandatory lines.
ORDER OF EASTERN STAR: This organization is Ulll·
doubtedly the largest organization of women in the world at the
pr,e sent time. It has approximately 12,000 chapters with a combined
membership of 1,800,000. Its ritual has been translated into German,
Spanish, Italian and Chinese. The view of the Grand Lodge of England, Scotland, Ireland, Pennsylvania and some other Jurisdictions is

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

2

3

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

that h should remain an organization exclusively for women. The
other believes that while it has no official connection with the Masonic
Fraternity, still the co-operation and assistance rendered .in cha~table
and humanitarian work entitle it to at least sympathetic consideration. There is not a trade, calling or profession that the ladies have
not invaded. Barber Shops have be;come Beauty Parlors, with a
similar change in other industries and activities. As the correspondent
of Alberta says: "Can we withstand the assaults of the ladies?", and
adds that perhaps there is something in the story of the man who
when he found that he had to be tried by a jury of women told the
Court that he wanted to plead guilty. He said, "I have been for the
last twenty years trying to fool one woman, how then can you expect
me to fool twelve in an hour or two."
ENTERTAINMENT: The Grand Lodge of California has at
various times been entertained and instructed through Masonic
dramas. Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio, Kentucky and far off
Nova Scotia have been guests at similar functions during the past
year. The Movies have popularized education throu.g h the eye and
presentations of Masonic history or incidents bring to the average
member a view point that cannot be supplied through lectures or
ritualism.
GRAND MASTER'S CONFERENCES: The belief that meetings of this kind will lead to the formation of a General ~r~d 1:-odge
we believe is held only by a few. We think such a poss1bi11ty is too
remote for serious consideration. The exchange of ideas and their
practical application derived from such gatherings cann~t help .but
be educational and productive of good results. There 1s certainly
room for improvement along uniform lines of some of the functions
of the various Grand Lodges. At a Conference held in Washington,
D. C. on February 20, 1928, there were 42 Grand Lodges represented,
32 of them by the Grand Master himself. The bugaboo of a General
Grand Lodge does not affect the relations of the Grand Lodge of
England, Ireland and Scotland. Their representatives last year met
in friendly discussion and came to an agreement with regard to the
initiation and receiving into the Order in each jurisdiction members
resident in the other two. The Deputy Grand Master of Ireland
states that this meeting was not only of importance to the three sister Grand Lodges but also of importance to Masonry and the world
in general, as it showed that the three Mother Grand Lodges of the
·world could be in the most absolute and perfect accord.
GRAND REPRESENTATIVES: With the exception of a few
Jurisdictions Grand Lodges are represented at meetings of other
Grand Lodges by a representative. Some States who have not fol-

lowed the system are seriously considering the matter. In one instance
the Grand Master recommended that the Grand Lodge furnish its
Representatives a special medallion for their use on official occasions, which was adopted.
INVESTIGATIONS: Grand Lodges, both at home and abroad,
are adopting questionnaires for the use of Investigating Committees.
This is not only an aid to the Committee itself but when used properly also gives the Lodges the benefit of the information. An applicant for insurance, a Fidelity bond, a bank loan, etc., to be accommodated must often furnish in writing intimate details of his personal
business affairs. We believe that a like requirement by the Craft
is also as proper.
LIFE MEMBERSHIP: The Grand Lodge of Wyoming made
an exhaustive and valuable survey and out of the mass of data submitted ascertained that of the 49 Grand Lodges of the United States,
29 approved some form of Life Membership, and 10 unqualifiedly disapproved it. Only ten jurisdictions have no law on the subject and of
these some permitted their subordinate Lodges to issue life membership.
MISSION OF MASONRY: William F. Kuhn, ·w ho during his
life was one of the outstanding Masons of the country, divided Masonry into three classes. First, the signs, grips, and words class, who
hold that if a man can perform the gymnastics and has a phonographic
record in his mind of certain words to be recited on occasion, he is a
well-posted Mason. Second, the King Solomon class who believe that
King Solomon was a member of the Craft, wrote its ritual and that
all his wives were members of the Eastern Star. Third, the philosophical class, whose heads are so encompassed by a fog bank of
mysticism that they cannot see cases of suffering and distress immediately at their feet.
The Grand Master of British Columbia outlined a practical way
that these might function, when he said:
"A new social order is in course of erection, the foreground is
strewn with disorganized material and the debris of the old. If we
are despondent this is all we may see, but faith in the purposes of the
Divine Creator, faith in humanity, and faith in our Institution, will
raise ·OUT eyes to the new and more glorious structure emerging out
of the old order.
The past has supplied us with an organization consisting of an
army of approximately four million men, selected for their intelligence
and moral worth. The possibilities of such a body working together

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

and actuated by a common purpose cannot be overestimated. If we
are true to ourselves and to the Craft we must in the future assume
the responsibility of supplying the directing force."
Brother Cheney, Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence
of New Hampshire, gives his definition as follows: "Masonry is an
organization of men teaching God in Fraternity."
!'AST MASTERS: Brother H. H. Moore of the "Masonic Home
Journal," of Louisville, Kentucky, in the following language divides
Past Masters into three grades.
"A useful Past Master is one who is diligent in his attendance
at the Lodge, one who did not go through the chairs perfunctorily,
but was in truth as well as in name a Master. His growth as a Mason
continues until the day of his death. He is a teacher who is always
a learner. His education as a Mason he feels is never completed. He
watches, with the closest interest, all the proceedings of the Lodge,
speaks whenever he can impart wisdom, and is silent when he has
nothing to say. He aids the Master in the skillful government of the
Lodge. He temporarily takes the chair for him when requested, and
is always able to perform the work Such a Past Master is both
useful and ornamental.
The purely ornamental Past Master is one who loses not his
interest in the Lodge sufficiently to be induced to remain absent from
it, but who, when present, is satisfied to sit in the army of his confreres of like grade, be perfectly quiet when business is under discussion, and exceedingly noisy while work is in progress. Such a
one may be a "good fellow," but he is only an ornamental Past Master.
He occupies his place, but does not fill it. He visits his Lodge for his
own amusement, not for the welfare of the Craft. He wears his jewel,
and wears his title, but he never wears himself.
The Past Master who is neither useful nor ornamental is one ·
whose name graces the Lodge roll as one of the P. M.'s, but who is
never present at a Lodge communication. He likely never should have
been Master, and the result is that practically he is not a Past Master.
He is never seen in the "noble army" to which he belongs. The fewer
the Craft has of these the better for its welfare and reputation.''
TIME LIMIT BETWEEN DEGREES: Fifteen Jurisdictions
in the United States do not require a waiting period between the conferring of Degree's, other than that a candidate must make suitable
proficiency in the preceding degree. In other Jurisdictions a specific
time is fixed. We believe it ,would work for the betterment of the
Craft in general if a minimum period of at least one calendar month,
together with suitable proficiency in the preceding Degree, was made

ADVERTISING
There continues to be methods, both direct and indirect, for advertising along Masonic lines. This activity may be divided into two
classes: First, that having to do with the affairs of Masonry as an
organization, and featuring as news the private affairs of a Lodge
or its activities. The desire for publicity along this line is unhealthy,
and might also be termed un-Masonic. Second, using Masonry as
a means for commercial gain.
We believe the only way to make the prohibition effective will be
to absolutely forbid the use .o f words or emblems by individual Masons
or associations of such for any purpose-commercial, political or
otherwise. No exceptions should be allowed where such advertising has
as its object profit of any kind to the user. Insurance companies
<;lealing with "Masons only'' and commercial activities of a like character may perhaps justly feel that they are discriminated against when
the privilege of using Masonic words and emblems is allowed Newspapers, Magazines, Cemetery Associations and Hospitals, or other
organizations operating for private profit, but not under the control
of a Grand Lodge.
Alabama (1927):
(Grand Master) : Grand Lodge has repeatedly refused to sponsor or
give its approval to Masonic journals. To suppress all such as did not
have its approval would, therefore, amount to an absolute suppression
of the freedom of the Masonic press. It would be very unwise for Grand
Lodge to give its endorsement and approval to a publication w.hich it
does not control and thus become morally, if not legally, responsible
for its utterances. As Masons, we 'profess to believe in freedom of
speech and of the press. We should certainly not belie our profession
by suppressing either in matters Masonic.
Indiana (1928):
(Grand Master): This year, I have received several letters from
Secretaries throughout Indiana, pertaining to the permissibility of the
use of the Local Lodge roster in connection with a privately owned and
operated business or enterprise.
The Grand Lodge is not for the purpose of, or has it the time or
inclination to operate cemeteries, publish papers, publish books, operate
building and loan associations, operate insurance agencies, run community
stores, further political interests, or to do anything except to endeavor
to build up its individual members toward a higher standard of manhood.

litical purposes is strictly prohibited, and the ostentatious display of
Masonic emblems is contrary to the spirit of Freemasonry.
"The Grand Lodge of Texas prohibits the use of the word ''Masonic'
and all like terms, as well as Masonic emblems, on signboards, business
cards or stationery, or in any other way for the purpose of advancing
the secular interest or business or political fortunes of individual Masons."
Washington (1927):
Sec. 262. Abuse of Masonic Name and Emblem. No Mason shall
exhibit any Masonic emblem upon any . sign, flag or banner, except in a
Masonic procession, nor upon any place of business or in connection with
any business advertisement ; nor use any such emblem or the word
"Mason" or the words "For Masons only" or "For Masons and their
famil ies only," or words, whether of ·similar or different import, constituting an appeal based on Masonic membership or relationship, or
make any reference thereto in connection with any private business or
any insurance or other business enterprise whatever, whether the same
be conducted by a stock company, a mutual company, association or individual, for the purpose of soliciting patronage; and any Mason who
shall accept employment with, or solicit business for, any person, asso- ·
ciation, company or corporation violating the provisions hereof, shall be
. guilty of un-Masonic conduct ; provided that this section shall not apply
to Masonic books, journals or periodicals, or to legitimate trade in
Masonic supplies, but any Freemason engaged in the business of publishing any Masonic book, journal or periodical who permits the printing
of any advertisement in any such publication, using the word "Mason,"
or words "For Masons only" or "For Masons and their families," or any
other term, sign or symbol of Freemasonry for any commercial or other
business enterprise, the use of which is prohibited hereby, shall be guilty
of un-Masonic conduct.

New Zealand (1926) :

. . (Grand Master) : I have no hesitation in saying that the fault must
he 111 our system. We must have failed somehow to impress upon our
brethren t~e fundamental object of F reemasonry, which I take to be
the mo~ld.mg of characters, which will, by the force of their example
and their mfluence, spread a light in the world and draw mankind closer
together. We may have. become too stereotyped in our Lodge working,
have devoted too much time to ceremonial, have paid too much attention
to the outside of the cup and platter, and forgotten that it is to the
heart that we must make our appeal. It may be that in our lectures
papers and addresses we have become too abstruse and idealistic and
have neglected to point out the practical application of our ideals.'
Philippine Islands (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : With regard to our amendment as. to non-attendance at Lodge and making a penalty therefor,
the Chairman Correspondence Committee of Manitoba states as follows :
"Youth jumps in where angels fear to tread, and so we find this
fourteen years' old Grand Lodge g rabbing the bovine male by the
horns an.d now the non-attender in that Jurisdiction is grouped with the
brother m arrears of dues. P ossibly one is as bad as the other but
'
some things have to be left to a man's conscience."
We might say, for the benefit of the review of Manitoba, that this
amendment has made trouble for the Fraternity and has not increased
~he attendance. Human nature is peculiar, particularly when endeavor
is made to force one to do certain things which should be left to the
sentiment and personal desire of the individual. No real permanent good
ever comes from an endeavor to force one to be good.
South Carolina (1927):

ATTENDANCE

(Grand Master) : The cry that goes up from every lodge is: "How
can we secure better attendance?"

Non-attendance at Masonic meetings continues to be one of the
great problems receiving attention in practically all of the Jurisdictions. Many members retain their membership and regularly pay
their dues who are never in attendance or take part in the active work
. of the Lodge. The rush of modern business life, change in living
conditions brought about by the automobile, movies and the radio,
are all contributing factors. A comfortable room, an interesting book
or magazine, and touch with the entire world through the radio, has a
stronger appeal for the average person than attendance at a Lodge
meeting, marked only by the constant repetition of Ritual, a handful
of Brethren with no interest in common other than mere attendance.

The answer to this question lies in the eradication of the idea that our
Lodges are organized for fun and frolic. Emphasis must be laid on the
fact that we are engaged in the serious and solemn work of making
better men out of. our members. Fun and frivolity makes such a wide
appeal, and so many of our members fail to see in our beautiful ceremo?i~s anything. but an opportunity to make sport of the candidate.

Iowa (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of
Wisconsin (1927) ruled it was "a violation of Masonic Law for a Master
Mason to place a Masonic emblem on the radiator of his automobile."
But the Jurisprudence Committee disagreed with him and the Grand
Lodge sustained the Committee. · It seems to us that the question is
open to argument.
If the Masonic emblem were placed on a car which was obviously a
business car, such as a delivery wagon or truck, we could readily see
how the action would amount to Masonic advertising. But where it is
placed on the family car or a pleasure car it would seem as though
that rule would not hold.

Kansas (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The writer most heartily
agrees with the Committee on Jurisprudence (Wisconsin, 1927) and even
goes further in questioning the mental capacity of one who claims to be
a member of the Masonic Fraternity who will have the poor taste to
place a Masonic emblem on an automobile. It would be just as consistent to place such emblem on the front window of a grocery store,
bank or any place of business, profession, or otherwise. The thinking
Mason is justified in questioning the motive of one who has such a
limited conception of the purposes of our time-honored Institution as
to use its symbols in this manner, as it means nothing more or less
than small knowledge and large pretentions.

North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A slight deviation from the
main thought of the above comes in the "State of Automobiles" when
it is ruled that it is a Masonic offense to wear the Square and Compass
on your radiator. It is made plain that one may wear said Squa~e
and Compass on his coat lapel, for that is personal adornment; but the
Michigan law denies that anything on the radiator of your car can be
construed personal adornment, and the Grand Master recommends

Masonry and are not supposed to comprehend the Michigan notion as to
such things; but, really, we are glad that the North Carolina law
·sort of contemplates that a man may put some of his personal adornments on his radiator as well as on his coat.
The question of the propriety of using Masonic radiator emblems ,
comes up again in Wisconsin. The Grand Master rules that a Masonic
radiator emblem is not inconsistent with the principles of Masonry, but
the Committee on Jurisprudence rules against him and is sustained.
The point is made that it is an easy step from an emblem on the
radiator of the car to an emblem over the door of the butcher, and so
forth. Just at this time we are not in a mood for lengthy exposition or
argumentation, and shall confine ourselves to the remark that we do not
discover Masonic emblems commercialized in North Carolina, nor Masonry in any form
Having just a few hours ago read that the Grand Master of

holding that it is proper to use such an emblem on said radiator, adding,
"unless it is used for commercial or other business ' enterprises." Of
course, the radiator emblem is less often capitalized for private gain or
advantage than the lapel emblem. To stop entirely the abuse of Masonic
emblems, we must follow in the footsteps of the English, among whom
. the use of any Masonic emblem outside of the lodge room is un-Masonic.
Sometimes we think this is the best plan, anyhow.

Iowa (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : In our judgment a Lodge
should go just a bit slow about establishing an official lodge publication, for

the paper comes to be pretty much of a Lodge boss.
Massachusetts (1927):
(Grand Master): I am strongly of the opinion that some form of regular publication, in which information of the policies and activities of the
Grand Lodge and of the Fraternity can be made available to the officers and
members of the Craft, would be a most valuable adjunct to our educational
work and would tend toward a better mutual understanding of our problems
and our aims.
There is a growing desire on the part of officers, past and present,
and of many interested Brethren for a greater knowledge of Masonry
and a closer contact with an understanding of the functioning of the
Grand Lodge and of the Fraternity in all its departments and activities.
A serious obstacle in the way of conveying this information is our lack
of any regular and adequate medium of communication.
Grand Lodge approved an effort .to obtain a sufficient number
of subscriptions to the Master Mason to secure the publication of a
Massachusetts edition thereof ; such Massachusetts edition to consist of
the regular edition of the Master Mason plus sixteen pages devoted
entirely to material furnished by this Grand Lodge and dealing with
the affairs of this Jurisdiction, and to be sent to all Massachusetts
subscribers and no others.
Minnesota (1928):
Your committee to which was referred the matter of a monthly
publication, recommended by Grand Master Albert F. Pray, said publication to contain at least sixteen pages, and to be sent to every member
of the Fraternity in Minnesota, have had the matter under serious
consideration.
The Grand Lodge of Iowa prints such a monthly Bulletin and sends
it to five officers of each Lodge, the Grand Officers and such of the

REPORT ON CORRESPONDl<.il'ICE

14

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

membership as are interested enough to make request for it. From
the Grand Secretary we learn that they circulate 8,000 copies to about
10 per cent of its membership. The Bulletin is usually 32 pages, but is
sometimes larger. The cost of the publication for the fiscal year ending
in June, 1926, was $5,760.05 and for the same period of the year before,
$5,757.08. So this may be taken as the average cost of a thirty-two-page
publication of 8,000 copies published monthly.
The committee has also secured information from the Grand Lodge
of South Dakota, which publishes a similar Bulletin quarterly. The
plan of distribution is practically the same as in Iowa. They circulate
1,200 copies, and the committee is informed that the cost is about $100
per month plus the postage of 1Y, cents each.
From the Grand Jurisdiction of North Dakota we learn that its
Bulletin is published bi-monthly, omitting certain numbers in the summer,
with practically the same distribution as in Iowa and South Dakota.
The Grand Secretary figures that the cost to the Grand Lodge does
not exceed $700.
The proposition before your committee is a somewhat different one
inasmuch as it involves the publishing of an edition of approximately
60,000 copies and their distribution to the entire membership of ·the
State. Such information as we have. been able to gather as to the cost
of such a publication is approximately $10,000 per year plus the postage,
which, if the publication could be entered as second-class matter, as it
could be for the most part, no doubt, would be 1 cent per pound for all
copies circulated outside the city of publication.
Besides this, an initial expense would have to be incurred for
mailing equipment, which cost the Brethren of Iowa $1,000. This expense
would be materially increased in our case, as by the plan suggested, the
edition of the Minnesota Bulletin would be 52,000 greater, approximately.
We understand that new plates for mailing equipment cost from 2Y, to 3
cents each, so that here is an expenditure of $1,300, probably. The
changes and additions would cost, stated very conservatively, $150 per
year-very likely more, judging from experiences of other mailing lists.
From the best information your committee has been able to obtain,
the cost to the Grand Lodge of the publication proposed, including cuts
and illustrative matter from time to time, would be $14,000 per year,
not taking into consideration any salary for the editor. Such a publication to be of value should be well edited, and it is doubtful if the services
of a qualified man could be secured permanently without compensation.
Such positions command from $1,500 to $3,000 per year.
Your committee was also instructed to inquire as to the possibility
of securing advertisi~g . N one of the publications referred to above
carry any advertising, and the committee has not been able to secure

15

much data on that matter. However, it is believed that, with a circulation of 60,000, some advertising could be secured, and a rate of $1 or $1.25
per inch might be asked, and, of course, the revenue derived from that
source would depend on the number of inches that could be sold. Your
committee believes that the carrying of advertising detracts from the
dignity of such a publication and that, if the Grand Lodge should
embark in such an enterprise, it would recommend that it be done
without advertising matter in its columns.
Your committee admits that, if such a publication could be financed
by the .Grand Lodge, without interfering with its benevolences, such as
the Masonic Home, it would be a useful avenue of information, which
the three jurisdictions referred to concede their publications to be.
From an entire survey of the situation, your committee believes that
the time is not ripe for such an ambitious program as this recommendation of Grand Master Pray contemplates and, therefore, reluctantly
declines to recommend it to the Grand Lodge at this time.

CANDIDATES
Reading the Reports of Committees on Grievances and Appeals
in various Jurisdictions, as well as the statistical tables of losses
through causes inclines one to the belief that there must be stricter
requirements as far as petitioners are concerned and a ·more thorough
investigation. 'Various methods have been tried to remedy this
trouble. In some cases it has been curbed by requiring separate
ballots each before each de.g ree, together with a waiting period between the conferring of the same. The most practical one we believe
is the appearance of the petitioner, together with those who recommend him, before a Committee composed of the Officers of the Lodge
and Past Masters or others competent to judge, for a personal investigation before the presentation of the application to the Lodge itself,
and the reference to a Committee. This is particularly true in large
cities, and if made mandatory on every Lodge it would work for the
ultimate good of our Institution. Too often the average Investigation
Committee resolves questions of doubt in favor of the individual rather
than for the general good of Masonry itself.

District of Columbia (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The nation adopted gold
for its money standard because it had value, not that we wanted to give ·
it value. The recommender of a petition and the committee to investigate
ought to select or recommend a candidate who has value, not that we
