quite a number who seek initiation into our Order have the Shrine as
their ultimate object. How to get there by the shortest and most direct
route seems to be their concern. The question is, "How do they
get that way?" What inoculates them with that bug?
I am of the opinion that they get the idea from us who are Shriners
by the emblems we wear. Very few brothers who join the Shrine can
resist the temptation to wear the Shrine emblem to the exclusion of the
Square and Compass. This, I think, is a mistake, and gives the idea to
those on the outside that we do not consider the Blue Lodge as important.
When Dr. Kuehn, the General Grand High Priest of the General
Grand Chapter, visited us five years ago he said that he had always
given the lapel of his coat to the Square and Compass in preference to
all of the other Masonic jewels ·or emblems he was entitled to wear.
I believe that if we would all do this we would soon create a different
attitude toward the Blue Lodge among ourselves, as well as among the
profanes.

Florida (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence -Committee): The censure is reported
of the proposer, seconder and committee of inquiry of a candidate who
was excluded from the Lodge for non-payment of dues within nineteen
months after being raised. The Grand Master held that they could not
have made proper investigation into the candidate's ability to meet his
financial obligations. In another instance a Brother belonging to two
Lodges was suspended because he proposed a candidate first in one
l!.odge, then when objections were raised withdrew the petition and
proposed him in the other Lodge. This is one of the instances of the
unfortunate working of dual membership, but this dual membership
made responsibility easier to fix than it would have been if the Brethren
had gotten someone else who was a member of the second Lodge to
propose the name, as shown in this instance by the fact that the seconder,
who was not a member of both Lodges, and the committee of the second
Lodge was not found responsible.

New Zealand (1927):
(Grand . Master): Some weeks ago one of our more learned and
distinguished Brethren drew attention to the fact that during the last
thirty years or so the stamp of candidates for admission to the Craft .
had in one respect greatly changed. Formerly they were, as a rule, men
of almost middle age; now they are much younger. From this he
deduced tw'o inferences: .First, that care in the selection of candidates
was more than ever important, and, secondly, that very careful instruction in the ideals and traditions of the Craft was essential.

18

REPOR'l' ON CORRESPONDENCl!;

The matter is of great importance. It is undoubtedly the fact that
many young men are now presenting themselves for admission, and a
glance around most of our Lodges confirms the fact that during the
last few years the standard of age of our younger Brethren is considerably lower than formerly. There is no reason to be otherwise than
thankful for this. The events of the last ten or fifteen years have
very probably made young men more thoughtful than formerly, and if
they find in Freemasonry something which appeals to them, it is not
only natural, but eminently satisfactory. But, on the other hand, it is
well to remember that young men are always impressionable and sometimes impulsive. They are m~re apt than older men to be moved by
curiosity in the first place, and perhaps to be less stable and persevering
when the novelty of a new experience has worn off. Of this danger we
ni.ust not lose sight. We of this generation have the great responsibility
of handing on the torch to those who are to come after us, and it
depends mainly on us and on the standard which we set that the light
of Freemasonry may continue to shine undimmed through the succeeding
generation.
North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We have seen Masons
poking fun at the candidates, drawing on their imagination for fool
suggestions and paving the way for a false start of a new Mason. We
saw a candidate once who had been told by some practical joker that
he must do certain · things in a certain way "when they let him get
inside the Lodge," and a solemn initiatory ceremony was practically
ruined thereby. There used to be a good old term in the psychology
of twenty years ago which we called "the Apperceptive Mass." The
Doctrine of the Apperceptive Mass teaches that any new experiences
adapt themselves in our minds in terms of the experiences into which
they fit themselves: that the effect of any new experience may be
changed by changing the associated experiences into which it is projected.
By this doctrine, the ceremony of initiation is highly colored for good
or otherwise by the experiences which precede it. This scribe believes
that there ought to be some sort of · mental preparation of every candidate prior to his initiation, by something to read, by a conversation
with some wise Mason or by some other means. Certainly he ought
not to enter the doors of Masonry with the impression from others
whom he believes to be Masons that, whenever he takes a step, the next
one is going to lead him into some sort of humiliating horseplay. They
do not do things that way in British Masonry, and the attitude of a
British Mason toward his institution is very beautiful, indeed.

Oklahoma (1928):

(Grand Master): In my judgment, the welfare of Masonry will be
best served, the interest of the candidate promoted and the dignity of
Masonry will be preserved if we do not make our laws, regulations
and customs flexible to the personal favor or desire of the candidate
or of the lodge. There should be a real emergency existing, and not a
merely imaginary one. For the last few years Masonry has been at a
low ebb, and there may be many contributing causes for this ; but most
of the leaders of Masonrv are agreed that the inactivity of a large
number of the individual Masons, in things Masonic, is caused by the
innumerable dispensations that have been issued in the past, and the
Brethren have not been adequately instructed and educated in the principles of Masonry and, therefore, were not sufficiently prepared to carry
out the aims and purposes of our fraternity, and many of them have
become drones in the hive of Masonry. I am informed by the officers
of several lodges that a large number of these Brethren have been
suspended for non-payment of dues.
Utah (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Lodge funds are not inexhaustible, and our observation convinces us that more and more lodge
treasuries are being drawn upon to relieve the necessities of their members
or certain of them. We are inclined to think that the opinion is gaining
ground quite generally, that Masonry is a beneficial order, and will take
care of anyone in its membership who may not be able to take care of himself, and this, even, under conditions which hardly justify such expenditure.

CLUBS
The development ·Of the Masonic Club has removed some of the
objections to this form of a'ctivities. Clubs are popular and fill a place
in the life of the average man. The social contact, which is the basis
of Club life and which unfortunately is overlooked in a large number
of cases in the Blue Lodge, is supplied by a well regulated Masonic
Club. It puts into practice one of the fundamental teachings of Masonry; to-wit, Fraternalism.

have perhaps been violated.

Idaho (1927):
(Gran,d Master): I feel this desire is a laudable one on the part of
these brethren, which would enable them to get together in their respective
communities and enjoy a program rendered for the benefit of the Craft,
bringing them together on a common ground to fraternize and indulge in
Masonic Fellowship permissible under such circumstances.
I feel that the matter of organizing Masonic Clubs should be referred
to the Master of the Lodge having jurisdiction, and if such requests meet
with the approbation of that Lodge, and the proposed club follows the
advice and guidance of the Master, much good can be accomplished, it
being understood the intent and purpose of such a club is for social and
study purposes only, and have no right to carry on any of the rights and
privileges granted a regularly constituted Lodge.

Oklahoma (1928):
(Grand Master): In every stage of civilization men have enjoyed
eating together. Eating together is a token of friendship. I do not know
of any place where men can get so close together as around the festal
board. I realize that we are going at such a rapid pace we hardly know
our next door neighbor, and we do not have time to get acquainted with
our brethren.
Through the Masonic Dinner Club we are brought in close contact
with each other, and we learn to know each other as men, as Masons, and
as brethren, and unite ourselves in promoting the interest of our noble
fraternity. In addition to the social contact much benefit is to be derived
from the hearing of various instructive talks. This branch has created a
wonderful interest and a great many of the lodges are emphasizing the
dinner club.
Washington (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A request from a Masonic
Club for assistance from the Grand Lodge of Alabama opens up a matter
which needs ventilation. Frequently we see so-called Masonic Clubs
located at some college, or near some United States Hospital, asking for
financial aid to build suitable club rooms, or for the maintenance of said
club. This whole question of the propriety of establishing outside organizations, such as clubs, by Grand Lodges is opened up by this request. It
is all very nice for students at our Universities to ask the Masons for
money to establish or to help establish a suitable meeting place for those
students who have already become Masons, but how about the fellow who
has to put up his hard-earned dollars for such a purpose?
,
Student life, if rightly conducted, is too full of more important matters connected with college work to really allow the student to become
active in such a club organization. It is evident also that there are Masonic
Lodges near all institutions of learning, where such students as desire can
gain the association which they need, and it is not necessary to organize
a Masonic club in order to do so.
The matter of Masonic Clubs connected with United States Veterans'
Hospitals is another matter. However, we have noticed in our experience
with such hospitals, that the government of the United States is spending

millions for these soldiers, and that the service rendered the veterans is
of a more substantial character than the great majority of the inmates
ever enjoyed before. In one hospital of that character, the largest, I believe, in the United States, there are on an average about 1000 inmates
present, and it takes about 2000 attendants to care for them.
It is very nice for these veterans to be helped by the Masons, and we
are not objecting because they are veterans, but we do think that there are
other members of the Masonic Fraternity who have just as clear a claim
on the Institution as they have, and who get very little attention. We know
of no set of individuals who have had the same generous treatment from
the public as have these veterans. Beside what is being lavished upon them
by the government, the Red Cross has exercised itself in their behalf for
the past few years in giving them extra luxuries which none of the rest
of us, or very few at least, can afforc;l. Such an attitude toward any class
of individuals will eventually pauperize the best character in the world,
and rob it of its independence.
CO-ORDINATE BODIES
Organizations having as a prerequisite membership in the Masonic Fraternity are not commanding as much attention as heretofore.
One of the Grand Lodges who established a rule requiring a time
limit between the time for receiving the Third Degree and petitioning
for membership in such organizations repealed the same. Two Grand
Lodges have placed a ban on member.ship in other organizations 'than
those now already in existence in the respective State. We hold no
brief for the Member of any ·organization who violates the teachings
or laws of Masonry or the law of the land through membership in any
co-ordinate body. Impressing on Masons through education the
obligation they owe to the parent body, or if necessary through
Masonic discipline will do more to curb excess enthusiasm or offences
than legislation.
We believe that the incentive for membership · of the average
Mason is based upon a desire for sociability, instruction or education,
not furnished through the Blue Lodge. In those countries where
Masonry is based upon the system of combining all Masonic activities
in the Blue Lodge we find none of these organizations. We think it
unfair to designate associations composed exclusively of Masons as
"warts," "barnacles," etc. If Masons or members of the "higher
degrees" or "playgrounds in Masonry" overstep the bounds of propriety, the fault is due either to the individual himself or lack of
education by the parent organization. The first can be remedied only
·by a stricter selection of candidates, and the second by the Blue Lodge
itself in social, educational and fraternal lines.

( C om~ittee on Grand Master's Address) : In these days when we

their membership on Master Masons, it is right that every Master Mason
be reminded of the force and effect of his Grand Lodge and of his obligations as a Master Mason. The Grand Lodge is not called upon to justify
the existence of any other organization or body. These other organizations or bodies must justif'y their own existence, and as a part of that

of Masonry as just outlined with respect to the Grand Lodge. Those
fundamental principles, or we may say the basis or heart of Masonry,
may not be compromised no matter how good the arguments or desires from
other sources may be.

My reasons for this are, that there is a vast difference between a
Masonic organization, and an organization of Masons. The Grand Lodge
has authority over the first, but none, as it is, over the second, although in
many instances they are organized for the purpose, to some extent, of
trading on the name and influence of the Fraternity. The heads of their
organizations at times attempt to speak with Masonic authority, although
representing only a small fraction of the membership. The conduct of their
affairs is not always. in line with Masonic principles, and their financial
difficulties are not in frequently alleviated by resort to lotteries, raffles, and
other money-making forms of entertainment which the Masonic institution
cannot countenance. Some of them undertake large building projects,
incur too much indebtedness, and become bankrupt, and their bills go
unpaid, all of which tends to impair the good name of the Fraternity, and
to erroneous impressions on the part of undiscriminating and uninformed
non-members.

Z6

In order to prevent the further multiplication of these hangers on, an
Edict was issued, early in the present year, forbidding membership in
organizations hereafter to be established, which require Masonic affiliation
as a prerequisite to membership therein, as follows:
Whereas, The establishment and continued existence of certain organizations or associations which require Masonic affiliation as a prerequisite
to or qualification for membership therein has not inured to the benefit of
Freemasonry; and
Whereas, The first duty of the Brethren is to this Grand Lodge, and
the divided allegiance to which they subject themselves by membership in
such organizations, creates a condition inimical to Freemasonry, and in
violation of the Laws, Usages and Customs of the Fraternity, in this
Jurisdiction ; and
Whereas, The Grand Lodge possesses, retains and exercises the right
to restrict and control the use of their Masonic affiliation, made or attempted to be made by its members.
Therefore, I, William M. Hamilton, Right Worshipful Grand Master
of Masons in Pennsylvania, by virtue of the powers and authorities in
me vested, do hereby order, direct and declare, that from and after the
date hereof, it shall be unlawful for the members of the Lodges in this
Jurisdiction to become associated, or in any way identified, with organizations hereafter to be established, which require Masonic affiliation as a condition necessary to membership therein, unless and until authority from
this Grand Lodge, for the creati.on of such organization, shall first have
been obtained.
This Edict shall be read at the next Stated Meeting of your Lodge,
copied in full in the minutes, and a copy thereof sent to each member of
the Lodge with the notice for the next Stated Meeting following its
receipt.
Given under my hand and seal, at the City of Philadelphia, this
Nineteenth day of March, A. D., 1927, A. L., 5927.
William M. Hamilton, Grand Master.
It is a gratifying fact that this Edict has been received by the members
of the Fraternity with practically unanimous approbation, indicating that
the basic esteem and reverence for the Lodge and for its perpetuation
unhampered by entangling alliances, is deep rooted in the hearts of the
Brethren, and that they are ready to yield willing obedience to provisions
which tend to preserve its integrity and well-being.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : In reading the proceedings
of the various Grand Lodges, we have come across many very interesting
matters which must eventually influence the action of the Grand Lodges
themselves. Among them we find the matter of extraneous bodies which
have attached themselves, at least in the minds of the public, to the
Masonic Institution. It matters not under what name these bodies masquerade, the very fact that they take their membership solely from those
who have taken certain Masonic degrees, is enough to brand such bodies
as Masonic in the view taken by the outside world. During the past fifty
years there have grown up a multitude of extraneous organizations of
this character, from Masonic Clubs to the Shrine and Grotto, all of which
are presumably taking their members, directly or indirectly, from Masonic
sources. Whether this is for the good of Masonry or not is a question.
In a way this reminds the student of the widespread agitation for so-called
Masonic Degrees which occurred in the eighteenth century. They seemed
to spring up almost over night, and their relationship to the Masonic
Institution was as tenuous as that which now exists between the Grotto
and Masonic Lodge. A general sifting out and a remodeling of the
remainder had to be undertaken before anything like order came out of
the chaos thus created.
The repetition of this craze for new degrees is causing alarm among
the wiser members of the Craft, and we find Grand Masters, and even
Grand Lodges, issuing their complaints over this condition of affairs, and
it begins to look as though some drastic action would become necessary
in order to free the Masonic Institution from the tightening grip of
these outside organizations.
In a sense they remind us of the tropic vines which cling to the
mighty trees of the forest for support, until there comes a time when
they choke the tree to death and rise above its ruins in parasitic strength
and usurped grandeur.
It has been maintained that Masonry can not prevent any Mason
from joining these extra Masonic bodies, any more than it can prevent
its members from joining the .Odd Fellows, the Knights of Pythias or
even the Church.
While this is true, yet we wish to call attention to the fact that,
when any such organization causes its members to violate their vows
as Masons, or to participate in acts which are under the ban of Grand
Lodges, such members at once become amenable to Masonic law and can
be dealt with personally for such acts.
The mere fact of belonging to an organization which allows or abets
the violation of Masonic law, or permits acts which are not permitted by
civil law, does not free any Mason from his allegiance to his Lodge nor
free him from his vows as a Mason.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

One Grand Lodge has found it necessary to order Masonic trials for
offenses against Masonic morality, and the Brethren so tried were found
guilty. The fact that the offense was committed under the guise of
another organization did not hinder or even inconvenience· the action of
the Lodge trying them.
The sad part of the whole matter lies in the fact that at the next
election of officers of the extraneous body, the principal offender was
re-elected to the highest office in the gift of the body. On the surface this
looks like a direct protest against any iii.terference from Masonic sources
against anything which the parasitic body wishes to do.
This attitude of Masons toward the highest authority known to
Masonry, is a sad · commentary upon the character of those who were
responsible for this practical defiance of the authority of Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master, in speaking of this matter says in part:
"Such lack of true allegiance to the sovereignty of Grand Lodge and
obedience to its constituted authority, which is the solemn obligation
of every Mason, may not pass without notice, and should be the serious
concern of any brother who has permitted himself to fall into such an
unfortunate habit of thinking. When obedience to the laws and regulations fails, and when Grand Lodge fails to enforce its authority, the
Institution will become a rope of sand, and the decay of Freemasonry is
at hand."
If Masons fail to remember their obligations and insist on violating
their Masonic vows, then it will be necessary for Grand Lodges to absa"lutely take charge of the offenders and throw them out of the Fraternity.
No halfway proceedings will do. The body of Masonry must be freed
from the parasites which threaten to choke it to death; the axe must be
laid at the root of the extraneous growth and the body of Masonry freed
from its encircling folds.
The above is written in sorrow over the necessity for harsh words,
and we recognize that this is delicate ground for any one to tread upon,
but we can not remain quiet when we see the danger, and realize that
it is imminent.
The danger is made more serious by the fact that the recent rush for
Masonic degrees leaves us in doubt as to the quality of some of the
material which we are now trying to assimilate, and the difficulty in
educating a crowd of candidates in the short time allowed. Again the
haste to get through the basic body in order to get to the "Play-ground;'
as some have called it, is a sure sign of lack of appreciation of the Masonic
Institution as such; and "in an age where commercialism has run rampant
through all ethics ; when the church has lost its hold upon the minds of
thinking men; when science is concentrating its every effort upon material
things; when the archaeologist is discovering the remains of primitive

man in strata of the earth's crust, which geologists tell us must be hundreds
of thousands of years old; when atheistic teaching is tainting our schools
and colleges ; when the physical body of man is be_ing gl~rified on the
athletic field and in the boudoir; when all culture 1s turnmg from the
spiritual to the material ideals ; it begins to look gloomy and dark for a
future of sane and honest religious belief."
The only hope that we can see is for Masonry, based as it is upon
the doctrine of monotheism and immortality, to hold fast to the eternal
verities and free itself from all entangling encumbrances. If we can
do this'. may it not be probable that, even under this discouraging set
of facts which are now features of modern thought Masonry may yet
become the rallying ground for the remnant of God fearing and reverent
men? As one Brother has graphically declared, "Can it be possible that,
our great Institution is yet to be the oasis in the desert of modernism
about which the forces of conservative religious teaching is to rally?"
In writing the above we have quoted freely from the words of Grand
Masters, of Reviewers, and others who are deeply interested in the question of keeping pure the fountain of Masonic ideals ; and while we belong
to some of these outside organizations, yet we feel deeply the danger
which seems to be growing out of the unwise action of enthusiastic
Brethren, and feel that it is only necessary to call the attention of the
average Mason to the suicidal tendency of all such untoward a~ts ~s have
been condemned so liberally, for corrective measures to be applied m those
organizations themselves. This question is one that is o~tstanding in its
importance, for Masonry is getting the blame for the actions of some _of
these "playful" Masons, and we see in the public press statements which
cause many a blush to come to the honest m~mber of the Fraternity.
It will not do for us to condone and forgive, because of the effect
that is being produced upon the public mind. Either the corrective m~a­
sures must be applied within the offending bodies, or they must be discarded by Masonry.

CRIMES AND OFFENSES
One of the sections of the Proceedings of a Grand Lodge that
a Reviewer must peruse with sorrow is the Report of the Committee
on Grievances and · Appeals, and that section of the Grand Master's
address which deals with the necessity for Masonic discipline. The
notes and criticism on the Proceedings reviewed on this subject when
assembled total nearly twenty pages of excerpts. They call attention
not only to the violation of Masonic law, but also the law of the land.
Criticism has been levied at those Jurisdictions which have
adopted the rule that a final judgment of conviction in a Court of law
for crime ipso facto terminates Masonic membership of the wrongdoer. Perhaps the best answer to this is that in a numiber of Jurisdictions the Grand Master has been obliged to revoke the Charters
of Lodges because they ·w ould not erase from their membership list,
through a Masonic trial, men who were notoriously unfitted or were
actually confined in the State prison. In some Jurisdictions there
are members in good standing who are such only by reason of a misdirected sense of charity or forbearance. Masonry cannot excuse
offences against the recognized laws of God and man. In Masonry,
as in every day life, the criminal or transgressor occupies the front

page while usually the decent law abiding, hard-working citizen does
not break into print. While it is the exception that proves the rule
in these cases, still in most instances the organization is judged by the
exception.
Alabama (1927):
(Grand Master ) : To the discredit of the Craft, it not infrequently
happens that the names of persons serving terms in prison after conviction
of crime are still carried on the roll of Lodges as Masons in good standing.
If our Constitution did not prevent, I would recommend that conviction in
court of a misdemeanor should operate ipso facto as a suspension, and
conviction of a felony should operate ipso facto as expulsion from the
Lodge unless the Brother within thirty days demands a trial by the Lodge.
British Columbia (1927):
(Chail-man Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master (Montana) recommended the enactment of an amendment, or addition to the
Code, by the terms of which a Brother convicted of a felony in a State
or Federal court would ipso facto be "suspended from all rights and
privileges of Masonry."
This is one of the most outrageous pieces of legislation that could
be enacted by a Grand Lodge. The Lord Chancellor, in Iolanthe, informs
us that
"The law is the true embodiment
Of every thing that's excellent,"
and we all have the greatest respect and regard fo r our judiciary, but
to make a Mason's membership in his Lodge contingent upon the decision
of the members of a jury, of whom possibly not one is a member of the
Craft, is asking rather too much. To support his recommendation, the
Grand Master said :
· "Note : -We have members of Montana Lodges at the present time
serving jail and penitentiary terms whom ' we are obliged to call Brothers.
Lodge Officers claim to me that it would be embarrassing to give them
Lodge trials or ·that .it would unnecessarily embarrass families. I ask why
they should be given Lodge trials after a jury of 12 men have found them
guilty."
We cannot believe that a Lodge or a family would be caused any
additional embarrassment by the t rial of one who was already serving time
in the penitentiary, and from our point of view the Grand Master's
recommendation looks like the passing of the buck.

(Grand Master) : Early in the year, I received a letter fro'? a Mast~r
f Lodge soliciting my help for a Brother who had become involved m
~ c~urt pr~ceedings through an automobile acc~dent which resulted in the
death of a woman. The request was th~,t I m1~ht help our B.rother who
"had been traveling in a foreign country. I replied as follows ·

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

35

"Our Grand Secretary .has forwarded your letter to me in which you
describe the plight in which Brother - - - finds himself. I am sure it
must be a trying experience for him, especially as the death of a woman
is involved in the unfortunate accident. But I do not see wherein Masonry
can be of any.help to him in his dilemma. If the accident was not due to
his negligence, I have no doubt the courts will exonerate him. But if he
was criminally negligent, and his carelessness has resulted in such a tragedy, what possible influence could the Grand Master of Masons in Maine
exert, to secure his immunity from the law? I can conceive of nothing that
would be any more detrimental to our Fraternity, than to have the
impression prevail that the Craft could or would exert any such unwholesome influence. Masonry does not stand for any attempt at interference
with the law of the land, or for any effort to exert an influence to bring
about a favorable decision for anyone involved in dealings with that law.
We must never make of Masonry even the slightest attempt to influence
the deliberations of the courts of the land, and if any of our Brethren
have any thought whatever that the Craft can be used for any such
purpose, the sooner their minds are disabused of the idea, the better it
will be for them and for the Fraternity. Sincerely I hope that our Brother
may be able to clear himself of any violation of law which brought about
such a tragedy, and may soon be able to proceed to his home and vocation.
If he needs testimonials of his personal character and worth, why not have
his friends of your neighborhood, who know him and know his worth,
write them for him. But do not try to bring any Masonic influence to
bear in the matter. At the very outset, that would be un-Masonic, and
unworthy of the great name we bear as Masons."
Any attempt by Masonry to interfere with the due process of
law in order to assist any member of the Fraternity is almost unthinkable. A person of sufficient intelligence to be made a Mason, who
has been admonished in every degree to be obedient to the laws of the
country in which he resides should be less entitled to our consideration
than one who has never had the benefit of Masonic instruction. Masonry
must and Masons should conform and submit to the civil laws.

The opinion is quite prevalent among non-Masons that Freemasons
are bound to assist one another to shield from punishment in all cases

delusion.

Nevada (1928):
(Grand Master) : I am also pleased to note the progress made in our
state by the Order of De Mo!ay. This shows that a good many well
meaning boys are becoming interested along fraternal lines. In my estimation we as Masons should encourage them in their work and do all we
can to see that they reach their majority through the channels of right
living.
(Grand Orator) : Then I say to you Brethren-One of the most important labors you can perform is to do what you can for the boys who
are coming along.
Some jurisdictions frown on !:Joys' work in connection with the Masonic .
order. I take issue with them, brethren. Millions of dollars are spent
annually for the education of the youth of our country in what you might
call mass production. The trouble with this system is that each boy is an
individual, and it is hard to mould them all . into one system by training.
He needs the personal touch, outside of his school work, to give him the
right balance.
You often hear the expression, Masonry is not a reform school. Even
so, Masonic work among boys is not of a reform character, but more in
the nature of guidance. It. strikes me that, if you can bring any percentage
of boys through to clean manly living and good citizenship, who otherwise
might not be, then you have accomplished one of the duties you owe to
God, your country, your neighbor, and yourself, as a builder, fol' the
future of your country and Masonry.
North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): What is going to be the
effect upon the Masonry of the future, of the De Molay organization?
It has become quite popular in the greater part of the United States. As
a character builder, we think it deserves that popularity. Boys of the
De Molay age need to be kept away from questionable places and occupations; and they need to be kept busy. We have seen the De Molay work
conferred several times, and have been much impressed by it. We have
seen many Grand Masters' Addresses, and allusions by the presiding officers of other organizations in the Masonic system, for which we write
reviews, in which there was a warning that the Order must not be looked
upon as a Masonic kindergarten, and we have uttered this warning in
person; but somehow, we are not impressed with danger from this source.

41

Perhaps the only remark that we should make originally about it, is that
we doubt that it shall be permanent and the interest in it self-sustaining.
That which holds the interest of boys must provide for the shifting of
interest from one activity to another, easily and frequently, in a sort of
progressive cycle. The De Molay may do this now, or may later do it,
to meet the inevitable boy-psychology; but if it does not, the De Mo!ay
Order will never be able to keep itself on a permanent basis. The principle
mentioned is the great secret of the success of the Boy Scout Movement,
which has proved the correctness of the psychological principle named,
in positive way rather than in negative manner.

Washington (1927):
(Grand Master) : The De Molay organization is one that came into
existence but a few years ago. Starting in 1919, with but nine boys, the
so.ns of Masons, it has expanded into a national organization with l,500
Ch~pters and a membership in excess of 275,000. There are some 20
Chapters of this organization within our Grand Jurisdiction. Some of these
Chapters have been sponsored by Scottish .Rite Bodies, some by York Rite
Bodies, and. in a few instances, by members of symbolic Lodges, as such.
The De Molay organization draws its membership from among boys
between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one, who are the sons of Masons,
or the chums of sons of Masons. I have been very much interested in the
work of this organization and its influence upon the lives of these boys,
the more so, because of the fact that a son of my own has been active in
one ·of the Chapters. I have been privileged to attend a number of
De Molay meetings in various sections of our Grand Jurisdiction, and
have familiarized myself with the work and activities of the Chapters in
general.
I have also conferred with Brother William S. McCrea, who is the
Deputy of the Supreme Council, Order of De Molay, for the State of
\V;ashington; with Brother R. W . Huntoon, who is Bro. McCrea's
Deputy; and with Bro. Roy E. Dickerson, who is director of program and
activitie.s of the Grand Council, Order of De Molay, and who recently
visited our Jurisdiction. Moreover, I, myself, have been a member of th~. ·
advisory Council of Seattle Chapter ever since its organization.
~.From- my' contact with this organization and those in general charge
of it~•activities within the State of Washington, I am satisfied that from
the standpoint of a general influence for good it must be considered highly
beneficial. The lessons taught by its ritual are pure and noble. There is
presented, howeve.r, from the standpoint of the Masonic Institution a question to which Masons should seriously address themselves and that is, il;l
respect to the influence that the De Molay org,anization may ultimately
have upqn the Masonic Fraternity. The Chapters are being enc9.u raged to
undertake activities along lines that would be improper for our Lodges to
undertake. F9.r instance, at the state meeting held last year' it ~a,s determined that the.Chapters in this State should undertake to carry out a
program of refor~~tation. "A De Molay Forest Every Year," or something to that effect, was adopted as a slogan. Moreover, in many of the
De Molay Chapters uniformed "patrols" are being organized. The officers
of the various Chapters are working in expensive robes. The question that
is presented is, what effect will the activities in the DeMolay Chapters have
upon our Masonic Lodges when tliese boys have attained to majority and
many of them have become members of the Masonic Fraternity, as many
of them naturally will? Will not those Masons who have had De Molay
training have a desire to see the Lodges engaged in the same kind of

activities in which the De Molay Chapters are interested ? Having become
accustomed to "Patrols," gaudily robed, will they not look for similar
accoutrements in our Lodges and not finding them, will not their interest
be lessened by their absence?
The De Molay organization has, in my opinion, come to stay. Its
general beneficial influence is of such a character that Masons, generally
speaking, want it to stay, but do not the circumstances which I have mentioned call for serious thought on the part of us all ? Perhaps the only
solution that we can arrive at is the more earnestly and studiously to
·bring to the attention of Masons the traditional character of our Institution, and thus prevent the growth of an influence or tendency to deviate
from its established customs and usages. I present this matter, not with
the idea that any action should be taken or expression: made concerning
the same, but only to challenge the attention of all who are interested in
the subject to the end that we may preserve the beneficial influence of this
organization for boys and at the same time, see to it that the Institution of
Masonry, as ·such, may not ultimately be confronted with the more serious
question of how it shall preserve its Ancient Landmarks, nor witness "any
deviation from our established customs."
Wisconsin (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : A year ago a special committee ( P . E. Is., 1927) was appointed to consider the question of fostering the Order of De Molay in their province. It reported that while the
institution is an excellent one indeed, as a junior organization, that after
careful investigation it does not believe that there is a sufficiently large
constituency in the Island for the organization of the Order. That
the young people at a very early age enter college and do not remain any
length of time in the Province after they graduate from high school.
We would think the Order of De Molay would be an excellent preparation with which to send the young people out into the world. Its objects
and teachings might save some of them from destruction.
DUAL MEMBERSHIP
As we have heretofore stated, we believe the advantages of dual
membership more than counterbalances the objections to it, most of
which are theoretical. One of the largest Jurisdictions found that
over twenty per cent of its members resided outside of the Jurisdiction,
but still remained members in good standing. In another State the
figures were higher and the same average had been maintained for a
number of years. Undoubtedly in a large number of cases sentimental
reasons cause this condition. If anyone has the time, inclination and
money to also assoc.iate himself with a Lodge at his permanent place
of residence it should certainly be permitted. The most often quoted

·44

46

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

· objection to dual membership is the one that Grand Lodge would not
know its exact membership. Masonry in the Countries and States
which allow dual membership do not worry about that detail. We
are continually told that Masonry is represented by quality and not
quantity, so this aspect of the matter should not be a factor in considering the matter from a practical standpoint.
For a precedent we might refer to George Washington, who was
raised a member in Fredericksburg Lodge in Virginia and remained
a member thereof until the time of his death, although he also became
a member of Alexandria Lodge and served as its Master for two
terms.

· Kansas (1928) :·
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The question of dual or
plural membership seems to be uppermost in the minds of some of our
brethren and like many other topics of the day is considered from a sentimental rather than a business point of view. It certainly is not based upon
the success attained in the few j urisdictions practicing this system; in
· other words, such jurisdictions have no knowledge whatever as to the
number df members on their rolls, which in itself should be considered
· of great imp<>rtance to any Grand Jurisdiction. So far, the writer has
been unable to ascertain the advantages, if any, to be derived from such
practice.
With an experience of almost thirty-five years as Grand Secretary
he possesses sufficient knowledge along these lines to justify the s~te­
' ment that the adoption of this dual or plural membership proposition will
demoralize, if not totally destroy, the splendid recqrd of membership as
· now kept by the Grand Lodges of the United States and some jurisdictions outside of this country.
We readily understand that in case of sickness or impaired health one
seeks relief through a physician or treatment through other sources to
remedy the ailment, and it would therefore be extremely foolish to call
for this help if we were enjoying the best of health and were physically
and mentally ·properly functioning. Why does not the same theory apply
. concerning this proposed dual or plural membership proposition?
At this day, in all affairs in life-commercial, financial, professional,
'educational or otherwise-statistics and correct account ing are indispensable. The day of a haphazard system has passed and it is no less important
that in Masonry we should have not only a correct accounting in the fiscal
departments, but also an equally correct accounting of the membership.
With no disposition to prolong this subject the writer will offer but
few comments.
In the earliest General Regulations, those of 1723, it was specifically
provided that no brother shall belong to more than one Lodge within the
. Bills of Mortality. This Regulation, however, was confined only to Lodges
h~ England within a certain geographic district. The custom, however, fell
into disuse later ori and from that time until. the present the United Grand
Lo.dge of England has been absolutely unable to furnish any authentic
fig1,1res on their membership.
'The practice . of dual membership is followed in the Grand Jurisdictions of Ireland, Scotland and several others, none of which possess
any system of tabulating their membership; indeed, it would be impossible
for them to do so when we take into consideration the privilege granted
members to join several lodges.

Illinois (1927):
(Chairman Conespondcnce Committee): The Committee on Dual
Membership (New York, 1927) called attention to the fact that there is
no prohibition against dual or plural membership anywhere outside of the
U. S. except in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick; also that
dual membership was abandoned in South Carolina in 1876, in Texas in
1869, and that Maryland investigated the subject and decided against it
in 1888. The committee, however, is of the opinion that the arguments
in favor of dual or plural membership ·o utlay those against it. Such membership is allowable in Massachusetts, Delaware, Rhode Island, Tennessee,
Virginia, and Wyoming. The committee recommended that plural membership be allowed both in and out of the state and that the Book of Constitutions be so amended.

The writer has noted that in practically alt cases where .this system
· is advocated the promoters are defending it on the basis that it will do
no harm.
One writer ridicules the idea that a member might hold office in several Lodges and thereby have an advantage in voting in Grand Lodge.
Under the system of dual mentbership why should a brother not bold
offices in several Lodges and be thereby entitled to more than one vote in
the Grand Lodge?
It is further argued that where a brother is a member of several
Lodges his suspension or expulsion would apply in all. We rise to answer
this by asking a question : How would the other Lodges recehre this
information, not knowing in what other Lodges the brother held membe.rship? Further, how many Lodges would receive this information even
if they knew where the brother's several memberships were held, Vo1hen
you take into consid.e ration the carelessness of the average Secretary?
The advocates of this system likewise claim that the practice of dual
membership would increase the attendance of Lodges rather than have
the opposite effect. Taking into consideration the average attendance at
Lodge Communications today we leave the question of the judgment of
such advocates to the thinking Mason and those who read this report.
As a conclusion to this proposition, one writer presumes to say that
facts demonstrate that the more Lodges a brother belongs to the more
constant is his attendance upon all. A more magnificent display of a lack
of knowledge of conditions could not be imagined.
Another argument in support of this proposition, which is manifestly
an injustice to many Grand Lodges, including our own, is the statement
that where a brother moves away from his Lodge he must terminate his
membership in that Lodge before be can become a member elsewhere. This
statement is not applicable in many jurisdictions today as we have a system
of transferring membership by means of certificates so that a brother's
membership is protected in the Mother Lodge, in case he is rejected on his
application accompanied by the certificate. This argument is defective in
another respect as dual membership would not prevent the rej,ection of a
brother any more than if he were a member of only one Lodge. The same
system of transferring membership applies in the establishment of new
Lodges and therefore does not jeopardize the brother's membership.
It is also stated that unless a brother is a member of the particular
Lodg~ he desires to visit fr~m time to time he never feels quite at home.
If this be true then we must eliminate the claim of the universality of
Masonry. The writer's experience along these lines is quite to the contrary of the one advocating dual membership. To his personal knowledge
ma?y brethren are enjoying the fellowship of members in Lodges to
which they do not belong, preferring to remain a member of their Mother

47

Lodge on account of a warm feeling of kinship, or because in that particular Lodge they have been made life members or served as Masters.
We maintain that the visiting or attendance upon the Communications of
Lodges by brethren not members of that particular Lodge is the strongest
argument in favor of the universality of Freemasonry. Therefore there
would be no more advantage to one being a member of two or more Lodges
than one, or in other words, to carry out the argument in favor of dual
membership, one would of necessity have to be a member of all Lodges,
and then it resolves itself again into the question of the universality of
Freemasonry.
Another statement concerns groups of employees in factories and the
like, forming Masonic clubs, which would not be the case if dual membership were practiced as they would then organize Masonic Lodges instead
of clubs. This we know to be thoroughly impracticable as places and
conditions might be favorable for a Masonic club but far from suitable
for a Masonic Lodge.
It is also stated that the supreme Masonic authority has no control
over clubs and the like, which is not correct as the Masonic scholar well
knows that Grand Lodges possess the inherent right to govern and control
the Masonic affiliation of members.
Reference is also made to members in England forming themeselves
into Lodges according to their profession or business. While this statement is true, yet it must be remembered that such Lodges are established
not for the purpose of doing Masonic work, but for social and other
objects. A member, therefore, under these conditions enjoys the same
privilege of visiting other Lodges as one who belongs to a Working Lodge.
One writer presumes to say that it is claimed by many that all argument in favor of dual membership is based on sentiment, and frankly
admits that such is the case, yet in defense of his argument in favor of
this proposition he states that sentiment goes for a good deal in Masonry.
We admit that sentiment does go for a good deal in Masonry, but its
influence has been toward the demoralization of our time-honored Institution rather than its upbuilding. Sentiment, for several years, on account
of' the late war, flooded our Lodges ·with undesirable material and today
the· deplorable condition in loss of membership through suspension is the
aftermath.
One surprising statement made by a supporter of this proposition is
that the Lodges in the United States have departed from tradition and
custom of the rest of' the Masonic world. This statenient proves beyond
a question of doubt that the supporters of this proposition are poorly versed
in Masonic history and the Ancient Charges and Regulations of the Institution because there is. no more connection between Masonic tradition
and custom in dealing with this subject than there is between the Constitution of the United States and the Bills of Mortality.

Massachusetts (1926):
(Grand Master) : The question is not one of the advisability or inadvisability of permitting dual or plural membership, Massachusetts has
its law and its practice which permit such membership, and feels that it
has worked well and is an advisable practice. But we freely recognize
the undoubted right of each Grand Jurisdiction to decide this question for
itself and we also recognize that full faith and credit ought to be given- in
each Grand Jurisdiction to the laws and decisions of other Grand Lodges,
acting within their territorial Jurisdictions; indeed we require our brethren
to obey the law of any recognized Grand Lodge within which they may
reside and accord full credit to proceedings for discipline ·had in other
Jurisdictions against m.embers of Massachusetts Lodges offending against
the Constitutions or Laws of such Grand Lodges.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This was a very important

comes the resolution which will henceforth permit dual 'membership. This
is aimed at the economic loss to the craft in having a large percentage of
its members at any given place non-resident. There are to be found in
these Reviews at the Illinois page, figures showing that eleven per cent,

\ f a man lives outside the city or the county in which his Lodge is located,
hi! is what the banks call "frozen assets" to that Lodge; he pays dues,
and that is all. But in that Lodge he was raised; it is his "Mother Lodge," ·
and therefore much sentiment attaches to his connection ~perewith, while
he .is a comparative stranger to the membership in the n·ew home. Hence
it is that such transfers have been very much more infrequent than would
have been salutary to Masonic activity. It is this sort .of co~ditions that ·
the practice of permitting dual membership aims to ameliorate. Dual
membership, or ·in many cases plural membership, has long been the established practice in England. The Masonic spirit is in England greatly
different from that in this country; and we· are compelled to believe that
the principle of multiple membership, coupled \vith an understanding that.
all Lodges are small bodies, closely compact, is responsible for the greate~
hold which English Masonry exerts upon its devotees. We regret one

another Mason fond of working up Masonic statistical tabfes, this dual

Wisconsin (1928):
(Grand Master ) : Many of our brethren removing from the city,
town or village in which their Lodge of membership is located, wish to
discharge the obligations of membership in the Lodge of their residence,
but for sentimental or other reasons do not care to sever their membership
in the home Lodge. Much good timber would unite in forming new Lodges
but for this dislike of breaking home ties.
Dual or plural membership would allow these brethren to form new
connections, at the same time retaining old affiliations. It is not an innovation. The Mother Grand Lodge of England has always permitted it
and in the United States the Grand Lodges of Delaware, Massachusetts,
Rhode Island, Tennessee, Virginia, Wyoming, New York, and perhaps
others, allow, under restrictions, membership in two or more Lodges. N;o
ill effects have been noted.

low. Generally the more costly anything becomes the more it is appreciated. Perhaps making membership .more expensive would also
have a tendency to curb the activities of. co-ordinate bodies.
Some Jurisdictions are struggling along under dues and fees
fixed years ago, when the producing power of th~ dollar was worth
100% instead of perhaps half of the amount, as it now is. This necessarily circumscribes the activities of a Lodge in carrying · out its
ch.aritable, social and educational work.

How far this modern idea of engaging all Lodges in the matter of
collecting dues for each other, appears, when we remember that originally
a man was made a 'Mason in a certain Lodge for a fee whi<;h gave him
certain rights in all Lodges, and that he incidentally became a member of
said certain Lodge for which he paid annual dues. The ceremonies of initia.tion evidently made him a member of the Fraternity at large, and the
membership in a certain Lodge was incidental to that fact. For the former
he paid a large fee and for the latter he paid dues to the local Lodge. The

·right of visitation was a part of the rights gaine? by becoming a memb:r
.0 f the Masonic Fraternity, and did not appertam to Lodge membership
alcim:. The right of visitations seems to have been subject to on!~ ?ne

debt to said local Lodge, and does not alter the delinquent's relationship
to any other Lodge. But the modern idea is to join all Lodges into a clo~e

set the idea of local membership in a Lodge.
The question naturally arises, is this in accord with Masonic justice?
Is the Lodge the paramount .object in making 'Masons? Or is there a
wider .and better view which can be taken, and which this age of the
making of many members is overlooking?
EDUCATION-MASONIC
We believe that the greater part of the new Masons desire to go
to school; they want an opportunity to learn •w hat Masonry stan~s
for and for what it will be to them. Unfortunately when a man is
raised the Fraternity devotes practically no further time to informing
him along these lines. If on his own initiative he desires to study
the Institution, books and periodicals are at his disposal, but even
without a guide he is greatly handicapped in this field. To carry out
the program of Masonic Education requires the expenditure of money,
consistent and voluntary effort, which must continue after the first
burst of enthusiasm has died out. The problem cannot be solved in
a day, or a year, but is one that will require "time, patic~ce and perseverance," which we are told will accomplish all thmgs. Grand
Lodges and individual Lodges must be in a position to answer the
question of the newly-made Mason, "What is it all about?" with
something other than mere platitudes or citing example from the past.

to the contin~ed success of the Order.

Man does not prize the things he receives lightly. Many of our
brethren do not prize Masonry because they know so little about it. We
· confer our degrees, decorate the faithful, conduct our funerals and call it
Masonry. But back of this are centuries, thousands of years, of tried and
tested principles.

Nebraska (1928):
(Chairman Correspondencc Committee) : Nearly all of the jurisdictions are engaged in promoting the cause of education, which falls
under two heads, the first of which is Masonic education, and the second
of which is public education.
Masonic education is capable of subdivision into two classes, the first
of which might be called general Masonic education, which is promoted
by the Grand Lodge libraries, traveling libraries, and libraries in subordinate Lodges, which have become numerous ; also by study clubs, the
efforts of historians, Masonic writers, lecturers, and publications, and
the second of which is ritualistic or technical in the hands of the custo. dians of the work, Grand lecturers or equivalent officers and their deputies
and the District Deputy Grand Masters, where such officers exist.
Public education is promoted by schools in the several Masonic Homes,
by student loan funds, some of which are very large, and administered in
different ways, but which we gather but cannot definitely say from the
proceedings, are unduly depleted by the failure of borrowing students to
repay the obligations, and by general promotion of the public schools
through the observance of public schools weeks, and special events .of
appropriate nature.
New York (1928):
(Grand Master) : Consider this picture ! On the one hand, is the
new member. He is an individual. He comes to the door of the Lodge
with only the vaguest of notions of what kind of thing Freemasonry is.
He has heard dim accounts of its mysterious history and vague rumors
of its hidden activities. He brings nothing with him but his own head and
his two hands, and he is perhaps a little timid and somewhat embarrassed.
On the other hand stands the great Fraternity, with all its complexity.
Behind it is the vast sweep of its history, with its ever-increasing richness
of traditions. Within it is its ritual, the strange form of which is so
baffiing, like speech ·in a forgotten language; its philosophy ; its
and symbols; its intricate system of jurisprudence; its peculiar system of
offices ; its truly bewildering complexity of activities ; like a vast machine
whirring, wheels within wheels. Around it are all manner of outgrowths
and undergrowths, concordant bodies, side orders, and social organizations without number.

How shall the individual find . his way into this strange, new world?
What are the paths for him to follow? Where shall he discover his own
approp~iate pla"Ce or station? How shall he learn to perform his duties?
How .can be become a Mason in fact as well as in name?
If he fails, he loses his interest, drops from sight, becomes a mere
name on the rolls, receives nothing except the satisfaction of calling himself a Mason, and gives nothing except his annual d1.1es. Or else, if he
hei>omes .active, he may do himself and the Craft more harm than good,
not from malice, but out of a complete misunderstanding of Masonry, its
practices, its rules, and its purposes; he may, for example, believe the
Lodge to be a social club, existing merely to give him a good time; or a
sectarian organization out to make war on some church or political party ;
:or act out .of some other misconception equally wild.

Nova Scotia (1927):
(Grand Master): The great vital need in this jurisdiction is more
light. We are turning out Masons who are Masons only in name, knowing
nothing or next to nothing of the teachings of Masonry, its philosophy,
symbolism, purposes, ideals, traditions. The Craft has left no mark on
their lives and characters. The smattering knowledge given them when
receiving their degrees is trivial, and unsatisfying and when they see
nothing further in Masonry they drift away, or are suspended. They
little realize the great services they can render to the world through a
better knowledge of Masonry.
What we need is not more "work" but more intensive teaching, more
addresses on our history, symbolism, ideals, philosophy, a wider circula·tion of well-edited Masonic journal, a closer interest in the work being
done by our N. S. Freemasons' H ome, and the Craft outside this jurisdiction. Until we do this in an intelligent way we cannot hope to hold
our membership and go forward to greater things.

Statistics composed from the reports of forty-eight States in
regard to the Student Loan Fund of the Grand Encampment, Knights
Templar of the United States, show that in the three and one-half
years from July 1, 1924, to December 31, 1927, $1,342,000 has been
invested in student loans.
The number of students helped is 8,398; 3,242 are now enrolled
in school and re<:eiving aid; 2,774 have graduated. It is stated that
393 have paid in full the amounts loaned; 1,384 have paid in part; 357
are in arrears and less than one per cent of the total, or 16, have
been charged off as a total loss. The entire expense of the administration of the fund from its inception six years ago is $3,303.66, or
less than one-fifth of one per cent.
A number of Grand Lodges have student loan funds established
either before or after the Grand Encampment established theirs. The
results, both from a monetary and educational standpoint, have been
highly satisfactory.

West Australia (1927):
· (Chairman Correspondence Committee): The very regrettable rush
for membership, following upon the late war, causing the admission of
ma1iy Masonic undesirables, has now practically cease<l, greater care being
exercised with regard to candidates. This is a hopeful sign for the future
of the Craft everywhere.
·A greater regard for Masonic education and research is being manifested. The "degree factory" is being gradually supplanted by Masonic
training. What subordinate Lodges failed to realize, Grand Lodges have
at last awakened to, namely, that to make Masons is something more than
a mill process; that the degrees are merely the gateways to a field of
knowledge comprehending the whole object and purpose of Masonry; and
that to enable the Mason to benefit from the field, it must be thickly
strewn with the plants of learning. . Therefore, everywhere we find Grand
Lodges providing facilities for making men Freemasons when once they
have been made members. Mason!c study, clubs, classes, research bodies,
Grand Lodge libraries, with encouragement to subordinate Lodges to form
their own libraries, the establishment of traveling libraries, the provision
of lectures and speakers on Masonic subjects, are all directions in which
· this goodly activity is being lined up. The reception given to these facilities, as well by the older, as by the .younger members with their newlycreated hunger for greater knowledge of the new country they have
entered upon, demonstrates the truth that degrees will make members
but only education will make Masons.

Georgia (1927):
(Educational Commission): During the past year the Masons of

North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : It is noted that the Grand
Lodge of Delaware has been presenting scholarships to certain classes of
students. It is recorded in this book that these students are told that these
should be refunded if, when, and as it is found possible to do this. We
think these aid funds ought to be in the form of loans outright, with
facilities for follow-up work, not to effect the return of the money so
much as to prevent the moral deterioration. of the beneficiary. Student aid
is worth while only in terms of its moral effect upon the student. Honorary
scholarships are good; but the most of the scholarships of which we know
are not too far removed from a tendency to pauperize the recipients. Many
loans, on the contrary, are without means of following up the beneficiaries,
and there arises a subtle temptation to postpone repayment. This is the
beginning of a moral breakdown and leads to an unwillingness to meet
just obligations. In this event, it were far better that the "beneficiary"
had never received aid, for he becomes potentially delinquent in his duties
inv.olving integrity. But loan funds when properly administered are vastly
beneficial.
Oregon (1927):
(Grand Master) : The income from the Educational Fund is distributed in monthly installments to those who have had left in their care,
with little or no financial provision, the children of deceased Master
. Masons. Only children of school age and in attendance in the public schools
of this state are eligible for assistance from the income of this fund. In
a number of cases this assistance has been the only means by which widowed mothers have been able to keep together under their own love and
care the children left them by the father's death.

(Committee on Revolving Student Loan Fu11d): We have loaned

arid other states during the past year.
We have collected $3,295.09 principal, and $278.31 interest on pre1ious

We have now a balance on hand of $2,015.09.
We may not be able to collect all we have loaned, but the loss will be
so small that the interest collected will probably cover it and leave the
principal to revolve on its helpful mission from year to year, and like the
echoes in Tennyson's Bugle "roll from soul to soul and grow forever and
forever."
It has been a pleasure to help these students in their struggle for an
education and to feel that the Masonic Fraternity is investing in the lives
of future men and women.

Recognition has been given the Grand Lodge of Egypt by a

Kansas (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): From the information at
hand it seems there is now a schism in the Grand Lodge of Egypt, .brought
about through the following circumstances: Idris Bey Ragheb, who for
many years had served the Craft as Grand Master, although it was believed that his services were to the disadvantage of the Grand Lodge,
refused to yield the Grand Mastership. The result of this refusal brought
about dissatisfaction, culminating in the election of Prince Mohamed Aly;
however, the Grand Master refused to give up the office and closed the
Grand Lodge before the newly elected Grand Master could be installed,
giving as his reason that the Prince was disqualified under their Constitution, he never having served as a Warden. The justice of this position
was recognized and the friends of the Prince proceeded to invest him with
the necessary ~ffices in order to qualify him for Grand Master. This
condition resulted in creating a new Grand Lodge, with Idris Bey Ragheb
as Grand Master of the origina: Grand Lodge and Prince Mohamed Aly
as Grand Master of the seceding one. We are informed that the Idris Bey

North Carolina· (1928) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Brother Arthur H. Tufts,
(South Dakota) Fraternal Correspondent, has prepared a most unusually
fine report for the Brethren which should be read by every Mason in
South Dakota. In the body of the proceedings is found a report which
reports adversely upon the National Grand Lodge of Egypt. This body
split up some three or four years ago, about the election of a Grand
Master. The overwhelming majority of the Grand Lodge; in fact all
except a dozen and a half, voted for Prince Mohamed Aly for Grand
Master, displacing Idris Bey Ragheb. The National Grand Lodge requires
by its. Constitution that its Grand Master must have been installed as a
Grand Warden. The Grand Lodge found as a fact that he had been made
an honorary Gr<1nd Warden, which fact was undeniable. The Grand Lodge
proceeded to act as judge of the qualifications of its presiding officer in
terms of its Constitution, and it adjudged Prince Mohamed Aly to be
qualified to be Grand Master under these requirements. As for us, we
feel that the Grand Lodge was within its rights in thus sitting in judgment
upon the question of whether its choice as Grand Master met the requirements of its own Constitution. We seem to observe that the Senate of
the United States sits in judgment upon the qualifications of its members
in terms of the constitution and statutes in such cases made and provided.
The Grand Lodges of England, Scotland and Ireland have taken the
position that this was correct; but the Scottish Rite people are all for the
other side, the Idris Bey Ragheb faction, if we are correctly informed,
because perhaps they are better acquainted with them.
All of this tends to point out just one thing of importance; these
non-English speaking people have not learned very well the principle of
majority rule and minority acquiescence; they are "not good losers", as
we say in politics. This was the cause of the Mexican schism some sixteen
years ago, in which the Scottish Rite sympathized with the side which
is at present not recognized by a single American Grand Lodge, so far
as we know ;-although as a matter of right in certain phases of the
question, the Scottish Rite's position was above question and criticism.

GRAND LODGES
The Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges reviewed show
practically only work common to the activities of all Jurisdictions.
In the main they have been simply routine matters. The system of
handling the affairs of a Grand · Lodge through a Board of General
Purposes as is customary in the three Mother Lodges, to-wit, England,
Ireland and Scotland and the Grand Lodges of Australia and the
Dominion of Canada, is a practical method for eliminating detail
which is of little interest to the general membership of a Grand Lodge.
In one Jurisdiction the Board of General Purposes attempted to
abolish a custom that had been in existence for over fifty years, but
were not successful. This shows that a Grand Lodge is not always
guided by the recommendations of a Board.
Some of the Grand Lodges while endeavoring to curb commercial activities among Masons directly assist by printing in their Proceedings complete roster of all of their members. This furnishes
ample opportunity for the compilation of what is generally known as
"a sucker list."
Decrease in the net gain in Masonic membership in the United
States during the past few years is also a matter of serious consideration. In 1927 it was the smallest in twelve years. The following figures taken from a survey mad.e in Wisconsin shows the net gain each

British Columbia (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of Iowa
says : "Can Lodge funds be used for other than Lodge purposes? There
seems to be some misapprehension as to the law on this subject. I have
received several enquiries as to whether a Lodge can contribute its funds
to assist in some worthy cause, such as the erection and maintenance of a
hospital, beautifying a city park, assisting the Boy Scouts, or making
donations to other charitable purposes. I held in all these cases, that
while Masons as individuals are encouraged to lend assistance to all worthy
undertakings, Lodge funds cannot be used for other than Lodge purposes.
This is a wise and necessary provision of our law and should be strictly
adhered to by every Lodge."
We do not agree with the above, and think our own Grand Lodge
has the better rule, viz. : That so long as a Lodge pays its debts and has
something for charity, the disposal of the rest of its funds is its own
business.

GRAND MASTERS
As we remember it, there was one Grand Master who stated he
welcomed letters requesting rulings on various subjects, even though
they were specifically covered by a law or regulation available to the
writer. He, however, was the exception. The address of practically
every Grand Master calls attention to the needless demands made
upon his time by these unnecessary and often foolish requests. Evidently some Masters believe it easier to make an inquiry, rather than
look up the matter up themselves.
Another outstanding Grand Master was one who believed that
dispensations were not in order to waive a law passed by the Grand
Lodge or Lodge itself, even though he had the power expressed or
implied.
District of Columbia (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of
Rhode Island suggested the term of office should in the future be
two years, which the committee also disapproved. This seems to the
writer to be reserving of grave consideration. It is the question
which was longer discussed than any question that came before
the Convention which prepared the Constitution of the Nation. Many great
men held that two years was too short a period to enable a President to
carry out a policy, and six years might be long enough to abuse his power,
and the term was limited to four years. We.have electetl Masonic office
bearers because it was their turn about as often as we have elected them
for their merit. Masters of Lodges have often completed their term of
office before becoming conversant in the duties. It is written in the Scriptures "By their fruits shall ye know them." To the writer it seems that
if we ~eally purpose making Masonry what the chesty orators urge, we
would increase the term of every office, but if we purpose electing every
good fellow whose turn it is and then continue our present custom of
politics and practice of sophistry, we will not.

tionalizing charity. Even when a Masonic Home is perfectly managed, there

Brethren as it is of their bodily wants and needs.

Maine (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): It was Hegel, one of the
profoundest minds of his time, who said that as a student of history he
had .noticed "the .Idea creates the Institution but in the end the Institution
smothers the Idea."
Signs are not wanting that something like this is insidiously overtaking and smothering the Masonic Idea. Our comparatively modern
Masonic Institutionalism, with its elaborately organized philanthropies,
was, in all probability, never contemplated by the original founders of the
Masonic Fraternity. We have only to read once more, those early constitutions, to see how far we have departed from the original intention and
spirit of the Order. Masonic Charity was a first-hand and a fi rst-aid proposition, not something to be done by proxy, or committee or anything
approaching a mere officialism. A re-reading or repeating of every obligation of the symbolic degrees would suggest that Institutionalism was
wholly foreign to the genesis and genius of Freemasonry.

REPORT ON CORflESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

On this subject of caring for dependents I have found two widely
separated lines of thought and action. One seems to follow the example of
the Good Samaritan. Finding the man who needs help and giving it to
him directly, quietly, among familiar surroundings and in the company
of old friends and associates. The other is institutional in ~haracter. The
dependent is carefully investigated by a Board, if his needs are established,
he is removed from his former location and placed with others to be cared
for according to certain established rules, in a place open to visitors who
are seeking a certain emotional thrill. Five years reading reports of
Masonic Home Boards has not converted me to the latter method. I am
more firmly convinced than ever that we are following the better course,
knowing that the dependents will receive the most fraternal and painstaking care, and that it won't cost us any $5,000.00 per capita to "foot
the bill."
Last year one Grand Lodge whose Home is "filled to capacity with
many applicants awaiting admission" candidly avows its conviction that
Masonic Institutionalism has gone far enough and now advocates the
adoption of the Good Samaritan policy, saying, "it is better now to adopt
a policy which encourages the aged man or woman who seeks the help
and guardianship of the Fraternity, to remain in the environment to which
he or she has been accustomed rather than accept lodgings in a new place
under strict and strange regulations and away from old ties such as home
friends and acquaintances." Of course the logical question to ask is
obvfous, that if it is better now, why indulge in such extensive, increasingly expensive and expansive Institutionalism at all?
In one Grand Lodge we notice that some scandal was started and
gained ground to the extent that a Joint Committee "recommended a thorough investigation that the truth or falsity of these serious charges may
be shown, and that such investigation shall include real conditions at the
Widows' Home." That, too, is one of the incidental penalties which
Masonic Institutionalism is bound to pay when such gossipy reports are
circulated respecting such Homes. In yet another. Grand Lodge this year
we read, "We should not permit ourselves to be disturbed by rumors now
and then that there is trouble at the Home. For you cannot bring together
such a large family of the aged and infirm without trouble." Of course
not, and a great deal of that trouble, we have noticed is brought into
the constituent Lodges when those of unsound mind, or cancer patients.
are rejected, under the regulations governing the Home; bitter feelings
are too often aroused, Lodges have been thereby disrupted and only too
often the matter gets into the public prints or on the tongue of ill-report
and the Fraternity suffers.
For nearly twenty years we have read the enthusiastic accounts of the
opening of these Masonic Institutions of various kinds, and somewhat

carefully followed their development and growth through the years. Our
observation has been something after this fashion : The corner-stone is
officially laid with great enthusiasm and most eloquent orations by eminent
Brethren, the next morning in session of the Grand Lodge, the Finance
or Ways and Means Committee, brings in its recommendation for a large
per capita tax to support the Institution and each initiate is mulcted a
fixed sum for the same purpose, under this process enthusiasm wanes a
little but the burden is borne on the whole rather cheerfully. Next year
the New Home is formally opened, enthusiasm waxes again, only .to wane
somewhat the next day when it is disco.vered that last year's per capita
is not sufficient and that increased taxation must be endured. In a few
years more comes the crying need for expansion, a hospital or at least
an infirmary annex must be supplied, taxation per capita again. By and
by some earnest and eloquent Brother advocates a Children's or Orphans'
Home, enthusiasm again, but rather chastened from the former years,
increased per capita of course, and so the accelerated and too often staggering process goes forward. Whether such Institutionalized Masonry was
ever contemplated by the original plan of Masonry may be seriously questioned, and it may well be that in the onward years this may be the rock
upon which the Order may founder in these engulfing and well-nigh
suffocating seas of taxation and accelerated financial burdens.
