North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Is there any danger that
Masonry will come to be regarded as a sort of insurance against all sorts
of things?
Here in North Carolina, if the Mason becomes helpless or his wife
or widow, there is a Home to which he may go; and if he dies, there is
the Orphanage for his children. The more we do in the way of organized
charity, the nearer does Masonry come to acting as an insuring organization.
The following paragraph from the address of the Grand Master of
Georgia (1927), holds our attention:
"Quite naturally our Institutional Work is the greatest undertaking of
our Craft. This work includes the Masonic Home and its associated departments, our Masonic Relief Fund for the Aged and Indigent, the
Alto Tubercular Cottage for Little Children, the Student Loan Fund and
the program for the Director of Masonic Welfare. When we read and
learn of the marvelous efforts and accomplishments along these lines of
other Jurisdictions, there comes the keel'l regret and sharp disappointment
that our Grand Lodge is so far behind in .comparison.
Is he correct? Is the · institutional work of Masonry the "greatest
undertaking of our Craft"? We are not persuaded that this is the case.

78

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

True, this institutional work is indeed the most spectacular work in which
Masonry is now engaged; but we are of the opinion that the greatest work
of Masonry is, and always has been, the shaping of the thoughts of
Masons. By this process, and not by institutions alone, do we make profanes to become Masons. By this yardstick we are able to measure the
force and the power of Masonry. When is Masonry most powerful?
Not when it numbers most of great visible institutions of brick and
stone, but when it can so influence its devotees that they will think and act
the spirit and truths of Masonry in daily life. If there were today in
these United States three and a quarter million of Masonry-minded men,
we should know that the Fraternity had reached its earthly millennium.
But alas, its influence is far too weak upon many thousands of those who
profess its name and wear its jewelry.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Home (Oklahoma)
has a Pleasure Fund which appeals to your. Reviewer. Where there are
children in an institution, there should always be a considerable amount
of pleasure along with the work and perhaps sadness of the child's life

have never been in favor of placing children in an institutional home,
having been director of several and always being able to observe the
apparently subdued or crushed appearance of most institutional children,
particularly when compared with children raised in a Christian home. I

be found a home where a father and mother would look after the child's
welfare rather than being a unit in a large crowd of children.

Mississippi (1928):
A man, a collector of curios, moved out of a home and left in this
home apd scattered around the premises some of the things that he had
there, some of the relics of his folly, and among other things .he left there
an ostrich egg. The new-comer moving around the house was a fancier
of poultry, and it so happened that a little rooster moving around the place
saw the ostrich egg. He eyed· it for a moment, and then he called his lady
friends around him. He said, "Now, I don't expect you girls to do this
well, but I just want you to know what they are doing in other places."

I like to feel about the Masonic Fraternity as the commercial traveler

"Now I lay me down to sleep,

If I should die I am not concerned,

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

My position just now reminded me somewhat of an old sailor, captain
of a sailing vessel. He was fearfully wicked and very rough with his
men, and they were as afraid of him as of lightning. The boat got caught
in a storm one day near the coast and was driven right on the rocks. This
old fellow cursed, swore, pulled and hauled and did everything he could
think of and the boat kept drifting on to the rocks. He turned around to the'
crew finally and said : "You all do the best you can, I am going to pray."
They all fell back aghast that he would pray. He dropped down on his
knees and said: "Oh, Lord, I know you can keep 'this boat off •of those
rocks, but I'll be damned if I can see how you are going to do it." I
am supposed to make you a speech, Brethren, but I'll be durned if I see
how I am going to do it.
South Australia (1928):
On one occasion the ancient King of Sparta was being visit.ed · by a
neighboring monarch. The visitor expressed surprise at the meager nature
of the defences of the historic city. The King of Sparta, pointing to a
handful of soldiers drawn up on the beach, said, "There are the walls
of Sparta, and every man a brick."

"We are living in a fast age. Old truths, like old keys, have grown
rusty and bent and no longer unlock the secrets of the universe. Old
philosophies and old creeds are falling. Ships are beating the air and
crawling the beds of the oceans. Men are calling to men across the seas,
speaking in sparJcs that span a thousand miles of space. The greatest
philosophers, the hardest-headed analysts and the most phlegmatic scientists of Europe are adventuring the empire of the dead, peering with eager
eyes and listening with credulous brains, for signs of the soul eternal. It
is a wonderful age! A great laboratory has developed a ray 'of light that
will hold your twin-six helpless in a tide of traffic, will stop the mightiest
airship in its flight or put out of commission the greatest engine that
turns the machinery of the largest factory in existence. Tonight a business
associate talks to you from some eastern center, which conversation
develops the necessity of a letter in return. Tomorrow's early morning
hours will find that letter a thousand feet above the mountains of Virginia, speeding to its destination as it greets the morning sunrise. A few
evenings ago I touched my radio and heard an official in Cuba announcing
the ·result of a bull fight. With the slightest turn of the dial I was
thrilled with beautiful music played by an orchestra on the top of an hotel
in Chicago. Again touching the dial, I heard a Jewish rabbi announcing his
text in clear-cut tones from his synagogue in San Francisco. And the
text, as it brought me back from the realm of wonderment to ·the .duties
of the hour, seemed like the thunders from Sinai: uExcept Jehovah build
the house, they labor in vain that build it.H

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Board of General Purposes (Queensland) met with determined opposition in its efforts to have
the "Macduff" done away with in the Scottish Lodges in Queensland. That
Nevada Masons who are not Scotchmen may know just what is a "MacDuff" and the reason for all the discussion thereto, we quote,
"The 'Macduff' has been in use in Scotland since about the year 1047.
It has been carried on all those centuries in Scotland, and it has been
carried on in Queensland for the last fifty years at least. During the last
eight or nine years a number of Brethren have returned from the war
with shell shock, and for this reason we did not give 'Macduffs,' and if the
matter had been brought on then it is very possible it would have been
carried.

"I desire to state that 'Macduff' is an integral part of Scottish Freemasonry. When Macduff defeated MacBeth, the King said he would
grant Macduff three great wishes in 1057, which he did. The Macduffs
were a people who were carrying on Freemasonry in Scotland at that
time. The Stone which the great Patriarch Jacob used as a pillow was
carried to Scotland by a Macduff, and the latest King of Scotland was

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

crowned on it by a Macduff. It was later removed to the Westminster
Abbey, and our Kings up to and including His Majesty King George V,
were .crowned upon it.
"The 'Macduff' was instituted at a Masonic gathering and has been
given in Masonic gatherings by Scottish Freemasons ever since. If in doing
this we are disturbing people at a late hour of the night, then we are prepared to consider our position; but if we have reason to think that we are
doing no harm nor causing any annoyance outside the Lodge room, then
we want you to leave us alone."
The motion to do away with the "MacDuff" was decisiveiy lost.

vicinity of Masonic Halls objected oh account, as claimed, that it disturbed
their slumbers at late hours of the night. Moreover it appears that the
Lodges were cautious of using it soon after the termination of the
European war when a number of shell-shocked brethren were returning
from the conflict, thinking the unfortunate veteran might mistake it for
a fresh breaking out of hostilities. But in the end the Macduff won out
and remains as an integral part of Queensland Freemasonry. It is indeed
gratifying to know that in some quarters the brethren will not permit any
interference with the ancient customs and usages of the Craft.

It is a question whether it will ever be possible to eliminate those

In recent years, our State has been disgraced by this super-government,

District of Columbia (1928):
Cases of intemperance are still in the trial records and grievance
reports. Political-prohibition has not ended intemperance. Masonry has
been passive on this subject, but has consistently obeyed the law. In the
clubs and by the wayside we hear of the preachers as the "power of the
land," which has made this trouble, but it is not true. It was sprung upon
us by the wily politician who was after votes, but avaricious preachers
caught the slogan and thought the contributions might increase. It will
not endure. The pastors who in our infancy threw round our cradles the
first rays of Divine Light are still dear in our memories, but many have
staggered from pristine christianity, and have violated every law in the
decalogue, even denying the Bible, and should not be a "power in the land."
Where politics have touched the outer garments of Masonry it has
been by subtle methods, and we have been the losers. The commercial
preachers who have been in the foreground have vied with the office
seeker for supremacy, and though there may be an increase in the contribution boxes, it cannot endure.
Michigan (1927):
(Grand Master): In view of the experiences I had during our last
political electiOns, I feel it my duty to bring to the attention of the Master
Masons in our Jurisdiction that Masonry discountenances political controversies, and it is. forbidden to use the institution or Masonic membership
for political purposes.
Some of our Lodge bulletins and Masonic papers have in the past
carried political advertisements, and some of these advertisements convey
the inference of Masonic membership or support; and in order to prevent
any further evils of this kind, and to maintain the historic and traditional
attitude of our institution toward political contests, I deem it necessary to
take immediate action.
I therefore order that no publication of any kind sponsored, authorized
or supervised by a constituent Lodge or representative thereof in this
Jurisdiction. shall hereafter carry in its reading matter or advertisements,
any notices of any candidacies for public office or discussion of controversial political subjects.

Montana (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Past Grand Master John
Milne, of New Mexico, presented the Correspondence Report. Montana
1925 was reviewed and he said:
"From the reports we note that several candidates for public office

was disapproved as it should have been."
That's hardly fair; we are fortunate in Montana in having in the
fraternity many members eminent in political life and to accuse them of
"campaigning" is not just. It is natural for ·them to attend Grand Lodge
sessions and meet their brethren even though an election campaign was
going on; our governor, state treasurer, auditor, clerk of supreme court
entire board of equalization, four out of five justices of supreme cour~
and many other state officials are members of the Craft, and many of
them like the governor are life-members of the Grand Lodge; why should
they stay away, just because of a political campaign being on.
North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : When a candidate for political office who is a Mason, puts his political advertisement in a
Masonic journal of circulation among the people whom he expects
to vote for him, is that act equivalent to making . use of Masonry
for private purposes ; and is it tantamount to dragging Masonry
into politics? The Grand Master thinks both questions should be answered
in the affirmative, and therefore directs that no Masonic Journal of Michigan Masonry shall in future carry such advertising matter. Admitting
that his conclusions are correct, we nevertheless fail to see how any line
may be drawn in regard to the advertising matter in such publication unless
all material which comes from a Mason or group of Masons in pursuit
of business, be eliminated. Why would Jones and Son, manufacturers
of automobiles and Masons, advertise in such a publication at · all? Obviously, because they want the business of Masons ; believe Masons will
patronize them. Is that not capitalizing Masonry?

RELIGION
Masonry has the greatest Creed for a foundation, as far as religion is concerned, of any institution. It is embodied in the Andent
Charge whereby all Masons are obligated to profess that "Religion
in which all men agree, leaving their particular opinions to themselves; that is, to be good men and true, or men of Honor and
Honesty, by whatever Denominations or Persuasions they may be
distinguished; whereby Masonry becomes the Center of Union, and
the Means of conciliating true Friendship among Persons that must
have remained at a perpetual Distance."

Colorado (1927):
(Grand Master) : Masonry requires of its members a belief in the
existence of one ever-living and true God and has always taught that one
of the seven days of the week is to be set aside as a day of rest and worship.
Our Book of Constitutions prohibits Sunday Lodge Communications,
except for the purpose of performing funeral services.
In spite of a seemingly widespread indifference to the observance of
the forms and ceremonies of organized religion, which persuaded that the
question of holding Sunday Lodge picnics would never be raised by any
well instructed Fellow Craft, and that if raised, even the least skillful
Master or Warden would refuse to entertain the suggestion.
In the eyes of the profane, Masonry stands sponsor for "Masonic"
affairs. Individual members of the Craft, of course, are entitled to the
fullest liberty of action, but in my opinion, "Masonic Sunday Picnics,"
given under the auspices of any Masonic organization serve no good
purpose, shock the sensibilities and offend the consciences of some members
of the very organization sponsoring the outings and ought not be permitted.

Kansas (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee ): The Bible, as understood
in Masonry, is that book, or writings, which reveal to Masons, universally,
the will of God. By this symbol is expressed Divine Truth. And, as was
observed in a former address, whatever book or writings reveal to a particular people the will of God ; gives the Divine Light ; is, to the Craft of
that people, a Great Light, to have place as indispensable on the Masonic
altar. If, for example, a Lodge is made up exclusively of Jews, the Old
Testament is to be that Light. For the adherents of Mohammed, the
Koran is that Light, as is the Vedas to the Brahman, the Book of Kings
to the Chinese, the Old and New Testament to Christians. By such a
symbol, sacredly kept, reverently believed in, do Masons, everywhere,
attest faith in the One God, Grand Architect of the Universe.
North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : One sees several divergent
views as to the Sabbath Day reflected in Masonic law and custom in the
several Grand Lodges. For instance, the cornerstone of the Louisiana
Grand Lodge Temple was laid and the dedication later occurred on Sunday ; President Harding laid a cornerstone for a Masonic building in
Alaska (under the Grand Lodge of Washington ) on Sunday; but the
vast majority of the Grand Lodges expressly prohibit such practices. To
a church a co rnerstone-laying is a religious ceremony; to a Masonic Lodge
it is labor. In all events, a picnic ought to be more secular pleasure, and
should not link the name of Masonry with a desecration of the Sabbath day.

Utah (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee ) : We would like to discuss
at some length the principle adopted by Missouri ( 1927), which requires
that the candidates for degrees in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Body
seeking recognition:
"• • * Shall have and express an unfaltering belief in a Supreme ·
Being as the father of all mankind • • •."
However, we can take space only for an observation or two.
'That requirement goes beyond a profession of a belief in Deity-tt
qualifies such professed belief by indicating an attribute of this Deity:
"the Father of all mankind." The Missouri Committee could not quite
shake itself clear of a characteristic of all creed-makers; its members in
common with human beings, generally, had to slip in a qualifying statement to indicate the sort of Deity contemplated. If this requirement should
be made, and the principles strictly applied, no candidate belonging to the
Latter-Day Saint organization could be, or would be accepted as an applicant for the degrees in the Grand Jurisdiction of Missouri, (yet Missouri has adherents of this organization in its membership), for it might
be exceedingly difficult if not embarrassing for a member of that organization or institution to select one of the many gods he believes in, as the
"Father of all mankind." Anyone at all familiar with the teachings and
doctrines of the institution referred to knows that from its beginning
(in fact, originating in the teachings of the first prophet), its leaders have
held to and have inculcated a belief in a plurality of gods.

The Grand Master of Manitoba made the following reference:
"I declined to permit a visiting Lodge from a foreign Jurisdiction
whose work differed from our own to confer the Third degree on a Fellow
Craft member of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction. The instruction the candidate would have received would have been of no service .to him in his
own Lodge and practically he would have to have the degree subs.equently
communicated to him."
This seems a very narrow way of looking at things. The members
of the Manitoba Lodge would be benefited by witnessing a form of work
different from its own, and would be brought to re~lize that Masonry .extends beyond the confines of Manitoba. As for the candidate, , we will
venture to say that at the conclusion of the degree he would not have
known whether he had received one work or the other.

One of the outstanding questions before the Fraternity today is
whether the correct rendition of the Ritual has not become the main
objective of the average Masonic Lodge. Religions and other Institutions have come into existence, flourished and decayed through a
strict adherence to the letter, rather than the spirit of their Creed or
Ceremonies. The action of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in
considering the advisability of doing away with the picturesque penalties of the obligations will undoubtedly be viewed by some Grand
Lecturers, Custodians of Work and Ritual worshipers with feelings
of alarm and horror.
Masonry, if it is going to survive and function as a worth while
Fraternity and Institution, will have to get in step with the changed
order and the development of the present day and age. Non-attendance at Lodge meetings, decrease in membership and other straws
show which way the wind is blowing.

North Carolina (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : There are in the excellent
Foreign Correspondence of Brother Joseph M. Lowndes, of Wyoming,
two quite valuable symposia. One of these deals with the nature of the
public grand honors of Masonry. From it we learn that in seventeen states
the public grand honors are the same as the funeral grand honors without
words; in 27 states, they are the three times three, but it is noted that in
Missouri there is no noise and in Alabama there is a stamping of the foot;
in Arkansas and Tennessee, the raising of the hands above the head and
three claps ; in Maine, cross arms on breast and bow ; in Rhode Island,
the same, three times; and in Pennsylvania there are no public grand
honors. The second symposium deals with dual membership, Massachusetts,
the Philippine Islands, Rhode Island and Virginia permit plural membership, we read ; Minnesota, New Hampshire and South Carolina in
addition to these permit dual membership but not plural; and Delaware
permits its members to belong to a Lodge outside of the state in addition
to one inside thereof. New York is recently added to the dual group.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : In the Jurisdiction under
. review (Philippine Islands) it is a Masonic offense for any Mason except
the Grand Lecturer, to have in his possession a written or printed Ritual,
whether in cipher or not. This law, it, appears, is violated in some quarters,
and, at the Annual Communication, an effort was made by one of the
Lodges to have the law so far amended as to permit of the use of the
cipher Ritual known in Southern California as "King Solomon's Key."
The reason assigned was not without common sense. "There is no doubt,"
·it was said, "that the memory of man is treacherous, and quickly forgets
·what it has learned. King Solomon's Key is an aid tci memory, and no
person not familiar with the ritualistic work can read it, especially if he
does not know English. Moreover, most of the Lodge Officers have a
large amount of work to attend to outside the Lodge, and cannot give' all
'their time fo Masonic work." The Custodians of the Work reported adversely, but recommended that as it might be found necessary at some
future time to adopt the use of cipher keys, these should be prepared in
both English and Spanish. This course was adopted. While it is quite true,
as the Custodians suggested, that the existence of such keys proved an
efficient aid to clandestinism, the practice of printed rituals is a growing
one, · and will probably continue to grow. As the Lodge moving in the
matter observed, human memory is treacherous. To that mental defect
speculative Masonry owes many of the debatable questions concerning the
ritualistic practices of our ancient Operative brethren as compared with
those of the Symbolic Lodges of modern times. It was not till the existing
Operative Lodges, less than a generation ago, allowed certain portions of
their carefully preserved written Ritual to become known to Symbolic
. Masons that at last some of those debatable questions were solved.
SECRET ARIES-LODGE
As a Grand Secretary, or like officer in a constituent lodge, is
generally responsible for the continued success or failure of the
lodge, for that reason the selection of a competent brother to fill
that office is of the greatest importance. The Secretary usually continues while the Master emerges from the ranks for only a brief

Idaho (1927):
(Grand Mastrr): But length of service is not the only standard of
measurement, and many others, though having served shorter terms, are
entitled to honorable mention. The office of Secretaty is exceedingly
important. It is a high type of service, and happy is the Worshipful
Master who is fortunate enough to have a loyal and capable Secretary
on whom he may rely for assistance. It would seem that in the Masonic
scheme of titles and honors there should be one to bestow on a Secretary
who has served his Lodge long and well. A member serves a year as
Master and, whether it be well done or otherwise, he retires with· the
title of Past Master as a recommendation of Masonic favor as long as
he lives. But one may serve as Secretary one year or twenty years, and
when he retires he carries with him no recognition of services or reward,
except the consciousness of duty well done.
It is a serious mistake to elect a Secretary from among the new
members. The Secretary, like the Master, should be a Mason of e'xpe·
rience. A few Lodges have elected Secretaries who have been Masons
but a few months, and almos-t invariably they have had to regret it later.
A very few Lodges are using the office of Secretary as the beginning
step in a line of promotion that is expected to lead to the Master's chair.
This also is a mistaken idea. There may be something said in its
favor, but the preponderance of argument is against it. The office is too
important to be made simply a period of preparation for higher stations.
To attempt to train a new Secretary every year is too costly an experience. Better start the line of promot ion from some other station.

TEMPLES
. Some one once said that a man would shoulder a rifle in the
defense of his Home, but never to protect a Boarding House. While
it is highly creditable for a Lodge to own its own Temple, still if it is
inadequately financed in the first instance, covered by mortgages and
the overhead too great for the income, it is not only a source of worry
but also a positive danger.
Without a desire to hamper those who are ambitious and able to
erect Temples, a number of Grand Lodges as well as some of the
co-ordinate Bodies, have adopted regulations calling for the submission of plans for such structures to some competent authority before
being allowed to proceed. It is a wise regulation. We know of a
number of cases where if this precaution had been taken, difficulties
both financial and otherwise would never have arisen.

THIRD DEGREE LECTURE

According to this scribe's way of thinking, the sooner we quit trying
to hedge a brother about who has been raised to the sublime degree of
Master Mason, and recognize that he is a Mason in deed and in truth
and is entitled to all the· rights and privileges of Masonry, the" sooner
will we discard the patronizing attitude toward those who are our equals
in Masonry.

The theory that you will make a better Mason out of the newly
raised brother by making him learn a lecture of the third degree does
not, perhaps, work out in practice as well as in theory. Some Jurisdictions after experimenting with it have repealed such a law, and
in other cases they have been followed more in the breach than in
the observance. While the idea of coaching lecturers may be to
enlighten and inform the candidate along Masonic lines, often. they
do not accomplish that purpose. In a number of cases they are
simply learned to be recited in a "poll parrot" fashion, to secure advancement or to be used to prove that the possessor is a Mason· for
visitation purposes. For the latter they are not as practical a~ would
appear upon the surface. When attempting to visit in a foreign Jurisdiction one usually finds that the method of examination is entirely
different from the one taught him in his home lodge.
·
The Popular idea that a man to become a Mason must commit
to memory a great deal of Ritual has prevented in~ny desirable men
from soliciting the privilege of Masonry, even though they had conceived a favorable idea of it. Some who were once proficient in these
coaching lectures have forgotten them. They hesitate to visit ano.t her
Lodge, even in their own or some other Jurisdiction, because they fear
they can not meet the requirements of an examining committee or
objects of suspicion or ridicule.

Oregon (1927):
(Grand Mast er) : Probably no sections of the Code are causing
more confusion in this jurisdiction than Section 203, Subdivision 8, and
Section 218, Article A, under Subdivision 1. Under an interpretation of
these sections, no brother is entitled to a certificate of membership,
nor is he entitled to sign the By-Laws of his Lodge, until after he has
passed satisfactorily an examination in the lecture of the Third Degree.
These sections, which raise the question, "When is a man a Mason?" are
·not popular with the Craft, and in the opinion of many, are in direct
conflict with the Fourteenth Landmark. The provisions of these sections
may be beautiful in theory, but in practice they are a nuisance and
should be amended in conformity with the true spirit of Masonry. Everywhere I have gone through this jurisdiction I have had complaint about
those sections. It is surprising, Brethren, how many Masons, how many
brethren who have been raised to be Masons in this jurisdiction who
have not signed the By-Laws of their Lodge and do not carry certificates
of membership. I was surprised the other day when one brother told
me in his Lodge they had twenty-fou; who had thus far failed to sign
the By-Laws, and when speaking about it to another brother last night,
he told me that was nothing, that in his Lodge they had forty such
brethren. I want to tell you, brethren, that when these brethren .get
out of your Lodge after you have raised them, it is not an easy task
to get them back to sign the By-Laws and secure their certificate of
membership. I know that everything that was right prompted the
brethren who provided this amendment to the constitution, but I don't
believe that it is working. It is causing a great deal of confusion. It is
causing confusion in connection with visitation, in connection with voting
in Lodge and has also made it possible for us to send Masons out of
this state who think they are Masons, but who do not carry proper
credentials. Time and time again the Grand Master is asked to give a
dispensation to allow a brother to receive the third degree out of time
in order that he may leave suddenly or that he may join the army or. go
into the navy, and what good is that dispensation, if we raise him and
send him out of the state without the credentials which will enable him
to prove that he is a Mason? I hope this section of the Code will be
amended~

The Proceedings from the Jurisdictions near the site of the
George Washington Memorial show that the Grand Lodges there
have generally met the quota fixed by the Association for them. In
Jurisdictions farther away and where it is not made mandatory for a
new member to pay the assessment, the payments have not been
very large.

The representative of the George Washington National Memorial
Association made his report and also read a copy of the minutes of the

"In 1911 the Masonic population of the United States was 1,317,123.
Today it is 3,134,703. Then our vision was undeveloped and naturally

103

"In 1916 we committed ourselves to a temple to cost not less than

~500,000. In 1920, upon motion of Bi:other Stockwell of North Dakota,
it was resolved that the plans for the temple should be made on a basis

Wisconsin (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Wisconsin never advised
that the memorial should be built and has never pledged it its support.
When the project was started it was only proposed to spend $100,000; now
it is said that $5,000,000 at least will be required. The brethren in Alex~
andria had some relics of Washington, and under the plea that they were
exposed to destruction by fire, asked the Masons of the United States to
build a temple for them in which to house these relics. Presumably, as
they expected the Masons of the United States to foot the bills, they made
a liberal allowance for the purpose. Their plans have increased in lavishness cif expenditure by leaps and bounds, and no one knows where it
will end.
They started with a plot of ground as a site for the memorial building,_
consisting of two and one-half acres ; this has been increas.ed to thirty-six
acres, which must for all time be kept by the Masons of the United States
in a park-like condition and which will afford a very convenient park for
the citizens of Alexandria, without expense. They changed the proposed
material of the structure from Virginia limestone to New Hampshire
granite at an added expense of $500,000. It will, no doubt; be the most
splendid and costly memorial ever erected to the memory of any human
being, but it will not furnish food for a single hungry Mason, clothe a
needy one or administer to the relief of a sick and unfortunate member
of the Craft.
Wisconsin Masons can make better use of the one hundred thousand
dollars or more that membership in the association will entail than to
put it into a pile' of cement and granite on a Virginia hill which not one
in a thousand of the members of this Grand Jurisdiction will ever see.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

The Seventh Annual Report of the Committee on Correspon<ience
was submitted by M. W. Brother Jesse M. Whited and is somewhat
of . the "topical variety" but so arranged that any specific subject can
be referred to with ease. It is the best arrangement of this particular
type of review which we have yet seen, and if this vari11ty, which seems
to be rather anathema to the majority of correspondents, must be produced, this is the way to do it. * * * * *
Citation at some length is made of your Maine Correspondent's Foreword on " Masonry, a Unifying Principle," covering nearly a page of
the review, while it is commended as one of the interesting Masonic
"Readings" of the year. This Maine correspondent cordially thanks
Brother Whited for such kin<ily references.

Their eighth annual observance of Public Schools Week again calls
our attention to something not done elsewhere. The observance this year
was the biggest success ever. * * * *
The reports of their several Boards of Rel.ief make wonderful reading. Here we find practical Freemasonry, carried on quietly but very helpfully. It is a marvelous story that California gives to us in this respect.
We cannot say very much about the Correspondence. Of couri;e it
is an extremely interesting document. But being written under topical
headings; .and not in the style of reviews of each particular Grand Lodge
proceedings, an analysis of the whole is so difficult that we do not
attempt it. Of its variety there could be nothing better. As a mere
job, it is a harder thing to do than the conventional.

A Field Day and a ball, organized in the interest of the Masonic and

The St. John's Mite Association is to supplement the activities of

brethren and their families, as well as to widows and orphans. The

by judicious investments to $22,000. Only the interest of the fund can
be used for· relief, under the terms of the will by which the original
amount was obtained.
The Home family is composed of 15 men, 36 women, 23 girls and
25 boys.

The Iowa Masonic Library started from an appropriation of $5 and

in arrears for dues.

South Carolina:
The grand total paid out for relief was $31,100.00 for the year. Th~
plan followed in the dispensing of aid to worthy distressed Brethren, their
wives, widows and orphans, has been found most satisfactory, · and its
continuation is recommended. Not more than $600.00 a year may be paid
to any one Lodge, during one year, for relief among the membership. The
limitation was found necessary because of the condition of the Relief
Fund and the many and widespread demands upon it. The fund, on
November 30th, 1926, amounted to $139,969.45.

Texas:
Texas has contributed somewhat over $65,000.00 toward the Washington Memorial so far.
The Grand Master by his firm stand in the matter of relations with
Mexican Masonry helped greatly to bring about a condition which is in
accord with Masonic laws as applied to English-speaking jurisdictions.
Texas is near the border, and partisanship accordingly is more ardent than
elsewhere. The Grand Master recommended that the fraternal recognition
accorded to the Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico be withdrawn and.
that Texas enter into fraternal relations, without reservation, with the
York Grand Lodge of Mexico. Grand Lodge supported the Grand Master.

Virginia:
The Virginia Masonic Home now shelters over two hundred children.

death, in the time in which it has been functioning.
The Charity Committee appropriated various amounts for relief,

In Fredericksburg is located an old Masonic Cemetery which was the
property of a Lodge which has been extinct for many years. Under the
existing laws the property came into the possession of Grand Lodge. It
was decided to transfer the cemetery to Fredericksburg Lodge which will
maintain it properly.

While in attendance at the Washington Memorial Association, the

at Fredericksburg said that Bro. Meier was the first Grand Master to
pay such a tribute to the mother of Washington. The wreath has since

131

An historical one-act play was presented under the direction of the
Grand Historian, who is the author. It deals with the organization of the
First Lodge at Halifax, in 1750, by the Duke of Cornwallis and others.
The ritual, the ceremonies, the lectures, charges, prayers, songs, costumes
and stage setting were those of 1750. The title of the play is "As It Was
in the Beginning."

Some difficulty arose with' the Grand Lodge of Scotland which had
established Lodges in th~ territory of the Grand Lodge of Chile. The
matter has been settled satisfactorily by Scotland's adoption of a resolution to recognize the Grand Lodge of Chile as a sovereign Grand Jurisdiction.
In June, 1926, a large group of English Brethren owning allegiance
to the United Grand Lodge of England asked the Grand Lodge of Chile
to grant them a charter for a Lodge which would work in their language
and use the Ritual of the Grand Lodge of England. The request was
granted. Thus came into being Prince of W ales Lodge No. 19, which has
made a most successful start. Two other Lodges already were operating in
the same manner. A German Lodge, No. 21, by permission, uses the ritual
of the Grand Lodge of Prussia.

Western Australia:
Brother Riley says things are very different from what they were
years ago when he and Past District Deputy Grand Master Frederick A.
Mullen were out on the goldfields; and what difficulty they had in getting
three Past Masters tog.ether to assist in an installation! He said once they
had three Past Masters at one installation, one English, one Irish, and
one Scotch, but that the difficulty then was to get them to agree about the
function. He settled the difficulty by saying, "You do the fighting and I
will do the installing."
The Grand Master's address mentioned one thing of which Western
Australian Brethren may well feel proud, besides other things. He says
that for twenty-five years he never heard of a Lodge failing to make its
payments to Grand Lodge at the proper time, and that the books, in all
that time, always have closed without one Lodge being in arrears.
Grand Lodge came into existence twenty-seven years ago and since
then has distributed in charity £29,903. The joint benevolent funds now
are £40,966.

Cuba (173 Lodges, 13,320 Members):
The sum of $1,975.00 was distributed among nineteen indigent Brothers and eleven widows of Masons.
The Grand Secretary reports that for the first time the United Grand
Lodge of England, "the Mother of Symbolic Masonry," has appointed a
Representative near the Grand Lodge of Cuba, "reposing this honor in a
Brother so distinguished and of such fame as he who for the past two
years has ruled the Craft with wisdom"-M:.W.'.Bro. Pineiro. The comment is added that England "always has been deliberate in such demonstrations of confidence and distinction," and that the act is of the nature of
a public recognition of the reputation of the Cuban Craft as a respectable
and respected body.
Mention is made of the opening of the Masonic Club at Habana, on
January 21st, 1927, under the auspices of the Lodge Fe Mas6nica. Active
membership is limited to the members of this Lodge, at present, but Brethren of other Lodges are admitted as associates. The announced object is
"to tighten more and more, by social activities, the bonds of fraternity and
to offer opportunity for entertainments compatible with the teachings and
the principles of the Institution."
El Zapato Escolar de la Habana is the name of an association which
supplies new shoes to poor school children. It has been in operation for
about six years, and in that time has furnished ten thousand children with
new shoes. Fifty Lodges cooperate in this worthy undertaking. Similar
organizations have been formed since in other parts of the Republic.
In 1925, the Trajecito Mas6nico was s'tarted by the Lodge Amor
Fraternal (Brotherly Love). Twenty-seven Lodges united with it for the
purpose of clothing poor children in the public schools. In the short time
of its existence, the association has provided clothing for two thousand
children.

Salvador (4 Lodges, 141 Members):
Freemasonry in Salvador has passed through serious difficulties since
it got under way, about thirty years ago, when the first Grand Lodge was
formed with eleven Lodges. Political changes led to its suppression. Ten
years later a new one was formed. Then followed a session of dissensions
and differences between members and then there were two Grand Lodges.
These became united again, in 1912, under the name of Grand Lodge
"Cuscatlan." One year later the handsome Masonic Temple was erected
at a cost of 35,000C. This was destroyed by an earthquake in 1917. The
collapse was so complete that there was no hope of restoring it and a
heavy debt still rested on the property. The Brethren decided not to
undertake any new building until that debt shall have been paid. For
eleven years they have been struggling to become clear of debt, at the
same time not neglecting the Masonic obligation of relieving distress
and helping the needy.
Venezuela (24 Lodges, 1,600 Members):
The Grand Master is elected for three years.
The Fund of Benevolence has contributed to the relief of distress of
many unfortunates-assistance to widows and children of Freemasons,
to Brothers themselves, helping foreign Brothers to return to t heir countries, supplying hospital room for the sick, paying for surgical operations
required by Brothers or relatives of Masons, etc.

Hamburg (54 Lodges, 4,888 Members):
The Grand Lodge of Hamburg sprang from the Provincial Grand
Lodge for Hamburg and Lower Saxony, established by the Grand Lodge
of England, in 1740. In 1811, the Grand Lodge ofHamburg became independent. There were four Grand Masters in the Provincial Grand Lodge.
In the 116 years of its independence, Grand Lodge has had only sixteen
Grand Masters.
Hamburg has two Lodges in Africa, one at Cairo and one at Alexandria; two in Argentina, one at Buenos Aires and one at Rosario de
Santa Fe; one at Valparaiso and one at Santiago de Chile, in Chile; one
in Mexico; and one at Constantinople, Turkey; four in Denmark, and one
in the Free District of Danzig.
At Hamburg six Lodges are under her jurisdiction; at Berlin, seven.
The Quarterly Communications are held in September, November,
February and May. The Annual Communication is held in May.

APPENDIX
AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish
Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized
proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction
is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the
Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the
Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests upon those who have
been regularly elected to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a
Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning " done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, tpe Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight

138

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Templar comes from the efforts of the · Christian Knights to take
the temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the
Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and the
degrees conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °,
inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to
30°; Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River); the degrees
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18°;
Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons- Commence their era with the creation of
the world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4000-5923.
Scottish Rite----Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 3760-5683.
After September add another year.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple
was commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.), "in
the year of discovery."
Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.),
"in the year of the deposit."
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization
of their order. Anno Ordinis (A.· 0.), "in the year of the Order."
From the Christian era take 1118. Thus: 1118 from 1923-S05.
Order of High Prie5thood-Dates from the year of the blessing
of Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis
(A. B.), "in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing: Thus : 1923
and 1913-3836.

Gustav Albert Hutaff
Grand Master 1928-1929

GUSTAV A. HUTAFF
Grand M&1ier
1929

Our sixty-second Grand Master, Gustav Albert Hutaff, familiarly and
lovingly by his friends called Gus, is physically the antithesis of his immediate predecessor, being more than six feet in height, fair of hair and
complexion. He is a na.tive of California, his birthplace being Santa Rosa,
on the 5th of October, 1879. His father was John Henry Hutaff; mother,
Marie Stauffer. His success in all business affairs stamP,s him as one of
the outstanding figures in the commercial life of the west coast. At this
writing he holds the responsible position of chairman of the Board of
Directors of the Bank of America of California, at Dunsmuir. He has
large property holdings in Siskiyou county, and has always during his
nearly thirty years' residence at Dunsmuir, interested himself in projects
which have for their goal the betterment of conditions in his home county
and elsewhere. One of his pet projects is the Masonic temple at Dunsmuir, he being President of the Association. This temple, which includes
a theater, was erected at ·a cost of one hundred thousand. dollars.
Brother Hutaff was educated in the public schools.of San Francisco
and the University of California, from which institution he was graduated with the class 0f 1900, winning the Ph.G. degree. He then engaged
in the drug business at Dunsmuir, which he continued until 1919. During
his college course he enlisted in the military service of the United States
and served in the Philippines during the Spanish-American war as a
member of the hospital corps, 1898-1899, and was th rice decorated by
the government for meritorious services.
Masonic record : Received his first degree September 26; second
degree October 17; third degree October 24, 1901, in Dunsmuir Lodge
No. 297. Served the Lodge as Marshal, Deacon, Secretary, Treasurer,
Warden and Master. Member of Cyrus Chapter 15, R. A. M.; Mount
Shasta Commandery No. 32; Sacramento Consistory Scottish Rite,
K. C. C. H.; Ben Ali Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S., Sacramento; Sciots;
Past Patron of the Eastern Star.
Grand Lodge record: Inspector for sixteen years; chairman Committee on Pay of Members; member of Finance and other committees;
Junior Grand Warden 1925 ; Senior Grand Warden 1926; Deputy Grand
Master 1927; Grand Master 1928.
On January 6, 1904, our retiring Grand Master was united in marriage
with Miss Alberta Moller, and this union was blessed with the gift of a
daughter, named Helen. Mrs. Hutaff is a woman who easily makes
friends, and is · of much charm and grace of person and manner. She ·
is indeed a helpmeet, and the domestic life of the family is ideal.

Almighty and Everlasting God! Source of life! In whom we live
and move and have our being. We offer to Thee our adoration and
homage. Invoking Thy Blessing as we assemble in Thy Name and
Presence. E nlighten our minds with. Divine wisdom, that we may say
and do only such things as are pleasing to Thee. May harmony and
brotherly love prevail among us. So guide and direct us in all our deliberations that the highest and best interests of our beloved Institution
may be furthered and its influence for good in our several communities
extended. Ever may the great principles of Masonry shape and control
our lives that we may exemplify before the world the sublime teachings
of our Fraternity. For all good things that h<1ve been accomplished during the p<ist year we thank Thee, and we pray for pardon for all that has
been done amiss.

May we as a nation, growing in- wealth and power, never forget

. the President of the United States, the Governor of this State, and all
others in authority. We also pray that Divine wisdom may be given to
those who are now in conference seeking to lay foundations for peace and

May they never falter in their stand for righteousness, truth and peace.
Comfort and relieve all our brethren who are sick or in any need.

Remember with Thy favor the wards of this jurisdiction, the children

To the Brethren of Grand Lodge:
Five year~ have elapsed since we celebrated our Diamond Jubilee in
this enterprising and beautiful city and, again we are the recipients of the
wonderful hospitality which characterizes our brethren of the Southland.
It is a pleasure and privilege to greet you in the true spirit of fellowship and bid you welcome to our eightieth annual communication. You
are here to take part in our deliberations and to share in the responsibilities of our proceedings. It is not for me to charge you with your responsibilities during this week, for you all realize the . important trust
which is yours in representing your respective Lodges. I know that
many of you will renew old friendships and form new ones and that you
will return to your Lodges inspired with higher ideals and renewed zeal.
In accordance with the requirements of the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge, I submit herewith, for your consideration, a detailed report of my
official acts, aims, and recommendations. It is my desire that this report
may be the means of conveying to you an adequate conception of the
scope of the work and the responsibilities which are ours in maintaining
the precepts and principles of our Institution on a high standard .
Necrology
We acknowledge the goodness of the Great Architect of the Universe
in sparing to us the lives of all our Grand Officers and Past Grand
Masters.
As we meet in our annual communication, it is proper that we should
pause in our deliberations to express our sorrow at the passing from our
midst of a number of our Grand Lodge members whose devotion to the
principles of Freemasonry makes this passing a distinct loss to our fraternity.
I leave to the Committee on Necrology the task of presenting at this
communication suitable memorials expressing the sympathy of our Grand
Lodge to the relatives and friends of our deceased brethren.

floods which swept through the State of Alabama, the following word
was received :
"Have not solicited outside of State for Grand Lodge, but any contribution gladly received; need is great." Accordingly, I directed our
Grand Secretary to forward to the Grand Master of Alabama our check

Visitations
The craft are to be congratulated on the peace, harmony and prosperity prevailing among the Lodges of our grand jurisdiction, for we can
truly appreciate "how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in
harmony."
We have 572 Lodges working under charters and six under dispensation, and during my term of office, by adopting the plan of holding
district meetings and joint installations, I have been able to contact with
512 Lodges in 105 of the Masonic districts.
It has been a source of great pleasure to have had the opportunity
of meeting so many earnest workers for the advancement of Masonry.
The cordial 'welcome and .courtesies extended to the Grand Master on
these official visits throughout the State are evidences of the loyalty and
interest of the brethren.
During my absence from the jurisdiction upon two occasions, in order
to attend the conference of Grand Masters in Washington, D. C., and to
visit with our brethren in the Hawaiian Islands, our capable Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, in accordance with the provisions of our
Constitution, exercised the official functions of Grand Master.
It was my pleasure to accept the kind invitation of the Grand Chapter,
Order of the Eastern Star, to attend their meeting at Sacramento on
October 16th, 1928. I was most cordially received and accorded all
honors due to me as your Grand Master. To the most cordial welcome
by the Worthy Grand Matron and Grand Patron I responded, extending
the felicitations of our Grand Lodge, together with the wish that their
session might be constructive and most successful.
Numerous other courtesies have been extended to me, as your Grand
Master, by the Knights Templar, Royal Arch, Scottish Rite, Shriners,
Sciots, and the students at the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley. On every
occasion I was impressed by the unbounded hospitality extended which
in a measure shows the respect of these institutions for the Grand Lodge.
On September 11th I paid my official visit to Western Star Lodge
No. 2 in· the old historic mining town in the shadow of Mt. Shasta, and
in the prese~ce of a large gathering conferred the Master Mason degree.
I found the brethren very appreciative of the assistance given them by
the Grand Lodge in the construction of the fire proof vault for the priceless relics of the pioneer Lodge, and learn that in the past year over 1500
people had registered as visitors. This I feel well justifies the investment.
On the occasion of my visits to the Lodges I have endeavored to outline to them the ainis and policies of Masonry, encouraging them to inter-

George Washington Masonic National Memorial
The nineteenth annual convention of the George Washington Masonic
Memorial Association was held in the historical Lodge room of Alexandria-Washington Lodge No. 22 at Alexandria, Virginia, on Thursday,
February 21, 1929, at ten o'clock. The meeting was called to"order by:
Most Worshipful Brother Louis A. Watres, Past Grand Master of Pennsylvania and president of the association.
Accompanied by our Most Worshipful Brother Albert E. Boynton,
Past Grand Master and a director of the association, I attended the sessions
of the association. It was a pleasure and inspiration to be present and
listen to the remarks of confidence and encouragement expressed by President Watres and officers in the progress of the building and its ultimate
completion. It is their hope to dedicate this memorial on the "twentysecond of February, 1932, when the eyes of the world will .be focused on
the city of Washington in the celebration of· the two hundredth anniversary
of the birth of George Washington, "The Man and the Mason."
Like all similar projects, it is a matter of finance, and it will cost
$1,709,624 to complete the Temple. Statistics show that during the year
1928 there were 126,402 admissions into Masonry in the United States
and, while the original plan was to collect one dollar for each initiate,
many jurisdictions, including our own, have adopted other methods of
paying the quota. Twenty grand jurisdictions have exceeded their quota,
7 range from 90 to 98%, 8 range from 52 to 89%, and the remaining
fifteen jurisdictions are below 50'}'o. · I estimate that by the year 1932, the
grand jurisdiction of California will have subscribed in excess of $150,000
.,.,.d I would recommend the continuance of the plan under which we are
maKmg annual payments on our quota.
The Conference of Grand Masters
I attended the Conference of Grand Masters in the United States
which was held in Washington, D. C., on February 20, 1929. There were
38 grand jurisdictions 'i;epresented and 31 Grand Masters were in attendance. The meeting was opened at 10 :30 in the morning by the Most
Worshipful Howard Cruse, Past Grand Master of New Jersey, who
welcomed the representatives. The organization for the conducting of
the business of the conference resulted in the election of Most Worshipful
Byrne E. Bigger, Grand Master of Missouri, to preside over the meeting,
and the Most Worshipful Claude E. Keiper, Past Grand Master of the
District of Columbia, was chosen to act as seeretary. The Most Worshipful Wisdom D. Brown of the District of Columbia then welcomed
the members of the conference to Washington, D. C.

425

The agenda presented to the Conference for consideration was as
follows:
1. Masonic Foundation, or Grand Lodge Charity Funds for Relief.
Should these be controlled and managed by Grand Lodge or a
separate corporation?
In addition to taking care of a brother, his widow and
children, how broad should the scope of such charity be?
Should these funds take care of all cases requiring permanent relief, or should they supplement the relief afforded by
·
subordinate Lodges in this respect?
Should Grand Lodge fix a minimum of receipts of subordinate Lodges to be devoted to charity before aid is given
from general fund ?
Should funds for organized Masonic charities be obtained
by per capita tax, special assessments, or by assessments on initiates and affiliates?
Endowment Funds-Should any portion of the initiation
fees so collected be set aside as a reserve fund for the care of
those who contributed them, or should they be used annually
for current expenses ?
2. Masonic Education. What is the best way to interest members ?
Masonic libraries, loan libraries, Masonic magazines, sale
of Masonic books?
Use of educational secretaries or directors, committees in
subordinate Lodges, films, etc.?
3. New organizations predicating their membership on Freemasonry.
How far should a Grand Lodge go in regulating other organizations which it is felt tend to injure the good name of
Masonry?
4. Masonic Temples. What action should a Grand Lodge take to
control the building of Masonic temples of subordinate Lodges
acting independently or in conjunction with other Masonic
bodies ?
Should plans, both of buildings and of raising funds, be
approved by the Grand Lodge, Grand Master, or Grand Lodge
advisory committee?

The subjects discussed were interesting and of vital importance in

The Hawaiian Islands
On Saturday, May 4th, accompanied by Mrs. Hutaff and daughter.
I sailed from San Francisco on the S. S. Maiolo for the Hawaiian
Islands. As we approached Diamond Head on the island of Oahu,
Brother Charles Pittam, Junior Grand Deacon, and Brother John A.
Madden, Inspector of the One Hundredth and Third District, boarded our
boat and extended to us the fraternal greetings of the brethren. On arriving in the harbor of Honolulu, we were royally welcomed by an enthusiastic group of brethren and their wives, who presented us with
exquisite leis, a beautifully symbolic custom of the islands. We were
taken to the Royal Hawaiian Hotel and from that time until we left,
three weeks later, every hour on the various islands was filled with entertainment for our pleasure. We visited the four large islands on which
are located the Masonic Lodges. Nothing could surpass the wonderful
cordiality and friendliness with which the brethren of the islands received
us. I wish to express my sincere appreciation to Junior Grand Deacon
Charles C. Pittam, Inspector John Madden of the 103rd District, Inspector Charles A. Shepherd of the 102nd District, the Masters of the eight
Lodges, and the individual brethren for their many courtesies. They made
every moment of our trip so delightful that it will be the outstanding experience in our memories.

The Lester A. Pelton Monument
As a lasting tribute to a beloved pioneer member of their Lodge, the
brethren of Gravel Range Lodge No. 59, and Brother Acton Cleveland,
of Camptonville, through their united efforts, erected a monument to the
memory of Brother Lester A. Pelton. The monument is placed on the
site of the cabin where Brother Pelton lived and worked. He was a pioneer of the State and invented the famous Pelton water wheel.
It was a pleasure to have our Past Grand Master George L. Jones,
who has always been interested in this project, dedicate the imposing
memorial. This ceremony· was · performed in the historical town of
Camptonville in the presence of several hundred people on the 31st of
August. The brethren of this Lodge of only thirty-eight members are to
be congratulated for their achievement.
Masonic Homes
Having made several visits to our Homes at Decoto and Covina, I
am pleased to report that they are in ~xcellent condition and reflect the
efficiency of all those concerned in their management.
Upon the receipt of Brother James B. Gist's resignation as Trustee
of the Masonic Homes, last October, I appointed Past Grand Master Will
H. Fischer to succeed him. He served for some time, but on account of
increased business responsibilities, asked to be relieved. Having appreciated the service which Brother Gist has rendered our jurisdiction during
a period of many years as a. Trustee of the Masonic Homes, I prevailed
upon him to again become a Trustee and accordingly I appointed him to
fill the vacan~y.
The report of the Masonic Homes will give a detailed account of
their activities during the past year.

Public Schools Week
Ten years have elapsed since our Past Grand Master Charles Albert
Adams inaugurated the custom of the observance of Public Schools Week
by the Lodges in this jurisdiction. I desigpated the week of April 22d
for this year's observance under his able leadership.
From the reports that have been received from the Lodges, it is gratifying to note that the citizens of our State are evincing a keen interest in
the work being accomplished and have cooperated with our brethren in a
fine spirit in this worthy movement.
The future success of these observances will ever depend upon the
continued interest of the officers and members of the Lodges and their
ability ,to promote community interest in the schools.
I wish to commend the members of this special committee who have
labored with the problems of attending to all details in connection with
this endeavor, and during this communication we will be pleased to have
a report on their activities.

Masonic Education
On November 12, 1928, the Grand Master held a conference with
the members of the Masonic Education Committee of the southern section
of the State and approved the plan of enlarging the committee and recognizing several new districts in the jurisdiction.
Under the very efficient direction of this committee, the scope of the
work is being broadened in various directions, so at the present time the
average Mason is more interested in the program than ever and there is
no doubt but what we are making a definite contribution to the educational life of our brethren. This is one of the means of awakening a real
interest in Masonry for we cannot expect a brother to be interested in a
subject that he knows nothing about.
This committee will .report at this communication, and without anticipating their report, I assure you that I am strongly convinced that
there is a necessity for the work they are doing and I urge the endorsement of their recommendations.

New Lodges
After careful consideration and investigation of petitions presented
for new Lodges I have issued six dispensations. In no case have I encouraged the formation of a new Lodge until I was firmly convinced that
there was a real need for its existence and that the interests of Masonry
would be well served.
The ambition of some of our brethren to form new Lodges without
consulting either the Grand Master or Inspector in advance of their intentions to organize and who hold preliminary meetings without authorization, has in some few cases caused an embarrassment to brethren who
had requested demits from their Lodges and this practice should be discontinued.
Decisions
The Grand Master has received a few inquiries asking for decisions
which are answered by the Constitution and Regulations. I invariably
replied with reference to the proper section or regulation. It is gratifying
to say that the necessity for formal decision on matters of Masonic law
are less each year, because the brethren are more familiar with our laws
and regulations.
My decision has been asked as to whether or not Acacia Lodge has
the right and authority. to confer the degrees of Masonry in the German
language upon candidates elected in other Lodges on the request of said
other Lodges.
The rights and privileges of chartered Lodges in the jurisdiction of
California are determined by their respective charters, and the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge.

432

PROCEEDINGS OF THE·

The facts as stated in' the petition of Acacia Lodge to work in
German as set forth in the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge in the year
1920, page 227, are that Acacia Lodge No. 438 was organized and granted
its charter October 14, 1913; that at the time the said charter was granted
the right to use the German language in its meetings and in the conferring
of degrees was also granted.
Thus by resolution of the Grand Lodge, Acacia Lodge is excepted
from the general rule as set forth in section 121 of the Constitution, as
are the Lodges specifically mentioned as exceptions therein.
These Lodges are thus given special privileges as Lodges tci confer
degrees in foreign languages.
Therefore, I held that no Lodge in the jurisdiction of California
other than those that are permitted to confer degrees in the German
language is permitted to allow degrees to be conferred upon candidates
elected in its Lodge by persons conferring them in the German language.
The above ruling applies in my opinion to all Lodges now permittr.d
to work under special privileges.
Clubs
The subject of Lodge clubs and internal organizations referred to the
Grand Master for investigation and study, has received my careful consideration and I herewith submit my conclusions :
Social activities undoubtedly have a place in all Lodges and, in
moderation, they are not a waste of time. 'However, when they are of
such a light and frivolous character as to be of the "slap stick" variety,
they deserve the consideration of Grand Lodge in order that the brethren
interested in internal organizations of this social character, may be
brought to see the light of wisdom and eliminate them from Masonic
affairs. We are deeply concerned with the problem of this type of club
which is of a non-charitable type and which conducts various forms of
ritual and ceremonies which are not in keeping with the dignity of
Masonry. For this type of organization, I have no sympathy, and recommend that any such clubs or other purely social organizations of this unworthy type within our Lodges be eliminated.
Clubs which have been formed for the commendable purpose of
rendering financial aid to the dependent members of the family of a deceased brother should be encouraged, providing they are firmly established
upon a sound financial basis. The past experiences of many such . organizations have not · been satisfactory and I would like to have the
brethren of our Lodges receive the benefit of expert advice relating to
their financial resources. I therefore recommend that a special committee
of three be appointed by the incoming Grand Master for the purpose of.
making a survey of these clubs and determining whether or not they are

GRAND LODGE OF UALIFORNIA

433

financially sound and to submit their recommendations at the next annual
communication.
Purely social activities can be adequately taken care of by committees,
appointed for that purpose by the Masters of the Lodges. In my opinion.
committees, working under the direction and leadership · of the Master,
can fill whatever needs may arise for the social enjoyment of all the
brethren.
Clandestine Grand Lodges
At the present time we have a special committee, at work investigating the status of several clandestine Lodges in the State. From my own
personal investigations it is quite apparent that many Filipinos are innocent victims of a small group, more interested in the mercenary than
fraternal side of the transaction. It appears that in addition to charging
them a fee they sell these men all sorts of regalia. A few of these
Filipinos have interviewed and informed me that gradually their fellow
countrymen are beginning to learn of the fraud being perpetrated upon
them and are taking no further interest in the affairs of these Lodges.
Financing of Masonic Temples
Several Lodges in our jurisdiction have submitted their plans of
financing the building of Masonic temples to the special committee authorized at our last communication, and are fortunate in having had the
cooperation of such capable brethren as M:.w:. Brother William P.
Filmer, Grand Treasurer; William P. J effries, Chairman of the Committee on Finance, and Brother Robert Greig, who have given freely of
their time in reviewing the applications for approval.
The legislation enacted has had a stabilizing effect, and has enabled
the brethren interested to become educated in the business end of the
transaction. While in all probability we will have fewer Masonic temples
erected in our jurisdiction, it will be the means of safeguarding the
brethren against financial embarrassment.
This subject has had the serious consideration of many jurisdictions,
was freely discussed at the conference of Grand Masters in Washington, D. C., and several jurisdictions .have already adopted similar legislation to ours.
Recommendations
Impressed by our lack of reliable information concerning the financial
status of Lodges, I endeavored to secure finan.cial statements of the net
worth of the Lodges as of January 1st, 1928, and as of January 1st, 1929,
in order to set up a guide for Grand Lodge officers. Also as an indicator
as to the general financial ·condition of the craft, not for publication but
for the files in our Grand Secretary's office.

The statements in many cases have not been complete, some have not
made proper appraisal of their holdings, others have not reported at all.
Other grand jurisdictions have authorized committees to make surveys of
the financial condition of their Lodges with good results. The functions
of the committees consists in collecting from the Lodges statistics and
information tending to show how near they are operating within their
income from dues, to appraise the net worth of Lodges and to assist the
officers of Lodges with their financial problems. Such a survey I .feel is
of importance and worthy of consideration. 1
During my visitations throughout the jurisdiction, I noted a tendency
to disregard the importance of safeguarding the health and safety of the
brethren by not providing proper ventilation and precaution against fire,
and earnestly suggest that these matters have the attention of officers of
Lodges in this classification. Furthermore in many of the pioneer Lodges
there are many valuable books and records of historical importance to the
pioneer Masonic history of our State, and I would recommend that the
brethren of these Lodges take proper steps to place them in fireproof
~afes or cabinets.
Grand Lodge Regalia
The regalia now in use for ceremonial occasions. has been in service
since 1906, and during all those years it has been shipped almost daily to
different parts of the jurisdiction. It has served its day well, but it is
now sadly worn, and to those of our brethren who have seen it on the
officers officiating at public ceremonies, no argument is needed that it
ought now to be replaced. I recommend that the Grand Secretary be
directed to provide a new traveling regalia set.

I sincerely regret that the real offenders cannot be segregated, thereby
preventing the duty which I feel is incumbent upon me, and it is only
after careful consideration that, under date of September 24, 1929, I
ordered the arrest of their charter, and recommend that this order be
kept in force until the next communication of our Grand Lodge ; unless
the incoming Grand Master shall in the meantime become satisfied that
the members of the Lodge are making a conscientious effort to uphold the
principles of Masonry and work in harmony. In which event he. be authorized to return to the Lodge its charter. In order that the property
and ·business affairs of the Lodge be properly conserved, I specially
exempted from suspension Brothers Walter Grant Campbell and the
Treasurer and Secretary.
Following is the text of my letter to the Master and members of
the Lodge:

434

Seal Rock Lodge No. 536
During the past ten months, due to the existence of two factions who
have embarrassed Masonry generally, the conditions prevailing in Seal
Rock Lodge No. 536 have been a source of much anxiety to the Grand
Master and other Grand Lodge officers.
At my request, Brother Chas. M. Wollenberg, Deputy Grand Master,
visited the Lodge on February 6, 1929, as my representative, and endeavored, to the entire satisfaction of all concerned, to adjust the existing
differences. As a result of this conference and in an effort to bring about
a conciliation, the Worshipful Master resigned.
After conferences with the officers of the Lodge, the granting of
special dispensations to reballot on candidates and to hold an election to
elect a Master caused by the resignation of the former Master, it has
been impossible to bring peace and harmony within the portals of the
Lodge, and the conditions seem to grow worse each month.

435

To Milo Bohall, Ma.rter, and the Wardens
and Brethren of Seal Rock Rock Lodge No. 536, F. & A. M.
BRETHREN :

My attention was called several months ago to grave violations of
Masonic law in your Lodge. In the interests of peace and harmony
and in the sincere desire to bring about an amiable adjustment of the controversies existing, I asked our Right Worshipful Brother Charles M.
Wollenberg, Deputy Grand Master, to visit your Lodge to ascertain the
real conditions and facts. He visited you and his overtures for peace and
harmony, as well as many efforts on my own part, have availed nothing.
Your Lodge is apparently split into two factions and bitter feeling
prevails. The followers of one faction are not allowing the election of
any candidate presented by the opposing faction. This condition is an
embarrassment not only to the members of your Lodge, but to Masonry
in general.
The foregoing facts have been established through very careful in~
vestigation. It is evident that under these conditions the usefulness of
your Lodge has been partially destroyed, harmony has vanished, and you
are not enjoying the true Masonic spirit that should prevail in your
Lodge.
It is, therefore, ordered that the charter of Seal Rock Lodge No.
536, F. & A. M., located at the city of San Francisco, be and the same
is hereby arrested and the work and business of the said Seal Rock
Lodge is hereby ·suspended until the next annual communication of our
Grand Lodge.
It is further ordered that . the charter of said Seal Rock Lodge
No. 536 be forthwith delivered into the custody of Very Worshipful
John Whicher, Grand Secretary.

Grand Master.

Conclusion
After twenty-six years of continuous service in the ranks of Masonry,
you honored me with the position of Grand Master. For this manifestation of your confidence I am deeply grateful. In accepting this distinguished honor I realized that it carried with it much labor and greater
responsibilities. I have at all times been faithful to the trust reposed in
me and when in a comparatively few hours I place the gavel of authority
in the hands of my worthy successor, I will do so with the knowledge that
I have endeavored to the best of my ability to discharge the various duties
incumbent upon me.
I sincerely trust that the spirit of kindness and brotherly love will
characterize all the proceedings of this communication and when our labors
have ended that we may all be permitted to return to our homes well and
happy with renewed ardor for our Fraternity.

Appreciation
All Grand Masters of our jurisdiction have received the loyal support
of the officers of the Grand Lodge and the brethren and the same cooperation has been accorded to me.
I wish to commend all the Grand Lodge officers for their attention
to all matters referred to them and their attendance at many of the special
communications and my visitations to the constituent Lodges.
While I realize it would be impractical to thank individually all who
have assisted me in administering the affairs of my office, I would be
remiss in my duty if I did not here acknowledge the generous and efficient
services of our Grand Secretary, John Whicher. He has at all times
been willing to render a service to the brethren as well as to the Grand
Master and I am glad to record here my sincere appreciation of his work.
To the Inspectors, I wish to express my deep appreciation for the
splendid support given to me. These are the men who, without financial
compensation, are giving unsparingly of . their time and energies in the
interests of Masonry.
Reception to the Grand Master and Mrs. Hutaf£
After traveling throughout the State and having had the pleasure of
meeting so many of the brethren, the journey was ended with the reception to the Grand Master and his wife.
The gracious hospitality accorded us at the Sala de Oro of the
Biltmore Hotel, Los Angeles, last evening will long be remembered. The
finished artistry of the entertainment and the informal greetings of the
representatives and their ladies left a warm feeling in our hearts.
The new acquaintances made and the many courtesies bestowed upon
us brought a further realization of the true spirit of fraternal love and
fellowship prevailing in the Institution.
