DUNSMUIR, CALIFORNIA
PROCLAMATION
TENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

To all Masons in the Jurisdiction:
In the past, men have learned that the advantages and opportunities
of life should not be for the individual alone, but for all. Due to the
educational system of our country it has been possible to equip a greater
number of our future citizens for the responsibilities of life, and it is
only by supporting such a worthy cause that we may hope to attain an
even higher standard of learning.
In the education of the children of our nation and in the promotion
of the sentiment in support of our public school system, Masonry has
aroused many of the citizens of our communities to a deeper realization
of the importance of our public schools.
It should be the earnest desire of all Masons that every child should
share in the fullness and richness of the opportunity for success which
is made possible through education.
Now, therefore, we, Gus A. Hutaff, Grand Master of Masons in the
. jurisdiction of California, do now proclaim the week commencing Monday, April 22, 1929, as Public Schools Week in the Masonic Lodges in
this jurisdiction; and we do request and direct that during that week
there be held in every community in California and Hawaii in which there
exists a Lodge of Masons at least one public meeting for the Tenth
Annual Observance of Public Schools Week.
We do likewise request and direct that wherever practicable the meeting be held in the auditorium of a public school ; and that it be particularly remembered that the observance of Public Schools Week is a community affair in which we seek the active co-operation of all local civic
organizations and the participation of all the people in the community.
We do furthermore request and direct that no "work" be done by
any Lodge on a night on which any meeting for the observance of Public
Schools Week is held in the town or city in which the Lodge is located.
Dated at Dunsmuir, California, this 11th day of February, 1929.
Attest :
]OH N WHICHER,
Gus A. HuTAFF,
Grand Secretary.
Grand Master.

Gus A. HuTAFF, Grand Master
DUNSMUIR, CALIFORNIA
MASONIC CLUB HOUSE AT U. C., LOS ANGELES

To All Lovers of School Students:
At our Annual Communication in 1928 a resolution was adopted as
follows:
Whereas, An effort is being made to secure funds with which to erect
a Masonic Club House at the University of California at Los Angeles ;
and
Whereas, This Grand Lodge looks with especial favor upon every
proper effort to minister to the mental arid moral well-being and development of our youth, and regards Masonic club houses at our great seats
of higher education as centers of usefulness and helpfulness to students
from Masonic families ; now therefore be it
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge hereby approves and indorses the
campaign to raise a building and endowment fund for a Masonic Club
House at the University of California at Los Angeles.
Our Los Angeles brethren, with their usual enthusiasm for all things
tending to the betterment of mankind, immediately set the necessary
machinery in motion to raise funds for the purpose indicated in the resolution. They succeeded, of course, as is their habit. The building is finished, furnished, and will be ready to receive student sons and daughters
of Masons, September 1st. The club will be particularly a haven for boys
and girls who for the first time are away from home and home influences.
It will be a place for clean social diversion, for relaxation from college
activities, and where the lonesome and homesick student may be associated
with those whose business it will be to serve them and direct them and
keep them happy-and altogether it will be a home worthy of the support
of the fathers and mothers of the students and of our members generally.
The Fraternity owes a debt of gratitude to the brethren who have
given so much of their time and thought and energies in the erection and
furnishing of the building, and I take this opportunity to thank the directors for their unselfish work.
All students having Masonic affiliation will be welcome, and assistance given to new students during registration week.
Elmer E. Beckman, 219 Security building, Pasadena, is Secretary of
the Masonic Oub, and brethren are requested to furnish him at once
necessary data concerning students in whom they are interested.
Gus A. HuTAFF, Grand Master.

To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:

By resolution of Grand Lodge the privilege of receiving this token
was confined to those veterans who had been members of Lodges within
our jurisdiction for fifty or .more years.
Several designs were prepared and submitted to the Grand Master,
who approved the one shown in the accompanying cut. Briefly described,
the design is a gold square and compass with the letter G on a blue field,
the circle being gold with the legend "Member 50 years F. & A. M. California" in blue, all superimposed on an octagon plate of gold representing
the old-time fifty-dollar slug so well known to all pioneers. On the back,
the name of the recipient veteran brother is engraved.

Section 36 of the Constitution provides that the Trustees of the
Masonic H omes shall make a complete report qf the property, condition and operations of the Homes for the previous year, to the Grand
Lodge. We have the honor of presenting herewith the report of our
stewardship for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1929, with a roster of
residents to and including August 31.

President, Charles M. W ollenberg, Deputy Grand Master ;
Vice-President, Will H. Fischer, term to 1931 ;
Chas. Albert Adams; te~m to 1929;
Albert E. Boynton, term to 1930;
Samuel E. Burke, term to 1932;
John Stewart Ross, Senior Grand Warden ;
Robert B. Gaylord, Junior Grand Warden ;
Treasurer, ex-officio, William P. Filmer;
Secretary, ex-officio, John Whicher.
In December, Vice-President Fischer, finding that his business engagements would not permit him to give to the H omes the attention he
believed should be given, resigned. The Grand Master prevailed upon
Brother J . B. Gist to again assume the responsibilities incident to work
on the Board, and at a meeting of the Trustees held on the 31st of December, he was elected Vice-President.
During the year the Board has held three regular meetings at Los
Angeles and Covina, and two at San Francisco and Decoto. The members at Los Angeles held meetings every week, and likewise weekly
meetings were held by the members living at San F rancisco.

The general condition of the residents of the Homes will be reported
by the respective Superintendents. Briefly it may be said that the children
are and have been free from serious illnesses and no deaths are reported.
At the Home at Decoto the mortality has been greater than in any
previous year, due largely to the epidemic of influenza which prevailed
last winter. We have lost by death in the year, 50 residents at the
Decoto Home.
The Homes are now caring for 140 men and 124 women at the
Decoto Home; and 96 boys . and 85 girls at the Covina Home, a total
of 445. In addition to those domiciled at th.e Homes, outside relief is
being extended to fortY-four Lodges for the support of 30 adults and
38 children. A detailed list of those receiving outside assistance appears
in the reports following.
Duririg the year, 58 men and women were admitted to the Home
at Decoto, and 25 boys and girls were admitted to the Home at Covina.
25 children were honorably .discharged.

One boy from Pentalpha Lodge No. 202, having mech~ical tastes,
has through the interest of members of his own Lodge, secured a place
as an apprentice in the shops of the Santa Fe Railroad at San Bernardino, and will learn to be a machinist. It would be well if Lodges general~y took the same lively interest in the welfare of their wards upon
leavmg the Home, as has been manifested in this case.

Graduations and Scholarships
Six girls and five boys, who were wards of the Home, were graduated from high school in June. These young people have not been set
adrift to make their own way as best they can; instead, for each of
them a vocational plan has been worked out, and in such cases as it was
deemed necessary, provision for their future training has been made
through the generosity of Lodges and friends who have con~ributed to
the Scholarship fund.
One boy from West Gate Lodge No. 335 has matriculated as a
medical student at the University of California at Los Angeles, where
his expense is being met jointly by his Lodge and the Scholarship fund.
One girl from Liberty Lodge No. 299 has entered the University
of California at Berkeley, intending to take a medical course. Her

One boy, who has attained distinction in high school athleties is
ambitious to become an athletic coach, and has been admitted to 'the
University of Southern California, where a scholarship has been provided
for him, his further expenses being provided by a group of Masons in
Los Angeles.
One girl from Hermann Lodge No. 127 plans to become a teacher
of physical education, and is now attending the State Normal College
at San Francisco. Her expenses are being defrayed by relatives with
some assi~tance from the Lodge and the Masonic Homes.
'
One boy had his heart and mind set on becoming a naval officer
and through the kindly offices of our good brother, United States· Senato;
Samuel M. Shortridge, he has secured an appointment to the United
States Naval Academy at Annapolis for the year 1930. In the meantime
he has enlisted in the navy and will serve as a "gob" until next spring.

Labor in Vacation Time
Twenty-three of the older boys and girls gave up the privilege of
enjoying the summer camp at Balboa during school vacation, in order to
accept employment and earn money to buy their own clothing, and thus
help in that measure to maintain themselves while in the Home. Their
employers were all passed upon by the Superintendent as being people
with whom the children would receive proper care and supervision.
These children all returned to the Home in time for school, each having
the proud possession of a bank account.
Building at Decoto Home
The new dormitory, immediately south and adjacent to the old administration building, is completed and occupied. The residents therein
are comfortable and are proud of their new quarters.
The administration building, erected in 1898 and badly shaken by
the seismic disturbance in 1906, has been torn down, and plans are
completed for a new structure to take its place. Contracts for the
building were let in the latter part of August, and construction work will
progress rapidly. The new building will be of steel frame with brick
exterior, and when completed will round out the general plan of the
group. This new administration building will add much not only to the
appearance of the Home, but will also add to the comfort of residents
and visitors, and make for economy of time on the part of the
management.
Brother Frank B. Hartman, who has been in charge of the Decoto
Home since 1909, maintains the same active, sympathetic interest for
:which he is justly famed, and under his fatherly care the residents are
happy and contented.
'
In this work he has the whole-hearted and able co-operation of the
genial Matron, Mrs. Minnie Richardson, who is beloved by all the
old folks.

Mrs. Lena Luckenbach, widow of the late John Luckenbach of East
Gate Lodge No. 290, died last fall, and by the terms of her will the
sum of $60,000 was bequeathed to the Masonic Homes. The fund is to
be known as the "John and Lena Luckenbach Fund," and the testator
requested that the principal sha11 never be expended by the legatee, but
that the interest thereof shall be used for the care of orphans or the aged
in Masonic Homes. This estate will be settled in about two years.
Another large bequest was that of the late P . W. Newhall, whose
entire estate (said to be about $200,000) was left in trust for the use and
benefit of his widow, and at her death, to the Masonic Homes.
A Matter of Policy
ln the booklet that was mailed to all Lodges in April last, g1vmg
rules for admission and general information respecting the Masonic
Homes, the following paragraph appears :
"The welfare of the child should be the first consideration of the
Lodge. No child should be sent to the Horne until every effort has
failed to find a place in a private home. The Trustees will co-operate
with Lodges in endeavoring to maintain the relationship and contact of
parent or guardian and child, even to the extent of a reasonable allowance
from the funds of the Homes."
Your Trustees, through long experience, observation and much study
of the problem of caring for dependent children, are inclined to agree
with the present policy of social and welfare workers throughout the
United States, that no matter how well managed they may be, institutions
or public homes cannot give to the child that degree of individual attention which obtains in a private home having a maximum of say six
cir eight children. The Masonic Home for children, maintained by the
brethren of California, we are proud to report, has the reputation of
being one of the best institutions of its kind in the United States. But
children do get heart-hungry for individual love and attention; they
need, and are entitled, to the opportunity to develop independence of
thought and initiative that is difficult to develop when raised in the mass.
Daily contact of two hundred children during a few hours each day

PROCEEDINGS OP- THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

at school is good; .but daily contact of the same number in an institution
which must be governed by set rules, where they are housed and fed
and instructed in the little niceties of conduct, is not, as to some children,
conducive of the best results.
And then, too, parental responsibilities should be considered and
encouraged, and wherever and whenever possible the personal relation
of child and parent ought to be maintained. It is true that some
children do develop morally, mentally and physically in the large institutional group, but there are many whose diffidence, sensitiveness, need
for individual attention or other special characteristics render them
unfitted for successful assimilation into institutional life. Therefore,
very careful investigation should be made not only by your Trustees but
by Lodges in every case to ascertain so far as possible if some plan
can be worked out whereby the child can be cared for under the
supervision of the mother or otherwise outside the Masonic Home.
There is no appeal to the heart and conscience greater than the
appeal of childhood. No Mason denies a child's need, and no philanthropy is so worthy as that which tends to insure the welfare of .the
child, who is aptly and properly called the hope of the future. There is
an obligation upon all men and women to help the weak, and this obligation applies with particular force to members of our fraternity. In
California, as elsewhere, there is an ever-growing spirit of Brotherhood
and social obligation being manifest by Masons, and we believe we will
have the whole-hearted cooperation of Lodges in our efforts to place
our dependent children, whenever possible, in private homes, or to assist
parents and guardians in maintaining personal supervision in their own
homes.
Recently, applications were made by a Lodge for the admission of
three children whose mother had died, leaving the father in what at
first appeared to be in a helpless domestic condition. The situation was
saved by the employment of a good, motherly wo"man as housekeeper,
thus permitting the family to remain intact and happy, besides furnishing
a worthy woman a home and means of livelihood.
In another instance there were four motherless children whose father
was endeavoring to maintain a home by .the employment of a housekeeper who proved to be unsuitable. The father was not temperamentally fitted to preside over the home even with a godd housekeeper,
although he was a good man and father. A boarding home was found
for these children in the home of a faithful, motherly woman near ·
the father's place of employment. This home is visited frequently by
a representative of the Masonic Homes to insure that the children are
being properly cared for. The father sees his little ones almost daily,
and contributes what he can towards their support, thus permitting and
encouraging him to maintain his proper sense of r~sponsibility.

Your Home at Covina, under the able and inspiring management of
Brother John M. Downen, is maintaining its high reputation as a banner
institution. We commend to your thoughtful consideration his report
of conditions and problems of the children and for the children.

468

469

Shifting by Children of Responsibility for Parents
Too frequently applications are made for the admission to the
Home at Decoto of aged men and women, when investigation discloses
that there are several adult children-in one case, six sons and daughters
-who, while not prosperous, are able to maintain their own homes, and
jointly could easily care for the old father or mother. They appear
however to want to shift this responsibility to the Fraternity. Father
or mother may be a bit cranky, but the children forget the deprivations
and loving care bestowed on them by the parents when they were babies,
and try to adopt the line of least trouble by foisting the old folks on
the Masonic Home. We have even had the sad spectacle of witnessing
a son or daughter driving up to the doors of the Home in a costly
automobile and calling on a father or mother who ought to' be in the
care and custody of the caller.
Responsibility of Lodges
In our annual report for the year 1925, and again in 1926, we
referred to the embarrassment caused by Lodges accepting as members
Masons who became immediate subjects for relief and who apply for
admission to the Masonic Home within the reasonable three-year limit
fixed by Grand Lodge. In 1925 we reported the distressing case of an
applicant who had received his Masonic degrees two years before, he
being at that time 72 years of age and having suffered from a severe
heart ailment for seven years. At that time we reported that the
responsibility for the care of this member was morally on the Lodge, and
denied admission.
In 1926 we reported to you the instance of a small Lodge having
elected to membership an aged brother who had been a member of an
Eastern Lodge for thirty years, and had been a resident within the
jurisdiction of California for six years. At the invitation of brethren
he affiliated with the Lodge near his home. He was at that time without
means and in poor health. The Lodge of course was within its rights
in accepting this responsibility, but it was not justified in asking the
entire fraternity to share the expense of maintaining this old brother
at the Home, and the Trustees denied admission on two grounds : First,
that he had not been a member for the required three years ; and second,
that the sole responsibility for his support was properly with the brethren
of his Lodge.
Other similar cases have heretofore been cited. Within this year we
were put to the embarrassment of denying to a Lodge the admission of

470

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

a member who had been elected to membership two years ago at the
age of 72, from a Lodge of another jurisdiction that had been remitting
his dues and furnishing him food. Our Lodge attempted to justify its
action by the lame statement that "the investigating committee did not
make a thorough investigation, and that it was having a hard pull since
the erection of its temple, and is not in a position to answer calls for
relief!"
A particularly sad case was that of an applicant for admission to
the Decoto Home who was 60 years of age, in good mental and physical
health, who was unable to secure employment because of his age. The
Trustees are well aware of the quite general present-day rule of
employers to refuse employment to men who are over the age of fifty,
but they are of the opinion that in cases such as this sixty-year old
brother, the members of the Lodge ought to assume the responsibility
for his care · and provide employment for him. The application was
denied for that reason.
Some of our brethren are prone to forget that the individual Maso'!
has obliga.tions to relieve distress and that all relief work is not to be
foisted upon the Lodge or the Masonic Homes.
We respectfully request that the per capita tax for maintenance for
the fiscal year ending July 31, 1930, be fixed at twenty-five cents.

C. M. WOLLENBERG, President,

J. B. Gist, Vice-President,

s. E. BURKE,

(HAS. ALBERT ADAMS,
ALBERT

E. BOYNTON,

JoHN STEWART Ross,
RoBERT B. GAYLORD, Trustees.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home

To the Board of Trustees:
I herewith present for your consideration the following report for
the year ending August 31, 1929.
Building Activities-During the past year there has been the usual
routine in the management of the Home. The year has been a very
important one. It marks the completion of the new south wing, consisting of four floors and basement. The first and second floors are
now occupied by married couples, and the third and fourth floors by
single women. The basement is equipped as a banquet room. This
,
room can comfortably seat 400 persons.
The old Administration building is now being torn down and will
be replaced by a five-story and basement steel structure. The first floor
as formerly will be used for administrative offices, reception rooms, etc.,
and the upper floors for residents and employes of _the Home.
The new permanent improvements have greatly enlarged the benevolent work carried on here by the fraternity and will enable the management to render a higher standard of service in the care of those who are
entering the evening of their lives and afford them more of the comforts
and quiet so much desired by them.
There are now at the Home 140 men and 124 women; 58 persons
were admitted-34 men and 24 women. During the year 50 have passed
away and 3 departures.
Health-The general health of the members of the family has been
good, with the exception of those who are infirm and feeble owing to
advancing years.
The facilities afforded by our hospital department enables our
physician and nurses to give every care and attention to those who are
ill. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance. There are at the
'
present time 34 persons being cared for in the hospital.
Industrial-All the members of the Home are encouraged to render
some service in keeping with their strength, and in their leisure hours
to interest themselves in healthful and wholesome diversions for their
general well-being. A number of the brethren have contributed by
their labor to the welfare of the Home by their services in the carpenter,
paint and upholstering shops, care of the garage, mail, passenger and
auto service, kitchen, pantry, vegetable room, laundry, store-rooms,
chiropodist, care of flower beds, lawns, clerical work, attending phone
calls and light work in a general way. During the year all minor
repairs have been attended by the brethren of the Home.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

483

The making, marking and mending of linen, sheets, pillow slips,
table cloths, preserving cloths, etc., is attended to by the ladies of the
Home. They also assist in preparing fruit and vegetables, work in the
kitchen and in the dining rooms and take care of their rooms, halls and
laundries and other parts of their departments and general household
duties.
Farm-There has been no change in the management of the farm.
The greater part of the hill ranch has, as in the past, been leased either
on shares or cash rental. Our share has been more than sufficient for
the needs of the farm department, the surplus being sold in the local
market. The orchards have supplied plenty of fruit for table use, the
surplus being either preserved or sent to the drier and stored for future
use. The garden has furnished a variety of vegetables and greens. The
chicken ranch has supplied all eggs for table use. All over and above
our needs have been preserved in water glass or sold in the San Francisco market.
The water supply has been plentiful for household, garden, irrigating and building purposes, also for fire protection.
Library and Club Rooms-There are now 5,800 books on the
shelves of our main library and branches located in the club rooms and
hospital department. The Masonic Hill branch of the Alameda County
Free Library continues to be well patronized and enables our family to
obtain many of the latest books. In addition, we are the recipients,
through members of the fraternity and friends, of daily papers, magazines and periodicals which are placed on the tables of the men's club
rooms, and ladies' reading and social rooms. A reading class for those
with impaired eyesight or entirely blind meets daily in the main library.
At that time the daily papers and subjects of interest are read to them
by good readers selected from the members of the Home.
Social Life-Many splendid programs and stage plays provided by
friends have been enjoyed by the members of the Home. The evening
gatherings often close with dancing. Every Thursday evening we all
enjoy a moving picture entertainment. Every Tuesday evening a social
is held in the Assembly Hall, where tables are provided for cards,
chess, checkers and dominoes, etc.
Choir practice every Friday evening. The usual services are held
every Sunday afternoon. These services are often conducted by Ministers accompanied by the choirs of their churches, after which a few
musical numbers are given by the Home orchestra.
A number of the members of the Home have radio sets installed
in their rooms. This privilege is partic11larly appreciated by those who
are blind and those who are confined to their beds in the hospital
department.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The
specials were those which were held on New Year's Eve, New Year's
Day, Lincoln's Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day,
Fourth of July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Arrangements have been made whereby members of the family, a
few at a time, may visit nearby Lodge and Eastern Star Chapters; also
sm~ll parties may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest. During
the year many trips are made to Oakland, San Francisco and towns in
the vicinity of the Home.
Grand Master Gustav A. Hutaff and Officers of the Grand Lodge
have made a number of visits to the . Home during the year, and a large
number of brethren from various Lodges have spent many pleasant
hours with us. The number of visitors and donations received this
year ·indicates an increasing interest in the welfare of the Home family.
I wish to extend my appreciation of the services rendered by the
officers and employes throughout the year and to express my sincere'
gratitude to the members of the Board of Trustees for the kindly
assistance they have at all times given and the many acts of courtesy
received.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

Report of Superintendent, Covina
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
Another year of the varied and interesting life of the big family of

childr~n in the Co;i~ .Ho~e has passed. While every day has brought
the tnals and anx1et1es which are to be expected in the developing Jives
of nearly two hundred children, the year's end brings the supreme satisfaction which comes with the feeling that many a child has been able to
make and hold substantial gains in physical development in mental
growth and in character.
'
Ours is a work of hope, facing as it does toward the dawn of life.
It is a privilege to have contact with the enthusiasm of childhood and
the energy of youth. The richness of our opportunity challenges our
best efforts. I am pleased to report that our staff of workers has labored
faithfully to discharge the trust imposed upon them.
A most important feat.u re in determining results in child training is
the proper selection of personnel. We exercise the greatest care to
c~oose housemothe;s and housefathers who possess those qualities of
mmd and heart which fit them to deal wisely with the children entrusted
to th~ir charge. In both the boys' buildings we have at the present time
~arned. couples as housefather and housemother, and this arrangement
is workmg well. In the Younger Girls' building we have two housemothers, each having under her charge about twenty girls: The Senior
Girls' building, housing some fifty girls, ranging in age from thirteen to
seventeen, has heretofore had the services of but one housemother· but
we are making arrangements for the coming year to give this group' part
of the time of an assistant housemother.
Health-The general health of the children in the Home has been
excellent. During November and December influenza which at that
time was epidemic in California, invaded the Home, filiing our hospital
full to overflowing. The disease was mild in form however and all
patients made a good recovery.
'
'
The average number of children confined in the hospital was four·
and t~ere was a daily average of sixty'-two clinical treatments, most!;
for mmor cuts and bruises.
The key note of our health program is prevention. An ailing child
is immediately placed in the hospital. Promptness of treatment is of
prime importance in preventing serious illness.
An important factor in our health program is dental work. Each
child is seen by the dentist twice yearly, and any needed work is attended
to. An important new feature introduced during the year has been the
establishment of orthodontic treatment for straightening the teeth of
children whose dentures show marked irregularities of conformation. We

504

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

now have some thirty-five children under this treatment, which in the
average case extends over a period of two years, and will result in
great benefit both to the appearance and future health of these children.
When Does Childhood End ?-Caring as we do for children ranging in age from four to eighteen, both boys and girls, we find no la~k of a
variety of problems. Roughly speaking, our work falls into two divisions;
the first dealing with childhood and the second with youth, the dividing
line being approximately the age of thirteen. Because little children
are ~ore easily managed and kept in order, we are liable to fall into
the error of concluding that our treatment of them is less important
than that of older children. We must never lose sight of the fact that
the younger the child, the more impressionable he is. The best modern
thought is giving increasing emphasis to the importance of the right
handling of children in the pre-school age. The little child who is being
wrongly handled may be docile and seem to present no behavior problems ;
but when the same child comes into the adolescent period a host of
difficulties will show their heads, resulting from the error of his earlier
mishandling.
About one-third of our charges are in the adolescent period, but
because of the greater complexities of the problems arising in this
period they require more of our attention than do the two-thirds who
are still in the period of childhood. The adolescent has the impulses,
ambitions and desires of an adult, but these are not controlled by the
judgment and common sense which only years can bring; hence arise
many problems which require the utmost tact, patience and wisdom.
This year eleven of our wards, five boys and six girls, were graduated from high school. All of these were aided in making choice of
vocations, and in each instance plans for vocational training were
worked out.
Not all of our children are fitted to complete the academic high
school course, and for these some other plan of training and adjustment
must be made. One boy, for instance, who was not doing well with his
studies, gave evidence of taste and ability to learn the sign painting
trade. At the age of sixteen he was placed in the Frank Wiggins Trade
School in Los Angeles. During the time of learning this trade he is
being cared for by us in a suitable boarding home in Los Angeles. By
the time he is eighteen he will have acquired sufficient skill in this trade
to be self-supporting.
Work and Play-Children develop character through both work
and play, and the proper proportion of these two factors at the various
ages is an· important factor in any well balanced program of child
care. Our children are called upon to bear their part in the work

GRAND ;LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

505

necessary for the conduct of the Home. Much of this work is necessarily monotonous, but we believe that work not intrinsically interesting
may, because of that fact, have distinct value in character formation.
Care should be taken, however, that the amount of uninteresting work,
exacted from any child should not be excessive in amount.
The recreational life of children, if properly devised is rich in
educational values. In planning recreations we should iook beyond
~erely giving children a good time. During the year we have materially
improved our provision for guiding the recreational life of our children.
We maintain in the Home an active and successful troop of Boy Scouts;
and for the boys who are too young for this we have other similar
activities suited to their needs. The child whose spare time is filled
with well-planned recreational activities is not liable to get into mischief; "mischief" is usually the undirected effort of the child to
provide his own recreation.
Our summer camp at Balboa ( Camp Tucker) is a splendid recreational asset. Here the children spend their summer vacation, living a
carefree outdoor life, with plenty of exercise, sunshine and fresh air.
In addition to these advantages for physical welfare, the Camp
fulfills an important recreational and educational need. The life of
institutional children inevitably tends to become routinized. From the
monotonous regularity of life in the Home at Covina, the Camp affords
a much needed relief. Camp life can without detriment be much more
unrestrained and free than at Covina during the school year. There is
a change of scene and a new set of activities. Duties and work in the
Camp can be much simpler. There can be much more free time, during
which the child is "on his own," and at liberty to fashion his activities
according to his own fancy. From his own resources and imagination
he can devise his projects and carry them out. The diversity of the
experiences which come to him in this way afford him recreation which
is truly re-creation ; and he returns to his school year with a new
reserve of vitality, not only physical but mental, ready to settle down to
the disciplined effort of another yeat's school work.

Swimming Pool-A greatly needed addition to our recreati.onal
facilities at Covina is an outdoor swimming pool. Indications are that
this need will be met during the present year.
"On the Home"-Some time ago a fifteen-year-old boy in the Home
asked for a new pair of shoes. His housefather, after inspecting the
clothing record, said to him, "Why, John; the record shows that you
received a present of a new pair of shoes from your grandmother only
two weeks ago." "Yes, I know," replied John, "but it has been six
months since I had any shoes on the Home, so that I thought I ought
to have another pair coming on the Home." This boy's reply represents

PROCEEDINGS OF. '!'HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

an attitude which comes about all too readily in any charitable institution,
an attitude which we regard as worthy only of a pauper and inconsistent
with the self respect our boys and girls should achieve as they come
into the years of accountability. We are endeavoring to build up, and I
think successfully, a sentiment among our older children which will
make them ashamed to receive as a gift anything which they can earn,
a sentiment of pride in getting beyond the stage of dependence, and a
feeling that they are under obligation to "carry their own weight" while
in the Home, so far as they may be able to do so. We are finding many
of our older boys and girls preferring to forego a summer of play at the
beach in order to take employment whereby they may earn money to
buy their own clothing and incidentals. Those who go to the summer
camp at Balboa in many cases obtain gainful employment while there.
In order to encourage their desire to earn their own money we have been
developing a plan of paying our older children for some of the work
which they do in the Home. If a boy needs a pair of shoes it is much
better for him to buy and pay for them with money he feels he has
earned than it is for him to receive them as a dole.
We see increasing evidence of the far-reaching beneficial effects of
giving our older children actual practice in the use of money. Inasmuch
as the affairs of every adult's daily life are intimately related to the
earning and spending of money, boys and girls who soon must make '
their own way in the world need training and experience in this respect.
It is surprising what a degree of industry and thrift, to say nothing of
increased self respect, is exhibited by children who are gaining this
experience.

not be put into words. The principles of Masonry, as he comes to
apprehend these through the very existence of the Home and its
protecting care of him, operate with powerful and lasting effect to shape
his ideals and form his character.

506

Unmeasurable Values-The highest values that can come from the
efforts which the Home puts forth in behalf of its wards cannot be
represented by statistics or statements of fact. But though they cannot
. be defined or measured, they are not the less real. No matter how complete may be the provision for the physical welfare of our children,
no matter how lavish may be the supply of material comforts, no matter
how thorough and skillful may be their mental instruction, results will
be barren unless their lives can be so touched as to enrich and purify
their emotions and awaken their ambitions to bear a worthy and noble
part in the world. Our supreme task is to aid each developing personality
to "find" itself, and to set out on life's journey with fine enthusiasm
and high purpose. The forces which may work to these ends are
manifold, and oftentimes difficult to command. Mother love, flowing
toward the child through the open doors of the Home, it may be from
a mother who has passed to the Great Beyond, in. many cases moves
with persuasive influence. The characters and personal examples of his
teachers and others in daily contact with him preach sermons that need

The Committee .is sure that it expresses the great pleasure of the
members of the Craft at the many visitations which it was possible for

the Craft to meet the Grand Master personally, to enjoy his hearty handshake and to be refreshed by his pleasant smile and courteous greeting.
It is a matter of special gratification that the Grand Master was able
to visit the Hawaiian Islands. These Lodges are so distant from California and need the stimulus of a visit from the Grand Master from year
to year. We are sure that the Grand Master's visit this year has infused
a new fraternal spirit and has intensified the fraternal feeling existing
among the Lodges of the Islands. We recommend that the matter of
the expenses of the Grand Master in his trip to the Hawaiian Islands be
referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Committee feels that the Grand Master is especially deserving
of commendation for his attendance upon the conference of Grand Masters.
We believe that it has long been the feeling of the Craft that the
various grand jurisdictions of the United States should be brought closer
together. The grand jurisdictions have many problems in common and
many activities of grand jurisdictions can and should be coordinated.
The Great War taught us how important it was for the grand
jurisdictions of the United States to be able to act togethe.r for the benefit
of Masons whithersoever dispersed and present-day national civic social
problems emphasize that necessity.
We trust that the succeeding Grand Masters of this jurisdiction will
find it possible to attend these annual conferences.

Your committee regrets, what seems to us, an unnecessary loss from
suspensions for non-payment of dues. This is something that for which
the Masters and Secretaries of the various Lodges are directly responsible.
If every Master at the beginning of his term would start out with the
idea of closing his year with a clean balance sheet suspensions would be
reduced to a minimum, if not entirely eliminated. There is really no
excuse for suspension for non-payment of dues. Too many members are
in the habit of allowing their dues to run 'along under the idea that they
will pay sometime during the year with the result that it is forgotten.
Dues are payable in advance and should be so collected. Failing response
to notice, the Secretary should follow up each delinquency, being assisted,
if necessary, by a committee appointed by the Master. If any case appears where it is a burden for member to pay dues the same should be
brought to .i:tention of the Master and after investigation remitted. We
would respectfully suggest that an official letter ?e sent to the Master at
each Lodge requiring him to make a personal report on delinquent dues
before the installation of his successor and that his report be spread on
the minutes of his Lodge.

ANNUAL ORATION
Rev. Dr. Tully C. Knoles, President of the College of the
Pacific, then delivered his annual oration, and on motion the
Grand Secretary was directed to secure a copy t hereof and
cause copies to be printed in sufficient number to supply
each Lodge in the jurisdiction. The oration was received
with a standing vote of applause and tha~ks. The full text
follows:
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
It is with unusual pleasure that I address you upon this occasion.
The .past year in association with my fellow Grand Lodge officers, it has
been a delight to assist our Most Worshipful Grand Master Hutaff in
several communications of the Grand Lodge for various services, and
also to be with him and the Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer upon
several occasions for Installations and other visitations.
Upon one occasion the friendliness and charm of our Grand Master
was shown in a remarkable degree. A brother approached him in the

537

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

anteroom, and exhibiting his apron said, "Brother Hutaff, you raised me
twenty-two years ago," arid in token of that he showed the signature of
Gus A. Hutaff. Instantly the Grand Master said, "Let me have the
apron," and he re-signed it "Gus A. Hutaff, Grand Master of the
Jurisdiction of California." You may be sure that such an exhibition of
friendship will be treasured not only by the brothers, but by all who have
come under the charm of our presiding officer.

And in particular should there be Masonic education concerning
foreign jurisdictions. The similarities as well as the differences should
be carefully explained, and when there is sufficient information to warrant
action World Wide Masonry may be united and toleration and brotherhood become facts of relationship and not words in a ritual.
Recently in a Masonic Lodge, I clasped hands with a member of a
Lodge in British India, and his Indian countenance lighted with sympathetic interest in our common service, and many of us have rejoiced in
the inspiration and fellowship of Chinese as well as of European Masons
-should not the process of unification be accelerated by education until
by knowing the Masons of the world our prejudices should be eliminated?
In the field of education which does not have to do primarily with
history and ritual, there is a wide range for the development of theories
of moral values and relationships, not only for Masonic relationships
within the body of the institution, but in the dealing of the individual
Mason with the outsider, not only that the outsider may thereby conceive
a good opinion of Masonry, but for the personal moral g_rowth of the
members.
Again, there is a vast field for the cultivation of the philosophy of
our order. So mu.ch of Masonic philosophy to which we have listened or
which we have read is stilted and unreal, is based upon far-fetched
symbolism or seeks mystical confirmation through appeal to strange signs
or numerical symmetries. Masonic philosophy should be interested in
life and in problems of human living, much more than in esoteric speculation.
My personal feeling is that the average Lodge is too satisfied, and
perhaps too busy with the work of the conferring of the degrees to spare
time for the consideration of the real problems of human living in this
most complex human age.
.
The modern American world is materialistic, mechanistic, and selfish.
It needs spirituality, personality, and altruism. Where can it secure solid
teaching to develop these ideals better than within Masonic Lodges? You
may ans~er-That is the function of the church. True, but Masonry
gathers round an altar upon which is an open Bible, every Mason has
declared in writing his belief in God and in immortality, and every Mason
has sworn not only to be just in his dealings but to limit his passions
with due regard for all mankind.
There is no question about the ideality or the sublimity of the declared tenets of Masonry, but there is a vast field for Masonic education
in the illustration of and inspiration to the applications of these elements
of philosophical disquisition to practical living. And it is my humble
opinion that the average Mason hungers in vain for the food of such
teaching. Brethren, our membership has not culled. all of the best of

536

In addressing you today, I am mindful of the old adage, "Shoemaker,
stick to your last," and the subject of "Education from a Masonic Standpoint" is enjoined upon me.
Naturally, the first consideration of this theme must have to do with
education concerning the history, customs, work and ritual, interfraternal
relationships, national affiliations, and the international coordinations
necessary and desirable for the securing of a world wide fellowship of
Masonic adherents.
There is ' required a great deal of research to present to the craft
adequate information in these fields. Our usual instruction contains such
a mixture of fact and fancy, of history and tradition, of reality and of
symbolism, that a serious attempt should be made to acquaint all of our
initiates with the areas of these various fields as well as an evaluation of
their comparative worth. Much of this instruction of necessity may be
given only in the sacred precincts of a just and legally constituted Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons, and much of it can only be given in periodicals, devoted to the interest of Masonry, in books of accredited standing written by those whose training and ability are such as to give them
a note of authority. The form and attractiveness of both books and
periodical~ should be such as to command the attention and respect not
only of the members of the order, but of the profane as well. Impossible
and fantastic claims should be eliminated and substantial facts substituted
in all cases.
In our interfraternal relations particularly there is a need for a full
and free discussion of all orders and institutions whose members are
drawn from Master Masons. Their advantages and disadvantages should
be clearly set forth by competent authorities, and their attractiveness
should never consist in their mysteriousness to a member of a Blue Lodge.
We plead also for a closer union among the various Grand Lodge
jurisdictions in the United States. There has been too much particularism
in Masonry in America. It is a splendid thing that the most Worshipful
,Grand Masters meet in unofficial groups from time to time, but in these
days of rapid growth in national organizations there should be the
strength of unity in our vast institution whose impact for good citizenship ·
and high morality would be greatly increased by a more closely knit
regular organization among the American Grand Lodges.

538

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

American life, but it has much of it, and it will respond nobly to intelligent appeal, and its response will be of such a nature as to enhance the
power of the Order ever the noblest impulses of unselfish lives.
My second consideration has to do with the traditional and present
relationship of Masonry to education in general.. Masonry has always
fostered• education and has been foremost in its support of the public
schools of the countries in which it is established. This is particularly
true in the case of the United States of America, where the public schools
hold a unique position.
Originally all schools in the American colonies were under religious
auspices, and it was not until 1821 that a free public high school was
founded in our land, and with one exception, all of our original colleges
and universities were founded under religious guidance, and many of them
retain that leadership until this day.
Masonry in America has always and rightly so, lined itself on the
side of public school as opposed to sectarian school development. It is
necessary for modern minded Masons to keep three factors of this
problem in mind. Sectarian education for, by, and of a religious denomination is one thing; religious schools open to students of all faiths
upon an equal footing, but with distinctively theological training either
restricted to separately organized schools of theology, or made wholly
elective is another thing; while public education in the American Democracy of necessity must eliminate all but the most formal of religious
exercises and indeed all religious instruction of all sorts. Unless we are
exceedingly careful this promises to be a very serious problem. There
are many strict adherents of this ideal of public education, who do not
stop to realize that the United States of America, Mexico, Russia and
China are the only great nations that do not have the sanction of an
established religion, and that of this list the United States is the only
government which has never had the sanction of religion. With these
exceptions, the public schools of other nations have religious curricula
as surely as they have curricula in any other field.
Unless we as Masons are very careful of our phraseology; we may
force ourselves to take positions on the matter of Masonry's attitude to
public education neither in harmony with our traditional attitude nor our
actual desires. Our traditional attitude has been opposition to sectarian
education, not religious education; to the use of public funds for the
support of sectarian education, not to the honest dev~lopment of moral
values and concepts.
·
In our earnest and rightful desire to protect ourselves and people
from sectarian education, we should not sanction and indeed demand an
atheistic education. Let me make my meaning clear. In our American
democracy we do not have a unified type of people and therefore we

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

539

have no national religion, formal or otherwise. But we have not yet
forgotten that in the beginning our fore fathers demanded that every man
should have the right to "worship God according to the dictates of his
conscience," and we must not forget that the separation of church and
state was not in a spirit of antagonism to religion, but in not ·only a
spirit of toleration, but in a spirit of appreciation of the fact that organized religion could and would care not only for the distinctive religious
needs of the people, but also for the total function of higher education.
This tremendous fact is too frequently overlooked by the over-zealous
partisan of our modern school system. Not many who frankly and rather
quickly respond to the tocsin to protect our public school system are
willing to follow the call to establish state and federal monopoly of all
education from the kindergarten to and through the University.
Rigid conformity to the highest educational standards should be
enforced upon all schools of all grades operating in America. Let us
note that the. secularization of schools has now reached a pproximately
nine-tenths of completeness in the elementary and secondary fields and is
increasing in the collegiate and university fields, but has not yet reached
fifty per cent of completeness, in spite of the size and influence of our
great and growing State Universities.
There is here a vital consideration. Our democracy is very inclusive,
as to peoples, creeds, economic theories, and social practices, and the
more inclusive our school system becomes the greater the number of
areas of s.ilences mapped out, and the fewer and more conventional and
the more materialistic the fields of untrammeled research. We are not
permitted even to attempt to solve our religious, social and political relationships with our intelligence, we must use our traditions and our
prejudices.
Masonry in California can point with just pr~e to the interest
created and sustained in public education as the result of a decade of
observances of Public Schools Week. Too much praise cannot be given
to the Committee which originated the plan, and to the successive groups
which have carried it forward. It has• been my great privilege since the
formal recognition of the week to have spent many days and nights in
travel and in speaking in the interest of our California school system.
I have only words of praise for the idea. But I also have a great deai
of sympathy for local committees which try to do successfully what is
desired. There are two extremes, both bad. Somewhere in between lies
the ideal. One extreme is to have an interesting program put on by the
children in the schools, a varied program which calls for the participation
of a great number of children. This calling out of a great number of
children will mean of course a large audience, for the parents and friends
of the pupils are out in great force. As a demonstration it is highly
successful, but it gives no opportunity for the stressing of the whole program, and I have learned by bitter experience that a speaker on such an
occasion, who usually gets the floor about nine-forty-five, is roundly
scored if he takes time to deliver the address which he has prepared, and

540

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

is considered ridiculous if he accepts the situation and passes it by with
"a few well-chosen words." The other extreme is where no program
has been arranged, save the address of the speaker. Very few occupants
of the seats of the Auditorium are present. The chairman deplores the
lack of interest, and the speaker loses confidence in his "drawing" power.
As I said before, somewhere between these extremes is the ideal situation.
It can be arranged so as to balance the program between the speaker and
the school production.

There are three general attitudes of opposition to a federal department
of education : The first is in the field of an increase of federal control
and interference. The successive bills that have been introduced have
carefully and consistently guarded the local interests at that point.
Federal aid and guidance, but not control, is designed.
In the second place there is fear for democracy itself in a government
controlled system of schools dovetailed into a federal system of education.·
An autocracy must control education in order to perpetuate itself· an
aristocracy must crumble if an 'aristocratic system of education does' not
sustain it. Democracy can only live where there is freedom of thought,
of speech, of publication, of teaching, and of research. Democratic
control of education by many is looked upon as a misnomer. But in our
opinion, a Federal Department of Education would foster all or" these
freedoms rather than restrain them.

Our schools today are doing so much more than they did a few years
ago, and a good, well-produced opening program, given by students, supplemented by an informational address by some one thoroughly interested
in education, followed by an hour given over to the viewing of an exhibition of the handiwork of the children, will make a program attractive
enough to call out an adequate crowd, definite enough to be of real educational value, and informative enough to be stimulating. I have seen this
plan successfully followed.
Nowhere else on the face of the earth are the citizens of a great
Commonwealth doing more in a material way to educate its young people
than in California. Far-reaching experiments are being tried. Particularly in the secondary field is California the leader. Here the total
adolescent population, representing every economic, social, financial, moral
and religious stratum in society is required to be present in a unified
school system. Problems of administration, and of economic adjustment
are very serious, but they are being attacked in a sane, whole-hearted way.
Masonry has undertaken through its Committee on Public Schools Week
to sanction, explain and popularize the great experiment in our beloved
state. May we not give the Committee our most whole-hearted support.
Then again, Masonry is committed to the ideal of a federal department of educatior1' with . a secretary in the President's Cabinet. It is
startling that America has left the education of her young so fully to the
care of states and local units. There are of course historical reasons for
this. When the Constitution was written, public education was in its
infancy, and in fact all education, as before mentioned, was looked upon
more as a local social and religious function than as a political one. Then
again in the controversy between nationalism and particularism the matter
of the control of schools in our diverse situation seemed more logical in
local hands.
Such scientific study as has been given by various groups seem to
indicate a need now not for federal control, but for national guidance.
The tremendous increase in the facilities for the intercommunication of
ideas, including the latest one, the radio, calls for national minimum requirements, and not local ones. The differences which have emphasized
local standards no longer exist, and our schools should reflect at least
approximate unanimity of standards. . Illiteracy is today criminal in the
United States, and a costly criminality at that.

541

Then there is a group of ultra-conservative church men not at all
confined to the Roman Catholic Church. This group fears th~ continued
secularization of educatiop until the state, federal and individual, should
gain a monopoly on education. There is little to fear in this field, though
the opposition thus far has been able to combine enough votes representing
these various attitudes to defeat each successive bill advanced. But
victory will come for education is now and always will be the most important factor in our social and political world, and its ·guidance cannot
be left to local interest, temporary caprice or superinduced hysteria· the
steadying continuous influence of national stability is essential.
'
It is also the wr iter's personal belief that Masonry should support
the proposition that at Washington, D. C., there should be located and
adequately supported by the Federal Government a great National
Graduate University, when all the resources of the Congressional Library,
and all of the opportunities of Congressional and of International Conferences should be at the disposal of students of America and of the
world. This is feasible and most desirable. What a capstone to the
great structure of democratic schools in our forward looking nation l
Here could be gathered the most eminent scholars of the world in every
field. Here adequate facilities could be provided them by the nation.
Laboratories in which experiments fraught with good to humanity might
be performed in every conceivable field. Here the library facilities and
artistic opportunities beyond compare might be developed for the utilitarian and cultural good of mankind. What a dream to stir the heart
of a patriot I
·
My brethren, these are my convictions : Masonry needs education in
her ow~ life and history. Masonry needs education in her own philosophy
~nd etht~s; and .the worl~ needs the power of her leadership in stimulating
mterest m public educat10n and in the education of the public from the
kindergarten to a Federal Department of Education and a National
University.

R E PORT OF THE BOA R D O F CO NT RO L
To the M. '.W.' .Grmid Lodge of California:
Your Board. of Control was created by legislation enacted by Grand
Lodge in 1926; and the year 1929 therefore marks the third year of
activity of said Board of Control.
Its first year as a committee of Grand Lodge was devoted to a
survey of the Boards of Relief of this grand jurisdiction in order that
its members might become acquainted with the organization, policies,
procedure and administration of said Boards of Relief. Thereafter
recommendations were made to and approved by this Grand Lodge, providing for uniformity of organization and procedure of Boards of Relief
the second year's efforts of your Board of Control were devoted entirely
toward making effective the legislation enacted by Grand Lodge and as
contained in the aforesaid regulations.
Chief among these recommendations were provisions for uniform
reports, filed at uniform periods; the keeping of uniform records; an
annual survey and audit of financial transactions ; the adoption of a uniform code of by-laws, and the requirement of fidelity and compensation
insurance.
The year just closed has been devoted to th~ further and continued
effort for a uniformity of procedure in the Board of Relief, and particularly as to the matter of compacts and Qy-laws of the several Boards.
Four meetings have been held during the year as follows .: At Los
Angeles on December 8th, 1928; at San Francisco on June 29th, 1929;
at Los Angeles on September 7th, 1929; at Los Angeles on October 7th,
1929. All of these meetings have been noticed to the respective Board
of Relief with request and invitation for representatives to attend and
present any matters of importance. Immediately following the close of
Grand Lodge in 1928, your Board of Control communicated with the
officers of the respective Boards of Relief, giving notice of the legislation
enacted by Grand Lodge and requesting the assistance and cooperation of
said boards in carrying out the Grand Lodge legislation thus enacted.

643

The response to the request of the Board of Control was most satisfactory. · In some minor matters, uniformity. is not yet general, but these
few discrepancies are being remedied and your Board of Control believes
that in another year all Boards of Relief, so far as possible, will be
working along the same lines. The members of your Boards of Control
do not mean to infer by this statement that we favor an unalterable,
straight-jacket procedure. Rather do we desire individuality, initiative
and personality in the procedure and in the reports. At the same time,
hewing close to the line laid down by Grand Lodge legislation, conferences have been held during the ·year with representatives of Boards
of Relief in an effort to bring about uniformity and a better relation
and understanding of Grand Lodge and Board of Control requirements,
where misunderstanding and suspicion theretofore existed. We are
pleased to report that there is now a complete understanding and with
it a better spirit and a very noticeable desire for harmony and accord.
Auditors' Reports
The legislation of 1926 provided for an annual survey and audit of
the work and financial affairs of each Board of Relief, such survey and
audit to be a charge against the respective boards.
Because of many complaints on the part of Boards of Relief that
said survey and audit was burdensome and expensive your Board of
Control at its first session following Grand Lodge session of 1928 referred. the matter to the respective Boards of Relief, with authority and
direction to secure an audit and survey and to report same to the Board
of. Control. In the main this plan has proved satisfactory, particularly
with the larger organizations, but some of the smaller boards neglect or
refuse to have such audit made. Your Board of Control has decided to
continue this plan of audit for another year, before going back to the
method of having the audit made by one firm of accountants.
Financial Report
Financial reports have been received by the Board of Control for
the period ending July 31 from all Boards of Relief, without exception.
Your Board of Control is of the opinion that the report blanks now
in use are not sufficient in their detail and do not convey to the Board the
ri~ht sort of information or enough information. It is respectfully submitted that the Board of Control, in the absence of objection, will draft
a new report blank to be furnished Boards of Relief before the next
communication of Grand Lodge.
Uniform Records
The respective Boards of Relief have at last yielded to the recommendation made by your Board of Control and approved by Grand Lodge

Requests for Reimbursement
In connection with the reimbursements heretofore referred to and
included in this report your Board of Control desires to call attention to
the respective Boards of Relief as well as to all the constituent Lodges of
this jurisdiction, the necessity of reporting to the Board of Control immediately, the neglect or refusal of any Lodge whether in the jurisdiction
of California or elsewhere, to reimburse such Board of Relief or such
Lodge for relief extended. By so doing the Board of Control will be
able to assist in securing the required reimbursement.
Scottish Life Members
Your Board of Control is in receipt of much comment and criticism
from Lodges and Boards of Relief regarding relief extended to so-called
life members· of Lodges under the Grand Lodge of Scotland.' In only
rare instances do these Scottish Lodges respond to appeals for relief and
in fewer instances do they reimburse the Lodges of this jurisdiction. In
response to an inquiry, Grand Secretary Whicher has been informed that
the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Scotland provides :
"Where Lodges have a fixed commutation fee, clear members
may commute their annual contributions by a single payment, the
amount of which shall be determined by the Lodge."
The Grand Secretary of Scotland writes: "Brethren who commute
their annual contributions are clear on the books of the Lodge, so far as
their dues are concerned, and receive from the Lodge a life membership
certificate."
The fee determined by the Lodges ta these commuters is usually a
nominal one and so, for a guinea or a pound and ten shillings or some
such amount commuters are sent out from Scotland to mingle with Masons
here who pay far more in one year than the Scots pay for the balance of
their lives. This situation is not objectionable, perhaps, until the Scotch
commuter gets into financial difficulties. He has no money, his lifemembership Lodge has no funds because he and many others have commuted and the California Lodge which relieves him cannot receive any
reimbursement. Your Board of Control does not make recommendation,
it would not be in accord with the fine spirit of California's Masonic
generosity to reject an appeal for relief, but your Board of Control does
wish to issue a word of solemn warning to our Lodges against the nondues paying commuter Scotchman and his financially stranded Lodge.

December 26, 1928.
"Will H. Fischer, Grand Master,
State of California,
1107 Edison Bldg.,
Los Angeles, Calif.
"Most Worshipful Sir:
"Because of the many requests which the Board has received
to assist in the reimbursing of other jurisdictions, for money expended in assisting the members of this jurisdiction, on November
10 at a meeting of the Board of Control administering the Outside
Relief Funds in this jurisdiction, the following resolution was
passed:
"Resolved that the Board is not justified in paying out funds
unless they are consulted before the expenditures are made.
Therefore, be it resolved that this Board notify Relief Boards of
all other jurisdictions in the United States and its possessions,
that they will not be responsible for reimbursing the Relief Boards
or Welfare Committees of Lodges in other .jurisdictions, unless
permission is first obtained to advance the relief.
"Inasmuch as the application for relief for any member of
this jurisdiction must come through the Lodge in which the brother
may hold membership, it is not the intention that the permission
be granted by this Board, but rather that it be authorized by the
particular Lodge in which the brother requesting relief holds
membership.
"The procedure governing relief from various Lodges and
the relief fund in this jurisdiction is already effective and known
to the Lodges in this jurisdiction.
"Sincerely and fraternally yours,
"F. HOMER NEWTON, Grand Master."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Your Board of Control, which was created by unanimous vote of
Grand Lodge at its annual communication in 1926, has now passed beyond
the experimental stage. Its functioning_in connection with the handling
of the problems of the various Boards of Relief and Employment_ Bureaus
in our grand jurisdiction has, we believe, demonstrated the wisdom of
its creation and merits its continuance as a . Constitutional Committee of
our Grand Lodge.
The legislation prepared by the Committee on J urisprudence and
adopted by Grand Lodge at the annual communication in 1926 covering
the appointment, duties, and powers of the Board of Control has been
most excellent and has adequately covered its operation. We recommend,
however that the matter of reimbursement of Lodges for funds expended
in matt:rs of relief be left to the discretion of the Board of Control in
order that immediate reimbursement may be made when warranted subject, of course, to the approval of the Grand Master.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption :
Resoli•ed, That a new section be added to the Constitution to be known
as Article VIII-a, setting forth the appointment, duties and power s of the
Board of Control and to read as follows :
SECTION 37: There is hereby created a Board o,f Control to consist
of five members to be appointed by the Grand Master. The term of office
of the members of the Board of Control shall be three years provided
that the members of the Board of Control as now existing shall hold office
until the expiration of their respective terms. Vacancies shall be filled
by appointment by the Grand Master for the unexpired term.
Sec. 37a: The Board of Control shall have control and supervise
the activities of Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus now existing
or hereafter to be created under the authority of the Grand Lodge of
California.
Sec. 37b : The Board of Control shall make such rules and regulations as it shall deem necessary for the effectual operation of the several
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus within this S tate, and shall
endeavor so to standardize the work that the operations of the several
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus may be conducted economically
and efficiently.
Sec. 37c: The Board of Control shall pass upon all applications for
the formation of new Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus and
shall submit all such applications to the Grand Lodge or Grand Master
with its recommendations and the Board of Control shall, with the consent
and by the direction of the Grand Master, have power the compel any

Employment Service
Organization, procedure, methods and administration have shown
marked improvement in the employment service institutions under this
Grand LOdge. Recommendations made by your Board of Control and
approved by Grand Lodge have been followed and there is general satisfaction over present conditions. Particularly in this case in Los Angeles,
Long Beach and San Diego. Employment service or rather unemployment. service is the big problem in all our Masonic centers and our organizations are to be commended by their splendid efforts for their
willingness to cooperate with Board of Control plans and suggestions.
, A brief resume of statistical information of the employment service
follows:

Employment Bureau-San Francisco
Due to the fact that a great many boys who regi~ter do so through
their affiliations as sons of local members, it is impossible to say how
many register from local Lodges. It is estimated that 15 per cent of
all registrations are from local Lodges.
During the year applications have been handled as follows: Applications received, men and boys, 3008; women and girls, 645. Positions
secured, men and boys, 1169; women and girls, 253. Temporary, 687.
Total, 2109.

556

Employment Bureau-Los Angeles
· A plan to establish an Employment Committee in each Lodge to
place members of that Lodge and to cooperate with the Bureau in other
ways, is meeting with some success. The committeemen and Masters are
furnished with lists of applicants and unfilled positions.
During the year applications were received and positions secured as
follows:
Applications received, men and boys, 3583 ; womeh and girls, 1304.
Positions secured, men and boys, 1217; women and girls, 197. Temporary
positions, 1006. Total, 2420. Funeral attendants furnished, 2772. Of
the total registrations 1596 were from local Lodges.

Employment Bureau-Oakland
The Employment Service is supported by thirty Lodges and six of
the higher bodies. Five Lodges do not contribute.
Applications received during the year, 1176. Positions secured during
the year, 961.
Employment Bureau-Long Beach
The bureau has been very successful this year, due to the large building program in Long Beach. Fully 65 per cent of the male positions
have been filled by men experienced in the building trades.
The service has had splendid cooperation from the Masonic employers,
the Social Welfare Employment Bureau and the personnel departments
of the oil companies. Also many local members have acted as "scouts"
to help fill the positions.
Statistics are as follows : New applications filed, male 583, female
270. Registered applicants called at office for work, male 3337, female
868. Positions secured, male 1306, female 326. Firms and individuals
using the service to secure their help, 710. Calls made on employers, 407.
Telephone calls in the office, 4311. Active applicants on file August 1st,
1929, male 246, female 73.
Employment Bureau-San Diego
The highly transient character of the applicants calling at this office
makes it difficult t o show the full amount of service rendered. Fully
300 temporary positions were secured the past year which do not show
in the records. Arrangements have been made to record all these temporary positions during the coming year.
Following is a summary of the statistics:
Applications received : Masons, 227 ; women, 176; non-Masons, 50;
De Molays, 48. Total, 501. P ositions secured: Masons, 165; women,
99; non-Masons, 26; De Molays, 38. ·Total, 328.
Twenty-five members of local Lodges were registered during the
year.

While our own Employment Service organizations are now functioning better than ever before, little, if any, progress has been made toward
bettering the unemployment situation in Masonic centers in the jurisdiction. The records still show that the placements of the Employment
Service do not compare favorably with the number of applicants. Again
our Employment Service in several localities is facing a loss of revenue
from the unwillingness of other Masonic organizations, which have
heretofore constituted to contribute further.
As our own Lodges increase in membership as more and more Masons
of Eastern jurisdictions locate in this state, the problem will become
greater, the conditions more acute.
California cannot withdraw from the good work it has begun. If
other M~sonic organizations fail in their duty this Grand Lodge must not
fail.
Again we commend to this Grand Lodge the consideration of the
appointment of a State Employment Service Secretary who will give his
whole time and attention to unemployment of Masons, the appointment
and organization of Employment Service Committees. We do not recommend this appointment now, but are respectfully submitting it for consideration because we believe the time is near at hand when such an official
will be imperatively needed in our state.
Again we commend to Grand Lodge as we commended last year the
authorizing and empowering in each district of the jurisdiction of the
Inspector of the district, when and where conditions may be advisable to
name an Employment Service Committee.

During the year over 19,000 pieces of literature, including the above
