circular letters were sent to all the Masters relating to the progress and
the work in general.
At the present time our mailing list contains approximately 1176
names. About 800 letters were received in connection with the work,
and approximately 1000 personal letters written. Several sectional conferences were held and the Chairman of the Committee, the members and
the ex~utive director visited approximately 126 Lodges.
A synopsis of the expenditures includes the following items:
Executive Director's salary, $2499.95; rent and stenographer for executive
director, $1500; printing, mailing and postage, $2445.36; telephone, telegrams and incidentals, $486.64; books, $15.10.
In addition to the above mentioned publications the Committee has
re-printe.d, in pamphlet form, the series of talks to be presented to
candidates and has sent two copies of this pamphlet to every Lodge. In
view of the emphasis laid upon this phase of the Educational program
this publication was thought highly desirable and the response from the
Lodges to the receipt of this publication has more than justified the same.
In August of this year the Chairman of the Committee addressed a
letter to the Masters offering in concise form certain suggestions as to
the manner of fostering the work; and in that letter a response was
solicited. You will be intensely interested to know that approximately
sixty-three per cent of the Masters sent letters of approbation and
comment. It has been a source of the deepest satisfaction to the Committee to know at first hand that the officers and members of the Lodges
are realizing ~ore and more as the years go by that the educational
program of our Grand Lodge is gradually taking its proper place as an
integral part of Lodge activity. In future years when those candidates
who have received instruction under the present program shall have.
succeeded to the various offices in the Lodges the program will then have
reached its full fruition.
The outstanding feature of the educational work during the last
Masonic year has been the organization and development of Lodge

561

GRAND I,ODG E OF CALIFORNIA

educational committees. The Master of each Lodge was requested to
name a Chairman to handle the work. The response on the part of the
Masters was very gratifying and at the present time these Committees
are organized and functioning in 440 Lodges.
The Committee feels it is fully justified in emphasizing the primary
importance of these Committees. For years the complaint has been heard
that too many Lodges are satisfied to initiate and raise a young Mason
and then pass him to the sidelines without any further instruction in the
teachings of our Order or explanation of the meaning of our sublime
ritual, and without any further effort to indoctrinate him in the rights,
duties and obligations of a Master Mason. The formation of these
Committees is a definite and constructive effort to meet this crying need,
and if we may judge from the reports received from Masters throughout
the jurisdiction the Committees hold the promise of the highest success.
In most Lodges, it is true, this Committee work is largely experimental
but as the brethren become more experienced in handling these gatherings
the movement will become more efficient and more effective. In some
communities the Lodge Committee has attained phenomenal success.
The basic fact is undeniably true that the more information and
instruction that is afforded our members, and particularly the candidates
as they are receiving their degree, the more appreciative will our members
be of the great principles of our fraternity.
For the coming year the Committee recommends that the regular
educational programs be presented but that the material submitted by the
Committee shall emphasize more particularly Masonic interests. It is
believed that the secretaries of the Lodges have on file a very large
quantity of non-Masonic material available for the Master who may
desire to vary his program, and except for an occasional paper on a
general and pertinent subject the program will be restricted to Masonic
themes. Some Masters prefer to arrange their own educational programs and to have speakers of their own invitation on specially chosen
subjects. We believe this policy should be encouraged, provided a complete report of the meeting be made to the Grand Master, and under such
conditions as he may prescribe.
It is our firm opinion that the success that has attended the operations
of the Lodge Educational Committees, to which reference already has
been made, justifies the earnest recommendation that this feature of the
educational work should be given special 'attention by the Masters and
every effort made to establish the Committee as an essential part of the
work of every Lodge, and during the coming year a consistent and
persistent endeavor should be directed to this end.
It would seem desirable also to encourage the formation of Lodge
libraries which would give the members of the local Lodge opportunity

for reading on their own account. There is available at the present

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON FINANCING
LODGE BUILDINGS
To the M.:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
At the 79th annual communication, Section No. 87 of the Constitution was amended to read as follows :
"No Lodge shall hereafter invest any of its funds in any manner
or obligate itself in any way for the purpose of acquiring or erecting
a Masonic Temple, Masonic Hall or other structure for the occupancy,
in whole or in part of a Masonic Lodge, until after the plan for financing
such building, and the plans and specifications of such structure, together
with estimates of costs, shall have been submitted to and approved by a
majority of a special committee, consisting of the Grand Treasurer, the
Chairman of the Finance Committee of Grand Lodge, and a member
appointed by the Grand Master."

William P. Filmer, Grand Treasurer; William P. Jeffries, Chairman
Finance Committee; and Robert Greig.
During the year twenty-seven Lodges or building projects have
conducted c01:respondence with the Committee. However, many of these
were minor matters. The Committee has reviewed and approved the
following projects:
Needles Lodge No. 326, F. & A. M., located at Needles. The most
outstanding example of the raising of funds for the construction of
a Masonic Temple during the year was Needles Lodge No. 326.
On November 13, 1928, the Master of Needles Lodge communicated
with the Grand Secretary regarding a lot which they proposed to purchase and on which they proposed to erect a building to cost $22,500.00
which communication was referred to your Committee and after some
correspondence the Chairman of Masonic Temple at Needles, Brother
W. R. Carty, called upon the Chairman of this Committee in Los
Angeles and discussed the matter of a new building.
The plans of the Brethren at Needles had been enlarged and they
had arranged to purchase a lot for $25,000, and erect thereon a building
to cost $60,000. Your Committee was very skeptical that the enterprise
could be successfully financed, but yielding to the enthusiasm of Brother
Carty we gave Needles brethren permission to proceed, with the understanding that at least $60,000 must be pledged before any contracts were
entered into.
On August 31st, Needles Masonic Temple Association informed
your Committee that their total stock subscriptions were $75,000.00,
on which more than $40,000.00 had been paid in, and that contracts had
been entered into for a total of $69,000.00.
When the building is completed and furnished, it will represent an
investment of practically $100,000.00 on which they will have an indebtedness of less than $25,000.00. They are assured of a rental income in
excess of $9,000.00.
It is the hope of your Committee that we may have more communities imbued with the same Masonic spirit as the brethren in Needles.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M. · .W. ·.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History .begs leave to render the folfowing report of its activities during the past year, together with its
recommendations as to further action on the part of your most worshipful
body :
At the last Annual Communication you directed us to prosecute the
work of gathering material relating to the early Masonic history of the
State and authorized the expenditure of $1,500.00 by this Committee dur-

566

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ing the year which has just closed. We have followed your mandate to
carry on the work and beg to report that we have expended slightly less
than $1,000.00. This entire sum has been devoted to activities other than
those of the members of the Committee, although several of them have
been busy with this work throughout the year and have traveled extensively. All of their serv,ices, as well as their traveling expenses, have
been furnished by them without any cost to the Grand Lodge.
The first thing that confronted the Committee was the urgent necessity of taking steps to preserve for future time various important mat. ters of information relative to the early activities of the Craft in this
state. The records of many of the early Lodges have been destroyed
by fire or otherwise and even during the past year the records of one
of the more important of the early Lodges were lost through fire. We
found it necessary to spend time in locating the records of some of the
early Lodges, particularly those in the Mother Lode section. Next we
had various early records studied and obtained notes, abstracts and quotations from them. This memoranda has been transcribed and put in permanent form. We soon found that the information thus obtained had to be
supplemented by interviews with early members of the Lodges who,
in many cases, had removed from their old homes, or from the families
of deceased members. We, therefore, were obliged to hunt up these
persons, establish an acquaintance, and interview them and put the information thus obtained in permanent and accessible form. Unfortunately,
in carrying on this work we were unable to employ one man for all of
his time on account of our restricted means and because we were feeling
our way, and the work has therefore been irregular.
During the year we have written more than six hundred letters to
various individuals or Lodges in connection with this work. Seventy-two
of the early Lodges have been visited personally by members of the
Committee. We have now obtained written data relating to one hundred
and six Lodges, which material is in our files. We have also personally
interviewed more than forty 50-year Masons. Expenses have been strictly
limited to typewriting, the expenses of the investigator, the work in putting the notes in permanent form and to the purchase of files and
stationery.
First, you should know what it is we are trying to find out-what
questions we wish to have answered. A few typical ones are these:
Who was the first regular Mason to become a resident of this territory? What did he do Masonically and otherwise? Was any attempt made
prior to the American occupation to form a Masonic Lodge here? If
so, how and where, and why did it fail? In what way did the early
Masonic pioneers, previous to the organization of Lodges, establish
Masonic relations? Of what practical importance were they? What

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

567

Masons were active as explorers in this region a century ago? Who were
the important Masonic inhabitants here during the fifteen years just
preceding the American conquest? What members of the Craft took
active part in the American conquest? What did Masonry have to do with
establishing our state government? What romances were connected with
bringing the first charters into this State? In what way did ·the Masonic
Lodge function in a typical Mother Lode mining town? What share
did the Army and Naval officers have in our early Lodges? What famous
early ship captains participated in our mysteries? What important early
charities were fostered by the Craft? Amongst the leaders in the civic
business and professional life of the early fifties, who were Masons?
What truth is there in the story that Mark Twain filled a station in one
of our early Lodges? How was Masonry regarded by the higher classes
amongst the Spanish population?
But this listing of questions ~ould be kept up to the exhaustion of
your patience, running through such matters as the furnishing of the
first Lodge rooms, obtaining the first Bibles, social activities, St. John's
Day celebrations, Masonic orations, public parades, cornerstone layings,
and dozens of other matters.
During the past year we first obtained authentic answers to many
of these questions. Let us give you one or two, as examples. The first
regular Mason to become an inhabitant of this State was Abel Stearns
from Massachusetts, who came here more than a century ago. He became
one of our wealthiest and most influential citizens and acted as secret
agent for the United States. He took an active interest in Masonic work
too. This last fact was not known even in the Lodge which he attended
until our research unearthed a misplaced Tiler's Register this year.
.On May 20, 1843, Captain John Paty of the American bark Don
Quixote arrived from Honolulu at Yerba Buena. He had been carrying
on business with McKinley and Fitch as partners as far south as San
Diego for several years previous, and was well known throughout
California. In the harbor was the American ship Vandalia, and with
it Carter Carew of Philadelphia. They were both Masons, and finding
several others in the settlement the idea was advanced that they found a
Lodge. So far as we can learn this was the first project of this sort
suggested on this coast. It failed from a curious circumstance. Business
was absolutely dominated by the priests. They controlled the Indians and
the hides. It was pointed out that the Fathers held Freemasonry to be
the work of the Devil. Carew wrote a letter from Yerba Buena to
his brother in Philadelphia, dated June 14, 1843, and in it he says that
they abandoned the idea of organizing at this time because the members
would be obliged to keep the fact of their membership secret. He wrote :
"I do not like secrecy in our great Society. It should be open to the

568

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

knowledge of all as to who belongs. Some day there will be a strong
Society of our Order here as more and more American~ come."
Jacob P. Leese became a resident of Yerba Buena in 1836. He was
later a member of California Lodge No. 1. He had previously resided
in Los Angeles with another prominent Mason-Isaac Williams. He
had just begun the erection of a residence at what is now Portsmouth
Square, at the end of June, and there he celebrated the Fourth of July,
1836, in a most lavish fashion and to the complete satisfaction of the
inhabitants. This was our first Fourth of July. As you know, Leese
became a rancher and a figure of note in later history. On one occasion
he took 1100 cattle to the mines.
But there was a country Mason who did something in a quiet way
which materially affected, and which is still materially affecting, the
entire world. No memorial has been erected to him save that which
the Lodge at Camptonville has put up during the past year ·with the
assistance of two members of this Committee. The funds were supplied
privately. In every place where great power is extracted from moving
water, the principle discovered and developed by our former brotherLester A. Pelton of Lodge No. 59 of Camptonvil!e-is employed. The
Pelton wheel is known the world over, but we have b~en content all
these years to remain ignorant regarding the romance connected with the
work of our brother.
In the Home at Decato there is an inmate of the age of ninety-five.
He is bright and active and has a clear memory. He began taking gold
out of the earth before '49 and was at Coloma in 1850. We believe we
should busy ourselves with him, that his recollections may be permanently
recorded.
During the past year we have carried on other activities, which do
not entail any expense on the part of the Grand Lodge. A start has
been made toward a California Masonic Library through the generosity
of several brethren and friends of the Craft. Dawson's Book Shop of
Los Angeles, Brother John Howell of San Francisco and Brother J. Gregg
Layne have been generous in presenting books which are arranged under
two headings- those dealing with the lives and activities .of prominent
Masons and those books of importance in the history of the state which
were written by Masons. We now have works dealing with Kit Carson,
Commodore Stockton, George Yount, Robert Semple and John W. Geary,
and books written by Brothers William Heath Davis and Captain Derby.
Several photographs have been obtained, and through the generosity of
Logan Jackson, brother of late Past Master Grant Jackson, and other
brethren, a set of lantern slides relating to Masonic History of California,
has been obtained which will be known as the Grant Jackson Memorial
Collection and which will be available for use by the Educational Committee, if it so desires.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

569

The devastation wrought by the San Francisco fire can never be
overcome. The loss of the Grand Lodge records is a tremendous
obstacle. Some of the San Francisco Lodges had very full recordsembracing photographs, newspaper clippings, letters and a mass of
material throwing light on the history of the City and even of the State.
We trust that individuals may yet be inspired to help fill up this void
by adding information regarding the past work of our Lodges and their
members.
During the year certain Lodges commemorated their seventy~fi fth
anniversaries with due ceremony and effectively. An impressive celebration was had at Santa Rosa, and Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 published
an illustrated book on its beginnings and had a dinner in addition.
In nearly every line of activity in this State interest in its history
has developed very markedly. Recently a book of 350 pages has been
written on the History of the Presbyterian Church in California. Banks
have issued elaborate productions dealing with the histories of the
numerous constituent elemental banks from which one bank is now
evolved. The Telephone Company has written up the history of its
service. During the latter part of the present week the Bench and the
Bar of this State will hold a joint meeting at Monterey and special
attention will be paid to history. The Supreme Court will convene in
old Colton Hall and the beginnings of our State government will be
rehearsed. So far, however, nothing is available to give us an accessible
and readable account of Masonry in this State; the study which we have
been making for four years convinces us that much material must be
gathered yet before any such work that will be of lasting value can be
attempted.
The question bef~re you is this-Is it worth while to carry on this
work? If so, it follows as a matter of business that we must go at it
more vigorously. The thousand dollars which we have spent has not
been most efficiently used because the limit on our expenditure forced us
to employ part-time and irregular work. We also need more direct
aid from members of the Craft. We are convinced that Masons who
are not members of the Grand Lodge will have to assist. The ideal
at which we aim is to inspire each part of the State to a general interest
in the part Masonry has played in its affairs, and particularly to help each
part of the State to adequately preserve and present the history of its
own Lodges and their members. .
We therefore request that an allowance of three thousand dollars
be given to the Committee for the ensuing year, five hundred of which
shall be the surplus we have saved this year. We ask also that the
Committee be authorized to appoint Master Masons in good standing
as Auxiliary Members who shall be recognized and referred to as such,

570

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

though not entitled to Grand Lodge honors. We also request the aid of
the Inspectors in helping us select such members. To effect this we have
prepared a resolution which we here respectfully tender for your consideration.
Resolved, that the sum of three thousand dollars be set aside and
appropriated to the work of the Committee on Masonic History during
the ensuing year, five hundred dollars of said sum being the surplus
yet on hand from the appropriation made for the work of said Committee
for last year ;
That said Committee is directed to devote particular attention to
gathering information and datit that is in danger of becoming lost and
to placing the same in permanent and accessible form;
That the various Inspectors are requested to transmit to the Committee the names of any Master Masons within their respective jurisdictions who may be of assistance to the Committee; and further,
That the Committee be authorized to appoint as Auxiliary Members
any such Master Masons, whether or not they be Past Masters, whose
services they may deem will be of value to the work of the Committee.
ARTHUR M. ELLIS,
LEON 0. WHITSELL,

REPORT OF COMMITT'EE ON RETURNS
To the M: .W: .Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns herewith submits its report.
It is with pleasure we report that the majority of the Secretaries
have sent in their annual returns promptly and accurately. But, like
the poor, delinquent Secretaries are always with us. Many Secretaries
did not report within the ample time fixed by the Constitution. Efeven
Secretaries failed t"o send returns until urgent telegrams were dispatched
·
to the Masters.
At the close of our last annual communication there were 572
chartered Lodges with a membership of 134,302. Since then the Most
Worshipful Grand Master has granted dispensations for the formation
of six Lodges, the details of which is reported by the V. W. Grand
Secretary.

571

There have been 6624 candidates raised, which is a falling off from
the previous year, and which is no cause for alarm.
Our present membership is 138,652, showing a net increase of 4350.
But the wastage has been heavy. We note that 1294 members have
been suspended for non-payment of dues and only the pitiful number of
305 were restored to membership. This would appear to indicate that
many Masters do not observe the letter or the spirit of Regulation No.
110, which reads as follows :
"It is the duty of each Lodge to have a committee on delinquent
members, whose duty will be to personally, or otherwise, interview each
member delinquent and ascertain the cause for such delinquency and
endeavor to have the same paid, or remitted, if unable to pay and
deserving."
It is a sad commentary that Lodges cannot keep a fraternal hold on
their members. Of course, some members may not have loved Masonry
well and some may have lost the love they had.
The following Masonic records of thirty-three suspended members,
taken from country and city Lodges, unfolds the following pathetic story:
One had been a member since 1885, two since 1893, two since 1902 one
since 1908, two since 1910, five since 1912, two since 1913, one each ~ince
1914, 1915, and 1917, and two since 1919. Eleven received their degrees
subsequently to 1920. These facts are submitted. You may make your
own comments.
Your Committee is of the opinion that it is just as good policy to conserve the membership we have as to congratulate ourselves on getting new
material and would suggest that Master and Secretaries keep in close
touch with their membership.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LIBRARY
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Viewing with no small measure of alarm the absence of proper means
to most fittingly and fully make reply to the many questions propounded
from time to time by the brethren of this grand jurisdiction, your
Committee on Library beg to report : The new blood coming daily to
mingle with our life-stream requires to know incessantly "Whence
we came," "Whither going,'' and most important of all, "Of what are
we in search." If the older generation expect to pass along the heritage

590

PROCEEDINGS OF

THE

of citizenship to their children, and they again hand it ·over unimpaired
to their successors, it devolves upon each of these generations to learn to
know the vital significance of the working tools.
Each new citizen should be required to meet the obligations we are
struggling to keep.
The world owes to Masonry the incentive of every advancing step
toward less of war and· more of peace.
She now stands-as ever-in the breach between ignorance, idolatry
begot of paganism, and a love of country and flag and its first born child,
preferred citizenship.
Freemasonry is sociology of the most intimate equation.
"Who best can work and best agree" is no idle foreword of purpose
and intent. We need missionaries everywhere.
Good books in the hands and minds of good men are necessary to
the proper promulgation of Masonry, peace and good will to men. Your
Committee beg to be allowed to function and to that end request of this
Grand Lodge the sum of fifteen hundred dollars to establish and
maintain a Circulating Library during the coming Masonic year. The
expenses incident thereto to be incurred and expended as needs develop,
when same have been vised by the Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge.
Awaiting your pleasure we are,
Yours sincerely and fraternally,

S. WAGSTAFF,
Chairman of Committee.

DENMAN

The report was adopted except as to the request for an
appropriation, which was referred to the Committee on
Finan<::e.

REPORT OF U. C. BERKELEY CLUB HOUSE
To the M.' .W.' .Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California, Inc., presents herewith its annual report of the affairs of
that institution.
Nothing can be added to what has been reported from year to year
in the past as . to the commanding position and continufog influence of
the Masonic Club on the campus of the University at Berkeley. The
same strong endorsements of our work have been given during the
past year by the President and other officers of the University and by the
Dean~ and members of the faculty. The attivities of the Club House
have been carried on in the same manner as in the past, very largely,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

591

in fact almost entirely, directed by the Masonic Council, compnsmg a
representative of each of the major activities functioning at the Club
House, which, expressed in other words, is that the Club House continues
to function under student control.
The splendid influence and quiet direction of Mrs. ]. H. Quinn, the
hostess, have contributed much to the spirit of harmony and good will
which marks the conduct of the "Masonic family" at the University.
The building and other property of the corporation have been well
cared for and carefully preserved under the direction of our superintendent, Brother Shepard. There is one matter, however, to which
attention should be directed. During the year, a defect in the heating
plant resulted in damage to the building and the destruction of certain
equipment by fire. The insurance companies adjusted the value of the
equipment, practically all of which had been placed in the building when
it was first erected, and paid $186.18, on the basis of a sixty per cent
valuation. To replace the equipment, an expenditure of $247.20 was
incurred. The damage to the building was completely repaired at a
cost of approximately $600, which was paid direct to the contractor by
the insurance companies, and did not pass through the hands of the
trustees. Inspection by the officials dfc the Berkeley Fire Department
revealed such a defect in construction of the building that the further
use of the furnace was prohibited until reconstruction, to eliminate fires
of a similar nature occurring in the future, requiring the remodeling of
the heating plant at a total cost of $1444. These last two items, appearing in the report of the auditor herewith submitted as replacement of
equipment and remodeling of heating plant, under the general head of
expenditures, should in reality appear as capital investment, and, so
placed, .would materially reduce the total of expenditures, which, on the
face, appear to have been considerably larger than the year previous.
During the year, a payment of $3000 was made from general funds
on the note held by the First National Bank in Berkeley. The amount
owing on this note on September 30 last was, therefore, reduced to
$9,350.90.
The books and accounts of the Trustees were audited at the close
of the fiscal year, September 30, by one of the auditors of the University
of California, who, among other things, reported having found "the books
and accounts well kept and any information desired was readily
furnished."
The Executive Committee has prepared, and we submit herewith,
the budget for the Club House for the ensuing fiscal year. It provides
two items not carried in the last budget, to-wit, depreciation, $525, and
payment against indebtedness, $3000. While the total budget appears on
its face as $14,110, the two items just mentioned, depreciation and pay-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ment against indebtedness, reduce the actual budget to $10,585, approximately the same amount as the budget presented one year ago, and which
was not exceeded during the past year.
Your Board of Trustees asks that its report be received and approved,
and that the present per capita tax for the support and maintenance of
the Masonic Club at the University of California be continued.
Fraternally submitted,

four per cent of the cost of the building. We then called for bids on

REPORT OF THE U. C. LOS ANGELES CLUB HOUSE
.To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Directors of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Los Angeles fraternally return this account of their efforts
and activities for the Masonic year now ending. At our last communi~ation we reported our confidence that the generous response to our
request for funds with which to erect a clubhouse would ultimate ·in
sufficient funds with which to complete a structure worthy of the dignity
and character of our fraternity and that the continuance of the campaign
would provide the funds with which to furnish it. By resolution you
authorized us to employ an architect, construct the building and continue
our efforts to raise funds for furnishings. Our first decision thereafter
to be made, after due inquiry among architects and contractors, was to
the effect that the spirit of Masonic service among them was such
that the building could be constructed without the payment of profit to
anyone. To combine this decision with a determination to know the
amount of our expenditures before contracting was a problem not free
from difficulty, but due again to the liberal and generous attitude of the
brethren in the building trades it was accomplished. After thoughtful

The recommendation of your Board is that the sum of Ten Thousand
Dollars be provided for the maintenance of the clubhouse for the ensuing
year.
We would be entirely remiss in our duty if we did not add our.
belief that the building erected is a worthy and beautiful monument to
Masonry. We have received commendation from many sources on its
appearance and the fact that it seems to be especially well adapted to
adequately render the service for which it is intended, which includes,
not only a contribution to the social life of the students, but a growing
degree of assistance and direction in studies, lodging, and self service.
On September 5th, the formation of a council among the students
patterned after the council at Berkeley was completed with two representatives from the University Masonic Club; two from Ptah Khepera, an
organization of Masonically affiliated men and women students; two
from Areme,- an organization of Masonically affiliated women ; two from
Phi Omega Pi, a sorority composed of Masonically affiliated women,
and one representative from the Board of Directors. This council is
directly responsible to your Board for the proper use of the building by
the students, and through it to the students is entrusted a large measure
of self government and self regulation. The employment of Mrs. Lida
W. Kempton as resident hostess completes an organization for the
proper use of the clubhouse which promises to make of it what was
intended by those whose generosity made it possible, a "university home"
for the Masonically affiliated students.
Fraternally submitted, by order of the Board of Directors,

IRA F. THOMPSON,
Chairman.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit my twenty-second annual report as Grand Lecturer.
I have at all times endeavored to perform the duties of my office to the
best of my ability, and have been richly compensated for my efforts
by the many friends and acquaintances I have won during my years of
service, and by the many evidences of loyalty I have seen wherever and
whenever I have traveled about the jurisdiction, all of which is most
gratifying.
I note in . the report on correspondence, in speaking of the ritual,
the following : "One of the outstanding questions before the fraternity
today is whether the correct rendition of the ritual has not become the
main objective of the average Masonic Lodge. Religious and other
institutions have come into existence, flourished and decayed through a
strict adherence to the letter rather than the spirit of their creed and
ceremonies."
I will say that any Lodge or set of officers that renders the ritual
in a dignified, impressive, as well as correct manner, will always receive
commendation and most favorable comment, and will tend to increase
attendance. The brethren all like to see good work. The success of
the Catholic Church is due in no small degree to the strict adherence to
its creed and ritual. The great danger to our ritual and the attendance,
is when Lodges confer four and five degrees in an evening, and try t o
keep the brethren present during the whole time. The officers are tired
and the brethren sleepy, and you cannot blame them. U nder such
circumstances it is impossible for the officers to do good work; hence
the brethren will not attend. Then, again, we now have so many side
orders that take the time and attention of the brethren from the Blue
Lodge. That is largely the reason why the brethren stay away. They
do not like to see the ritual butchered. As I have often stated, the
ritual is not the end, but certainly is and always will be the means to
the end. Carlisle has said, "Such ideals are like stars. You will not
succeed in touching them with your hands, but like the mariner from
the vast expanse of water, you will use them as your guide, and following
them, reach your destination."
At the last session of the Grand L odge, Grand Master Fischer
suggested a revision of the funeral ceremony and the shortening thereof,
to the extent of blue penciling the-lugubrious and sepulchral phraseology
of the old days when death was considered the "King of Terrors," leading men in chains which bound them to the grave. Even the church has
quietly dropped much of its old phrasing of worms and decay, into
something more in keeping with our modern thought and a radiant

598

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Christian faith. The rev1s1on of this ceremony was referred to the
Ritual Committee. We have accomplished that duty and the,, result of
our labors will be presented for your consideration. The ceremony has
been changed simply by a process of elimination, with some slight
changes in the wording; and as Brother Fischer said, by striking out
some of the unnecessary mournful and harrowing notes.
I have received reports from all the Inspectors. They report all of
their Lodges doing good work and most of them in fine financial condition, although candidates are not as numerous as in the past: I owe
much to the Inspectors for their loyal support and assistance.
It has been my pleasure to have accompanied the Mo~t Worshipful
Grand Master on many of his visits. These meetings were all well
attended and thoroughly appreciated by the brethren.
I am indebted to the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary ~nd his
assistant, Brother Hobbs, for many courtesies and the helpful assistance
given me at all times in his office, which is very much appreciated.
The Inspectors of San Francisco will confer the third degree on
Wednesday evening, October 9th, at 7 :30 o'clock at Sunset Temple,
Pico and Orchard Streets, under the auspices of Sunset Lodge No. 352.
Trusting that my efforts have met with the approbation of the Grand
Lodge and thanking the brethren for their co-operation and helpful
assistance,
Respectfully submitted,
THOMAS

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON TENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
Los Angeles, October 8, 1929.
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
To report in detail the extraordinary success of the Tenth Annual
Observance of Public Schools Week would be little more than a reiteration of what was said in the reports for the last preceding three years.
We therefore purpose devoting this report in the main to a statement of
the growth and development of what was in its origin an experiment to
meet a war-time emergency.
Public Schools Week in its inception was a Masonic event. It has
become a community affair; and in many communities is the outstanding

599

feature of the school year. Originally observed only by Masons in their
lodge rooms, the participation is now by all the friends of the public
school. In the smaller communities the Masonic Lodge naturally continues to be the motivating factor in the observance; but in the larger
towns and in the cities, the Fraternity functions best where it serves only
as the nucleus of the organization through which the arrangements for
the observance are made, and which includes representatives of the Parent-Teacher Association, American Legion, the various service clubs in
the community and other fraternal and civic organizations. Evidence of
the development of the observance into a community undertaking is furnished by the fact that there are several cities in which the arrangements
are now made by the Chamber of Commerce through a committee of its
selection.
Whether the arrangements are made by a committee appointed by
the Master of the Lodge in the small community, or, in the larger centers, by a Masters and Wardens Association, or a citizens committee,
or the Chamber of Commerce, almost everywhere the burden of providing the program has been assumed by the school people. We say burden
advisedly; because in many instances, particularly where exhibits of
school work constitute a part of the program (and this has become a
very important and attractive feature) it involves prodigious labor.
Superintendents (city and county) and their deputies, supervisors, principals and class room teachers are all now apparently not merely willing,
but anxious, to make each observance held in the respective communities
more attractive, interesting and instructive than was the preceding one.
The extent to which the school people now participate in the observance deserves especial mention. From the very start we had the earnest
support and hearty cooperation of the most prominent educators and
school administrators in the state; but in certain communities there was
an apathy, and in some instances what appeared to be almost opposition.
on the part of the local school trustees, which of course influenced the
principals and teachers. The apathy was, of course, due to the fact that
the worth and importance of Public Schools Week was not at once
sensed; and what appeared to be opposition may have been nothing more
than a hesitation, not at all unreasonable or improper, to give official
sanction to an undertaking initiated by a fraternal organization. That
that apathy has now been dispelled, and that instead of any opposition
there is now cordial, hearty and extremely valuable cooperation on the
·part of all the friends of our public schools is of course due to the fact
that it has become evident that the institution of Public Schools Week
was not for the aggrandizement of the Fraternity but solely in the interest of the public school system of this state.
The two factors primarily responsible for the success that has been
achieved are the active cooperation of the school people and the publicity

601

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

received from the newspapers and broadcasting stations. There is a
correlation in this to which attention may well be called. In an address
delivered before the National Education Association by Dr. Glenn Frank,
President of the University of Wisconsin, on "The Responsibility of the
Press in Interpreting the Schools to the Public," he commenced by saying
that if any of his hearers expected him to exhort the newspapers to .
devote more space to news about the schools they would be disappointed ;
because as an old newspaper man (Dr. Frank was formerly the editor
of the Century Magazine) he recognized the fact that it is the function
of a newspaper to handle news, and not to convert itself into a preaching
agency in behalf of even the best cause. He then went on to say that
if the press was to do more toward. interpreting the schools to the public,
the primary responsibility rested with the schools; and that if the school
men wanted more publicity in the press with respect to school matters
they must do more things that have legitimate news value in the minds
of the editors. He suggested that the school people "try to make it
increasingly clear that press and school have a joint responsibility in
seeing to it that there is thrust into the stream of public thought, in terms
that men who haven't a Ph. D. can understand, those new ideas, new
idealisms and new spiritual values that have been thrown up as by-products of the sciences, philosophies, and practical adventures of the modern
mind."
Now there can be no question as to the correctness of the position
.. taken by Dr. Frank. The difficulty confronting the school people is
to find the opportunity. In California that opportunity has been furnished by Public Schools Week; and the school people were not slow in
availing themselves of it. When the schools hold "open house" for
visitors during which the parents of the children and the people of the
community may personally see just what the schools are doing, and what
is being taught, and how ; when the schools provide a program for every
service club in the community during Public Schools Week, and when
one of these service clubs holds its noonday meeting during that week in
a school at which the luncheon is served by the pupils of the domestic
science class ; when a pageant is arranged (as was done this year in one
city as the culmination of the week's observance) in which 3000 school
children participate; and when the school people of a community arrange
for a display in the Civic Auditorium of an exhibit of every phase of the
work being done from the kindergarten to the high school and including
the part-time and pre-vocational schools attracting an attendance of
20,000 people, that is news. ·
What has resulted is just exactly what Dr. Frank anticipated.
In our report last year we referred in detail to the extraordinary
amount of publicity that had been received, calling attention to the fact
that it included not only extended news reports of the happenings of the

week, profusely illustrated by photographs, but also long editorials and
special articles on educational topics. This year the newspapers were
even more generous in the, amount of space devoted to school matters
and to awakening the interest of the people in their schools. We have
in mind one newspaper which published a special two-page section prepared by the principals, teachers and students of the schools of that
community. It was the second year that that service had been rendered;
and it was, quoting from a long editorial, "a part of this newspaper's
contribution to the celebration of Public Schools Week." Incidentally,
by the way, the editor although not a Mason paid a glowing tribute to the
Masonic Fraternity which he stated was "rendering a fine piece of educational service in arousing people to visit the schools, to attend programs
prepared by them, to listen to talks by school leaders, and in general to
familiarize themselves with the school program in California and its
results."
\Vhat was done by the publication to which we have just referred is
but typical of what was done by the newspapers generally throughout
the state; and the publicity, by the way, was not confined to this state.
Not only did Masonic journals in other jurisdictions make mention of
our observance, but a noted editor and columnist, probably the most widely
read in the country, referred to our observance in a syndicated article
published in a chain of newspapers extending from coast to coast ; and
commenting on our public schools said, "In California, Public Schools
Week sets a good example to the rest of the country."
Whatever may be the fact elsewhere, no school man or woman in
this state will doubt that the press is to the uttermost discharging its
responsibility in interpreting the schools to the public.
The broadcasting stations were all likewise extremely generous in
giving publicity to the events of the week and to the work being done in
the schools. In more than one instance the entire program was broadcast by the local station. That we do not mention by name any particular
newspaper or broadcasting station is due only to the fact that it would
be obviously impossible to mention all to whom credit is due. It is for
the same reason that we have made it our practice not to refer by name
to any community in which a particularly successful observance was held.
This year there were more meetings with a larger total attendance
than was reported even last year; better prepared programs ; more musical and dramatic features; a larger number of, and more ~ttractive, exhibits of school work; more original features ; an increased number of
instances in which the observance extended over the entire week; and
what is especially gratifying, more interest and enthusiasm manifested
in certain communities which had not theretofore attained the high mark
set by especially successful observances. As an evidence of the interest

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

manifested by the people in certain communities it is worth noting that
not only did the merchants permit the use of their show windows for
the display of school exhibits, but they also devoted all, or part, of the
space usually occupied by their advertisements in the newspapers to the
publication of announcements concerning the schools and the week's observance.
With some hesitation we make mention of the fact that there were
a few reports received which indicated an unwillingness on the part of
the Masons of the community to share with any other organization the
credit for a succ·essful observance of Public Schools Week. This is of
course to be regretted because it is not in consonance with our aim and
purpose; and in this connection we quote from a splendid article on Public Schools Week appearing in one of our most influential Masonic publications. Referring to the fact that the Fraternity was "very wisely
allowing the public authorities, the civic and social bodies, and the staffs
of the schools to take first place in the programs," the editor wrote,
"there may at times come to the minds of the brothers a regret that
Craft sponsorship and initiative are not kept in the front; they are apparently fearful that the good work done by the Fraternity may not be
fully credited, or that the movement may in time be otherwise attributed.
But those most thoroughly committed to the work are not seeking praise
for what is being accomplished . . . . then again with Masonry, as with
other institutions, any general idea that this particular society was mainly
concerned in pushing such a movement would arouse some antagonism,
and thus its force would be weakened. Masonry is and should be at all
times ready to forego any special credit, and merge itself with the whole
community in work that is for the common benefit."
There were so many reports of particularly successful observances,
and such was the wealth, originality and value of the programs throughout the state generally, that it is extremely difficult to select the few to
which we are necessarily limited for special mention. Indeed we call
attention to these few only with the purpose of encouraging those who
are inclined to believe that the results are not even yet commensurate
with the effort entailed, and as suggestions for others who may desire
to arrange a program different from that heretofore presented, or a more
elaborate one than they have yet attempted. In accordance with our
custom, all identifying references are omitted.
The Master of a Lodge which has observed Public Schools Week
successfully only during the. last two years reported: "It (the observance) has become one of the outstanding events of the year. Last year
. we filled the auditorium of our largest elementary school which accommodates approximately 800. This year we endeavored to make the best
showing possible and the auditorium of the High School which holds
approximately 1500 was practically filled on the evening of the program.

At no time did we make mention of Public Schools Week as being a
Masonic event; but it was known as a community affair backed by the
Chamber of Commerce. We did not confine the activities of Public
Schools Week to the program only but featured the entire week as
follows:
"Monday the Rotary Club's program was devoted to a speaker from
the University of California.
"Tuesday the Lions Club's program was presented by the principal of
the high school.
"Wednesday a meeting and tea of the combined Parent-Teacher Associations was addressed by another speaker from the University of California.
"Thursday the Kiwanis Club's program was presented by the superintendent of the elementary schools with some of the children participating. This was followed Thursday · evening by the program held in the
auditorium of the high school.
"Friday was featured as 'Visitors' Day' and the schools reported
the largest attendance of visitors had in any one day. This was followed
Friday evening by the dedication of the new - - - School which had
just been completed at which time sixty members of the girls' and boys'
Glee Club presented a three-act operetta.
"The program in the auditorium was designed to inform the audience
of the accomplishments of the schools. It included a playlet dem6nstrating the ability of the pupils in the line of dramatics with instrumental and
vocal selections by individuals and groups demonstrating the training the
pupils are receiving in that line."

schools are attempting"'to do.

The report from a Lodge whose Master last year complained th~t

the program, while approximately 300 more remained in the gym~asium

because the right method of arousing public interest had not yet been
adopted was made evident by the success achieved this year. There was
no other community in the state in which there appears to have been
more interest displayed by the public, or in which the observance was
given greater publicity by the newspapers. This was due to the fact
that the committee had very wisely made a radical change in the nature
of the observance. Instead of the plan theretofore pursued, the committee arranged for an extraordinary exhibit at the Civic Memorial Auditorium of the work being done in the schools, ranging from kindergarten
to the high school and including the part-time and pre-vocational schools.
There were on display dresses, coats, modish hats and dainty lingerie
made by the pupils, products of the domestic science class, and exhibits
of metal work, together with furniture and all sorts of articles made
by the boys in the pre-vocational departments. The muMc was provided
by the pupils of the schools. Commenting on the showing made, one of
the newspapers in an editorial on Public Schools Week, said, "The display is a 'fair' showing the things boys and girls learn to equip themselves with for making a living, making homes and enriching their lives
after they leave school. A view of the finished products is apt to convince the observer that the things the pupils learn are eminently practicable and not to be viewed in the non-essential class. The work of the
classes is the test of the instruction received and carries conviction ...
Public Schools Week, although a display of the work of the pupils, is a
school for the parents and citizenry in which they see how old ideas and
new are being blended in the educational melting pot. Although the
schools may not be perfect, the exhibit demonstrates that the present day
educational system is a wonderfully progressive institution."
The exhibit was open for three days, each afternoon from 2 to 5
and each evening from 7 :30 to 10; and the observance closed with a
final program which included a band concert, singing and folk dancing.
That the interest of the public has been now awakened is made evident
by the fact that the exhibit and closing program attracted a total attendance of more than 20,000 people.
That the observance to which we have just referred served its purpose must be evident to everyone. There can be no doubt that never
before did the people of that community have the knowledge they now
have of what is being done by their schools; and it is certain that there
will be hereafter a closer contact between the public and the school
people. As was said in one of the editorials published during the week,
''There is need of a Public Schools Week to remind the public in general
and parents in particular of the importance of the schools in the community, and of the need of cooperation between parents and schools. .

making. In some few instances, announcement of the Week .and the

:Each school was left to its own initiative to work out the program
best suited to its community and its own internal requirements. The

Attractive exhibits of the work being done by the pupils were displayed not only in the schools, but also at ten "downtown" locations secured

of Commerce. The program of entertainment was the most varied and
instructive ever provided by the public schools of that community and
included operettas, field and track meets, a doll parade, orchestral concerts and an international oratorical contest. Careful check of the visitors
to classrooms and at the special programs showed a .grand total of 19,730
persons.

college of another city. The pageant symbolized the progress· of health

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON OFFICE ROOM
FOR GRAND LODGE
.To the M.'.W.'.Gmnd Lodge of California:
It will be remembered that at the last annual communication the
special committee on meeting place of Grand Lodge rendered a report,
recommending the purchase of a site and th~ erection of a permanent
Grand Lodge building in which would be a suitable auditorium capable
of seating 2500 representatives, · with reception and committee rooms,
space for library and museum, and offices for the Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge and the Recorder of the Grand Commandery. The
estimated cost of such a building and furnishings was placed at $750,000.
This was referred to the Committee on Finance, which committee
reported that while such a building is needed and desirable, the expenditure of the amount of money required was not at this time vitally
necessary. The Finance Committee, in its report, conceded that more
commodious quarters for offices and committee rooms were actually
needed, and recommended "that the incoming Grand Master, the Grand
Secretary and the Grand Treasurer be a committee with authority to
arrange with the directors of the Masonic Temple Association for
additional space on the fourth floor of the Temple, and that th\!Y be
authorized to expend from the funds of Grand Lodge a sufficient amount
to remodel the quarters and refurnish the same." This was adopted.
Pursuant to this authorization, your committee arranged with the
directors of the Temple Association for three more rooms on the fourth
floor, all contiguous. In order to secure this additional space it was
necessary to .rearrange the office rooms heretofore occupied by the Grand
Commandery and the Board of Relief, which necessitated the removal
of some ·partitions. The work is now completed and the offices and
committee rooms for the use of Grand Lodge will be adequate for many
years. In addition to the office rooms for the Grand Secretary, there
are office rooms for the Grand Master, Grand Lecturer, and Masonic
Homes, which rooms will be available also for the Committees on
Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes, Finance, Grievances, and
possibly two others.
Gus. A. HuTAFF,
WILLIAM

P. FILMER,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
To the M :. w:.Grand Lodge of California:
"The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie
down in green pastures : he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul: he lea<leth me in the paths of righteousness for his
name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of
death, I will fear no evil: fo r thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff
they comfort me. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the
days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever."
How comforting indeed must these cheering words of the Psalmist
h.ave been to. the hearts of those members of this Grand Lodge, who,
smce the period covered by our last report, have laid aside the cares
and vexations of this life, and placing their trust in the Supreme Grand
Master, have gone to partake with H im the everlasting joys of that
existence, the sweetness of which can only be experienced by those who
have entered into it through the Valley of the Shadows whose very
darkness is but the harbinger of the coming perfect day.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We who remain will not mourn for our brethren who have preceded
us, but rather look hopefully forward to the time when they shall greet
us as we emerge from the Valley of the Shadows into the glorious
Sunshine of the presence of the M~st High, who doeth all things well.
Among the names shown in this report, happily there does not appear
the name of any officer of this Grand Lodge; we have, however, to
chronicle the death of Past Grand Master of Nevada, Brother Augustus
Muhlenberg Van Bokkelen, who at the time of his death was a member
of Charter Rock Lodge No. 410 of the city of Berkeley.
Brother Van Bokkelen was raised in Mount Moriah Lodge in the
city of San Francisco in 1860, and later moving to Nevada, became
charter member of Escurial Lodge No. 171 under the Grand Lodge of
California, and its first Senior Warden. This Lodge later became
Lodge N~. 7 under the Grand Lodge of Nevada, which Brother Van
Bokkelen served as Grand Secretary for a number of years, and in 1872
became its Grand Mas~r. For thirty years he served as Treasurer of
the Diocese of California of the Episcopal Church.
The roster of our departed members is a Roll of Honor, and contains the names of many of those who have helped to make the history
of California, Masonic and otherwise. Your Committee wishes it might
include in this report even a brief statement of the accomplishments of
each of these brethren, who through the years have so freely and so
unselfishly given of their time and substance to promote that spirit of
amity and good will which should ever characterize those who bear the
title of Mason. The many deeds of these men would fill many more
pages than can be allotted to our use; however, the statements of the
Secretaries of the various Lodges are on file in the office of the Grand
Secretary as a permanent record of their services.
Among the outstanding names on our Honor Roll, are two from our
fair dty of Los Angeles: Brothers Frank P. Flint, ·Past Master of East
Gate Lodge Nb. 290, and Charles S. Walton, Past Master of Albert Pike
Lodge No. 484.

These three brethren were all distinguished for their services to
their country as well as to their Lodge. Brother Cooper was Chairman
of the Committee of Safety at the time of the revolution, and read the
proclamation abolishing monarchical government. He variously served
as a member of the Advisory Committee of the Provisional Government,
Circuit Court Judge, Minister. of Foreign Affairs, Minister of .Public
Instruction, Attorney General, Minister of the Interior and of Fm~nce,
President of the Board of Health, Acting President of the Repubhc of
Hawaii, and was first Secretary of the Territory of Hawaii.
Brother William Thomas Rawlins was noted as a student of the Language and Folk Lore of Hawaii. At the time of his death he had in. co~r~e
of preparation a History of Hawaiian Traditions and Customs, which 1t is
anticipated will soon be published. He served his cou?try as Rc;fe~ee
in Bankruptcy, Deputy Attorney General, High Sheri~, and D1st~1ct
Magistrate. He was several times a member of the Legislature, servmg
on important committees. For five years he was Assistant United States
Attorney. His life was one of great service and it is agreed that he
has left a strong impress on the affairs of the Islands.
Brother James Arthur Rath was known in Honolulu as a welfare
worker. He gave the most of his life to the rehabilitation of mankind
in his Island home. He took over the philanthropic work of the Palama
Settlement and under his administration the scope and character of the
.work of the settlement was tremendously broadened.
During a period of about twenty-five years, from a small mission
chapel the work grew in volume until it now maintains eleven baby
clinics, a general dispensary and several other clinics where twenty of
the leading physicians give their services to the people of Honolulu,
besides sending twenty-two visiting nurses among the poor where for
some reason hospitalization is not required. To relieve the distressed
is a duty incumbent on all men, particularly on Masons, an admonition
taken very seriously by Brother Rath. He was a saintly man. God
give him the rest he so richly merits.
From Redwood City Lodge No. 168 comes the remarkable record of
Philander Peregreen Chamberlain, who during a membership of sixty
years, served thirty-four years as an officer of his Lodge. ~uring this
period he filled all the chairs except Senior Steward and Jumor Deacon,
and was ten times elected as Master. In addition to this great service to
his Lodge, he served his County as Treasurer for forty-four years.
Truly a life well worthy of commendation and emulation.

REVISED FUNERAL SERVICE
Suggestions for Lodge Room Services
The entire service may be held in the Lodge room. After the Lodge
is opened, the Master states the object of the meeting and calls off. The
public may then be admitted. When the funeral party arrives at the hall,
the officers remain seated and the Master, with gavel in hand, goes to
the outer door and escorts the procession into the hall. As the funeral
party reaches the room, the Junior Warden calls up the Lodge, the
Master goes to his station, and the casket is placed directly west of the
altar, the mo1miers in preparation room, and the pall bearers in the west.
When the casket is placed in position the Lodge is seated. The service
is then commenced:
"Brethren and Friends," etc.
After the first anthem the Master reads the sacred roll, and says:
Almighty Father ! Into Thy hands we commend the soul of our
beloved brother.
The Master then delivers the roll to the Secretary, who immediately
deposits it in casket.
Music may here be introduced.
The officers shoitld remain at their respective stations and places,
seated, except when called up. Master and Marshal approach casket
for apron ceremony and deposit of acacia, after which they return to their
places. Senior Warden approaches foot of casket only for his part in
service, then resuming his station.
The service is then remmed: "Once more, my brethren," etc., down
to b1tt not including the paragraph beginning, "S oft and safe," etc.

The Master says:
Musicians, if any

The Marshal will now take charge.

The Marshal then forms a procession in column of twos on the
north of the hall, facing east, and marches 01tt of the hall on the south,
and lining up at the front door. After the mourners have viewed the
remains, the casket is closed and the proc.ession is formed, the Master
at the head of the casket, the mourners following the casket to the hearse.
After the casket is placed and the mourners are in their carriages, the
procession disbands and the officers and members return to the hall, the
Master and such members as can, going to the place of sepulture, where
the ritual is completed, followed by the benediction.

The service is then commenced by the Master as follows:
Brethren and .Friends: From time immemorial it has been the
custom among the .Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons, at the
request of a brother, to accompany his remains to the place of interment,
and there to leave them with the solemn formalities of the Craft.
In conformity to this usage, and in accordance with the duty which
we owe to our departed brother, we have assembled in the character of
Masons to offer up to his memory, before the world, the last tribute of
our affection; thereby demonstrating the sincerity of our past esteem for
him, and our steady attachment to the principles of our beloved Institution.
The great Creator having been pleased, in His infinite wisdom, to
remove our brother from the cares and troubles of this transitory life, thus
severing another link in the fraternal chain by which we are bound
together-let us, who survive him, be yet more strongly cemented by the
ties of brotherly love; that, during the brief space allotted to us here,
we may wisely and usefully employ our time, and, in the reciprocal intercourse of kind and friendly acts, mutually promote the welfare and
happiness of each other.

(An anthem, or other solemn music, may here be introduced, after
which the Master reads the sacred role and says:)
Almighty Father l
beloved brother.

Into Thy hands we commend the soul of our

(He drops the roll upon the casket, and then says:)
Our brother has reached the end of his earthly toils. The brittle
thread which bound him to earth has been severed and the liberated spirit
has winged its flight to the unknown world. The silver cord is loosed; the
golden bowl is broken; the pitcher is broken at the fountain; and the
wheel is broken at the cistern; the dust has returned to the earth as it
was; and the spirit has returned to God who gave it.
While we pay this fraternal tribute to his memory, let us not forget,
my brethren, that we, too, are mortal; and that our spirits, too, must
return to the God who spake them into existence. "Man that is born
of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. He cometh forth as a
flower, and is cut down; he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not."
The almighty fiat has gone forth-"Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt
thou return"; and that we are all subject to that decree, the daily observation of our lives furnishes evidence not to be forgotten.
Seeing, then, my brethren, that life is so uncertain, and that all
earthly pursuits are vain, let us no longer postpone the all-important

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

623

concern of preparing for eternity; but let us embrace the present moment,
while time and opportunity are offered, to provide against that great
change when all the pomps and pleasures of this fleeting world will pall
upon the sense, and the recollection of a virtuous and well-spent life will
yield the only comfort and consolation. Thus we shall not be unprepared
to enter into the presence of that all-wise and. powerful Judge, to whom
the secrets of all hearts are known; and on the great day of reckoning
we shall be ready to give a good account of our stewardship while here
on earth.
With becoming reverence, then, let us supplicate the Divine Grace
to insure the favor of that Eternal Being whose goodness and power
know no bounds, that, on the arrival of the momentous hour when the
fading taper of human life shall faintly glimmer in the socket of existence,
our Faith may remove the dark clouds of doubt, draw aside the sable
curtain of the hidden world beyond, and bid Hope sustain and cheer the
departing spirit.

(The Chaplain then repeats the following prayer:)
Mcist glorious God l Author of all good, and Giver of all mercy l
Pour down Thy blessing upon us, we beseech Thee, and strengthen our
solemn engagements with the ties of sincere affection l Endow us with
fortitude and resignation in this our hour of sorrow, and grant that this
dispensation from Thy hands may be sanctified in its results upon the
hearts of those who now meet here to mourn I May the present instance
of mortality remind us of our approaching fate, and draw our attention
towards Thee, the only refuge in time of need ; enable us to look with
the eyes of faith toward that realm whose skies are never darkened by
sorrow; and after our departure hence in peace and in Thy favor, may
we be received into Thy everlasting kingdom, to enjoy the just reward
of a virtuous and well-spent life. Amen l

Response.

So mote it be.

(Solemn music may here again be introduced, after which the
Master continues.)
Our Brother has been raised in blissful Lodge which no time can
close, but which will remain open during the boundless ages of eternity.
In that Heavenly San\:tuary, the Mystic Light, unmingled with darkness,
will reign unbroken and perpetual. There, amid the sunbeam smiles of
Immutable Love, under the benignant bend of the All-Seeing Eye, in that
Temple not made with hands, eternal in the heavens-there, my brethren,
may Almighty God of His infinite mercy, grant that we may finally meet
to part no more.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The apron is then taken from the casket by the Marshal and hat!ded
to the Master; the casket is deposited in the grave (or conveyed into the
vault); at!d the Master continues:

thy resting place, and there may the sweetness of the summer's last rose
linger longest! Though the cold blasts of autumn may lay them in the
dust, and for a time destroy the loveliness of their existence, yet the
destruction is not final, and in the springtime they shall surely bloom
again. So, in the bright morning of the world's resurrection, though
thy mortal frame be now laid in the dust by the chilling blast of death,
thy spirit shall spring into newness of life and expand in immortal beauty,
in realms beyond the skies. Until then, dear brother, until then, farewell!

This lamb-skin apron is an emblem of innocence, and the peculiar
badge of a Mason. It is more ancient than the Golden Fleece or Roman
Eagle, and, when worthily worn, more honorable than the Star and
Garter, or any other Order which earthly power can confer. By it we are
admonished that purity of thought and conduct are essentially necessary
to gain admission into the Celestial Lodge, where the Supreme Grand
Master forever presides. (Drops it upon the casket.)

The Benediction will then be pronounced b31 the Master (or Chaplawi,
if one be present) as follows:

Taking the Acacia in his hat!d, he continues:
This Evergreen, which once marked the temporary resting place of
one illustrious in Masonic history, is an emblem of our enduring faith
in the immortality of the soul. By it we are reminded that we have
an imperishable part within us, which shall survive all earthly existence,
and which will never, never die. Through the loving goodness of our
Supreme Grand Master, we may confidently hope that, like this evergreen,
our souls will hereafter flourish in eternal spring. (Deposits Acacia.)
Unto its final resting place we consign the body of our brotherearth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. We shall ever cherish his
memory in our hearts ; we commend his spirit to Almighty God. We
trustingly leave him in the hands of that beneficent Being who has done
all things well ; who is glorious in His Holiness, wondrous in His Power,
and boundless in His Goodness; and it should always be our endeavor so
to live that, on the great day of account, we, too, may be found worthy
to inherit the kingdom prepared for us from the foundation of the world.
We extend to the bereaved friends and relatives of our departed
brother our sincere sympathy in this hour of sorrow, and we pray that
"He who tempers the wind to the shorn lamb" will give them His divine
comfort and consolation, and that they may be brought to realize that
the spirit of our brother is happy in his Father's house, where "God
shall wipe away all tears from their eyes, and where there shall be no
more death, neither sorrow nor crying, neither shall there be any more
pain, for the former things are passed away."
(Music)

Master then says:
Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy earthly bed! Bright and
glorious be thy rising from it! F ragrant be the cassia sprig that there
shall flourish! May the earliest buds of spring unfold their beauties o'er

Response. Amen! So mote it be !
Thus the services et!d. T he procession will reform and return to
the Lodge room, and the Lodge will be closed in the customary manner.
