627

To the M.".W.".Gra11d Lodge of California:
Your Committee appointed to consider the Grand Lecturer's report
begs leave to submit the following:
It is at once evident that the Grand Lecturer has maintained the
ritual to a high degree of efficiency and we feel that the care he has
shown in the performance of his duties is certainly conducive of very
great benefit to the Craft. He has not, however, lost sight of the fact
that a perfect ritual is still a means to,an end. The Committee also feels
that such an attitude on the part of our Grand Lecturer shows that he
has taken a v~ry practical view in. corelating the theoretical with the
practical side of Masonry.
The point which the Grand Lecturer makes relative to closing the
sessions of th~ Lodges early is very well taken indeed and the Importance
of this cannot be impressed on the officers of the Lodges too strongly.
Certainly it is asking too much to expect the brethren to attend Lodge
regularly and to stay through a prolonged ceremony which they have
heard innumerable times, even though it is given perfectly. However,
if the meeting is conducted properly and without unnecessary delay then
an early closing will be possible which will do much toward stimulating
attendance. The report also mentions the presence of too many side
orders which are also a cause of division of interest. To this we
heartily agree and suggest that members be impressed with the fact
that their Blue Lodge has the first as well as the strongest claim to
their support.
The Committee is particularly pleased to learn that the funeral
ceremony has at last been changed and has had its "Terrors" removed.
Certainly our former ceremony was not overly burdened with comforting
sentiment for the bereaved, and it seems evident that the words employed
in the old service had more the tone of a warning rather than that of
comfort and consolation. It may be that the harshness of our old ceremony deterred many families from asking for a Masonic funeral for
their deceased Masonic relatives.
. The Committee recognizes the fact that the California Grand Lodge
is particularly fortunate in having the services of a Grand Lecturer
who is so fully blessed with a beautiful personality and nature. All of
the Grand Lodge know, as well as the Craft at large, the hnniense store
of patience and kindness possessed. by our good Brother Baker. We
marvel that he continues night after night, year in and year out, going
over the same work always .in the same friendly and amiable manner.

PRO~EEDINGS

628

OF THE

Not only is he adin.ired for his knowledge of the ritual but we are particularly impressed with his tact and good judgment, all of which have
justly earned for him the honor, sincere esteem and love of his brethren.
Lastly, we thank Divine Providence for having favored us so long
with his cherished association and advice, and may the future continue
to favor him with health and happiness.
Respectfully submitted,
]AS. A. LYNCH,
SAMUEL T. GILLISPIE,
RoY H. PARKINSON.

Report adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Repoi:ts from the Lodges under dispensation, six in number, but
one of these not to be given a charter at this Annual Communication
as explained hereafter, show members under the following classifica~
tions: Charter members from California Lodges, 75; same, other Grand
Jurisdictions, 32; affiliates from California Lodges, 22; one affiliate from
another Grand Jurisdiction, 1 ; Master Masons raised, 41; or as shown
in the report of the Grand Secretary read here Tuesday, a total of 171
members.
The work of a committee like ours, is of the most pleasant nature.
Its members and chairman sense a peculiar interest and joy in being the
committee on whose recommendation Grand Lodge acts to welcome the
probationary Lodges into our great family and fellowship of 572 chartered Lodges. We are always pleased to meet the advocates, the eager
representatives of these Lodges under dispensation, as they seek from
Grand Lodge an approval of their work since they were honored with
the name their organizing members chose and with the grade of "U. D."
They approach this Committee, seeking its recommendation and in most
cases, in past years as well as this one, their records have disclosed their
right to such approval.
We have felt that the examination of records only might not justify
chartering, the giving of the organic instrument that completes their
Lodge. The law requires an examination of its work as well as of its
proceedings. (Consti. Sec. 75.) There is no one better acquainted with
the wor~ of a new Lodge than the Inspector to whom it has been
assigned, and who, in most cases, conscientiously gives the infant organization more care and attention than he does his older Lodges.
For the past five years then, this Committee has followed the plan
of asking attendance upon its sessions, with the represen!atives of the

629

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Inspectors for the petitioning Lodges· concerned. There are probably few
offices in the Masonic order that present as many opportunities as have
the Inspectors to perform difficult and faithful, important and pressing
loyal work, with as few encomiums and outward rewards. At all times
they have ably co-operated in the work of this i;harters Committee and
we take this opportunity to say we appreciate it.
Altadena Lodge U. D. at Pasadena, to whom a dispensation was
issued April 30, 1929, do not now petition for a charter for the reason
that they have not yet obtained a safe and suitable Lodge room in their
own citi·. They have been meeting in Pasadena and they ask that their
dispensation be continued until the next Annual Communication. Affirmative action to that effect by Grand Lodge is necessary under our law, else
the activities of this Lodge under dispensation must instantly cease ; and
we recommend that the dispensation be continued until the next Annual
Communication.
In one case, certain corrections were necessary but were cheerfully
made by the representatives on the request of this Committee on Charters,
and this Lodge is now included in the following recommendations, in all
of which cases, the examination proved satisfactory and showed compliance with our law. We therefore recommend to Grand Lodge that
charters be issued to the five Lodges, and that they be assigned the
following names and numbers on the registry :
San Clemente Lodge No. 671, at San Clemente, Orange County;
Laguna Beach Lodge No. 672, at Laguna Beach, Orange County;
Far West Lodge No. 673, at San Francisco;
Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674, at Long Beach;
Modesto Lodge No. 675, at Modesto, Stanislaus County.
RALPH A. CHASE,

ERNEST WEBSTER,
HENRY EisSLER,
LEO BRUCK,

Committee.

The report was adopted, and charters ordered to be issued accordingly. The dispensation for Altadena Lodge was
continued until the next annual communication.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

SERVICE OF SUMMONS
To the M. '.W:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances herewith offers the following resolution:
· Resolved, that Section 199 of the Constitution be amended to read
as follows:
"Sec. 199. If the accused be within the jurisdiction of the Lodge,
the summons and copy of the charges shall be issued and served upon
the accused at least ten days prior to the day appointed for the trial, and
shall be served personally by the Tiler or some other member of the
Lodge authorized by the Master for that purpose, or shall be left at his
ordinary residence or place of business. If he be without the said
jurisdiction, but within the State, and his residence be known, they shall
be issued and served upon the accused at least thirty days before the day
of the trial, and shall be forwarded to his address by the Secretary, by
mail or other usual mode of conveyance, and service shall be complete
from and after depositing the same in the mail upon due proof thereof.
If he be without the State, and his residence be known, they shall be
issued and served upon the accused at least ninety days before the trial,
by the Secretary forwarding the same to his address by United States
' mail with postage thereon prepaid, which shall be sufficient service. If
his ·address be unknown, the Master shall order the trial to proceed at
once upon the testimony, ex parte. In the event the trial shall be held
ex parte, the record shall contain a full statement of the facts constituting
due diligence in the effort to locate the accused.

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred Trial Record
No. 614, Covenant Lodge No. 527, containing the proceedings of the trial
in said Lodge of a member of Euclid Lodge No. 519, beg to report as
follows:
The record shows that the charges of unmasonic conduct as originally
preferred contained nine specifications. The accused was tried and
acquitted on specifications one to seven, inclusive. The eighth and ninth
specifications were held by the Master to be insufficient and were by him
stricken out. While the Master may have been correct in striking out
the eighth specification, he committed a grave and prejudicial error in
striking out the ninth specification. We, therefore, offer the following
resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the findings of the trial Commission on specifications
one to seven be approved; but that the action of the Master of Covenant
Lodge No. 527, in striking out the ninth specification of the charge on
which the accused herein was tried, be and the same is hereby disapproved;
and that the matter be sent back to Covenant Lodge No. 527, or such
other Lodge as the Grand Master may designate, with the direction to
try the accused forthwith on the offense charged in said ninth specification,

GRAND LODGE SEAL
To the M:.w:.Grana Lodge of California:
A Special Committee was appointed to examine into the heraldic
character of the present Grand Lodge seal, and if the same was found
deficient in any respect, to submit a design for a seal which would be
correct according to the recognized canons regulating heraldic devices.
The Committee is indebted to John H. Logie, a member o.f the Committee, for his painstaking research and scholarly presentation of the
matter of the seal, and your Committee offers as its report the letter
written to the chairman of the Committee by Brother Logie, and respectfully recommends the adoption by this Grand Lodge of the seal proposed
by Brother Logie and described in the proper tci-minology by him in the
letter attached hereto:
First Seal-At the organization of the Grand Lodge, April 19, 1850,
a committee consisting of Jonathan D. Stevenson, John H. Gihon and
Charles Gilman was appointed to procure a suitable seal for the use of
the Grand Lodge.

640

At the first Annual Communication, held at Sacramento, May 7, 1850,
the Committee reported that they had ordered one to be executed, which
would be ready before the next Communication. The report was received
and the Committee continued.
On Tuesday, November 26, 1850, the minutes of the Grand Lodge
state that "The Committee appointed at the first Communication to
procure a seal for the use of the Grand Lodge, reported that they had
attended to the duty assigned to them, and presented a seal, with the
bill for the same, amounting to twenty-five dollars ; which report was
received, the Committee discharged and the bill ordered paid.''
The first seal was correct according to the rules of heraldry. It
might well have remained the seal of the Grand Lodge of California for
all time. The only point that might be raised against it is that it did
not show descent from both the "Ancients" and "Moderns." The Grand
Lodge of California was formed by representatives from the Grand
Lodges of the District of Columbia, Connecticut and Missouri. The
District of Columbia was formed from Lodges of Maryland, and Maryland from the Moderns of England, from the Moderns of Massachusetts
and from the Ancients of Pennsylvania. Connecticut may be traced from
St. John's Grand Lodge (Modems) of Massachusetts, while Missouri
was formed from L6dges chartered by Pennsylvania (Ancients) and
Tennessee (Mixed). So that California is of a somewhat mixed blood;
but descended from both the Ancients and Moderns, and its seal should
show the A~ms of bot4.
The original proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California for the
years 1850 to 1854 do not show the seal; its first use appearing in 1855.
At the Twenty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
October 8, 1872, Grand Secretary Abell . reported as follows: "The seal
of our Grand Lodge has now been in use for some twenty-two years, and
is much worn. It never was a thing of beauty, and it is suggested that
'as a new one should be provided, it would be well that its design be one
more appropriate and significant. A sketch for a new device has been
prepared under the direction of the writer, which is herewith submitted
for consideration, and which may be briefly described as follows : A
shield quartered; the first quarter charged with the Arms of the State
of California, for the jurisdiction of our Gra.nd Lodge; the second with
the Arms of the Grand Lodge of England, for our descent from that
progenitor of· all American Grand Lodges ; the third, with the Arms of
the first used by the Freemasons at York, for the Rite which we practice,
and the fourth with the two implements of the Craft, which are its
principal symbols in every land, for the universality of our fraternity.
Supporters : Dexter, a female figure representing Faith; and Sinster, a
female figure representing Hope. Crest: The upper portion of a group

This seal fails to show the date of organization, a thing that historians wish every seal to show. It is incorrect in its blazoning,
arrangement tinctures, etc. Its supporters are wrong. Its crest is
questionable' and has no support. A crest, according to heral?ic rules,
must rest on one of three things : a ducal coronet, a cap of mamtenance,
or a wreath. It rests on neither. The Arms of the Ancients and
Modems are given second place and the symbol of California the place
of honor-Dexter chief. The tinctures are wrong and not in accordance
with the grant of Arms "to either the Anc.ients or Modems. Brother
Abell says that probably very few would understand it. While that may
be true it is also a fact that letters from the Grand Lodge of California
bearin~ this seal are sent to countries that do notice and are very
particular about such things.
The Grand Lodge of Arizona has evidently copied our present seal,
exactly as we have it, mistakes and all, except that in Dexter chief they
have substituted what seems to be a deer for the California symbol thai
we have. As it now stands, Arizona and California are the only two
States in the Union that have the same se'a!.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
GENERAL PURPOSES
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes respectfully reports
as follows relative to the various matters submitted for its consideration:
Restoration to Membership
1. T. A. McMillan of Euclid Lodge proposes an amendment to
Section 119 of the Constitution by changing the word "three-fourths" to
the word "two-thirds."
The said section provides that if a member suspended for nonpayment of dues neglects for a period of two years to pay said dues or
have the same remitted by the Lodge, that the member shall not be
restored except by three-fourths vote.
It is argued that the Constitution requires a two-thirds vote to
restore a member suspended for unmasonic conduct and that it is illogical
to require a larger majority for the restoration of one suspended for a

645

The Committee on Jurisprudence having concurred in
the recommendation, the report was adopted, and Section
119 of the Consti"tution was amended as stated above by
unanimous vote.
Change of Place of Meeting
2. Hugh C. Dougherty, Past Master of Van Nuys Lodge No. 450,
proposes an amendment to Section 93 of the Constitution by adding the
words "and the appointed hall therein" after the word "charter" in the
third line of said section.
The effect of this amendment would be to require a proper resolution
and the approval of the Grand Lodge or Grand Master to the removal of
the place of meeting of a Lodge from the appointed hall named in the
dispensation or charter.

It is the opinion of your Committee that a Lodge should be permitted
to remove from one hall to another upon proper action on the part of the
Lodge and without the approval of the Grand Master.
We recommend that the amendment be not adopted.

Report adopted.

· The Lodge has adopted a by-law providing for such change and the
application has had the approval of the Grand Master.
Your Committee can find no reason why the request of this Lodge
for change of name should not be granted, and therefore respectfully
recommends that the name of Workman Lodge be changed to Temple
City Lodge.

Report adopted, and the name of Workman Lodge was
ordered changed to Temple City Lodge.

Remission of Dues
5. The Masonic Officers' Association of the 70th and 71st Districts
propose amendments to Sections 128 and 41 of the Constitution.
The proposed amendment to Section 128 provides and adds to that
section a provision that a Lodge may, by its By-Laws, resolution or
otherwise, remit the dues of a member who has been a member in good
standing of a Lodge in this jurisdiction for ·a period of forty years or
more.
The proposed amendment to Section 41 exempts the Lodge from a
per capita tax on the members of forty years' standing whose dues have
been remitted. The form of these amendments has had the approval of
the Committee on Jurisprudence and are attached hereto.
The argument presented in support of the proposals is that many of
the Lodges have members who have been members for forty years or
more and who are in reduced circumstances. Many of these members
regard the remission of dues as a charity and their pride leads them to
forfeit the membership rather than to become the object of the charitable
ministrations of the Lodge.
We are of the opinion that members of the Lodges who are so circumstanced that they can pay their dues should continue to contribute to the
support of the Lodge arid Masonry, regardless of the length of time they
have belonged to a California Lodge. There should be no "retired list" in
Masonry. We are of the opinion, however, that each Lodge should have
the prerogative of remitting iti advance the dues of such of its brethren
as have been members of a California Lodge for forty years and who,
in the sound judgment of the Lodge should, by reason of misfortune,
inability or other good cause, be exempt from the payment of dues.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the proposed amendments,
to read as follows:
Sec. 41. (Last paragraph) And the Grand Lodge may levy, in
addition to the above, such other contributions as in its judgment may be
required. Provided, nevertheless, that no contribution of any sort, in
the nature of a per capita tax, shall be payable by a Lodge upon any
Master Mason who has been exempted from payment of dues by reason
of his having been a member in good standing of a Lodge in this jurisdiction for a period of forty years or more as provided for in Section 128

647

The report was adopted, and Sections 41 and 128 of the
Constitution were declared amended as above set out, by
unanimous vote.
Petition for Additional Degrees
6. A recommendation has been receivoed, signed by forty-five
brothers, recommending that Part VII, Article iii, Section 246, Question
13, of the Constitution be amended to require a promise of a petitioner
that he will not within twelve months after receiving the degree of
. Master Mason petition for or receive any degree in any body, order, or
organization, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person
be a Master Mason. The proposal extends the period of six months now
provided in our law to twelve months. We believe that our present
requirement is salutary and .wholesome and is to the benefit of our Lodges
and their initiates, but we think the statute should always be reasonably
restrictive and that six months is probably a reasonable period of restraint
in this matter. So far as we are able to learn, the present law is meeting
with general approbation and in the main is satisfactory to the members
of the Craft. This being the case, it does not appear to us that a change
should be made at this time. We therefore respectfully recommend that
the proposal be not adopted.

The Number of Colusa Lodge
10. Colusa Lodge No. 240, by resolution, requests this Grand Lodge
to change the registry number of the Lodge from 240 to 142. It appears
that on March 22, 1882, the Grand Master made an order authorizing the
consolidation of Colusa Lodge No. 142 and Equality Lodge No. 240: and
that on April 1, 1882, the consolidation was perfected under the name of
Colusa Lodge No. 240. The Lodge for forty-seven years has been
known as Colusa Lodge No. 240. While the Lodge passed the resolution
asking for the change of name, an objection to such change has been
presented. Unless some very clear and definite reason exists therefor, we
do not think it desirable to change the registry number under which this
Lodge has operated for nearly half a century and therefore recommend
that the resolution be not adopted.

"I promise I will not within six months from the date of receiving
the Third Degree of Free Masonry petition or apply for other degrees
of Mason.ry."
We think the present question as framed in our law is unambiguous
and aptly stated and that no improvement would be made by accepting
the proposal, and therefore recommend that it be not adopted.

Report adopted.
Fee for Dispensation

7. A proposal has been submitted that the fee for a dispensation to
form a new Lodge be twenty-five dollars instead of seventy-five dollars.
The reason given is that it is desirable that a greater number of Lodges
be constituted and Grand Lodge should encourage the creation of new
Lodges.
It is our ·opinion that the present fee is reasonable and that the
same should not be reduced, and therefore we recommend that the
proposal to change the fee be not adopted.

Report adopted.

Educational Committee
11. Your Committee again directs attention to the fact that this
Grand Lodge has engaged itself in the work which has been placed
under the direction of the Educational Committee and is disposed to
continue its policy in that respect until it is fully and finally determined
that the educational work is successful or unsuccessful. Your Committee
feels that the work is still in the experimental stage and that a determination of the value of the work should soon be arrived at. The efforts of
the Committee should be confined to Masonic subjects and interests, and
the Com~ittee should resist every effort to expand its activities beyond
Masonic fields. An ambitious program of general education will lead to
certain defeat. We cannot compete with the high schools, academies,
junior colleges, and universities in our pedagogic efforts. Our members
desire Masonic instruction and information. The Committee should
strive to meet their needs and requirements. The establishment of
Masonic libraries in the Lodges, as suggested in its report, is · one of the
proper activities of the Committee. We are deeply appreciative of the
earnest and active work of the members of the Educational Committee,
. and Grand Lodge is hopeful of results which will justify the large expenditure of money, and the time and effort of many earnest and diligent
Masons.
Past Grand Master Sherman does not join in, and disapproves of
this report, but the remainder of your Committee respectfully recommends
that the educational program as laid down at its Session in 1925 be
continued.

Report adopted.

Dual Membership
13. Your Committee has considered the subject of dual membership
on the occasion of several Annual Communications of this Grand Lodge,
and now has before it a resolution that dual membership be ~dopted.
We again remind Grand Lodge that the principle of dual membership
was adopted in 1922 but that this Grand Lodge has refused to adopt
proposed legislation to carry the principle into effect and has also failed
to rescind the formal action taken in adopting the principle of dual
membership.
Sixteen Grand Jurisdictions now permit unrestricted plural membership. The Grand Lodge of South Carolina permits it by dispensation
from the Grand Master. Massachusetts, Virginia and Rhode Island have
had dual membership for many years. New York and Kentucky adopted
the principle last year. The Grand Lodges of England, Ireland, Scotland.
and those of many of the English Dominions have always permitted it.
Seven Grand Lodges permit plural membership between members of the
Lodges under their jurisdiction and members of Lodges under other grand
jurisdictions, but prohibit such memberships between Lodges within their
own jurisdiction. Alabama, New Hampshire and Washington are numbered among these seven Grand Lodges. In Delaware plural membership
is not a Masonic offense. The report of a committee on dual membership
of the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin states that the committee is unable to
discover a single Grand Lodge that has at any time adopted either plural
or dual membership later to abolish it.
It is interesting to note that Virginia has permitted the practice since
before 1777 and has 1100 plural members out of a total membership of
48,500. The Grand ·Lodge of Wisconsin in 1929 adopted plural membership and enacted appropriate legislation with respect thereto.
Your Committee makes no recommendation on this subject and
presents the foregoing for the information of Grand Lodge.

Report adopted.

Fifty Year Veterans
16. That portion of the Grand Master's message relative to emblems
for veteran brothers has been referred to this Committee. The Grand
Master suggests an amendment to our resolution relating to these buttons
to include those brethren who have become members of our jurisdiction
by affiliation and who have been Master Masons in good standing for a
total of fifty years, the last ten of which having been in a Lodge in
our jurisdiction.
.
Your Committee believes that a beautiful sentiment has been expressed by the presentation of these buttons and that the recipients have
been cheered and pleased by the recognition given to them. Your Committee agrees with the suggestion of the Grand Master and goes a step
further, for it believes that buttons should be given to each Master Mason
now affiliated in .our jurisdiction, who has been a Master Mason in good
standing for a period of fifty years. No harm could follow the presentation of buttons to those who would meet this qualification, and some good
could be ·done and much pleasure given by recognizing our half century
members'.
Your Committee respectfully recommends that the resolution be
amended to provide for the presentation of the golden veteran buttons to
members of Lodges in our jurisdiction who have been Master Masons in
gbod standing for fifty years or more.

Report adopted.

Board of Control
20. Your Committee has considered the report of the Board of
Control and has also considered its proposed recommendations for the
amendment of the Constitution substantially to provide for the matters
now partly in the Constitution, partly in the Standing Resolutions and
partly in the Proceedings in this Grand Lodge for 1926. Your Committee
fully approves of the said report of the Board of Control except as to
the proposed legislation, and with respect thereto your Committee believes
that there is no difference of opinion regarding the duties and powers of
the Board of Control as the same has heretofore been established, but that
there is some difference of opinion as to the manner in which those duties
and powers should be given expression. For this reason your Committee
feels that the best interests of Masonry would be served by a postponement of action on the proposed amendment until the next Annual Communication in order that divergent views may be brought into accord and
that differences of opinion may be harmonized. The proposed legislation
has been approved as to form by the Jurisprudence Committee.
Your Committee, therefore, respectfully recommends : I. That the .
matter of the legislation proposed by the Board of Control be postponed
for consideration until the next Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge, and, 2. That the said report of the Board of Control be adopted
except as to the proposed legislation.
Past Grand Master Sherman dissents from the views as above
expressed and the recommendations of the Committee approving said
report.

. The report was not concurred in, and the report of the
Board of Control, including the proposed additions to the
Constitution (Article viii-a, Sections 37, 37a, 37b, 37c, 37d,
37e) were adopted by a five-sixths vote.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
JURISPRUDENCE
Rights of Members of Suspended Lodge

T..;;--t-h_e_J.._f_...-w-.-.-:c--r_a_n4-:L7ii"ie7/•C~lifo-;:~ia:
1. In considering the matter of the arrest of the charter of a· ..
Lodge, we have concluded that Section 133 of our Constitution as it
now stands necessarily works great injustice to many of the members
of a Lodge, the charter of which is arrested or forfeited . . It provides
that the forfeiture or arrest of the charter of a Lodge mvolves the
suspension of all its members from the rights and privileges of Masonry,
except those who may be specially exempted from ~uch effect. The
plain effect of this is that pending the arrest of the charter of a Lodge
every •member except those specially exempted by th: Grand ~a~ter
from the effect .of such arrest, is no longer a Mason m good standirt~.
Without any charges preferred against him personally for ~nmasomc
conduct; without any formal trial of any charges of unmaso?ic conduct
at which he is given opportunity to appear and defend hi~self, a?d
without any conviction by a trial commission, he. is by the simple e~ict
of the Grand Master arresting the charter of his Lodge, for the time
being placed beyond the pale of Masonry. He cannot visit any ~odg~,
if he · be in distress he cannot be given assistance by the fraternity, if
he die he dies as a non-Mason and cannot receive Masonic burial, and
his widow and his children are entitled to no recognition at the hands

655

of the fraternity. And all this although he personally may be altogether
innocent of any act amounting to unmasonic . conduct, which is probably
the situation with regard to the great bulk of the membership of the
Lodge whose charter is arrested. Such a situation appears to us to be
intolerable.
It is true that as the law now reads, the Grand Master in arresting
a charter may specially exempt certain members from this effect, but
it is clear that in most cases, especially where the membership is a
large one, it would be impracticable for the Grand Master to investigate
sufficiently to enable him fo fairly determine who should · be specially
exempted. And a more grave objection is that this places it in the sole
power of the Grand Master, without charges, and without a trial offering
the opportunity of full defense, by his simple edict, to temporarily
deprive a Master Mason of all his rights ~nd privileges as such.
Regardless of the exalted position of a Grand Master, and of the
unlimited confidence in him of the members of the Craft, we feel that
no Grand Master should have such power with regard to Master Masons
in good standing. It savors too much of the divine right of kings,
and is not in accord with modern ideas of Masonry. We long ago
repudiated the ancient rule as to the right of the Grand Master to make
Masons at sight. More obnoxious still is the idea of unmaking a Mason
at sight.
Nor is any such provmon essential to any purpose to be accomplished by the arrest of a charter. The whole purpose in such a case is
to prevent a Lodge from functioning as such, pending proper trial on
proper charges of the question whether the charter of the Lodge should
be revoked by the Grand Lodge for any of the reasons specified in
Section 132 . of our Constitution, being in every case some course of
conduct or omission on the part of the Lodge itself. We note as one
of such specified reasons, the failure of the Lodge "to meet within a
period of six months."
The situation as to the consequences in the event of forfeiture of
the charter, which can only be accomplished upon charges against the
Lodge, presented to and investigated in the Grand Lodge, of which
· " · charges the Lodge accused shall have had due notice, is perhaps not
· · so serious. There will then have been something in the nature of a
trial and opportunity for defense. But again the questions at issue in
such an investigation are as to the conduct of the Lodge as a Lodge,
rather than as to the conduct of any individual members.
We have concluded that what we believe to be a deplorable situation
can be remedied by the amendment of Section 133 of our Constitution
in' such a way as to accomplish all the protection essential to the

656

PROCEEDING!;; OF THE

fraternity without what we conceive to be an improper deprivation of
Masonic standing of any member of the Lodge whose charter is arrested
or forfeited.
We propose that Section 133 of our · Constitution be amended to
read as follows:
Effect of Forfeiture or Arrest
Sec. 133. During the pendency of the arrest of the charter of a
Lodge, the status of each of the members thereof shall be that of a
non-affiliated Master Mason in good standing, subject, however, to
charges and trial for unmasonic conduct to the same extent and effect
as if there were no such arrest, provided always that any such charges
shall be presented to the Master of a Lodge which would have jurisdiction of the matter if such suspended Lodge were not in existence, and
all further proceedings therein shall be in accord with the then existing
law governing trials, penalties and appeals.
In the event of the forfeiture of the charter of a Lodge, each of
the then members of such Lodge shall have the status of a non-affiliated
Master Mason in good standing, subject, however, to the disposition,
according to law, of any charge of urtmasonic conduct already made
and then pending against him, as well as to the subsequent institution
and prosecution of any charges of unmasonic conduct on account of
matters occurring prior thereto, and it shall be the duty of the Grand
Secretary to issue to each of said members his certificate under seal of
the Grand Lodge evidencing such status, which certificate shall serve
all the purposes of the ordinary dimit.
We recommend the adoption of the proposed amendment.

On motion duly made and seconded, the report of the
Committee was adopted, and a vote being had upon the proposed amendment to the Constitution set forth therein, the
same was adopted by a five-sixths vote of the Grand Lodge.
Arrest of Charter of Seal Rock Lodge No. 536
2. As is shown on pages 434-435 of his address, the Grand
Master, after careful consideration, under date of September 24, 1929,
arrested the charter of Seal Rock Lodge No. 536, _effective until the
present Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge. He recommends
to the Grand Lodge that his order be continued in force until the next
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, unless the incoming Grand
Master shall in the meantime become satisfied that the members of the
Lodge are making a conscientious effort to uphold the principles of
Masonry and work in harmony, in which event he be authorized to
relieve the Lodge from such arrest and return the charter.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

657

This action of the Grand Master was taken only after full investigation and very earnest consideration, and was based upon his conclusion
that such action was essential to the proper protection of harmony in
the jurisdiction. According to his address, it was apparent that the
Lodge was for some reason split into two factions, between whom there
was so much bitterness that, regardless of the merits. of any candidate
for the degrees, the mere fact that he was proposed by a member of
one faction insured his rejection by the other faction, with the result
that no candidate for the degrees could be elected. There seems to have
been no suggestion by the members to the contrary. It is obvious that
such a well settled attitude and practice on the part of the membership
of a Lodge is a· violation of the recognized usages of the Craft, and
that if continued it must bring not only the Lodge itself, but also the
Craft into disrepute. The Grand Lodge has held that where there is
no hope for harmony in a Lodge, it should cease to exist.
The necessity and propriety of the action of the Grand Master were
apparently not serio;msly questioned by the Lodge, such action was in
accord with precedents established by this body.
A petition has been filed at this communication signed by sixty-four
of the members, asking that the order arresting the charter be dissolved,
it being the opinion of the signers that harmony has been restored and
that a true Masonic spirit wi}! again prevail.
We have had the benefit of the views of both the Grand Master
and the Deputy Grand Master upon this matter, including such petition
for relief from arrest. They are both hopeful that it may develop
within a few months that the deplorable situation in this Lodge may be
obviated and that differences may be so adjusted that the members of
this Lodge will live together in the harmony that is essential to a full
discharge of their Masonic duties and obligations. But they can see no
solution of the existing difficulties in an immediate restoration of the
charter. We believe that the action of the Grand Master should be
approved and that his recommendation should be adopted, with additional
provision to the effect that if within six months existing conditions be
not remedied to the satisfaction of the Grand Master, charges, with a
view to the forfeiture of the charter of the Lodge, be presented by him
. for investigation by the Grand Lodge.
The effect of the amendment to Section 133 of our Constitution
made this day, is that the status of the members of this Lodge will,
pending such arrest, be as provided in the amended section.
We recommend that the action of the Grand Master be approved
and that his recommendation be adopted with the additional provision
specified by us.

The report of the Committee was adopted.

Foreign Language Lodges
3. The M. W. Grand Master has not burdened his message with
reports of his decisions upon questions asked as to which the law of this
jurisdiction is thoroughly settled or which are answered by plain and
unambiguous language of our Constitution and Regulations-a practice
we believe to be entirely commendable.
As a result of this practice his address contains but one decision upon
any such question.
This decision is to be found at pages 10 and 11 of his message. It
is to the effect that no Lodge in the jurisdiction of California, other than
one expressly permitted to confer degrees in a particular foreign language,
may allow a degree to be conferred therein by persons conferring it in
such foreign language. The decision is directed against the practice said
to have been followed of a Lodge working in the English language
allowing the conferring of a degree in its Lodge by a visiting team
working in a foreign language. It has no application to a case where
a foreign-language working Lodge confers a degree in its own language
for an English-working language Lodge, at the request of the latter, under
the provisions of Section 155 of our Constitution.
The decision of the Grand Master was in our opinion correct, and we
recommend that it be approved.

departure from our general rules with regard to jurisdiction of Lodges,
and therefore it was provided that in such cases the territorial jurisdiction
of a particular Lodge might, after full investigation, be expressly defined
by a resolution of the Grand Lodge, to the exclusion of each and every
other provision of the Constitution in the matter of jurisdiction. Recognizing, however, the absolute necessity of great care in such an important
matter, it was expressly provided in such section that as a prerequisite
to the adoption of such a resolution, there should be a recommendation
of such action by the Grand Master. This requirement contemplated an
' investigation by the Grand Master as to the necessity of such action
in so far as the particular Lodge was concerned and his recommendation
based thereon, in order that the Grand Lodge have the benefit of his views
before acting.
In the cases before your Committee the Grand Master has made
no recommendation. He indorsed his "approval" thereon solely "for the
purpose of giving jurisdiction to the Committee on Jurisprudence," whose
favorable action is also required in the event he recommends such action.
He did this without making an investigation and without any intention of
recommending the action requested. This is not such a recommendation
as the law requires.
It follows that, in view of the lack of recommendation by the Grand
Master, the express language of the Constitution precludes the granting ·
of either application, and we recommend that both be denied without
prejudice to a new application.

Restoration After Suspension for Non-Payment of Dues
8. The Committee on Policy having recommended the adoption of
the resolution to amend Section 119, and it appearing to your Committee
on J~risprudence that the proposed change is desirable, we recommend that
Section 119 be amended to read as follows :
Sec. 119. Provided, that should any member suspended for nonpayment of dues neglect for the period of two years to pay said dues or
have the same remitted by his Lodge, said member shall not be restored
except by a two-thirds vote by ballot of all the members present at the
next stated meeting after the petition for restoration is presented.

Report adopted, and Section 119 was amended by unanimous vote.
Service of Summons
9. Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred a proposed amendment to Section 199 of the Constitution, which amendment
is offered by the Committee on Grievances, report as follows :
The purpose of the amendment primarily is to provide not only for
the issuance of summons at least ten days before the day appointed for
the trial, but also for its service for at least the same period of time.
While it has been held that summons should be so served upon the
accused, yet we feel that the amendment is desirable for the purpose of
clarity and definiteness, and we therefore recommend its adoption, as
follows:
"Sec. 199. If the accused be within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, the
summons and copy of the charges shall be issued and served upon the
accused at least ten days prior to the day appointed for the trial, and
shall be served personally by the Tiler or some other member of the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

661

Lodge authorized by the Master for that purpose, or shall be left at his
ordinary residence or place of business. If he be without the said jurisdiction, but within the State, and his residence be known, they shall be
issued and served upon the accused at least thirty days before the day of
the trial, and shall be forwarded to his address by the Secretary, by mail
or other usual mode of conveyance, and service shall be complete from and
after depositing the same in the mail upon due proof thereof. If he be
without the State, and his residence be known, they shall be issued and
served upon the accused at least ninety days before the trial, by the Secretary forwarding the same to his address by United States mail with postage thereon prepaid, which shall be sufficient service. If his address be
unknown, the Master shall order the trial to proceed at once upon the
testimony, ex parte. In the event the trial shall be held ex parte, the
record shall contain a full statement of the facts constituting due diligence in the effort to locate the accused.

The report was adopted, and Section 199 was amended
by unanimous vote.
Provisional Dimits
1-0. Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had referred to it a
resolution presented by the San Diego County Officers' Association,
proposing an amendment to Section 248 of the Constitution in the form
of a provisional <limit. While this legislation seems to possess some merit,
we find on examination that it would require the amendment of several
other sections in order to make it effective; and in the limited time
afforded us, we have been unable to determine the full extent of such
necessary changes.
We, therefore, recommend that the proposed amendment be not
adopted.

Audit of Accounts
Your Committee employed Ruckstell & Land, certified public accountants, to · examine the books and records of the Grand Secretary and
Grand Treasurer, as well as those ·of the Masonic Homes of California
and Endowment Fund. These accountants have certified that all books
and accounts are correct. This audit discloses that the net worth of the
Grand Lodge on July 31, 1929, was $787,911.68, an increa5e for the fiscal
year of $19,513.81. Of this amount $588,050.00 is represented by stock
of Masonic Temple Association of California.

We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $750.00 is hereby appropriated from the
funds of this Grand Lodge to purchase seventy-five shares of stock of
the Masonic Temple Association of California.

Reimbursement of York Lodge No. 423
Your Committee has had before it the request from York Lodge No.
423 for the reimbursement of Grand Lodge dues paid on Brother Joseph
C. Smith for the years 1925-1928, inclusive. It appears that Brother
Smith was a resident of the Soldiers' Home. He was discharged from
the Home and the Lodge lost track of him.
·
Later, the Secretary wrote to the Pension Bureau in Washington to
ascertain the whereabouts of Brother Smith and was notified that he
had died on March 19, 1925, hence your Committee feels that this was
not a neglect on the part of the Secretary and therefore recommends
that the amount of such dues be returned.
. Resolved, that. the amount of Grand Lodge dues heretofore paid by
York Lodge No. 423 for the years 1925-1928, inclusive, on Brother
J o.seph C. Smith be ascertained by the Grand Secretary and remittance
be made to said Lodge for said amount.
0

Purchase of · Masonic 'Temple Stock
Alta Lodge No. 333, located af Bridgeport, is the owner of seventy. five · share.s· of stock in the Masonic Temple Association of California,
located at San Francisco. The Lodge. is very desirous of building a new
halt and is in need of the funds for that purpose. Your Committee on
Finance, therefore, recommends that the seventy~five shares of stock
be purchased by this Grand Lodge.

Library Committee
Referring to the request of the Library Committee for an appropriation of $1500.00 for the purpose of furnishing the membership with a
circulating library consisting of Masonic books and other literature:
Your Committee is of the opinion that this field is being covered by
other agencies and recommends that the request be denied.
Benicia Lodge No. S
Referring to the resolution of Benicia Lodge No. 5, dated September
4, 1929, requesting that funds be appropriated by this Grand Lodge to
buy a building at Benicia erected in 1850 by Brother A. Riddle and used
by the Masonic Fraternity until 1888, when it was sold to Solano county.
Your Committee is of the opinion that funds should not be appropriated for this purpose and recommends that this request be denied.

Masonic Club of the University of California at Berkeley

Resolved, that the sum of $9000.00 be and is hereby appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge for the maintenance of the Masonic
Club House at the University of California at Los Angeles for the fiscal
year 1929-1930.

Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the report of the Trustees
of the Masonic Club of the University of California, located at Berkeley,
and feel that it is being properly operated and in the interest of the sons
and daughters of Masons of this jurisdiction.
The maintenance of this Club calls for an annual expenditure of
approximately $10,000.00.
There is an unpaid note held by a bank in Berkeley for $9350.90, the
annual interest on which amounts to approximately $600.00. Your
Committee is of the opinion that this note should be paid.
The Trustees had on hand September 30, 1929, $2047.00. They
have available during the year 1929-1930 an amount in excess of $13,700.00
received from the 10 cent tax levied at the last Annual Communication,
making a total of approximately $15,800.00.
Your Committee recommends that an appropriation be made by this
Grand Lodge of $3000.00, which would give the Trustees of the Masonic
Club at Berkeley a gross of $18,700.00, out of which they are to pay the
note at the bank and leave sufficient funds for operating during the coming
year.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Rtsolved, that the sum of $3000.00 be and is hereby appropriated out
of the funds of this Grand Lodge, to the Trustees of the Masonic Club
of California, located at Berkeley.
Masonic Club of the University of California at Los Angeles
I

Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the report of the Board
6f Directors of the Masonic Club of the U. C. L. A., and their request
for funds for its maintenance during the fiscal year 1929-1930.
At this time we desire to congratulate the brethren ·and to commend
the Masons of California, and particularly the Board of Directors for
their excellent work in securing funds and the erection and dedication of
a building free from debt at the University of California in Los Angeles.
This Board of Directors have submitted a budget on which they have
placed an estimate and made a request for an appropriation of $10,000.00.
This budget contains an item of $3300.00 for taxes and insurance,
but as we are informed that no taxes, except on the land, will be paid
until October, 1930, we feel that this budget can be reduced to $9000.00
without hampering in any manner the operation of this club.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:

Masonic Education

auditors have been unable to establish the particular fund to which this
amount can be allocated. The F inance Committee, therefore, recommend
that it be deposited to the credit of the Endowment Fund of Masonic
Homes.
The present bookkeeping system of the Grand Lodge was installed
many years ago when the membership was small and annual cash income
less than $25,000.00. With the growth of the fraternity, and a present
am-1ual cash income of more than $450,000.00, we believe that the present
system is inadequate to meet our growing needs.
Your Committee would, therefore, recommend that the incoming
Grand Master be authorized to install a system that will more nearly
meet the present requirements of this Grand Lodge.

Your Committee on Finance has had under consideration the report
of the Committee on Masonic Education and its request for an appropriation of $10,000.00.
Many of the brethren have called on the Finance Committee and
discussed with them the educational program of this Grand Lodge, and
ha'l(e expressed the opinion that the membership was not getting value
received from this expenditure. Your Committee, therefore, feels that
a smaller appropriation might suffice for the coming year, and therefore
offer, the foll_ owing resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $5000.00 be and is hereby appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge for the use of the committee for
education during the coming year.

Grand Lodge Activities Week
Masonic History
Your Committee on Finance has had before it the report of the
Committee on Masonic History and its request for an appropriation of
$3000.00 during the coming year.
After considerable discussion with the members of that committee,
as to their program for the coming year and the assurance that this year
will practically complete the work of the committee in examining the
records of all the pioneer Lodges, we concur in their request for this
appropriation.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption :
Resolved, that the sum of $3000.00 be and is hereby appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge for the use of the Committee on
History during the coming year.
Committee on Accounts
The attention of the Finance Committee has been directed to the fact
that some of the committees of the Grand Lodge, in expending appropriations, have failed to submit their bills for approval to the Committee
on Accounts.
· The Constitution clearly provides · that all the bills shall be audited
by the Committee oh Accounts, and your , Finance Committee is of the
opinion that this should apply to all expenditures being made by any
agencies of the Grand Lodge with the exception of the Masonic Homes
and Masonic Club Houses and Masonic Employment Bureaus.
Grand Secretary's Office
During the last twenty-five years there has accumulated a surplus
in the suspense account of the Grand Secretary the sum of $1288.05. The

It has been customary during the last several years at the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge to pay the bills of the Grand Lodge
·· Activities Committee.
The Committee in Los Angeles has requested an appropriation of
$3000.00, which is in accordance with the recommendation of this Finance
Committee at the last session.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:·
Resolved, that the sum of $3000.00 be and is hereby appropriated
from the . funds of this Grand Lodge to reimburse the Grand Lodge
Activities Committee for money expended during the present session.

Euclid Lodge No. 519
Your Committee has reviewed the request of Euclid Lodge No. 519
for a reimbursement of $535.32 for expenses incurred for stenographic
reports in Trial Record No. 614, for the following reasons:
The accusers in said Trial Record No. 614 were all members of
Lodges other than Euclid Lodge No. 519 ; that the trial was held in Covenant Lodge No. 527; that Euclid Lodge was in no way connected with
the trial, although the brother against whom the charges were preferred
was a member of Euclid Lodge.
'
The trial commissioners allowed extraneous matter to go into the
record which greatly increased the cost of the stenographic report, which
your Committee feels was very excessive.
· As Euclid Lodge is small and can ill afford this large expense, and
as your Committee feels that Euclid Lodge was not at fault in the
matter, we believe that the Lodge should be reimbursed ; however, our

722

GRAND L ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

. recommendation for this reimbursement shall, in no way, be construed as
a precedent for the reimbursement to Lodges for expenses in trials in
general.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $535.32 be and is hereby appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge to reimburse Euclid Lodge for the
payment of the stenographic report of Trial Record No. 614.

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
October, 1929
By JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith is submitted my Ninth Report as Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee. As usual, the views expressed under
the various topics are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
We also desire to express our thanks to the Secretaries of the
several Grand Bodies and of .the Grand Lodges of the United States,
the Editors of Masonic publications, and to other writers who have
directly or indirectly fttrnished material which has furnished the
basis for some of the opinions expressed in the report.
Brother Louis Block, Committee on Fraternal Correspondence
of Iowa, says that as he conceives of it the Report on Foreign
Correspondence is destined to serve as a post-graduate course in
the school of Masonry, of which the writers form the Faculty.
Whether .or not this Report will serve as a text book is something
that the reader must judge for himself.
In the nine years that the writer has been privileged to serve
as Chairman of this Committee there are various questions that have
generally been prominent at the same time in a number of the Jurisdictions. Some have been considered, with action taken to write
them into the laws of the Fraternity, while others are still under
discussion. Among them may be mentioned: in the order of time
in which 1:hey have arisen are, physical qualifications, Masonry in
the World War, the relation between co-ordinate Bodies, the Ku
Klux Klan, changes in the Ritual to take care of the large number
of petitioners, Masonic Clubs, Education, both public and Masonic,
large Lodges, the Masonic Service Association and the National
Masonic Tuberculosis Sanatorium. In the Report we have endeavored to consider those topics that are at present receiving the
attention of the Craft and others, that like the poor, will be always
with us.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Within the limits of the Report cannot be considered all of
these and for that reason only a general statement can be included.

"side orders," would soon establish the fact that while all Masons
are not members of these co-ordinate Bodies still all members of
them are Masons. This method might have ~ more salutary effect
than mere preachments.

2

CIPHER CODES: In some of the Jurisdictions the use of
cipher codes, "keys" or "exposes" is a Masonic offense, but some
Grand Lodges have even adopted aµ official cipher. The Grand
Master of one Jurisdiction advanced the following reasons for his
recommendation to adopt a cipher code; that this is a day of multiple
interests and the average man is too much engrossed with the
details of business, social affairs and other activities to take the
time to go through the parrot-like process of learning the said
questions, that Masonry is more concerned in having a good man
interested in Masonry and active in its work rather than the particular way in which he learned it; that the large sums of money
paid for salaries, expense of Inspectors, Lecturers, etc., would be
saved, and the law that it is a Masonic offense to possess these
books is more honored in the breach than by the observance.
A visit to the average book store, the perusal of Masonic
journals, histories, etc., demonstrates that there is very little of the
esoteric work of Masonry, if any, that is not available to an interested party in some form or other.
COORDINATE BODIES: The extent to which the Grand
Lodge of England goes to prevent its members from becoming members of any organization that has any resemblance to Masonry is
shown in the report .of the Board of General Purposes wherein they
view the Loyal Order of Moose, which lately started in England.
They caution their members to seriously consider the organization
from a purely Masonic standpoint before joining, until the Grand
Lodge had made a thorough investigation. They based their warning on the ground that the Moose talked good fellowship, harmony
and benevolence, that they had a ceremony of initiation, and that
while their governing body did not use the same titles as a Grand
Lodge, still the system of government was similar and some of the
claims made by the organization could not be regarded as otherwise
than Masonic.
The Shrine, the Grotto, and other like organizations are criticized or commended in various jurisdictions according to the viewpoint of the Grand Master or the Grand Lodge itself.
We have always held the view that if the Blue Lodge offers to
its members the same advantages, real or imaginary, as are found in
these organizations they will cease to play an important part in the
Masonic system.
Discipline' of offenders against the Masonic law in the Blue
Lodge, even though the act was committed in one of the so-called

3

MASONIC EDUCATION: The various views on this important topic, which is now actively before a large number of the
Jurisdictions, if set forth at length, would more than fill the entire
Report. We quote from an editorial 'from the· " Missouri Free
Mason," entitled "Catching Them Young," which ably summarizes
this matter:
"The first year or so of . Masonic life are to the members of
our Fraternity very much what the years of childhood are to the
adult. In them those conceptions and impressions are received
those habits formed, which dominate later life. The young Maso~
is in a receptive state, he craves for explanation and instruction. If
he does not receive it, he is apt to gain an unworthy or at least
an impoverished idea of Masonry, which generally prev;nts his ever
making any real advance. Therefore, the question of arousing the
interest of the newly initiated brother is of paramount importance.
What we have to do is to encourage the newly-made Mason to
follow the injunction given to him to 'approach the East.'
"~ surv~y of the present situation does not seeJll to help us
much m finding a remedy except insofar as it gives the key to the
weaknesses which must be eliminated. Ther e are in this country
more than three millions of men who wear the square and compass.
Of these three million possibly three per cent know any more about
Masonry than was told them on the nights they received their
degrees. Thus we are faced with a staggering problem. The overwhelming majority of American Masons know no more than the
bare ritualistic elements of Masonry and most of them only the
merest confused smattering of that. These Masons form the various
~ategories. of 'button Masons.' Some of them attended Lodge at
. irregular intervals, others on anniversaries, when elections are held,
others when refreshments are served, and still worse, some never
come at all.
·
" If strenuous efforts are made on those members who are at
present uninterested observers of the workings of the Cr aft and we
neglect those who are coming up the ladder of initiation, a constant
supply of uninterested members is being created and our . work is
endless. It might be stated with certainty that concentrating on
the other horn of the dilemma leaves the already dying timber to
the final ravages of dry rot and decay. It is for both the old and
the young Mason that we have to work, but strategically the latter
is far more important for the future.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

"These objects, however, need a two fold treatment. The two
dasses cannot be reached by quite the same methods, although in
the final analysis the same principles and the same material must
be employed. The educational efforts of various Grand Lodges,
the mechanism of Study Clubs fostered by the N. M. R. S. are
directed very largely towards the greater and senior class of Masons,
and it is only by such means that they can be reached. But the
task· 'difficult. The subject of the effort has been initiated perhaps
several years previously, and the enthusiasm of the early period has
died out, and must be revived. This phase of Study Club work will
require the hardest effort and will prove the least fruitful. The other
phase of Study Club work comes in bringing the new initiate into
the fold of thinking Masons. There is a preliminary step to this
work and it is being worked with considerable success in many
cases. We refer to the presenting of pamphlets, magazines, or
books to the newly initiated Mason as he climbs the three steps.
The value of this lies chiefly in the fact that it shows the young
Mason that there is more than a mere ritualistic formula to the
Order, and while his enthusiasm is still at its highest, encourages
him to make a start in 'approaching the East.'
"Thus far we have seen a possible remedy to a bad situation.
We probably never will see the day when Masonry is composed of
readin·g or at · least thinking members, even to the extent of one in
three, but a reasonable goal at this time would be ~me in ten, and
that might, and ought to be a_ccomplished before very many years are
past. It is not research students that Masonry wants, however.
They will develop if this idea can be worked out. It is interested
members that are needed; men who are capable of intelligently performing the official duties of the Lodge, men who. when they take
part in a ceremonial understand whereof they speak, and do not
merely repeat a meaningless formula memorized after the fashion
of a parrot, or ground out mechanically like a gramophone, with
less effect or conviction than the bird of green and iridescent plumage says, 'Polly wants a cracker.'
"Doubtless every field of knowledge has been obscured with wild
theories and · the baseless fancies of writers with more imagination
than knowledge, but none to the extent that Masonic scholarship
has been. There are more hobby-riders, more constructors of systems on the basis of scraps of disparate facts, among so-called
Masonic scholars than in any other subject of research. While of
those who sincerely try to weigh all evidence and confirm every
step taken are conspicuous by their rarity.
"It is this state of affairs that makes the task of educating
Masons so difficult. Misunderstandings arise and corrections have

to be made and the earnest seeker after truth, who has not sufficient
time to read everything of importance that has been written and
weigh it for himself, becomes disgusted and joins the army of
uninterested Masons.

4

5

"As long as the type of scholarship remains what it is the task
of overcoming the lack of interest in Masons is going to be difficult.
There are two aims that must be fostered, first, to increase the
interest of new members and in those old initiates . who can be
reached, and second, to increase the number and the quality of
authentic yet popular works on Masonry."
GENERAL GRAND LODGE: This bugaboo, we think, will
never be more than an academic question regardless of Grand
Masters' Conferences and other meetings of a like nature. The
thought that any one of the Grand Lodges would delegate their
authority or prerogatives to any general body is scarcely within the
realm of possibility. As the Correspondent of West Australia says:
"A general Grand Lodge operating merely in an advisory capacity
would be about as useful as a soleless shoe without uppers."
The Grand Masters' Conference, which is held annually at
Washington, however, does serve a useful purpose by perhaps .
bringing to the attention of the various Grand Lodges certain conditions as might be made uniform, without infringing upon Grand
Lodge sovereignty. The Proceedings of these meetings show that
even in such questions, where some change might profitably be made
there is a great difference of opinion, largely due to local conditions.
LANDMARKS: Just what is a "Landmark" is interesting
more from a historical standpoint than otherwise. Dr. Kuhn of
Missouri stated there are only ' two landmarks, namely a belief in
God and a belief in the immortality of the soul. West Virginia has
adopted the following eight:
1. Belief in God, the Creator, Author and Architect of .the
Universe-omnipotent, omniscient and omnipresent.
2. Belief in the immortality of the Soul.
3. A "Book of the Law" as an indispensable part of the
furniture of the Lodge.
4. The government of the Fraternity by a Grand Master.
5. Secrecy: Applied to the modes of recognition, certain symbols,
the ballot, obligations, signs and pass words, and forms of
initiation.
6. The legend of the Third Degree.
7. Ancient Craft Masonry includes only the degrees of Entered
Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason.
8. A Mason must be a man, free born and of mature age.

6

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Some Jurisdictions have ten;· others the twenty-five listed by Dr.
Mackey; one has thirty-eight, and another has stretched the limit
to fifty-four.
The ones adopted by West Virginia seem to embody those which
are absolutely vital to the Masonic system and have never been
tinkered with.
MISSION OF MASONRY: We believe that the following
from the Report of the Chairman of the Correspondence Committee
of Washington presents this question from a number of angles and
is worthy of perusal:
"This is a question which can be discussed from many angles.
To the man who desires rank and position for himself, it appeals
only so far as he can use the Institution to elevate himself for a brief
authority. To him who wishes to use it for social or business
advancement it soon wears out and is discarded. To the student of
antiquities it appeals for its age-old wisdom. To the ritualist it
brings satisfaction for .. its wonderful ceremonials. To others its
social features are deemed paramount. To the superficial it appeals
for its possibilities of spectacular display. To the thinking mind it
furnishes a world of speculative and moral principles which have a
· beauty all their own and furnish much food for thought. But the
highest an~ noblest consideration of all comes to him who judiciously
accepts the great moral truths taught in history and ceremonials,
and honestly tries to apply them in the building of his own personal
character.
"Masonry, as an institution, does not pretend to correct the
evils of society except through its influence over the individual
Mason. It reprobates the use of the fraternity for political or
sectarian purposes, although it tries to teach those age old truths 'of
Morality, Friendship and Brotherly Love, as the very foundation
of social activity. Its impression is primarily made on the individual,
and it is only through the individual that it proposes to influence
society.
"This truth must be recognized as the fundamental ideal of all
our efforts or the Institution will eventually pass out of existence
like so many other societies which have flourished for a 's eason and
then been discarded. That it has lived so long in a changing world,
has survived through revolutions and cataclysms of moral degeneration, is an evidence of its virile hold upon the minds of thinking men.
Its principles are old, yet ever new. Its ideals appeal to the best
there is in mankind, and if we give way to the mad rush of
so-called wider field of influence, we may find the seeds of disruption
growing in our selected garden sooner or later."

PUBLISHED PROCEEDINGS .O F GRAND LODGES: One
of the outstanding events of the year 1928 was the action of the
Grand Lodge of Texas in deciding to stop the custom of printing
in their Proceedings the entire roster of members, and has thus
·made unavailable for those engaged in preparing "sucker lists" one
of the sources of supply.
This example could be followed by other Jurisdictions without
objection from Chairmen of Correspondence Committees who have
to peruse them. It would also result in a large saving to the Grand
Lodge itself. Michigan, which is a great State in many respects,
still stands at the head of the l~st with a book of over 1,200 pages.
REPRESENTATIVES: Massachusetts, which is one of the
few Jurisdictions who do not appoint Representatives to other Grand
Lodges, has adopted the system. It came into existence in the
United States in 1838 . in New York, through the adoption of a
recommendation made by the Grand Secretary reading as follows:
"I recommend that in every Grand Lodge with which this
Grand Lodge is in correspondence, some well known and respectable
Brother of the rank of a Past Master, be appointed as the representative of this Grand Lodge at the discretion and on the warrant
of the Grand Master; said representative to be a resident of the
State or Kingdom in which the Grand Lodge to which he is commissioned holds Masonic jurisdiction and his duties to be prescribed
by this Grand Lodge. And also, that all foreign Grand Lodges, in
correspondence with us be allowed a resident representative in this
Grand Lodge. Such representatives to be always clothed in the
peculiar costume of the Lodges they severally represent and to be
allowed the privilege of speaking in Grand Lodge on all subjects
of general interest to the Craft, or the Grand Lodge they represent
in particular, but without a vote."
As a general rule we cannot find where these Representatives
have ever functioned. In some of the Jurisdictions, both at home and
abroad, the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence has
endeavored to draft the Representatives from their Jurisdiction by
asking that they review the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge to which
they are accredited. Even then there has been Jack of results.
One Jurisdiction decided to present its Representatives with
an appropriate jewel to be worn when attending functions of the
Grand Lodge where they were supposed to be honor guests. This
may produce something.
TEMPLES: Some of the larger Jurisdictions, including
Illinois, Indiana and New Jersey, in line with California, have

REPORT ON CORHPJSPONDENCE

adopted the rule that proposed temple projects to be undertaken by
a subordinate Lodge must first be approved in some form or other
by the Grand Lodge. Ambition and optimism have often entailed
serious financial losses not only upon Lodges but individuals.
An argument advanced against this supervision by the Grand
Lodge is based on the practice of today of "too much legislation."
It is contended that a subordinate Lodge should be the sole judge
as to what it wishes to do in such a matter. As a Grand Lodge
perhaps by law might ultimately become responsible for the debts
of a subordinate Lodge it would be right and proper that they
should be consulted. The old adage that "two heads are better
than one" can usually be invoked to good advantage.
Lodges .have undertaken building projects beyond their capacity
or means, and this has indirectly caused not only a heavy burden
upon the Members but also indirectly commercialized the Lodge
by efforts to meet their temple obligations. The result has been
the lowering of the standard of membership, naturally reflecting
not only upon the Lodge but on the general membership.

TRIALS: Masonic trials, in a number of Jurisdictions by
reason of the procedure have resulted not only in the miscarriage
of justice but also has entailed a vast amount of work on the
Grievance and Appeals Committee and the Grand Lodge itself. In
some the offender is tried by the entire body of the Lodge; in
others by Trial Commissioners selected by the Master or the
Lodge; in others by a body appointed by the Grand Master or
District Deputy Grand Master for each particular case, from Past
Masters who are members of Lodges other than the one in which
the trial is to be held.
The main objection to a trial by Commission appointed by the
Grand Master comes from Jurisdictions covering a large territory.
Even in such cases there could undoubtedly be a plan arranged as
would overcome this objection. A large number of cases are sent
back for re-trial by reason of the unfamiliarity of the Trial Commission with the technical rules of procedure adopted by the Grand
Lodge for handling trials. The appointment of a Board or Commission by the Grand Master, composed of Members who have had
experience and are therefore familiar with Masonic trials would
undoubtedly eliminate a large amount of the work.

ADVERTISING
Grand Masters, Committees on Jurisprudence and others in
authority still continue to endeavor to bring home to misguided
members the stigma that is placed upon the Fraternity by using the
word "Masonic" or any of its emblems to further political, commercial or social preferment. Perhaps one of the difficulties is the exemption of certain endeavors, or businesses. In their nature they
are doing a legitimate service to the Fraternity or its members, but
they are, when all is said and done, business propositions.
We have always inclined to the opinion that there should be no
exceptions, and that the word " Masonic" should be strictly taboo
for everything that is not under the absolute control of the Grand
Lodge.
In some instances the Grand Lodge itself is at fault by publishing in the Proceedings the roster of its members. In numerous
cases the newly initiated Mason is disillusioned by experiences with
book-sellers, insurance companies, real estate firms, etc., peddling
their wares with the Institution as a background. Masonry in no
sense should be used as a link or a method for securing political or
commercial preferment. The general public is also often "taken in"
in the same manner. A great deal of criticism has been directed
against companies organized to insure " Masons only" and yet one
of these companies has in a number of cases financially assisted
Jurisdictions in Temple projects which might other wise have resulted
in disaster to the Grand Lodge or the subordinate Lodge undertaking the work in question.
Colorado (1928) :
(Grand M aste1·) : During the year my attention has been called to
certain practices that are being indulged in by representatives of socalled "Masonic" insurance companies {that is to say, companies or
associations that insure, or agree to pay benefit to, Masons exclusively,
even though the word "Masonic" may not appear in the names of such
organizations), · who call upon newly-made Master Masons and state
that it is their duty to carry life or other forms of insurance, often
times intimating that in some way their companies are connected with
the Masonic F raternity.
T he accusation has been made that even Masters and Secretaries
participate in these practices to the extent of circularizing the names of
newly-raised Master Masons, for a fee or other consideration.
In, that previous resolutions have been adopted by this Grand
Lodge, condemning the use of the word "Masonic" in connection wit!i

11

business enterprises, and disclaiming any connection with "Masonic"
insurance companies, it is obvious that they have not curbed the practice,
and to evade the liability, the offenders are oftentimes careful to avoid
the use of the word "Masonic."
Jn order that the responsibility for the act may be placed upon the
individual and the proper discipline exercised, I offer the following
resolution and recommend its adoption:
"This Grand Lodge has in no manner authorized, and is in no way
responsible for the creation of insurance companies or mutual benefit
associations, called Masonic, or any other company or association that
insures, or agrees to pay benefits to, Masons exclusively; nor, is this
Grand Lodge, or any Lodge under its jurisdiction, legally or morally
r esponsible for any agreement, contract or other act of any such companies or association." "Any Mason who shall make representations in
conflict with the above declaration, to induce any person to join or
become interested in any such company or association, is hereby declared
to be guilty of un-Masonic conduct."

Section 44, Grand Lodge By-Laws makes the use o.f Masonic
Symbols in business a Masonic offense. If the offender is a Mason he

hy a person not a Mason he or she can be proceeded against under the

(Clu:iirnu:m Correspondence Committee): Recently it has come to

to be advertised, apparently as a matter of news, such matters as the

Now, while there does not appear to be any valid objection to advertise the holding of the meetings of subordinate lodges, your Board

most improper and un-Masonic should be stopped.
