Section 41, Chapter 18, of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Nova
Scotia and under no circumstances contain any reference whatever as to
what occurred in the respective lodges or the names of the persons
joining the same.
Texas (1928):
Resolved, That Article 631, "Masonic Laws of Texas," be amended
so as to hereafter read as follows:
:'The use of Masonry or use of the faith and credit of Masonry by
individuals, associations or corporations for business or political purposes
is strictly prohibited, and the ostentatious display of Masonic emblems is
contrary to the spirit of Freemasonry. Provided that nothing herein
shall prohibit a corporation, association, firm, or individual from engaging
in activities intended for the service, protection, education or relief
of Master Masons or their dependents. Provided further, that before
engaging in such activities in Texas such corporation, association, firm
or individual shall first submit its plans and purposes to the Grand
Master and obtain his consent thereto.
The Grand Lodge of Texas prohibits the use of the word "Masonic,"
and all like terms, as well as Masonic emblems, on signboards, business
cards , or stationery, or in any other way for the purpose of advancing
the secular interest or business or political fortunes of individual
Masons ."

BIBLE-PRESENTATION OF
While no criticism can justly be made of the effort of a Lodge
to impress upon a new member the value and symbolism of the Book
of the Sacred Law, by presenting him with a Bible, from a practical
standpoint we fail to see where it can or will accomplish very much
good. Perhaps in the main the Book will only be regarded as a
souvenir or observing of a custom.
The same purpose could undoubtedly be served ·if a newly initiated candidate was given some form of Masonic literature that
would bring home to him the importance of the Bible in Masonry.
If he was presented with a work such as Brother Street's "Symbolism
of the Three Degrees," Joseph Ford Newton's "The Builders,'' "The
Dollar Masonic Library" or something else equally as good, the
same effect would be produced. In addition it would furnish the
newly made Mason with something useful with which to start his
Masonic education.
On a par with the presentation of the Bible is the giving of the
Constitution and Regulations of the Jurisdiction wherein the Lodge
is located to a new member. That Masters of Lodges, who should
be familiar with the law often request rulings on matters that are
speeifically covered, is evidence that those who should use such a
work do not. If that is the case there seems to be little hope thaf
a lay member will make use of any printed manual or code.

CORNERSTONES

(Chairmaa Correspondence Committee): With a touch of gentle
irony in refer:ence to the presentation of Bibles to newly made Masons
he said: "The good aimed at might be better attained if some plan could
be devised for its careful and regular study." This conviction always
overwhelms us whenever we witness the ceremony.

The laying of cornerstones of public buildings under Masonic
auspices has existed almost from "time immemorial." Sometimes
it becomes a matter of public moment when objections t o it are made.
They are generally based upon the erroneous assumption that
Masonry is endeavoring to advertise itself or serve an ulterior purpose.
Embarrassment might be saved the Fraternity, ·with the attending
bad results, if in such instances the ceremony was abandoned. ·
One of the questions producing discussion is whether or not
cornerstones for churches should be laid on Sunday. The answer
of course depends upon the viewp~int of the Jurisdiction. The
church authorities undoubtedly regard the event as simply a ceremony and "the better the day the better the deed." In the main
however, the Fraternity regard it as Masonic labor, which is ex~
pressly or impliedly prohibited by a regulation.
In the olden days Lodges were permitted to a ttend church in
their regalia, ·while in the present day and age this is considered a
form of advertisement.

Massachusetts (1928) :

(Deputy Grand Master) : · Just how remote in the mists of antiquity
rests the origin of the custom of laying cornerstones with attendant ·ceremonies, no man knows. There is evidence from which we may conjecture
that it is almost, if not quite, a~ old as recorded history itself. We have
reason to surmise that the custom may have originated when man first
began to erect his shelters and edifices on firm and enduring foundations.
There is an existing record of such a ceremony participated in by King
Thotmes III about 1600 years before Christ. An excavation in 1853
disclosed a cornerstone, enclosing a box and contents, with an inscription
showing it to have been laid by King Sargon of Assyria, some 800
years before Christ. We thus have actual proof of the great antiquity
of the custom of laying cornerstones.
As to the form of the ceremonials attending the laying of ancient
cornerstones, we can be guided only by tradition. The ceremonies which'
you have just witnessed are substantially the same as those recorded
as performed by the Grand Master of Masons of Scotland· on September
13, 1753, and precedent for the ceremonials then used goes back to the time of King Henry the Seventh, who presided as Grand Master, on
June 24, 1502, in the laying of the foundation stone of the Chapel bearing
his name at the east end of Westminster Abbey.

The Grand Lodge of New York approved of dual membership at
its Annual Communication last May, and regulations have been adopted
to govern such membership. The constitution was amended to permit a
Master Mason in good standing to become and continue as a member
of two Lodges, by regular affiliation, or by joining as a petitioner in
the founding of a new Lodge. He shall be liable for the payment of
the affiliation fee in the second Lodge, and dues in both Lodges ; can
hold office in both Lodges but cannot be a Master of more than one
Lodge at the same time; and involuntary loss of membership in any
Lodge shall work loss of membership in both Lodges.
A member of a Lodge under the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of New York cannot become a member of a second Lodge outside of
the State of New York unless the Lodge happens to be in a Grand
Jurisdiction permitting membership in more than one Lodge. If a
Master Mason in good standing outside of the State of New York desires
to affiliate with a regular Lodge in New York, without surrendering
membership in his present Lodge, he may do so, providing that the
Grand Secretary certifies to the New York Lodge that the petitioner
hails from a Grand Jurisdiction permitting one of its members to belong
to more than one Lodge.
The principal reason for dual membership is to permit sojourners
to affiliate with a Lodge in a city or town where they may reside without
terminating their membership in their old Lodge. Whether this can
be done depends upon the law of one or more Jurisdictions. The Grand
Lodges of the three States bordering on Connecticut now permit such
membership, and as many of our members may desire to affiliate with
a Lodge in one of these Jurisdictions and still remain a member of his
old Lodge in Connecticut, he should be permitted to do so. It is also
true that some members of those Jurisdictions may desire to join a
Lodge in Connecticut without severing their membership elsewhere.
This can be done now only by filing a demit. There is a deep-seated
sentiment against relinquishing one's membership in his mother Lodge,
and while he is willing to visit a Lodge occasionally, accept its hospitalty
and mingle with the brethren, he still feels that he is only a guest and
hesitates to wear out his welcome. Having no status as a member of
the Lodge he visits, no responsibility to support it, nor opportunity to
render service, he soon loses interest and seldom makes his presence

much depending upon what the accurate number is. England, however,

be verified to the last dot, no doubt explains why her figures are intimated

Wisconsin (1929):
(Committee on Dual Membership): Your Committee, instructed to
investigate plural membership as practiced by other Grand Jurisdictions

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

25

~d ordered to report their findings together with their recommendations
at this Annual Communication, offer the result of their labor for your
consideration and such action as you may see fit to take.
In the understanding of the Committee, plural membership is a
term used to designate that condition brought about within a Gran,d
Jurisdiction through its adoption of regulations governing its constituent
Lodges permitting a Brother to assume active membership . in two. or
more Lodges at one and the same time. Single membership restricts
such membership to one Lodge, while dual membership permits active
membership in two Lodges but no more. Life and Honorary Memberships may enjoy such privileges as a Grand Jurisdiction sees fit to
sanction.
With these definitions in mind, detailed inquiries were made of the
sixty-nine Grand Lodges with which we are in fraternal correspondence
as to the customs and regulations in their various Jurisdictions, and
m ch valuable information was received from most of. those wh~ replied,
11
sixty-four in all. To read this data in full would re~u1re more t1i:ne than
you care to devote to this subject, therefore, as bnefi~ as pos~1ble, we
wiff endeavor to place before you the gist of the mformatton thus
received.
Sixteen G1and Jurisdictions-British Columbia, Canada, England,
Ireland Kentucky, Massachusetts, Manitoba, New York, Nova Scotia,
New z~aland, Rhode Island, Scotland, South Australia, Virginia, Victoria
and Western Australia-permit unrestricted plural membership. The
Grand Lodge of South Carolina permits it by dispensation from their
Grand Master.
Of those in the United States, Massachusetts, Virginia and Rhode
Island have permitted the practice for many years and speak in glowing
terms of the advantages derived. New York and Kentucky adopted
plural membership last year and report little experience. England, the
mother Grand Lodge of the world, Ireland, British Columbia, Canada,
Nova Scotia, Scotland, New Zealand, South Australia, Victoria. and
Western Australia have always permitted it with no ill results. Manitoba
adopted plural membership in 1918, and opinion in this Jurisdiction is
mixed.
Seven Grand Lodges-Alabama, Alberta, Quebec, New Hampshire,
Philippine Islands, Saskatchewan and Washington-permit plural membership between members of Lodges under their jurisdiction and members
of Lodges under other Grand Jurisdictions but JJrohibit the same between
Lodges within their own Jurisdiction. In Delaware this form of plu.ral
membership is not a Masonic offense while in Maine there is a gro~m!5
sentiment in favor of it. In the Philippine Islands, dual ·membership is
permitted in the case of new Lodges.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

26

27

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Alberta, Quebec, Saskatchewan, and possibly others prohibit actual
plural or dual membership within their own Jurisdictions but at the same
time permit their members to hold Honorary and Life memberships
which, under their regulations, carry all the privileges of active membership including those of holding office and paying dues. This in effect
results in plural membership under another title.
Four Grand Lodges-Alberta, California, North Dakota and Oregon
-report they will act on some form of plural or dual membership at
their next Annual Communications.
Thirty-eight Grand Lodges-Arkansas, Arizona, Connecticut, Colorado, California, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Montana, Mississippi, Maine, New Mexico, Nevada, North Dakota, Nebraska,
North Carolina, Oregon, Oklahoma, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Prince Edward
Island, Missouri, New Jersey, South Dakota, Texas, Tennessee, Utah,
Vermont, Wyoming and West Virginia-do not permit or have never
taken legislative action on the question of permitting their. membership
to belong to more than one Lodge. In a few it is a Masonic offense
while in others there are no regulations governing. Your Committee is
unable to discover a single one of these Grand Lodges that has at any
time adopted either plural or dual mmbership later to abolish it.
Five Grand Lodges-Cuba, New Brunswick, New ~outh Wales,
Queensland and Tasmania-did not reply to our inquiry. This is unfortunate since it is probable some of these Jurisdictions permit plural membership and their experience could be of value to us.
A study of the material and comments received reveals that of the
Grand Lodges who have ever adopted plural membership not one has
abolished it and all are decidedly satisfied the system is a distinct benefit
to them. The only criticisms are from those Grand Jurisdictions who
have never worked under this system.
A digest of the comments from the various Grand Lodges that permit
plural membership establishes four advantages the Craft in Wisconsin
might derive should we alter our regulations to permit active membership in more than one Lodge.
1. Since a Brother could assist in forming a new Lodge without
severing his membership in his original Lodge, it might result in more
new Lodges, especially in the larger centers.
2. In removing to another city or State a Brother could assume the
obligations of membership in the city or State of his adoption without
breaking home ties. It might also result in fower exclusions.
3. A member of a large Lodge, that might offer little scope for
advancement, ' could join another Lodge in which he might hold office
or perform other duties, without ceasing to be a member of his mother

Lodge. Perhaps this privilege would stimulate Masonic enthusiasm
among some of our inactive members and gratify a laudable ambition
on the part of some Brother to be of more service to the Craft.
4. Weak or dormant Lodges could be strengthened by affiliating
Brethren willing to assume obligations of plural membership.
Among possible objections set up we have noted but two worthy
of consideration :
1. Possible confusion as to exclusions, suspensions, and expulsions
unless records are properly kept.
2. Additional work in the Grand Secretary's office and the difficulty
of computing net membership.
These do not appear to be serious objections for if Grand Lodge
dues are required of each member of every Lodge it is hardly likely
there · will ever be a great many plural members in Wisconsin. The
Grand Lodge of Virginia which has permitted the practice since before
.1777 and lists only 1,100 plural members out of a total membership of

48,500.
Your Committee can tiiscover no good reason for not extending to
'our membership the privileges, advantages and obligations of plural
membership should they desir e to avail themselves of it. The experience
of those Grand Jurisdictions permitting it has been uniformly satisfactory
while those who do not and never have permitted it obviously have no
experience to report.
DUES
A question confronting a number of the Jurisdictions i1 the objection ot subordinate Lodges to increasing their dues to meet expenses.
We have always inclined to the theory that Masonry is not a necessity in the strict sense of the word and that those who avail them, selves of the privilege of joining should be willing to pay for it.
With the decrease in the purchasing power of the Almighty Dollar,
and the increase in necessities and luxuries, it seems almost unthinkable that Lodges supposed to be conducted by business men and
along business lines, can expect to take care of their obligations on
dues that were sufficient ten or fifteen years ago.
The Reports of Boards of Relief and the records of Grand
Lodges in the Southwestern part of the United States, who are
caring for tuberculosis ca:ses, clearly show that a large amount is
expended for sojourning Brethren without hope of reimbursement.
The small dues generally paid by the member requiring financial
assistance is given as the excuse for not making reimbursement.

Arkansas (1928):
( Gral«i Master) : It is interesting to note that practically all these
appeals for aid originate in Lodges charging less than $30.00 for the
degrees and less than $2.50 for dues. I feel that if our Lodg(;!s would
increase their fees and dues to an adequate figure, there would be fewer
of these appeals, Lodges being in position to carry their own financial
burdens rather than requesti~g that such burden be passed on to other
Lodges who are really making an effort to make their own way.
Every worth while thing which you and I enjoy costs something.
In all too many Lodges our fees are too low, our per capita tax is
too small and our dues are inadequate. Too many Lodges are satisfied
to educate their members as far as the first few pages of the Masonic
Primer, when, if they would half try, and ·expend just a few cents, they
could give all their members who desire it a university course.

the financial condition of the delinquents and their mental attitude with
relation to a continuation of membership. A desire on the part of the
member to ·definitely withdraw from all Masonic work and interest is the
only valid reason why a member should be suspended for non-payment of
dues. The Master of every Lodge should appoint a committee composed
of members who have a knack of reaching the hearts and the pocketbooks of men. This committee should, if possible, interview every
delinquent member, appeal to his pride, if necessary, and urge him to
continue his membership. Explain to the Brother that .if he is ill or
out of employment or otherwise in distress, the dues will be remitted and
a receipt given him for the amount of his dues. On the other hand,
if the committee ascertains that the brother is living beyond his means
they can gl~e him good and timely advice. Many large and prosperous
Lodges use this plan with satisfactory results.

Illinois (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Referring to the tendency
in all sections of the country to increase Lodge dues the question has
been asked why is this necessary. Freemasonry for many years conducted its affairs with great success and charged a minimum of dues.
A good oyster supper or some ice cream and cake at the conclusion of
work in the third degree. Now the lodge sets up an elaborate dinner at
six o'clock and invites everybody in. Secretaries used to serve for twentyfive cents a night. It now happens that most secretaries draw one dollar
for each member reported at the Annual Meeting. Many other instances
could be cited to show that Masons demand more in every way. Much
of this demand is, of course, unnecessary and could have been gotten along
without, but it is the spirit of the times to be extravagant and waste and
lack o( self-control manifests itself in the Masonic Fraternity just as
it does elsewhere. Those Masons who insist upon being indulgent must
be willing to pay the price and that price is increased fees and dues.
Somebody has said that the luxury of tooay becomes the necessity of
tomorrow. Then it is going to be very hard to return to the old order
of things when Masonry was distinguished because of its simplicity, its
adherence to old ideas and its genuine brotherhood and fraternal feeling.

Texas (1928):
(Grana Master): One of the things which needs correcting in a
great many of our Lodges is the amount of annual dues paid by the
members to the Lodges. The amount of dues of which I learned ranges
from fifty cents per year, which is one dollar and seventy-five cents less
than the Grand Lodge dues, to twelve dollars per year.
I have found that almost with~ut exception the Lodges which charge
the least amount for dues are the ones which in many respects are
furthest from the standard of what a Masonic Lodge should be, and that .
one of the results of this is that in most of such Lodges the dues are
harder to collect than in those which charge more. This is but natural.
A Lodge which charges only a little more than enough to pay its
Grand Lodge tax has almost nothing left with which to pay current
expenses, make its hall attractive, relieve distress, fu~nish social feat~res,
and otherwise function property. This, of course, is not so true m a
Lodge whose treasury is not dependent on its dues (there are a few
such Lodges in the State), but even in such Lodges if the dues are too
small the effect on many of the members is to cause them to regard
Masonry as being so cheap that it doesn't amount to much. It should
not be our desire to cheapen Masonry by reducing the dues and fees for
degrees in an effort to make it appeal to the man who is too stingy or too
needy to pay· for it.
Many of the members of one Lodge which I visited contend that
they should pay to the Lodge only what the Lodge pays on them to the
Grand Lodge. Such members have a very limited conception of Masonry
and its obligations. A member does not pay dues to his Lodge merely to
enable it to pay Grand Lodge dues or to provide a home after his death
for his widow and children as if it were an insurance proposition; which

Washington (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We note that Brother
J. Edward Allen in his reviews asks the pertinent question: "Have we
reached the limit in Fees and Dues?" And doubtless this question has
been suggested by an appeal made by a good Brother in Grand Lodge
against too much interference with the right of a Lodge to set its
own · charges. This seems to have grown out of a declaration of the
Grand Lodge that the fees shall not be less th~n $35.00.
When we wrote our screed on the danger of excessive expenditure
of the monies collected from our Lodges, we were taken to task by one
reviewer who said in effect that we were not paying nearly enough.
There are two sides to this question If we actually believe that
Masonry does not regard a man for his worldly wealth or position, we
must acknowledge that the poor man has as much right to be a Mason
as any one else, and his ability must be recognized whether small or
great. If we wish to make a rich man's club out of the Masonic
. Institution · we seem to be headed the right way.
We always have the poor with us, and it is our duty to assist
as we can, but there exists a great difference between extravagance
and the satisfaction of real needs. Nor are we required to take upon our
shoulders all the ills of humanity. It is a wise saying that we should
undertake the duty that lies next to us, rather than to try to assume
the other fellow's burden.
DEMOLAY-ORDER OF
The Order of De Molay is NOT a Junior Masonic organization,
this fact is forcibly impressed upon every young man making application, and the same effort is being made to establish this idea among
those not familiar with the organization itself. The Order of De
Molay we believe is performing a service to communities in which
it exists. When it is taken into consideration that nearly half a
million young men have passed into and out of the organization in
the eight years that it has been in existence, all taught the ideals of
clean living, clean speaking and clean thinking, it certainly is productive of good, not only to its members but the public in general.

Wisconsin (1929):
(Grand Master): In 1921 the then Grand Master, William F.
Weiler, granted a dispensation to an organization of boys known as
the Order of :De Molay to meet in Masonic Temples in Wisconsin.
Not since the organizatic;m of the Masonic Fraternity back in the
centuries has the Craft had an opportunity of doing so much good in
any one of its activities as is offered in the promotion of the Order of
De Malay. It strikes right at the very foundation of the superstructure
and enables us to produce the Perfect Ashlars so much needed in the
work of rebuilding and edifying our Masonic structure. It is a fact
beyond dispute that we select the future Mason from our own environment largely from sentiment aed becau!le of the ties of blood and
relationship, whereas the candidate for Masonic honors has no knowledge
of what is before him. Sometimes, many times, he petitions for Masonic
light out of curiosity mingled with a desire to follow in the footsteps
of those he knows and trusts to help him in the paths he has not known.
All this is well; but when you begin training your boy in the
tenderest years of his life, to place upon him responsibilities connected
with mystery, you at once help to broaden him out and build the foundation of manhood upon a higher plane. Take any well-conducted Chapte~
of the Order of De Molay--and be it said to our shame that only a
fraction of the Masons have ever witnessed the impressive ceremonies
of this organization-and you will be absolutely astounded at the impressive work done. Sit with me, as I have sat with others, in almost
breathless silence during a working session and watch the masterful
manner in which the officers conduct the work, and as the hour of nine
arrives, look around and see every member of De Molay on bended
knee while the chaplain offers prayer, a prayer which implores God's
blessing upon father and mother, and including the Masonic Institution
which your hands and mine helped make possible, upon all the guests
living there. Try it on, those of you who have never visited a Chapter;
and you will come away converted to the cause of this wonderful,
helpful fraternity, the strongest arm in the Masonic Fraternity of the
future.
These are my views . on the Order of De Molay.

West Australia (1928):

themselves within the Masonic circle. Speaking on the Eastern Star, the
Grand Master of Canada said:
· "It must be understood that we are not expressing any disapproval
of the Order named, its membership or its purposes. The resolution to
which I have just referred is part of the traditional policy of the Masonic
Order. Conservatism is sometimes the indifference of an indolent mind ;
it is sometimes the wisdom born of experience and this conservatism is of
the latter kind. Freemasonry does not lend itself to co-operation with
other societies. It is not a service club; much less is it a benevolent
institution. It is a great fraternity, which can neither admit or permit
anything that might create divisions among its members or disturb the
harmonious workings of its Lodges. Its perfectly balanced system has
come down to us out of the past, tried by the most searching of tests,
the test of time. And experience has shown that within the limits set by
. the ancient landmarks there is safety and ample opportunity for service
while without there is difficulty and danger and usually Masonic disaster."

EDUCATION-PUBLIC
The idea. of "Public Schools Week," as established by the Grand
Lodge, F. & A. M. of California, has been and is being copied by
other Jurisdictions. Masonry stands for Education and Enlightenment. There can be no better way of translating that into service
than a consistent and active campaign on behalf of the Public School
system.
Masons of the early days played an important part in the formation and establishment of our Public Schools, and there is thus a
sentimental reason for helping them. It is an activity in which
partisanship should have no place. The Equality of Opportunity,
which is the fundamental doctrine of this Republic, is one that must
be developed to the greatest limit.
The Student Loan Fund of the Grand Encampment of Knights
Templar and those of a number of other Grand Lodge Jurisdictions
have produced results that have been highly satisfactory, both from
a monetary and educational standpoint. President Hoover in calling
the Public Schools "The Central Power House of our Nation,"
spoke not only in engineering but also in practical terms.

FUNERALS
The custom is gradually growing throughout the various Jurisdictions to make a Masonic funeral more of a private ceremony than
a public function. This is shown in the continued attempts to
change the funeral service of the Fraternity so as to make it fit in
with this thought.

40

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

In a number of cases the duty of attending Masonic funerals is
carried out where there is the greatest opportunity for public display.
Often on such an occasion the great harm is done by the manner in
which the service is conducted. Being only an occasional ceremony
often the Officers are not proficient in the ritual, and as "they are
on parade" the impression is anything but favorable. This criticism
is voiced by a number of Grand Masters and is perhaps an added
argument for privacy.

is the unusual : Eight persons were burned to death. One of them was

Michigan (1928):
(Grand Chaplain) : Through the lapsing years there has been manifested a growing indifference to attendance at funeral services. You
cannot successfully deny that this is true. From all parts of our Jurisdiction, from the Brethren of other Jurisdictions, goes up the plaint
that it is difficult to get a respectable number out to attend a funeral. I
myself have observed this growing disinclination to honor the memory
of the dead. I have gone long distances to attend Masonic funerals,
when my feelings and my pride have been hurt by the impoverished attendance. I have seriously wondered whether the spirit of brotherhood
is fading away; whether our Institution is finally to become an exponent
of mirth, fun, jollity and pastime. If we really have appreciation of the
merits of the dead and sympathy for those who are left to mourn, are
we unwilling, through self-indulgence and indifference, to make our
appreciation and sympathy manifest.
To such an extent have the Brethren become negligent of this
appreciative and sympathetic manifestation of brotherhood that it has
led in some quarters, to the formation of members into a club, or society
devoted to a reverent respect for the dead as shown by attendance at a
funeral.
One Brother, so impressed with the indignity of this thoughtless
neglect, wrote to the M. W. Grand Master asking his opinion upon the
subject of the formation of such clubs or associations. A copy of his
letter he forwarded to the Grand Chaplain. I was glad to know that in
some sections of the Jurisdiction the Masonic conscience was stirring.
I felt sure that the disgraceful treatment of our beloved dead being
recognized, there would eventually be found a remedy. But I felt sure
that the best remedy would not take the form of coercive or semicoercive measures. I felt sure that the iron hand of compulsion would
not bring the best results.

North Carolina (1929):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The status of Masonic
funerals differs greatly in the several parts of the Masonic world. We
are told in the book before us that "wearing of regalia at Masonic
funerals is discouraged"; that a Masonic funeral is not permitted except
by dispensation of the Grand Master ; and that the reading of the
Masonic burial service when the Brethren are not in regalia is not to be

Masons to attend the funeral of a sister, wife, mother-in-law, daughter
or other relative of a Mason. This is prohibited henceforth.

So far as cao be ascertained there are no regulations under the
Grand Lodges of Ireland and Scotland with respect to Masonic burial
beyond those requiring a dispensation to appear in Masonic . clothing,
but the Book of Constitutions of the latter provides a ceremonial to be
.used at the house of the deceased Brother and thereafter at the grave, as
well as a ceremony for a funeral Lodge.
From inquiries made at the Australian Grand Lodges, as well as
New Zealand, the Board has ascertained that, with the exception of
Tasmania and South Australia, dispensations are issued without the
Grand Master being first assured that a Masonic burial was the expressed wish of the deceased. It has also been ascertained that the
wearing of regalia at funerals is d.iscouraged, and in no case can a nonafliliate receive Masonic burial. In England the practice has fallen
entirely, or i!lmost entirely, into disuse. At this stage the Board desires to
call the attention of Grand Lodge to the resolution carried at the First
Australian Masonic Conference, "That the wearing of regalia at Masonic
funerals be discouraged."
As a summary of the position it may safely be stated that the practice
of Masonic funerals in regalia has almost died out in Australia, as it
has in England. While the wearing of regalia at funerals is governed
by our Regulation 180, B. of C., and is in the hands of the Grand
Master, all the old regulations make it clear that a Masonic burial is
not conferred as a mark of honor, but in order to meet the wishes of a
deceased Brother.
There still remains the question of reading the Masonic Burial
Service at the grave of a deceased Freemason without the Brethren
appearing in regali~. Such requests are of frequent occurrence, and
the Grand Master has wisely laid it down as a rule that permission will
not be granted unless he can be assured that in giving the requisite
authority he is acting in accordance with the · wishes of the deceased
Brother. Some Lodges, and a few Worshipful Brethren, are of the
opinion that the reading of the Masonic Burial Service without regalia
requires no permission, but your Board is in entire disagreement with this
attitude.
There remains to be dealt with the more difficult question of Lodges
inserting notices in the press inviting Brethren to attend the funerals
of relatives of members. From what the Board can gather this seems
quite a modern practice, .and has no doubt arisen through one Lodge
following the example of another in a sincere desire to show sympathy.
The question arises-Has the Master power to insert such an advertisement in the 11ame of his Lodge in the public press ? The Board is of the
opinion that the Master has no power to insert an advertisement in the
public press inviting members to attend the funeral of a non-Mason, and

West Australia (1928):
(Board of General Purposes) : For some time past the Board has
had under consideration the question of Masonic burials, their origin,
and the regulations respecting the government of the same in various parts
of the world.
The first reference to Masonic funerals which can be found is
under the heading of "Funeral Processions,'' and is contained in the
Constitutions of the Grand Lodge of England of 1754-56, when a regulation was adopted which prohibited the . wearing of regalia at the funeral
of a Freemason without a dispensation from the Grand Master. At
this time Preston laid down certain conditions,· which, by general consent,
became the law of the Order, and they appear in the English Book of
Constitutions as .late as 1873 in the following form:
"No Mason can be interred with the formalities of the Order, unless
it be at his own special request, nor unless he has been advanced to the
degree of a Master Mason. When the wish of the deceased shall have
been communicated to the Master of the Lodge of which he died a
member, the Master may apply to the Grand Master or Provincial
Grand Master for a dispensation.
"A dispensation having been obtained, the Master may invite other
Lodges to attend in form, but the whole ceremony, unless the Grand
Master or his Deputy, or the Provincial Grand Master · or his Deputy,
be present, must be under the direction of the Master of the Lodge to
which the deceased belonged; and he is accountable for the regularity
an<l conduct of the whole proceedings.
"The Lodges rank according to seniority, the junior preceding (except
the Lodge to which the deceased belonged, which in every case is to go ·
the last) , and each Lodge forms one division."
The above differs slightly from the original of 1754, which provided for foreigners and sojourners receiving Masonic burial on request,
but not without a dispensation from the Grand Master.

and that an announcement was made that the profits were to be devoted
· to the Masonic fete. All this is contrary to the spirit of Freemasonry.
The work and the appeal should be confined to our own members, and
as for this going from door to door pressing people to buy tickets, I
regard it as absolutely derogatory to the dignity of our Institution.

. (2) That for the future Lodges shalt not insert advertisements in the
public press inviting members of the Craft to attend the funeral of a
non-Mason.
'
Adopted.
GAMBLING
There appears to be less comment or legislation against gambling
in connec~ion with affairs · held under Masonic auspices or by organizations composed exclusively of Master Masons. This is as it
should be. We also believe that the practice is becoming generally
taboo.
The Regulations of the United States Post Office and legislation by States has had a great deal to do in producing this result.
This comes from a gradual change in public opinion. Gambling,
like other forms of amusement, is perhaps not as fashionable as it
used to be but there still remains in all of the descendants of Adam a
wish at sometime or other to "take a chance."
In the early history of our Country, and as we remember also
in Masonry, it was not thought out of place to finance the erection
of public buildings, Lodge rooms and Masonic Homes by affairs
wherein an opportunity was given those so inclined to try their luck.
New South Wales (1928):
(Grand Master) : Brethren, there is one other matter that has
given me a good deal of concer~ during the past few weeks. You all
know that the Masonic Schools' Welfare Committee, who are doing such
splendid work in taking the boys and girls in hand after they leave the
schools and hostel, and finding them positions in life, have in their
wisdom decided to hold a fete at the town halt at the end of next month.
They wrote and asked for my patronage, and I gave it gladly, on the
understanding that the appeal was to be to Freemasons only. I found
later on that the committee arranging the fete had resolved to hold a
"queen competition," which I very much regret, and if they had asked
my permission I say unhesitatingly that they would not have received it;

North Carolina (1929):
(Chairman Correspo11dence Committee) : Grand Master Cruickshank (Alberta, 1928) in his formal address reports that he has been
several times asked to sanction a lottery for the purpose of raising
funds with which to build a Masonic Hall. Of course he refuses alt
such. The fact that these requests are heard in many places throughout
our country leads us to inquire why they persist. One answer is . found
in the fact that many lotteries or near-lotteries are actually conducted,
even though in violation of law throughout the country. We heard a
man lecturing to a service club of a national reputation say just a few
days ago that he helped conduct one somewhere in Oklahoma, being a
sale of tickets on an automobile, which netted the organization promoting
it twenty-one thousand dollars. The attractiveness of easy money causes
people to undertake practices which sometimes are not proper to
examine closely.
Nova Scotia (1928):
(Grand Master) : I was asked to officially sanction a scheme to raise
a large sum of money by means of a Canada-wide lottery, for the purpose of erecting a Masonic building.
The suggestion was to distribute tickets at one dollar each among
the Craft all over Canada-the inducement to purchase same being the
chance of drawing a big cash prize (cir prizes).
The absurdity of the proposal must be apparent to any one professing Masonic education or principles.
It is worthy of note, only because it reveals and illustrates an
unwholesome trend of thought, inspired and fostered I believe by the

47

knowledge that heretofore lesser infractions of our country's laws covering such procedure, have been overlooked by the civil authorities, and
that our own Fraternity has not been wholly without blame in· this
connection.
I wish to emphasize our duty as Freemasons and as citizens to
maintain, obey and support our own code of ethics, as well as the laws
of the land in which we live.
The Freemasons of this Jurisdiction are not ignorant of these laws
as concerning lotteries, and I submit that this Sovereign Grand Body
should not regard with inOifference or toleration any violatiop of them,
under Masonic auspices.
Tennessee (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A Grand Master was
much impressed by an edict issued from the office of the Grand Maste}'
of West Virginia, dealing with all forms of raffles, lotteries and games
of chance, conducted by bodies basing their membership upon membership
in the Blue Lodge. He concurs with the opinion that no Mason should
be concerned in or participate in any game of chance no matter by what
organization it may be sponsored. He also condemned the use of the
name "M.asonic" in connection with clubs and associations without the
sanction of Grand Lodge, saying, "Clubs of this kind have become detrimental to the Fraternity in other Jurisdictions." Grand Lodge concurred
in both statements.
GRAND LODGE
While it is only a small cloud on the horizon a start has been
made in some of the Jurisdictions by adopting the. English custom
of conducting the routine business of the Grand Lodge through a
Board or Committee, and eliminating from its sessions a large
amount of detail work.
·
The present is an era of "Big Business," and systems that have
worked satisfactorily there will sooner or later be reflected · in the
conduct of fraternal organizations. Indeed, if it does not, the average
session of a Grand Lodge will become more and more of a bore, ·
with the resulting decrease in attendance and interest.
As a communication of the Grand Lodge is the only time where
the Craft have an opportunity to become acquainted, that should be
the outstanding aim of the session.
Illinois (1928):
The Committee on Finance made several recommendations looking
to a more systematic and businesslike method of handling finances by
subordinate 'Lodges. From their recommendations we excerpt the
following:

"l. A standard form of accounting should be prepared and adopted
by the Lodges so that studies, such as has been undertaken by this com.
mittee, can be easily and accurately made.
"2. Masters should prepare a budget of the Lodges' expenditures
for the year and have such' budgets approved by the Lodges.. They
should then see that the budget is carefully followed out durmg the
year's operations.
"3. The District Deputies should co-operate with the Lodges in the
preparation of budgets and give their counsel in using them. In addit~o~
the Grand Lodge could well afford to employ several accountants to v1s1t
the Lodges, install the standard system of accounting, and educate them
in proper financial methods.
"4. Lodges should file with the Committee on Chartered Lodges,
or other designated body, a financial statement of Lodge expenses, income
and investments at the end of each year. The necessity of filing such
a report at the end of his year will bring home to each Master a sense
of his responsibility for the finances of his Lodge and will also enable the
Grand Lodge to determine which Lodges are making progress and which
need more assistance.
"5. While, according to Masonic law, the Master is supreme, some
method ought to be developed whereby the Lodges have more voice
in the handling of their finances, so that there will not be a change in
policy from year to year. It ought not to be possible for a ~ast~r,
whose Lodge has been making progress for several years, to arbitrarily
plunge the Lodge into extravagance and at the same time dissipate its

assets."

Masons, who are stockholders in this organization, and the Grand Master
being its head, must attend to a voluminous correspondence, and tremendous demands of a fraternal and social nature are made upon his t ime
and energy.

Michigan (1928):

(Grand Master) : These Lodges should consider well their Blue
Book before writing such letters to a Grand Master. There are no
objections to a Lodge discussing the merits of any Grand Lodge action
or law enacted; in fact, it is encouraged for Masonic enlightenment.
But when a Lodge refuses to comply with the Constitution, Regulations
and By-Laws of. this Grand Lodge, or feels that it should be exempted
above all other Lodges who enact by legislation the laws of this Grand
Lodge, then it would seem that the proper method to pursue would be
to return their charter to the Grand Lodge and stop writing letters to
blame the Grand Master for the discharge of his duties.
Montana (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Absolute peace and harmony seemed to prevail in New Hampshire-no recommendations of the
Grand Master to fight over; no Jurisdiction Committee report to squelch
proposals for changes in the fundamental laws ; no Grievance Committee
to report. Makes us think of a picture of a thoroughly contented soul,
with an Uncle Sam's whiskers, and half a suspender holding up a pair
of overalls, with the legend: "I know nothing, I owe nothing, I want
nothing, I own nothing- so I am perfectly contented."
The simile is not intended as a reflection; we merely meant to
bring out the last phrase of the expressions used.
New Hampshire (1929):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Here is some real common sense: It was ruled, and approved, that any Master Mason, member
of a Lodge in Nevada, was eligible to be elected ·or appointed to any
Grand Lodge office. That jibes to a nicety with our individual opinion.
The resources of membership should ever be available for Grand Lodge
use. Were it otherwise, then the Grand Lodge is either gagged or
wearing handcuffs, self-imposed.
North Carolina (1929):

(Grand Master): Under the existing law, if a Brother is appointed
Junior Grand Steward and is advanced through the various offices to
that of Grand Master, it takes him ten years to reach the latter office.
During that time he is required to occupy at least two offices which,
to my mind, serve no purpose, unless, perhaps, to furnish two more
appointments for the Grand Master, or two more steps to be taken in
the ascent to the Grand East. If the Grand Lodge has any use for the
offices of Grand Sword Bearer and Grand Pursuivant, I must confess

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

49

that I have never been able to discover it. The Grand Lodge line is too
long, and should be shortened by abolishing these two offices, so that
the Brother m;iking the trip from the lowest to the highest would not
die of weariness on the way up, or succumb to the ravages of old age
before he arrived. A shorter .line would be an incentive to better work,
would make a more efficient organization in Grand Lodge, and would
not, in any way, deprive the Grand Lodge of the services of any useful
officer, as the duties pertaini~g to these respective offices have seldom,
if ever, been performed or their performance been invoked by Grand
Lodge. I therefore, recommend that the office of Grand Pursuivant be
abolished, and that the office of Grand Sword Bearer be abolished.
The following from Mississippi will be interesting to our North
Carolina readers. A' resolution was adopted, reading : "Due to the
fact that several distinguished visitors are in attendance and that the
Craft are anxious to hear from them, it is hereby resolved, That in our
night session for the election of officers that all nominations and seconds
shall be limited to two (2) minutes each and only one nomination and
second for each candidate nominated be allowed."
Based on North Carolina practice, we suggest that henceforth they
dispense with all nominations and let the visitors have still more time.
The Grand Lodge of Kentucky has for a long time retained in its
constitution a clause which prohibits electioneering for office by or on
behalf of any candidate. One of the Past Grand Masters now offers
the following resolution, which is adopted :
"Resolved, That the adoption of a resolution by a Subordinate
Lodge, stating the qualifications and recommending one of its members
for an elective office in the Grand Lodge and the mailing of said resolution to the Subordinate Lodge and Masons in Kentucky shall not be considered as a violation of that part of the constitution which prohibits
electioneering."
We leave it to our readers to judge how close this comes to being
a case of destroying a clause in the constitution by the process of interpreting it to mean what it was not originally intended that it should mean.
Texas (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): One of the Decisions of
Grand Master (of Connecticut) in effect holds to the doctrine that a
member of a constituent Lodge may be assessed by Grand Lodge for
such purposes as the George Washington Memorial, etc. In this Connecticut is not alone, still we are of the opinion that such a doctrine is
error. Grand Lodge may unquestionably fix her budget and provide
by the · levy of necessary .tax or assessment <IS against her constituent
Lodges to meet the demands of her purely Masonic engagements, but

50

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

we maintain that members of Lodges should not be subjected to direct
assessments in excess of amounts provided for in the By-Laws of their
respective Lodges. If such assessments are authorized for the one purpose and for any additional sum or sums, we would ask where is the
limit to be found? If answer is made, "In the wisdom, discretion and
justice of Grand Lodge," we readily agree that hardships and injustice
may rarely be encountered, and yet we would rather depend upon
the quickened consciences of the individual Brother.
West Australia (1928):
( Chair11u111 Correspondence Committee) : Another matter receiving
favorable consideration in New York was the consolidation of the work
of a number of committees into the hands of one body called the Board
of General Activities. Of course, in most British countries the body
which discharges similar functions, and many others besides, is called
the Board of General Purposes, to which Masonic conservatism inclines
the writer, even at the risk of hearing it styled, as a Los Angeles (Cal.)
paper did at the time of Sir Alfred Robbins' impending visit, "Board of
General Purchases."
GRAND MASTER
As the Grand Master is "a law unto himself" so do the results of
his administration reflect his individuality and ability. In a number
of cases there is an inclination on the part of Grand Masters not to
use their prerogative of granting Dispensations, and this cannot help
but have a beneficial result.
From an abstract point of view we fail to see why the Grand
Lodge should pass laws, establish uniform codes, etc., and then give
a Grand Master authority to set them aside. Sometimes Dispensations are necessary and advisable, but often they are requested as a
means to avoid trouble or save time.
British Columbia (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : It does not seem necessary that because a Grand Master is given certain powers he is compelled
to use them. A man owning a high-powered motor car does not feel
obliged to travel at seventy-five miles an hour simply because his car
can do it. Grand Masters to whom such power is given should remember that all things may be lawful, but all things are not expedient and
should cultivate the quality of self-restraint.
Some time ago a Grand Lodge was called to refreshment to allow
the wife of the Grand Master to come in and kiss her husband, and

Being about to retire from the Chair the Grand Master put in a
good word for his successor in the matter of expenses. The Grand
Master of Kentucky receives no salary, but is allowed one thousand
dollars for expenses. The Grand Master felt that this is not enough,
as· "No man with any business of his own. can be faithful to his duties
as Grand Master except at heavy loss to his own private business
affairs." The tendency in the United States for some years has been
to make the <Srand Master a sort of chief clerk, and he is called upon
to attend 'to a lot of work that could, and should, be done in the Grand
Secretary's office. In our opinion no one should ac~ept the office of
Grand Master who has not the time and money to enable him to properly
discharge the duties attached · to it.

Manitoba (1928):
(Chairman Corresponde11ce Committee) : The Grand Master of
Arkansas had the usual diatribe with reference to what he considered
unnecessary correspondence concerning law interpretations. Until such ·
a time as we can create or develop a superman who is able to write
laws which cannot be misconstrued I imagine Grand Masters and Grand
Secretaries will have to stagger along with pen in hand and a typewriter
on the desk. A couple of years ago our Constitution was amended,
making it absolutely imperative that Lodge dues must be paid yearly
and in advance. That all looks simple enough on the face of it, but
questions like this will loom up. If a Brother on January 1 pays one
year in advance and in May or June applies for and is granted his demit
is he entitled to a refund of the moneys paid covering the year. When
a Brother makes application for affiliation should such form be accompanied by a year's dues to be placed to his credit if accepted for membership. With honors and responsibilities comes work, and while the
"law shark" sometimes seems an infernal nuisance, yet occasionally he
might be termed both a useful and necessary evil.
So many Jurisprudence Committees in United States Jurisdictions
seem to consider that it is their duty, not to mention pleasure, to rip
the Grand Master's decisions "fore and aft" that a report such as presented in this instance is notable: "We recommend that his decisions be
in all things approved."
The powers and prerogatives of a Grand Master constitute a very
debatable question. Tradition ascribes .unbounded power. Constitutions
and Masonic customs limit. Language is a wonderful vehicle for transmitting thought, but does not always convey the meaning. Some Con-

Montana (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): On a motion of the
Grand Secretary a resolution was adopted by the Grand Lodge of
Arkansas expressive of admiration and appreciation for the wife of the
Grand Master for the manner in which she aided him in the performance of his duties as Grand Master during his administration.
While this was a nice act and no doubt a great heart prompted it,
we doubt very much the wisdom thereof, either as a precedent or otherwise. The wife of each Grand Master is, or should be, proud of the
honor conferred on her husband and should be ready to go the limit of
usefulness in his behalf during his term of office; his father and mother
if living, and his children, his sisters and brothers, uncles and aunts,
are happy over the honor and doubtless do all they can to make it
worthy; but to start in thanking them or any of them for it is beyond
the needs of the occasion.
New Hampshire (1929):
(Chairman Correspondenc(! Committee): To us it has ever been
surprising to find so many decisions reported. It would seem, even
after some thought upon the subject, that by this time Masonic law
ought to be pretty well established. But here is a new one in Colorado.
The Grand Master decided that it was the right of a Master to
exclude from casting a ballot, and from the room if necessary, a member
who had been judicially decreed to be mentally unsound and for whom
the court had appointed a guardian.

. HOMES
Financial problems incident to the maintenance of Masonic
Homes is an acute one in some Jurisdictions. There are two schools
of thought-one that relief can best be administered through .institutional means and the second by direct aid to the party entitled to
help. Of c~urse those Jurisdictions that have Homes will never
abandon them, but the opinion is growing that greater good can be
accomplished through the Iowa or English methods.
We call especial attention to the very able report of the Colorado
Committee with the statistics compiled by them.
Colorado (1928):

(Committee on Robt. Russell Foundation): 1n keeping with the
spirit of the discussions on the report of the Committee one year ago,
the Committee this year has made an extended study of Homes and
Orphanages.
Early in its work, the Committee felt it was necessary t? obtain
information concerning the Masonic Homes and Orphanages, m other
Jurisdictions. A rather careful survey was, therefore, made ~f these
institutions to obtain amount of investments, costs of operation, the
number of aged and orphan in such homes, cost of operation per gue~t
and number of guests in these homes per thousand members. From this
survey it is found there are twenty-one Grand Lodges maintaining
homes for both the aged and orphans. There were 5,689 guests in these
homes being an average of 2.65 guests per thousand members. The
avera~e value of the home property per guest is $3,132.00. The cost
of maintenance per guest averages $416.00.

be decided upon. The petitioner should appear personally and be
subjected to a searching investigation along lines prescribed by the
Grand Lodge, together with such other inquiries as the Committee
might wish to make.
There is also a heavy responsibility resting upon the members of
a Lodge who recommend an Applicant. These Brethren should also
be required to appear personally and furnish their · reasons for
approval of the Applicant.
It is no argument to say that if a Lodge wants to adopt such a
plan it is within their province. To accomplish the greatest good for
the Fraternity it should be made mandatory on every Lodge, and
where this system has been adopted it has produced beneficial results.
The investigation by the Lodge committee should be supplemented and in addition to the first one. There are often cases where
there might be an objection to an individual becoming a member of
a particular Lodge that would not warrant his rejection by it. Such
a preliminary investigation would allow. him to withdraw his application without being subjected to the formality of a ballot. It is no
excuse to claim that if Lodges want members they will take in
undesirable men, regardless of any safe-guards that might be established. . Such instances are perhaps infrequent.
Investigation through every possible method required by positive
regulation will accomplish more than where they are voluntarily
established by individual Lodges.

Alabama (1928):
(Grand Master) : There shall be a standing committee on information to consist of seven members, appointed by the Worshipful Master,
in such manner that the terms of two shall expire the first year, two the
second year and three the third year. This committee shall have a
chairman and a secretary to be designated by the Worshipful Master,
It shall be the duty of the committee to obtain information from all
applicants for the degrees or for affiliation, and from their recommenders
avouchers and references touching their character and fitness, and t~
furnish this information to the committee of investigation.
The information obtained by this committee is to be given to the
regular investigating committee of three, who may use or reject it.

Canada (1928):
(Grand Master) : The employment of questionnaires may serve
a useful purpose, but I should like to sound a note of warning. When
you accept a candidate for admission to your Lodge, you accept him
with the intention of making him one of yourselves, and no system
of questions, however skilfully devised, can take the place of a report
that is based upon personal knowledge and personal investigation. The
time when you rely upon a system is the time when it is most likely
to prove a broken reed.
West Australia (1928):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Worshipful Masters who
imagine that the occupant of the Chair is the radial point of activity,
will not find Brother Charteris (Grand Master of Montana 1927) on
their side. To him the most important person in a Masonic Lodge is
the Brother on the Investigating Committee. The one question that
committee should ask itself is, "If we admit this person, will he attract.
other good men to us, or will he repel the good and attract those of
the undesirable strata?" Until a committeeman is able to answer this
question he is not ready to report. There is considerable common sense
in this view of Brother Charteris'. However, with us, as with most
Empire Jurisdictions which base thei~ laws and customs on those of the
Mother Grand Lodge, this importance of the committeeman in no way
detracts from the importance of the Worshipful Master, whose prerogative it is to appoint committees, and to exercise his own discretion therein.
JEWELRY
The following extracts express the two views in connection with
the wearing of Masonic jewelry, promiscuously and otherwise. In
the United States perhaps it is a question of personal taste, while
in England and other Jurisdictions it is a matter of custom. Possibly
the result of carrying a custom to extremes will do more to discourage the display of Masonic "hard-ware" than argument.
North Carolina (1929):
( Chairma11 C orrespo11dence Committee) : 'l'he reviewer of West
Australia discusses our views concerning the public wearing of Masonic

59

HEPORT ON CORRESPONDE.I'fCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

jewelry at considerable . length. He seems to have discovered quite
accurately, too, what our views are. Lest we shall not make the matter
clear to the present reader, we remark that Masons in Great Britain
and in Australia are not. permitted to wear Masonic jewelry in public.
In America, this practice is not forbidden, and in every jewelry catalogue
or jewelry store one finds these articles. We do not like the thought
of a Mason's overloading himself with any sort of jewelry; nor do we
relish the thought that some Masons have a stock of Masonic jewelry
which in extent and value is far out of proportion to both their knowledge
of Masonry and their worth to_ the .Institution.
But after all, these do not represent true American Masonry. The
real, representative American Mason is neither ostentatious of his jewelry
nor ignorant of his Masonry, nor yet is he worthless to the Fraternity.
He is a Mason because he wants to be ; he is a Mason in spite of the
fact that a dozen or more other organizations claim his efforts and his
evenings. Many good Masons scarcely have a single evening free at
home in a fortnight. They have social clubs, service clubs, professional
organizations, business organizations, and civic duties of swidry sorts.
And in spite ~f these, Masonry survives; yes, and there are not lacking
good men to shape its destinies. On the continent of North America
there are nearly four million Masons. In the possession of each of these
there is one or more Masonic emblems. He travels. In Pullman cars,
in hotels, in other public places, these men feel free to converse with each
other, and .they do so. We have seen these scenes time after time; and
we have also observed similar groups of Englishmen, who remained
silent and aloof in just the same circumstances. The Englishman's
attitude. in these public and accidental contacts is just as characteristic
of him as is the opposed attitude of his American cousin in similar circumstances. The attitude of the English Mason toward Masonic jewelry
in public is just as much a part of him as the other; and the attitude of
the American toward Masonic jewelry_ is psychologically related to his
attitude toward a half dozen men, perfect strangers, in a Pullman smoker,
with whom he forthwith proceeds to make the passing of time in transit
tolerable by the usual American practice.
Americans wear much less regalia than the English Masons, in
the tyled Lodge; they wear jewelry when and as they please in public.
English Masons wear much more regalia in their Lodges, and leave it
all off in public. We have no desire to complain at the practice prevailing
in England, though it is the accepted practice of fewer than a half million
Masons altogether, perhaps; and we feel quite sure that our Brethren
in Great Britain, the Australian Grand Lodges and elsewhere will not
complain that the Masons of North America, to the number of three and
a half million and more, follow the impulse of their own Masonic

psychology, even though that does seem to include a button on the coat
or a device oh the watch chain. It is our way of letting ourselves, and
others, know that we feel a pride in Masonry. Is it a sin to do this?

West A ustralia (1928):
(Chairmati Correspondence Committee ): Brother J. Edward Allen
is again the reviewer of Foreign Correspondence, and in his review of
the Proceedings of seventy-nine sister Grand Lodges, furnishes a document not only worthy. of his reputation as a scholar, critic and Masonic
student but containing nearly three hundred pages of deeply interesting
matter.' And it is none the less interesting for the light it throws upon
what is done in North Carolina, where, it would seem, without sacrifice
of Masonic usages, customs and principles, Masonry is made to adapt
itself to the conditions of the country. Brother Allen was somewhat
handicapped by a necessity for cutting down the space usually allotted
to his reviews, but the latter in no wise suffer for it. In his review
of Western Australia for 1925-26, he notices certain observations of
mine opposed to the personal use of Masonic jewelry outdoors, and his
reply suggests that he views the position from a different angle. My
view is that ( 1) the wearing of a Masonic emblem is no sure indication
of Masonic membership. Such emblems are purchasable at all American
jewelry stores by Masons and non-Masons alike; as a matter of business,
a jeweler I met in Los Angeles, who was a Roman Catholic, sold them.
Thus, they are unnecessary as an indication of membership. (2) As
articles of personal adornment they should possess no value for the man
of good taste; it is considered "bad form" in a man to wear jewelry
other than a ring and a scarf-pin. (3) It smacks of advertising one's
membership, and Masonry, being a · secret organization existing for
Masonic purposes only, there is not and should not be any need for such
publicity, either for prideful or some politic reason. It is quite true
that practically throughout the British Empire the practice is prohibited
by our Grand Lodges; it is equally true that in the United States, with
a larger Masonic population, it is not prohibited, although it is no more
general than is the custom of wearing regalia in public processions, or
attendance at Divine worship, which is prohibited in some Jurisdictions.
It is no less true that a few years ago, the then Grand Master of
Arkansas referred in scathing terms to the same practice, and although
he did not actually condemn it, he said he felt that a person who joined
every branch of the Institution merely to wear jewelry was not benefiting
himself. Unfortunately, undue importance is attached by some Masons
to this practice. I myself have seen Shriners in an American State
who "had 'em all on," bar the apron-wearing the jewelry of Blue and
Red Masonry and the so-called "higher degrees," besides the Shrine

jewels, in a procession. My Brother asks me: "Will he be a good
sport and let the decision of the great majority stand, remembering that
we are as close to the fountain-head as he is, even though that fountainhead happens to have adopted his view about the matter since we began
our separate existence?" I fancy my good Brother would have an
unenviable task in attempting to prove that in the earlier days of
Masonry either in England or the United States the practice of wearing
Masonic jewelry existed. Indeed, Masons of old standing in America
have assured me that the practice is comparatively modern-not more
than three generations old, if so long. N.o r is it a· matter of my being
"a good sport" ; it is one of Masonic conformity to Masonic rule, as
that rule has come down to us.

limited. In what I shall say on this topic I do not want any Secretary
who has done his best to think that I am criticising him personally. My
criticism _is on the Lodge rather than on the man. Brethren, let me
insist that when you elect officers next year you take pains to elect a man
for the office of Secretary who is competent to fill it. All men serving
you now may be good men, I do not question their goodness or their
integrity, but some of them are not good Secretaries. They cannot
write well enough to keep good records of the business transacted by
the Lodges, they cannot compose a letter, they cannot spell, they know
very little about the correct use of the English language. When I heard
a former Grand Master pass some criticisms on Secretaries who were
not competent, I wondered if he were not a little severe. I know now
why he made those criticisms. Please think of these statements when
you hold your next election. All this may seem harsh to some of you,
but I assure you that I do not mean it that way. The office work of the
Grand Master would be reduced fully one half if all of the Lodges had
competent Secretaries. Many Lodges have excellent Secretaries. It is a
pleasure to communicate with them. The office of Secretary is second
in importance 'to none in the Lodge.

Wisconsin (1929):
(Chairman Corresponaence Committee): A modest Masonic button
worn on the lapel of one's coat is one thing, but such a sign to attract
business is quite another, just as the hoisting of an American flag over
a school house is an entirely different act than to use one to decorate a
garbage cart.
LODGE SECRETARIES
Experience has demonstrated that generally the efficiency and
standing of a Lodge depends upon the Secretary. His zeal, ability
and Masonic knowledge are naturally reflected in its activities,
because he usually occupies the office continuously. Of course he
may become "atrophied," the only remedy for which would be the
selection of a capable successor.
In 1926 the Grand Master of Nebraska made a recommendation
to provide for the attendance at Grand Lodge of the Secretaries of
local Lodges, with an allowance for mileage and per diem. It was
not adopted.
The Grand Lodge of Oregon last year had submitted to them a
law to replace the Junior Warden with the Secretary as a member
of the Grand Lodge. Under their procedure it was to be considered
at the 1929 session. Their proceedings have not been received so we
are unable to state whether it became a law or not. The proposition
has some strong arguments in its favor, although strictly speaking it
might be a violation of the "landmark" that every Lodge is entitled
to be represented in Grand Lodge by its Master and the Warden.
Alabama (1928):

(Grand Master): I would not be unkind, knowingly or intentionally, to any man, especial.ly to one whose educational advantages were very

Idaho (1928):
(Grand Secretary) : But length of service is not the only standard
of measurement, and many others, though having served shorter terms,
are entitled to honorable mention. The office of Secretary is exceedingly
important. It is a high type of service, and happy is the Worshipful
Master who is fortunate enough to have a loyal and capable Secretary
on whom he may rely for assistance. It would seem that in the Masonic
scheme of titles and honors there should be one to bestow on a Secretary
who has served his Lodge long and well. A member serves a year as
Master and whether it be well done or otherwise he retires with the title ·
of Past Master as a recommendation to Masonic favor as long as he
lives. But one may serve as Secretary one year to twenty years, and
when he retires he carries with him no recognition of services, or reward,
except the consciousness of duty well done.
It is a serious mistake to elect a Secretary from among the new
members. The Secretary, like the Master, should be a Mason of experience. A few Lodges have elected Secretaries who have been Masons
but a few months, and almost invariably they have had to regret it later.
A very few Lodges are using the office of Secretary as the beginning step
in a line of promotion that is expected to lead to the Master's chair.
This also is a mistaken idea. There may be something said in its favor,
but the preponderance of argume~t is against it. The office is too important to be made simply a period of preparation for higher stations.
To attempt to train a Secretary every year is too costly an experiment.

Kentucky (1929):
(Grand Secretary) .: I am confident that the carrying of the blanket
bond on the Secretaries and Treasurers of our Lodges has resulted in
much good. Many losses have occurred and although the bonding companies have raised their premium 25 per cent I recommend that this bond
be continued.

mend that Sections 5 and 106 be amended to provide that each constituent
Lodge shall be represented in Grand Lodge by its Master, Senior Warden
and Secretary. That the Master and Secretary be paid their actual
traveling expenses, provided that if the Secretary can not come in person,
that he may give his proxy to another, but that the holder of such
proxy shall not be entitled to receive any expense money.

Montana (1928):
(Chairman Correspondmce Committee): We thoroughly agree with
one of the reviewer's ideas to the effect that in many Lodges Secretaries
of long standing become petty tyrants of the Lodges ; they want to
dictate everything ; frequently will delay and not carry out orders which
seem to be against their wishes; are in a hurry to get through with the
work as speedily as possible ; seem to forget that they are only
paid officers of the Lodge and not dictators. As against these it
is refreshing to note occasionally Secretaries who are obliging and
painstaking; unobtrusive in their views and cheerfully bowing to the
will of the Lodge; such Secretaries are jewels and command the love
and affection of the Brethren; we happen to know both kinds, and the
latter appeal to us as the real men and Masons.

Victoria (1928):
(Grand Secretary) : During the past year the work effected by the
Secretaries of Subordinate Lodges has been most gratifying and encouraging, and I have suggested to the Board of General Purposes that
a second conference of Secretaries be held in September, 1928. The
first conference was held in 1923, when 230 Secretaries attended, out
of a total number of 320 Lodges. As a result of that conference much
improvement has been made in connection with the carrying out of
the Constitutions, and the adoption of uniform systems in connection
with the admission of candidates, and the keeping of Lodge accounts.

Oregon (1928):
(Grand Master): Experience has taught us that the Secretary of
a Lodge is usually a very efficient and faithful Brother, and that it is
common practice to re-elect him year after year as long as he will accept
the position. His duties are legion, and it is to him that the Brethren
are accustomed to go for information concerning the affairs of their own ·
Lodge and the Grand Lodge. Not only is he required to keep the records
of his Lodge, but he must be familiar with the provisions of the code in
order to properly perform the duties of his office. Any changes in the
substantive law or in the rules of procedure are of vital interest to all,
but it is frequently left to the Secretary to see that the Lodge is made
acquainted with such change.
By reason of his intimate knowledge of all of the details incident
to the business of his Lodge, and the fact that he is at all times in close
touch with the office of the Grand Secretary, he is perhaps better qualified
than any other member to represent his Lodge in Grand Lodge and to
:vote intelligently on the various. questions that come before us for consideration and determination.
As at present the organized membership of the Grand Lodge includes
the Master and Wardens of all constituent Lodges. I believe that the
Secretary of each Lodge in the Jurisdiction should be a member of the
Grand Lodge and should have his expenses paid. To allow each Lodge
four representatites, would, in my opinion, be unwise. I therefore recom-

MEMBERSHIP
The decrease in membership generally, not only in the !l)'lllbolic
Lodge but also in coordinate Masonic Bodies, is a sign of the time.
Some claim it is a post-war condition, others a laxity on the part of
Secretaries in collecting dues which results in a large number of
suspensions, and others that Fraternal organizations under the

Illinois (1928): .
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : A review of the proceedings of the several Grand Lodges shows that in not a few instances there
has been a loss in membership for the past year. The net gains have been
reduced to a very great degree from what they have been previously.
One of the large Jurisdictions in the United States shows a net loss for
the year of sixty-two. Another Grand Jurisdiction has its net gain
reduced to just one-fourth of what it was two or three years ago. All
this goes to show that men are not flocking into the Masonic Fraternity
as they once did and it also shows that the Fraternity is not only losing
large numbers by suspension but by death as well. It must be expected
that the death rate will continue to increase because many in the
Fraternity are advancing in years and must ultimately pay the last debt.
There is nothing alarming in this falling off in Lodge members. In
some respects it may be looked upon as rather a good omen. It should
indicate that the Fraternity was commencing to stabilize and that as
soon as it can pass through the period of adjustment in the matter of
suspensions it will reach a point when the net gain per year will attain
normalcy. In times past there has been entirely too much stress placed
upon numbers. We have been brought to estimate the value of the
Fraternity by its net gains in membership, overlooking the fact that
the real growth of the Fraternity lies in the development and expansion
of the principles for which it stands. A little education is needed along
this particular line in order to impress Masons with the real value and
worth of the Fraternity, which is inherent.
In a good many quarters the marked decline in petitions is a matter
of comment. No little inquiry has arisen as to the cause. It can be
traced directly to changes in our method of living and the fact that men
are seeking other pursuits for their personal satisfaction. The chief
cause for diversion of Masonic interests is chargeable by a great many to
the automobile. A large percentage of cars sold are bought on the ·
deferred payment plan. The result of it is that many families find
themselves burdened not only with the monthly payments on their purchase but likewise heavy upkeep. By the time they pay the family expenses and keep the car going ·they have exhausted their income. Financiers agree that people are heavily in debt for radios, ice machines,
electric washers, and what not, all of which have ·been bought on the
installment plan. As a result the average man has a place for every
dollar of his income. As a consequence he has very little money for
investment in Masonic degrees. It will be quite a period before an
adjustment can be made and things reduced to a normal condition. It
cannot be doubted that men are seeking other means of fellowship. It
used to be the Lodge was a favorite diversion of many, particularly in

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

65

the small town. The Lodge meeting was looked forward to with great
anticipation because it afforded an outlet for the desire of fellowship.
But all this has been changed. Nowadays we have the country club
and the city club, the golf club, the theater, and the moving picture, to
say nothing of the automobile, all of which make a direct appeal to man's
desire for pleasure and recreation. Freemasonry has strong competition
in this day and age of the world and it can only meet that competition
by making its Lodge meetings attractive and pleasant so that men will
be drawn toward the Masonic altar to find there something that they
cannot gain elsewhere.
This is well worth thinking about. Installment buying and the
abundance of entertainment and diversion are assigned as a major
cause of the decline in· the volume of work.
