of the Craft. The const ituent Lodges are charged with the more essential

trombone, while serviceable elsewhere, are not for us.

faction. The Lodges realize at last that the admission of undesirable

everybody in our ranks in order to be able to carry on the good work. We
want not followers but leaders, not crowds but guides. To make our
work more thorough and lasting, we must accept under our banners
only the very best, leaving the rest of humanity to receive the benefits
of our activities and profit by the lessons of our conduct and actions,
because we work for others and not for ourselves.

No attempt is made by him to answer these interrogations and we
feel somewhat disappointed, as we have frequently asked ourselves
these questions and have been baffled in an attempt to answer them.
Permit your scribe to offer one suggestion for considerat ion: Perhaps
it is merely human nature. Nearly every human being is possessed
with a large bump of curiosity, and Freemasonry appeals to this phase
of their being just as the riddle of the Sphinx in Egypt does, or the
Mona Lisa smile in the famous painting. They join our Fraternity
because they have an irrepressible curiosity to know just what it is all
about, and they find they cannot satisfy that curiosity in any other way
than by joining the Masons. When their curiosity has been satisfied
they become lukewarm in the pursuit of knowledge and seek other means
to gratify their desires. Many a marriage has been contracted from no
other motive, simply to find out how it seems. When the novelty wears
off the divorce court settles the matter. In Freemasonry they simply
drop out.
GEORGE WASHINGTON MEMORIAL
The views expressed by the Chairman of the Correspondence
Committee of British Columbia and Manitoba present the condition
surrounding the George Washington Memorial MINUS patriotism,
local interest and enthusiasm.
We have not changed our opinion from that expressed in our
Report nine years ago to the effect that a great National university,
founded on the lines set forth by Washington himself, would be a
bigger and better monument to him than the one in question.
We cannot subscribe either to the viewpoint that any Jurisdiction
that did not formally become a member of the Association by joining
in the Articles establishing it; and has not met the advancing financial
demands made by an Association of which they are not members,
should be branded as slackers in any way, Masonic or otherwise.

illustrations happen at the present time to be very much to the fore in
Grand Lodges of the United States, they are only used to point the moral
and not based upon any imaginary line creating a difference between that
country and ours. The thought a t issue is this: Is there a Masonic
principle involved? Will it spread to our Grand Lodge and is it right
or wrong? Take for instance the George Washington National Memorial. As one writer expresses it, "Alexandria Lodge conceived the
thought and then sold the idea to the whole United States."
Urged by patriotism and lashed by local pride the original construction
costs have been gradually raised fr om an estimated one hu~dred thousand
dollars to over five million dollars, and the building is not even yet
completed.

discussed, which is even more worthy, and that is the proposal for
hospitalization for all tubercular Masons in the United States.
We are glad to hear that common sense is being spoken about this
great venture, for unless someone does speak out, we will soon be
swamped by further philanthropic proposals.
PAST GRAND MASTERS
In some Jurisdictions there is an opinion that Grand Lodge is
governed entirely by the Past Grand Masters. In some instances
perhaps this may be justified. Past Grand Masters who have served
well and faithfully are entitled to all the honors that may bt accorded
them.
Attaining this rank must necessarily be a source of pride and
satisfaction to one who has filled the high office, but perhaps not all
who have been honored feel or believe that they should sink into
oblivion.

72

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

About the only remedy for this condition would be to have
practically a hereditary Grand Master, as in England, or one elected
continuously, as is the practice in Maryland.
Illinois (1928):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): It is often said that a
chosen few run the Grand Lodge and in most instances this is true.
Much of the work of all our Grand Bodies is done in committees. The
committees come before the Grand Body and report and the Brethren
vote yea. Unfortunately, many who serve on Grand Lodge committees
are men who have served their time in the work of the Fraternity and
are in reality on the retired list, and others who because of personal
influence and political pull, seek appointment on committees in order to
get their railroad expenses paid to the city where the Grand Lodge
holds its sessions. As a result many of our Grand Lodge committees
are not made up of men who are active in the work and who are
thoroughly acquainted with the demands of this modern age. As a
result they report different matters according to their own notions, and
the Brethren vote yea and then go home and criticise the Grand Lodge
for the action taken. It is refreshing to notice that in one Grand Jurisdiction this year that a certain number of Lodges asked for the passing
of legislation which they seemed to think would be a benefit to them.
It was as usual referred to a committee. The committee reported
adversely and the representatives voted down the committee's report by
. an overwhelming vote, and passed the legislation which they so much
desired. If representatives only knew it they hold the balance of power.
If the platform rules the Grand Lodge it is generally because representatives haven't backbone enough to stand up for the things which they
believe to be right.

POLITICS
Peace and harmony among the Fraternity can only be secured
by strictly adhering to the doctrine of the Founders, that politics
and religion have no place in the Masonic Institution. Both of these
subjects are part of our earthly existence and, as has •been truly
stated, when you attempt to say to three million men that they shall
not concern themselves with either, you are undertaking a big
contract. In making this statement we interpret the word " politics"
not in its broader aspect but as partisanship. Until perfection is

Mississippi (1929):
(Grand Master): It has come to the attention of the Grand Master
that perhaps the harmony of some Lodges is being disturbed by political
communications or discussions in open Lodges.
It is unmasonic for any political communication, any circular, or
paper which refers directly or indirectly to politics, political party, or
any candidate for office, to be read in open Lodge. It is likewise unmasonic for any political discussion to take place in open Lodge, or for
any Lodge to pass any resolution touching political views or candidates.
It is therefore ordered by the Grand Master that no political paper,
letter, or communication be read in open Lodge, that no political discussion of any kind take place in open Lodge, and that no Lodge pass or
promulgate any resolution political in its nature.

* * * * *
(Grand Master): Thirty-eight years ago the then Grand Master,
and now our venerable and beloved Senior Past Grand Master, M. W.
John W. Vrooman, in his Annual Message said:
"Many years ago our Craft was not only wickedly persecuted in
this State, but socially and politically ostracized; and the principal
excuse of our persecutors was that Freemasons were using the Fraternity
for political gain or preferment. Our Brethren submitted to this cruel
and unjust persecution without a murmur, and their prudence and
fortitude challenged the admiration and secured the sympathy of the.
people.
"We must maintain our standing by demonstrating to all mankind
that our aims are confined to moral, charitable, and religious problems,
and hence we must live above and beyond suspicion of self-interest. The
moment we seek to divert Fraternal devotion into political channels, that
moment we bring ourselves into disrepute and become the object of
just criticism."
·since then other Grand Masters from time to time have sounded
a similar warning. Only three years ago M. W. William A. Rowan,
. Grand Master, said in his Annual Address:
"The large membership of the Craft, with its constantly increasing
numbers, opens a large field fo r political venture. For this there should
be permitted no opening wedge. Masons as citizens in politics, yes;
the Institution of Masons in politics, never I"
Notwithstanding these admonitions there seems to be an almost
irrepressible impulse to drag the Fraternity into partisan politics from
time to time. This was manifested during the political campaigns of
last year. Letters were sent out by various members of our Fraternity
making appeals to our members to support particular candidates for
office at the November elections. In some of these the Masonic character
of the appeal was vague, and left more or less to inference from the
language used. In others, it was direct and unequivocal. One of the
most ·flagrant of these was a letter sent out by the Secretary of one of
our Lodges over his official signature, and with the title of Worshipful
prefixed to his name, indicating his previous position as Master of the
Lodge; This letter called attention to the candidacy of a member of the
Fraternity for a high office and contained among other matters these
sentences:

76

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

"This is an opportune time to show our sincere appreciation and
friendship for our good friend and Brother, and prove to him that work
in the Quarries of Masonry brings results.
"Might I therefore suggest that you address the Brethren o r write
them and make sure we roll up a vote for our Brother and friend ...
of which we may justly be proud?"
This letter was brought to my attention just before the election, and
I promptly suspended the Secretary from his office.
Subsequent investigation satisfied me that this particular Brother
had acted upon the advice of other Brethren in sending out this letter,
and that he was not fully aware of the nature of his unmasonic conduct
in so doing. Those who advised him knew, or should have known, the
nature of his offense. I felt therefore, that to prefer charges against
the Secretary and let those even more guilty go free of censure or
punishment, would be unfair. Accordingly, I restored the Brother to
his office after the election with a reprimand and admonition against
future like conduct.
That the Fraternity is not to be used for political purposes is a law
so well established by custom, edicts and admonitions as to give it
practically the force of a Landmark. Evidence of this was presented
in the fact that complaints to the Grand Master from the rank and .file
of our membership were frequent, complaining of the political activities to
which I have referred.
The importance of the subject needs no emphasis. For our Fraternity
to indulge in political controversies, would be to sound its own death
knell. The only way to prevent this is to suppress every attempt to
use the Fraternity for political purposes. If we disregard a minor attempt
to introduce politics into the Fraternity, we encourage a greater attempt
of the same kind. Thus step by step, we shall find ourselves enmeshed
in political affairs, and our Fraternity at the end of its usefulness.
Philippine Islands (1928):
(Grand Master): "If you are willing to have strife and discord in
your Lodge; if you desire to see its charter taken away and its name
blotted out on the rolls of our Grand Lodge, all you have to do is to
introduce politics into the Lodge. Like a corrosive acid, discussions on
such subjects make bitter feelings and enmities, contrary to the teachings
of .our Institution, and tend to destroy the Masonic fabric built on peace,
umty and brotherly love, by creating confusion, hatred and spite among
the Brethren. If Masonry is to endure in these Islands or anywhere,
it should and must avoid political discussions of any nature whatsoever."

PROHIBITION
As the discussion of this matter is constantly before us, so
does it find a place in the Proceedings of some of the different
Jurisdictions.
As Masons we are enjoined to obey the moral and civil law,
which is the position that the Craft must assume towards the 18th
Amendment, and the laws passed in connection therewith.
Arkansas (1928):
(Grand M aster) : It has repeatedly come within the personal observation of your Grand Master that an increasing number of members of
organizations whose prerequisite for membership therein is based upon
a membership in the Masonic Fraternity, are prostituting meetings or
gatherings of these organizations into orgies of gambling, drunkenness
and debauchery.
When such gatherings of members of the Masonic Fraternity degenerate into clownishness and buffoonery, the great Fraternity of Freemasonry must necessarily bear the brunt of just criticism, no matter
under what name or guise they may be assembled.
"A Mason is obliged by his tenure to obey the Moral Law" and
therefore membership in no fraternity or organization can give him
license to appear anywhere in a drunken condition, with or without the
insignia of that other order to which he may belong.
It is therefore ordered that hereafter any Mason under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas who shall, while under the
influence of intoxicants, so disport himself as to bring just criticism upon
the Fraternity by reason of such intoxication shall, upon presentation
to his respective Lodge of due proof thereof, be by his Lodge indefinitely
suspended; and· any Lodge failing or refusing to take immediate, proper
action against such offending member shall immediately forfeit its charter.

Quebec (1929):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We agree with him in
his attitude toward the Eighteenth Amendment. But we do not anticipate any ready acquiescence to its enforcement on the part of all Masons.
Masons in their Lodges have learned a love of liberty and a hatred of
oppression. The fact that this oppression is under the guise of law
does not make it more attractive. Nor even if it is for the best of all
the people, do liberty-loving persons care to be told what they shall eat
or drink by a paternalistic government. In America since the davs of
the Boston Tea Party, Masons have been against such oppressive methods.
They have even rebelled against law, iniquitous or not, more than once.
If people obey the law supinely, how shall our lawmakers know the
people's will? "Nullification" is no new word in American history.

RITUAL
The time. is approaching when the Ritual of the Fraternity
should be abridged to keep step with present day conditions. Some
one ventured the criticism that we make too great a fetish of our
past, of our ancient constitutions, of ways and customs better suited
to the need of operative Masons of five hundred years ago than to
the civilization of our twentieth century. We have been too much
interested in the fading beauties of the sunsets of a departing age to
appreciate the glorious dawn of a new day that calls to us.
That ritualism as such does not appeal to the Lodge member of
today is. clearly shown by the l~ck of attendance and the tendency
of .the .Blue Lodge to become a mere degree mill. On this particular
pomt 1t ma~ be as Mark Twain said about the weather, "everyone
talks about 1t but no one does anythini"."
In too many instances perfection in rendition of language and
floor work has become the ambitio'n of the average Master and Lodge
Officers.

Grand Master Dunkum of the District of Columbia is of the
opinion that the existing limitation might be changed "without detriment to the orderly manner of conferring the degrees and that the
number of candidates to receive a degree at one time might be increased
to seven."
We cannot see how the increase would in any way be detrimental
to the "orderly manner of conferring the degrees." Laws of many
Grand Jurisdictions which prescribe the maximum number of candidates
also allow dispensations for an excess number. As Grand Master, we
have issued such dispensations for good and sufficient reasons and there
has been no detriment to the ceremony of the degrees. To our mind, a
law is not much of a law, if it can be nullified by the power of dispensation. Then, too, Freemasonry, where it can, must adapt itself to
the changing times. After all, the degrees are only "the cloth that
cloaks the clay."

The Grand Master of the District of Columbia expressed the belief
that the number of candidates receiving the degrees at one time might
well be increased. Prior to 1903 maxima of five for the E. A., the
same for the F. C., and three for the M. M. degrees were constitutional,
but that year five for all degrees was prescribed as the maximum. The
Grand Master favored increasing· the maximum to seven. An amendment to this effect was presented, but was laid over till the May (1928)
Communication. The United States is a country of "big" Lodges, and
it naturally follows that at times there is almost a plethora of candidates
for degrees. In such circumstances, it is not surprising that our Brethren
consider it necessary to make special provision for not keeping their
candidates waiting an unreasonable time. In most of the Jurisdictions,
too, they are faced with the difficulty that arises out of their adhesion to
the principle of exclusive jurisdiction of subordinate Lodges and their
aversion to dual or plural membership. All these matters enter into
consideration when candidature for degrees is under notice. British
Masons rarely experience these troubles, and most of us believe that
the comparatively small membership of our Lodges has a great deal
to do with our. freedom. Certainly we do not have the experience which
an American Worshipful Master mentioned to this writer a few years
ago: "We have sixty candidates waiting, and I am half through my
year of office," he said.
What may happen in a country which dramatizes its degree ceremonies was shown in the petition for reinstatement in Illinois after expulsion from membership. The petitioner while a candidate in the third degree
"resisted one of the workers by returning violence for violence." This
took place upwards of twenty years ago, a~d the Committee on Petitions
in recommending his restoration told Grand Lodge that it appeared "that
this man was as much sinned against as sinning, that he is now a respected
business man of his community, and that this occurred more than twenty
years ago, when the ceremonies of the second section of the third degree
were less dignified than now." This had weight, and Grand Lodge
sanctioned the erring one's reinstatement. But "less dignified!" What
must that section have been in 1905, when the event took place? This
writer has witnessed a big, hefty creature as "the worst of them all" in
that precious second section, and he will need more than "another think
coming" to discern any dignity at all in it. Moreover, protests against
over-dramatization continue to be heard in various quarters.
The evil genius who too often appears to dog the Masonic footsteps
in Oregon, turned his attention to the flag ceremony, necessitating the

RELIEF
Unfortunately there appears to be an idea not only among the
public, but also among a large number of members, that the Masonic
Fraternity is an Institution possessed of fabulous wealth and amply
able to take care of all and sundry who make application for aid.
Indeed in some cases this has been the thought in the mind of some
applicants. The establishment of elabor~te _Homes a?d ~he advertisement of activities in connection therewith 1s a contributing factor.
If it could forcibly be impressed upon an applicant that Relief is not
the chief activity of the Fraternity, it might remedy conditions.
A .strict investigation of the financial condition of every Applicant, the number of people depending upon him for support, whether
or not he carries life insurance, the possibility of him becoming a
charge through physical or financial· reasons, and higher initiation
fees and dues would undoubtedly minimize the calls made upon Grand
Lodges or individual Lodges for assistance.

Utah (1929):
(Cha frman Correspondence Committee) : Under "Relief" the Grand
Master of North Dakota made pretty strong statements concerning the
duty of the Lodge to look after its own, who are in need. And from
one point, this can hardly be over-emphasized. On the other hand, we
have the feeling that Masonic organizations are teaching their members,
and the idea is passed on to the profane, that Masonry is a sort of
insurance society, which will care for its members and their families,
regardless of any other consideration; that Lodges are in existence
primarily to care for the sick, and to bury the dead and to educate the
orph~s, and that they can be drawn on to any extent. That it is the
plain duty of Lodges to afford relief when necessary, there is, and can
be no question, but this is liable to abuse. We have known of instances
where Masons have assured their families that they have nothing to do,
but to draw on the Craft for whatever may be needed. We have in mind,
cases where expensive funerals were arranged for by the family and bills
sent to the Lodge without so much as consulting the Lodge in question.
One of our Lodges her; in the city received bills amounting to between
seven and eight hundred dollars for a funeral, and other Lodges have
been called on for excessive amounts on the understanding that Masonic
bodies obligate themselves to care for all such, and other expenses. We
do not so understand this matter. Our point is, that often the impression referred to, is due to unqualified statements by Grand Masters and
others, concerning this feature of Masonic work.
West Australia (1928):
(Chairman C orresponde1lce Committee) : Amongst other subjects
dealt with in the address of the Grand Master of Louisiana was the

be restricted to the afffuent, Brother Haller considered that care should

Washington (1928):
The Grand Lodge of California was fortunate in having a good
Grand Master to preside over its destinies at the convocation of 1927.
The picture of Grand Master George Louis Jones and a short sketch
of his life are the first things to attract our attention upon opening the
Proceedings of this Grand Lodge, and we naturally expected good things
from him as soon as we saw his face even in pictured form. We were
not disappointed, for upon reading his message we rejoiced with the
Brethren of California over the work that he <lid.
The Grand Lodge seems to have entered upon a novel method of
supporting the school system of the State, in that they urge the Lodges
to sponsor public meetings in the various communities throughout the
State, at which will be discussed the various phases o f the public school
system. These meetings are not to be Masonic in any character, but the
Masons are urged to take the initiative' in organizing such meetings, and
they seem to have been a success.
The California Brethren contributed liberally to the aid of the
Masons who suffered from the Florida hurricane and the floods of the
Mississippi valley.
Brother Jones speaks very positively concerning the right of a
Lodge to organize a club for political purposes.
He speaks wisely of the need for Masonic education among the
newly made Masons.
The report of the Committee on "Public Schools Week covers
fifteen pages of well written stuff, which shows how the . Brethren

101

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

of California are taking the lead in interesting the general public in the
idea of a closer scrutiny and better understanding of what the schools
are really doing. The idea is a good one, and the public should be taught
in some way to take a deeper interest in what is being done in and for
the schools of the land. But, the question naturally arises, what will be
the ultimate effect of such a leadership as is indicated in the report, upon
the Lodge itself? So long as wise leadership is used all may be well,
but it is so easy for enthusiastic leaders to step beyond the lines laid
down by all Grand Lodges, and to border upon the introduction of
political questions into Lodge discussions, that we have our doubts as to
the wisdom of such a course.
A stirring oration was presented by W. Brother Fletcher A. Cutler,
Grand Orator, which dealt primarily with citizenship and the relations
of Masonry to it. As a document it reads well and in its delivery must
have struck a responsive chord in the hearts of his hearers, for when
he concluded the Grand Lodge raised as a body and cheered.
The reports of the activities of the "Homes" of the California Grand
Lodge are very interesting and complete.
The report on Correspondence is written by Brother Jesse M. Whited
and is in the topical form. It takes up special topics which are of interest
just now and gives numerous quotations from the proceedings of other
Grand Lodges thereon. He is not chary of giving his own opinion, and
then backs it up by quotations.

to the quotations. The whole review, however, is well worthy perusal,

Maine (1929):
During the year several impqrtant historical events were celebrated
in California, notably at Coloma, where a kind of historical pageant of
the days of '49 at Sutter's Mill was presented. California is specializing
in these historical events and the Grand Master believes they will give

progress.
The Masonic Homes of California are conservatively administered
and much space is given in their Annual Proceedings to these institutions.
The report on Correspondence is of the topical variety and written
and compiled by R. W. Brother Jesse M. Whited. It is the despair of
this Maine reviewer and judging by the comments of other reviewers,
they also find it difficult to review because of two things, the nature of
the review and the extended excellence of it. It is good, it is illuminating,
it is constructive, but it is the trial of this reviewer's life none the less.
The fact is it ought to be printed en exte11so for the enlightenment of the
Craft everywhere. *
The whole review is preceded by five
pages in heavy type giving Brother Whited's comments on world
Masonic problems and issues. These comments are always lucid and
constructive and something of the breath and finer spirit of the Fraternity beats through it all. Perhaps there is no finer tribute to pay his
review than to quote the Great Light which says, "thes·e words are spirit
and they are life." There is an atmosphere, an aroma like that of a
bouquet gathered in many fields-which breathes throughout this review,
and to try to capture in words the fragrance of meadow violets, and arbutus
and the score of other odors from New England woods · and fields 1s
beyond our limited powers. We leave it untouched and unprofaned.

New York (1929):
The Grand Lodge of California has had in lVL W. Brother Fischer
an outstanding, most effective Grand Master. The record of the year's
work is a most gratifying one. Ideas and plans have been set under
way which no doubt will bear rich fruit in the future, not only in California but in Jurisdictions outside. Keen observation, clear-headed judgment and the courage to enforce what he believes to be right, appear to
1
blend perfectly in him.
The Grand Master reports concerning the Conference of Grand
Masters and the Washington Memorial Association, held at Washington,
D. C.; M. W. Brother Fischer's virile talk at the social session of the
Conference is remembered by all who attended, as an outstanding feature.
We recall particularly his searching question: What is the Conference
doing to compensate busy men who travel long distances to attend it?
He himself had come all the way from California to take part in the
C_onference. The · question needed no stronger emphasis. The result
was that steps were taken to assure a program for the future which will
make every monument count.
A unique feature of the history of the year was the celebration of
the seventy-fifth anniversary of several pioneer Lodges which started
under way in the days of the gold rush. The manner of celebration was
unique. · With camping out in the open, and in other ways getting a taste
of the spirit of the olden times, there were pageants and all that, carried
on as could not have been done anywhere else as strikingly as in
California.

Jesse M. Whited has found a way for making a Correspondence
report serve two purposes, that of giving brief notes characterizing in a
way the. various Masonic Jurisdictions, and that of setting out Masonic
Topics and gathering under appropriate headings all that the year
brought out in Proceedings with reference thereto. It works out well
with him, because he is in it heart. and soul and has good Masonic judgment.. He believes that what has given rise to the multiplication of
bodies drawing their membership from Master Masons is that the Lodge
does not fill the bill as regards strict selection of material for admission
and does not meet the desire of many for sociability and really worth
while Masonic instruction. In other countries, where more care is
exercised in the acceptance of candidates and where full opportunity is
given to satisfy reasonable desires· for sociability and mutual advancement
in intellectual and artistic departments the need for side-organization
is not felt so keenly. Hence the difference between these and ourselves.
That is about how Brother Whited sees the situation. The report is
commended to all who wish to get a general view of the topics now to the
fore in the United States.

The Grand Lodge has a committee known as "The Lodge Study

Connecticut:
Pawcatuck, Connecticut, the home of a Connecticut Lodge, and
Westerly, Rhode Island, home of a Rhode Island Lodge, are separated
by a narrow stream. The Connecticut and Rhode Island Lodges are
both permitted to meet in a common Lodge-room in Westerly, but the
territorial jurisdiction of neither Lodge is thereby affected.
Delaware:
Delaware has a very high percapita rating in the support of the
Washington Memorial Fund. It is excelled by only four Grand Jurisdictions: New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia. The
first named standing not far from 200 per cent, while the rating for
Delaware is 118.4 per cent.

Indiana:
There is a waiting list of twenty adults for admission to the Indiana

Iowa:
The Masonic Home is taking care of 127 children and 140 old people,
besides providing for 22 wards outside of the home.
An important discovery was made during the year in going through
a number of old pamphlets which had accumulated; it is a copy of the
Cole's Constitution of 1762. This find completes the set of the Constitutions. Iowa now has all four of them. Hitherto there has been only one
known complete set, and that is in the library of the Provincial Grand
Lodge of Worcestershire, England.

The membership of the Masonic and Eastern Star Home consists

Florida:
Some say Constituent Lodge, others use the designation Subordinate
Lodge. Vermont frequently substitutes the term Secular Lodge, but
Florida says Particular Lodge.

Maine:
The Grand Lodge of Maine has paid 90 per cent of her quota to
the Washington Memorial" Fund and hopes to be able to send the remaining 10 per cent before the close of the year.

Idaho:
One Lodge has a "refreshment club," which meets once a month for
dinner followed by a brief address on some Masonic topic. In another
Lodge the Master appoints each year a member as chairman of the
educational work; one meeting is held each month for Masonic addresses
and their discussion. In other Lodges, a '(\1asonic textbook forms the
basis for monthly discussions through the year.

100. The Committee on Library, which had arranged the program, felt ·

of 1928-29.

Minnesota:
During my stay in Washington I visited the Congressional Library
as I wanted to get some information on a certain phase of Masonry. I
was referred to a Masonic department where I found a brother Mason
in charge, who seemed pleased to rende,r all assistance possible. I was

The old By-Laws of the Minnesota Masonic Home permitted the
admission of "Sisters of Master Masons." The provision was deleted on
recommendation of the Trustees. The Home had sixty-eight residents
during the year 1927.
The Eastern Star appointed, in 1921, a "Patriotic and Masonic Home
Committee" for the purpose of raising $75,000 to b~ used for the furnishing and equipment of the Home. The money was secured and $65,146.95
expended for the designated purpose. The Eastern Star Committee reports. that it has a balance of about $10,000 to be drawn upon for further
needs.
Grand Lodge adopted a recommendation by voting a per capita
assessment of $12.50, payable either in full or in five equal yearly
installments, to meet the liabilities resting on the Masonic Home.
Attention has been called to the good Masonic work sponsored by
Grand Lodge at Rochester, Minnesota, to render personal service to the
many Masons and blood-relatives of Masons to be found among the
thousands who go to the famous Mayo Institute there each year to be
treated for physical and mental ailments. Grand Lodge appropriated
$3,300.00 for the continuance of this worthy undertaking.

New Jersey:
A most important departure advocated was the recommendation that
permanency of policy and program in the work of Grand Lodge and a
closer co-ordination of its Committees could be achieved best by the
establishment of a Board of General Purposes, such as has functioned
successfully in the Grand Lodges of England and the British Empire
generally. The recommendation was adopted and marks a distinct progress in the management of affairs.
The Board is to be composed of the Grand Master, Deputy Grand
Master, the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, the Grand Treasurer
and the Chairmen of the Committees on Constitutions and By-laws,
jurisprudence, Ritual, Appeal and Grievances, Foreign Correspondence,
Masonic Service, Masonic Bureau, as also the Chairman of the Board of
Governors of the Masonic Home and the Chairman of the Board of
Trustees; besides one member to be appointed by the Grand Master.
The Grand Secretary will serve as Secretary of the Board which will
hold at least three meetings each year. Five members shall constit.ute
a quorum at any mee.ting.
The Board is charged with the execution of all matters as may be
referred to it by the Grand Master, to co-ordinate the work of ·the various
Committees, to recommend to the Grand Master whatever wilt be necessary that will be to the welfare and good government of the Craft.
On the Grand Master's recommendation the office of Grand Historian was created.
The Masonic Bureau is reported to have secured positions for over
four hundred applicants.
Sisters of Masons were made eligible for admission to the Masonic
Home.

One of the many schemes set in motion within or from without the
Fraternity, to commercialize Masonry, was brought to the Grand Master's
attention by the Grand Secretary of England; it had to do with a
touring proposition advertised as "Masonic." England has been annoyed
quite often of late by so-called "Masonic Tours" patronized by Masons
in the United States. Commercial enterpri'ses of this ·type turn up in
one form or another, and only constant watchfulness can save the Fraternity from discredit in this direction.

Texas, too, has established a Students Loan Fund. A resolution was

Virginia:
The Grand Chapter of the Eastern Star of Virginia offered to
present to Grand Lodge the building and site of the Eastern Star Home
of Virginia. Connected with the gift were the provisions : The Home
is to be known as the Masonic and Eastern Star Home of Virginia;
proper provision is to be made for the care of all dependent members of
the Eastern Star in Virginia ; that the Grand Chapter 0. E. S. is to have
representation on the Board of Governors of the joint institution. Grand
Lodge did not deem it wise to accept "this most gracious offer."
Nearly all the original Lodges in Virginia forming the Grand Lodge
in 1777-1778 held charters from either England or Scotland-only one we
believe held a charter from another source, Cabin Point Royal Arch,
which in 1786 became No. 8, was chartered by Joseph Montfort, "Grand
Master of America." The original charter is still in this office; written
on parchment or leather, and in a fair state of preservation. Bears the
signatures of Joseph Montfort, G. M. A. (Grand Master of America);
Cornelius Harnett, D. G. M.A. (Deputy Grand Master of America); and
W . Brimage, P. G. Secy. ( Provincial Grand Secretary) . It is dated
"under the Seal of Masonry, 13th April, Anno Lato'm 5775, Anno Dom.
1775."
As Montfort in this document says: "Whereas His Grace Henry
Somerset, Duke of Beaufort, &c. Grand Master of the Most Ancient &
Honorable Society of Free & Accepted Masons hath been Graciously
pleased by Patent dated the 14th day of January, Anno Latomorum, 5771
Anno D. 1771, at London) to Constitute me Provincial Grand Master of
& for America," etc., this Lodge, too, was of English origin.
Even after Grand Lodge of V irginia was formed and these Lodges
had given up English and Scotch charters and received Virginia charters,

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Grand Lodge of England kept them on its register until 1813, when all
American Lodges were stricken off. The record reads at the time the
Ancients and Moderns United, but history tells us that a very important
transaction was going on between England and America beginning in
1811, and while the end was in sight when these Lodges were struck off
English registry, the event was not concluded until 1814. Of course
this had nothing to do with the American Lodges being "written off the
list." It was just a coincidence.

The Grand Master warns Lodges to be circumspect before entering
upon any building undertakings. The enthusiasm . which gives rise to
the idea is too precious an asset to be discouraged, but prudence demands
that the cost and future maintenance shall be fully considered beforehand,
preferably in consultation with an experienced financier. T he exam~le
of one Lodge is cited which, after having been among t~e m~st act~ve
Lodges of the jurisdiction, became so involved in financial d1fficulttes,
owing to the building of its temple, that it had to suspend labors altogether.
With the aid of the Grand Master the members of that L odge were
brought together again and the Lodge is at work now in modest but
suitable quarters.
A fund for supplying shoes to needy children is maintained, and
clothing is provided. The Masonic Home is progressing satisfactorily.

Philippine Islands:
The Filipinos and particularly the Chinese, of whom there are
many in the Islands, have great reverence for the dead. This, the Grand
Master says, has made it easy for him to favor the establishment of
Masonic cemeteries. Most of the municipal cemeteries are ill-conditioned,
and Masons are excluded from those maintained by the dominant church.
Beautiful Masonic cemeteries have been supplied, and their number is
growing.
Porto Rico:
Fifty-three Lodges; 4,000 members; cash balance, $21,886.13.
A Latin-American Masonic Congress is to be held at San Juan,

Forty-four Lodges; 3,950 members.
The subject uppermost at this Communication was the action of the
National Grand Lodge of Germany at Berlin, in breaking fraternal relations with Zt4r Somie. The reason assigned for the rupture that some
Lodg~s of the latter Grand Lodge had been permitted to place upon
their altars a White Book, a book of blank leaves on the cover of which
was imprinted in large golden letters the name of God. The practic~ has
been carried on for over half a century. The idea was that a candidate
who believed that God's Revelation to men was not confined to the Bible,
could mentally inscribe upon the white pages whatever other Divine Inspired Writings to him. represented the fulness of the Revelat.ion, the
Lodge meeting thereby the religious scruples of men of other faiths, the
Mohammedan and Buddhist, for example. The outcome of a prolonged,
lively discussion was that the Grand Lodge Zur Sonne a~opted a reso~u­
tion permitting the Lodges to continue to place upon their altars, beside
the Bible, the White Book. The following explanation was added:
"The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge Zur Sonne affirms
that the Three Great Lights of Freemasonry are The Bible, Square and
Compasses, are unchangeable parts of its common symbolism, according to
Section 51 of the Grand Constitutions. Every candidate is obligated on
these Three Lights."

The teachings of the Order are revealed .Progressively in eleven degrees: the three degrees of the St. John's Lodge, three of the St. Andrew's
Lodge, two of the Steward's · Lodge, and three of the Chapter.
The charities are administered by a Board of Benevolence. The
annual budget amounts to about 100,000 Nor. Kr., or approximately
$25,000.00, which are expended chiefly for annuities and grants to widows
and others in distress. The balance goes to the support of the. Masonic
Home for Infants and the Masonic Home for aged Masons and surviving
relatives of deceased Brethren. Further contributions for the support
of the Homes are derived from subscriptions by individual Brethren and
aggregate from 25,000 to 30,000 Nor. Kr., a year.
The Endowment Fund of the Home of the Aged amounts to 700,000
Kr. and that of the Home for Infants to 400,000 Kr.
The funds are subscribed mainly by the Lodges of Oslo. The other
Lodges throughout the country maintain local charities of their own,
varying in scope according to the number and financial ability of the
Brethren.
The magnificent Freemasons' Hall, at Oslo, is headquarters of the
Grand Lodge. It was completed in 1894. Six halls are set aside for
Masonic meetings : one for the E. A. and F. C. degrees, one for the M. M.
degree, two for the St. ·Andrew's Lodge, and two for the Chapter.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATIONS-MONTH OF MEETING
AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish
Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized
proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is
by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the
Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the
Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests upon those who have
been regularly elected to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a
Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter."
.
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a C-Ommandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. · The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the
temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the
Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and the
degrees conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfecton, 4° to i4°,
inclusive; Chapter Rose Cr-0ix, is• to is•; Council of Kadosh, i9° to
30°; Consistory, 3i 0 to 32°; Supreme Couru:il, _33°.
In the N orthem Jurisdiction (which includes all States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River); the degrees
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 • to 14 °, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, is• and i6°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and is•;
Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
